summary: The Food Inspector took a sample of lal mirchi powder from the grocery shop of the respondent. On analysis by the Public Analyst it was found in exhibit PW 1/C that the sample contained nine living meal worms. There was no other evidence in support of the case of the prosecution that the Lal mirchi seed was adulterated and he accordingly acquitted the respondent, but the High Court in appeal reversed the acquittal order of the trial court. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The word 'insect ' is defined in the Oxford Dictionary as "small invertebrate segmented animal having head, thorax, abdomen and three pairs of thoracic legs, usually with one or two pairs Of thoricars (1) 1973 (Prevention of Food Adulteration Cases) 257. The term 'insects ' is not defined in section 2(1)(f) of the Act. According to the Shorter Oxford English Dictionary (1962 edition), 'worm ' means "a slender, creeping, naked, limbless animal usually having a body divided into segments, and several pairs thereof. The phrase 'or is otherwise unfit for human consumption ' can be read conjunctively as well as disjunctively. If it is read disjunctively, that is, in association with what precedes it, sub clause (f) with slight consequent rearrangement and parenthesis would read like this: "If the article is unfit for of human consumption on account of (a) its consisting wholly or in part of any filthy, putrid, disgusting, rotten, decomposed or diseased animal or vegetable substance or being insectable, (b) or on account Of any other cause". In this view of the sub clause proof of unfitness of the article for human use is a must for bringing the case within its purview. [470B C] 2. The fact that the appellant was not out of difficulty in this case does not make it necessary to refer the case to a larger Bench. [473C D] 3. In the instant case, the Public analyst has found in the sample only nine living meals worm and he has neither stated that it is insect infested nor that it was unfit for personal consumption on the account of the presence of the meal wyorms the sample was unfit to be human consumption. [472E] 4.

The appellant was an agriculturist and was not liable to the penalty under the Bihar Foodgrains Dealers ' Licensing Order, 1966. He was prosecuted under section 7 of the Essential Commodities Act for violation of cl. 3 of the order. The trial court rejected the evidence on the ground that the lease deeds were not registered and were not admissible in evidence under section 49 of the Registration Act. The Sessions Judge did not accept this ground and convicted him. On appeal by special leave, HELD: (i) The appellant had successfully proved that he was an agricultural agriculturist and the presumption under para 3(2) could not be drawn against him. [901 B] Manipur Administration vs M. Nila Chandra Singh ; , followed. (ii) The presumption under paragraph 3(1) could, therefore, not be raised against him because of the exemption which agriculturists enjoy. On the whole, it was easy to see that the evidence which was 'brought for ward of witnesses deposing orally was not concocted to set up a false defence. Indeed no adequate reasons were given for rejecting the testimony of witnesses. [ 901 C] Manipur administration vs M/s. Nita Chandra Singh, ; , referred to. (iii) The fact that the appellant was in fact carrying on agricultural operations does not make him an agriculturist. [900 D E] Manipur Adminis tration vs Mastu Chandra Singh; , followed and Manipur Administration v M.Nila Chandrai Singh, , distinguished. (iv) The evidence of one witness on the other showed to have been granted to him. He also produced receipts of payment of lease money and he cited witnesses who deposed orally were held by him for purposes of cultivation. If that be so, then, he is an agriculturist, and it is easy to say that the said evidence which he was 'a 'b 'rought ' for ward off of witnesses depose orally was never concocted to make a false plea.

The defendant was a monthly tenant in respect of the suit premises. He had been paying rent to the Receiver several months before the Kabuliyat was executed, and the rental amounting to Rs. 1,000 per month was paid by him to the defendant several months after the expiry of the second annual lease. The plaintiff contended that the defendant was at no point of time a monthly tenancy under the plaintiff or his predecessor, and that he had acquired permanent rights in the land under the Prodhan 's Patta of 1913 and continuous occupation of it since then for more than 12 years. Held, that on the facts of this case it would be quite proper to hold that the tenancy of the defendant wag one from month to month since its inception in 1924. The agreement between the parties was certainly not to create a monthly lease. It was not an operative document at all and could not consequently fulfil the requirements of section 107 of the Transfer of Property Act. The Kabulianyat in the case before this Court was undoubtedly a registered instrument, but ex ceptedly it was not a valid document at any stage and could therefore be construed as a lease under the Transfer Of Property Act, even though no rent was demanded by the landlord after 1926. The contract to the contrary, as contemplated by section 106 of the , Transfer of property Act lays down that "in the absence of a contract or local law or usage to the contra a lease of immovable property for agricultural or manufacturing purposes shall be deemed to be a lease from year to year, terminable on the part of either lessor or lessee by six months ' notice expiring with the end of a month of tenancy. In these circumstances it could not be said that the agreement between parties was really not to creating a monthly rent. The lease was intended to be for a period exceeding one year, but as the intention was not expressed in the proper legal form, it could no be given effect to. It is one thing to say that in the absence Of a valid agreement, the rights of the parties would be regulat ed by law in the same manner as if no agreement existed at all; it was quite another thing to substitute a new agreement for the parties which was palpably contradicted by the admit ted facts of the case. The question whether payment of rent amounted to payment to payment of the plaintiff himself, though this question was left open by the High Court on the previous occasion, was whether payment to the receiver amounted to payments to the plaintiff itself.

The appellant, Trilok Chand Jain instituted a suit for recovery of Rs. 1,39,722.86 against the defendants, M/s. Dagi Ram Pindi Lal and Smt. Budh Wanti Gulati, w/o Shri Pindi lal Gulati. During the course of proceedings in the suit, when evidence was being recorded, the plaintiff obtained summons from the court requiring the Income Tax Department to produce in the Court records relating to the Income tax Assessment of the defendants M/S Borizeon Industrial Products (P) Ltd., and Bishamber Nath Kaul. That record was also sent by the IncomeTax Officer in a sealed cover alongwith a letter, dated November 1, 1972 claiming that the said record was privileged under Section 137 of the 1961 Act. The Income Tax officer to whom the summons were issued, sent the record in a separate sealed cover along with a letter in which it was submitted that no disclosure of information regarding income tax pertaining to an income tax assessee could be made. It considered the first question in the following four situations: (a) Where the documents, records etc., in respect of which privilege is claimed were filed by an assessee or a third party after April 1, 1964, in respect for assessment years 1964 65 onwards, and (b) where the documents record, records, etc. in respect thereof were filed on or before April 1 1964, but before April I,1964 in respect to assessment years 1962 63 and 1963 64 in proceedings for the said assessment years taking place under the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922. The assessee also applied for and obtained summons requiring the income tax Officer to produce the Incometax record relating to M/ s Borize on Industrial Products. That records was also send by the Incometax Officer in sealed cover with an Inspector along with letter, which it had submitted that there were no circumstances justifying its refusal. Disclosure of information prohibited (1) All particulars contained in any statement made, return furnished or accounts or documents produced under the provisions of this Act or in any evidence given, or affidavit or deposition made, in the course or of any proceedings under this Act other than proceedings under Chapter XXII, or in the record of any assessment proceeding, or any proceeding relating to recovery of a demand prepared for the purpose of this act, shall be treated as confidential and notwithstanding anything contained in the Indian Evidence Act, 1872 (1 of 1872) no Court shall save as provided in this Act, be entitled to require any public servant to produce before it any such return, accounts, documents or record or any part of any such record, or to give evidence before it in respect thereto. The provisions of Section 138(1)(b) of the 1922 Act were, as is seen, almost identical to the provisions Of sub section (1). Under the original Section 138, before the necessary information could be furnished or cause to be furnished to an applicant, the Commissioner was to be satisfied that there are no circumstances justified its refusal and that it would be (sic) in the public interest to produce or furnish the documents. The Commissioner, has to make an order after being satisfied that it is in the Public interest so to do, to furnish or cause or causeto be furnished such information and that decision of the Commissioner is immune from challenge in any court of law. The finality which has been attached to the order if the Commissioner under Section 138 (1)(a) of 1961 Act is applicable only in cases where application is made to the Commissioner by a party or any other person for receiving documents or information.

One Mammotty was ill for a long time and was in hospital and he was discharged uncured a month before the execution of the gift deed and remained in his mother 's house afterwards. There were conflicting versions about the nature of the disease and a plea was taken in the case that the gift was made in contemplation of death and was voidable. The trial Judge and the first Appellate Court did not accept it. After the death of Mammottty, the present suit was brought by Kunhamu an eider brother of Mamman for partition and possession of a 6/16 share of the property which he claimed as an heir under the Muhammadan Law, that is to say, by the father or his executor or by the grand father or by his executor. The plaintiff 's case was that when succession opened out on the death Of Mammothty, his widow Seinaba was entitled to the enhanced share of 1/4 as there was no issue and the remaining 3/4 was divisible between 552 two sisters, Kunhamunu and his two sisters. The first three defendants (the appellants) were entitled to a 3/16 shares each. In other words, the plaintiff 'S father) claimed that when inheritance opened out of the death Mammetty, he was entitled lo the enhanced shares of 1 /4 as they were unaffected by the invalid gift in faVour of Seinha and accepted on her behalf by her mother. The Trial Court dismissed the suit holding that the donor and donee lived together an overt act only was necessary and this rule applied between husband and wife. On appeal, the High Court held that there was a declaration and a tender by the donor Mammastty and as the gift is by a registered deed no question in this behalf could arise. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant (i) that neither express acceptance nor transfer of possession was necessary for the completion of a gift when the donor is himself the guardian or the de facto guardian orquasi guardian; and (ii) that there is no rule of Muhammadan law which permits such acceptance and delivery of possession (qabza). HELD: The appeal must be allowed. There can be no question that there has been a complete intention to divest ownership on the part of Mamammotti and to transfer the property to the donee. If there is any such person one can be chosen and appointed by the donee to whom possession can be made over to manifest the intention of departing from the property gifted. [557 C] In the present case there was delivery of Possession and the deed also records this fact. Possession was not delivered to Seinsufficient to establish the transfer of Possession. The gift was not given to the minor 's father or guardian and the donor could nominate a person to accept the gift on behalf. of his wife who had attained puberty and had lived with him, for after the celebration of marriage a husband can receive a gift in respect of minor wife even though her father be living; but the mother was not the guardian of the person of Seinsha. [554 D] In such cases the benefit to the 5th defendant and the completion thereof for his benefit is the sole consideration. As there was good authority for these propositions in the ancient and modern books of Muhammadans law and in decided cases of undoubted authority, the gift must be accepted as valid and complete.

The Madras Religious and Charitable Endowments Act 19 of 1951 was enacted to provide for the better administration and governance of Hindu Religious and charitable institutions and Endowments in the State of Madras. The Act provided that the Government may make rules to carry out all or any of the purposes of this Act and not inconsistent therewith. Section 76(1) provides that the Commissioner shall pay the salaries, allowances, pensions and other beneficial remuneration of the Commissioners, Deputy Commissioners, Assistant Commissioners and other officers and servants (other than exeutive officers of religious institutions) employed for the purpose of this act and the other expenses incurred for such purposes including the expenses of Area Committees and the cost of auditing the accounts of religious institution. The respondents who were trustees of the Venkataramana Temple at Mulki, District South Kanara moved a petition in the High Court challenging the validity of the demand. The High Court upheld the plea on the ground that no rules had been framed under section 100 of the Act and therefore the demand for levy of contribution was without jurisdiction or authority of law. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the Commissioner had not determined the audit fee under section 76(2); (2) the High court erred in holding that no rule had been made under section 80(2) of the Madras Act and that the demand was premature; and (3) the rules framed by the Government were invalid.

The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the notice issued by the High court. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on the ground that no appeal lies to this Court under section 19 of the Act from an order rejecting the prayer of the alleged contemner for bearing the case piecemeal. In appeal to this court, it was contended on behalf of the respondents that an appeal does lie to this Supreme Court as a matter of right under section19 of the . Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: An order merely initiating the proceeding without anything further, does not decide anything against the alleged contemnor and cannot be appealed against as a matters of right tinder section 19. [512C] Baradakanta Mishra vs Justice Gatikrushna Mishra, ; , referred to. Baradikanta Mishra v Justice Gitikrushnna Mishra; , distinguished. Barabadakata Mishra vs justice Gatirushna Misra, A.I.R. 1976 S.C. 1206, distinguished. The appeal is, therefore, dismissed as being not maintainable. [511E F] Barbadakanda Mishra vsJustice Gatikakrushta Mishra, , referred. Barbakanta Misra vs JusticeGatikrunna Mishra ; , distinguished and held inapplicable. Bardakanta Das vs Justice S Gatikushna Kumar Mishra, A C.A. No. 15 of 1975 dated the 2nd April, 1975, approved.

The appellant was prosecuted along with another, in the Court of the Magistrate First Class, Delhi under section 6(1 A) of the , for possessing a wireless transmitter in contravention of the provisions of section 3 of the Act. The trial court upheld the conviction but reduced the sentence to the period already undergone plus a fine of Rs. 500. On revision, the High Court confirmed both the conviction and the sentence. Held, that the words " unless a different intention appears, the repeal shall not affect the continuance of any such amendment made by the enactment so repealed and in operation at the time of such repeal". The word " text " is comprehensive enough to take in the subject as well as the terminology used in a statute. Another escape from the operation of section 6 A of the was sought to be effected on the basis of the words ' unless a separate intention appears. The repealing Act does not indicate any intention different from that envisaged by the said section. Further, the object of the 1952 Act is not to give it any legislative effect but to excise dead matter from the statute book. The word ' text " in its dictionary meaning means " subject or theme". When an enactment amends the text of another it amends the subject or proposal of it though sometimes it may expunge unnecessary words without altering the subject. Held further, that section 6 (1 A), inserted in the Act XVII of 1933 by the amending Act of 1949, is either covered by the provisions Of the , or a surplusage not serving any definite purpose. Khuda Bux vs Manager Caledonian Press Chakravartti, C.J., neatly brought out the purpose and (XIII) that section 4 of the Repealing and Amending Act of 1952 applied to a case of repeal of an amending Act.

The appellant was the managing Shebait of a deities from 1926 to 1930 and as Shebait, he executed a Hatchita in favour of one Nanitosh Chakraborty some time in April 1928 on the basis of which he received advances of money from time to time from the latter. The last entry in the Hatchitita was made in March 1929 and the total amount borrowed up to that date came up to Rs. 3,801. Adwaita Charan Roy died in March 1930 and after his death, Satish Chandra Roy became the managing trustee and continued to act as such till his death in 1940. There was an adjustment of accounts between Nanitash and the creditor in whose favour the H 39 Matita executed by the Chakrabortys in favour on July 26, 1940, was a fictitious conveyance made in favour by Aghore Nath Roy in favour Of one Nanitaosh Chakraborty. The trial judge decided in favour both the applications holding that the appellant was not entitled to have two compromise decrees reopened and on the passing of new instalments decree to have the properties, which were in possession of the real decreeholder, restored to the deities in terms of section 36(2)(c) of the Bengal Money Lenders Act. The High Court dismissed both the appeals. In appeal by special leave: Held, that the object of restoring possession of properties sold in execution of the decree to the judgment debtor is to enable the latter to pay off the decretal dues, but it is to be remembered that the sale itself is not annulled and in case of default in payment of any instalment, the properties are returned to the decreeholder purchaser. The Court has not only the right but is under a duty to make an enquiry as to whether the ostensible purchaser at the execution sale or the person who purports to have acquired an interest therein under a subsequent transfer from the decree holder purchaser, has bonafide acquired such rights within the meaning of clause (b). But it does not agree with the learned Judges of the High Court that in making a new decree under cl. (a) of section36(2) and giving the judgmentdebtor consequential relief under cl.(c) to the sub section, the court can at all enter into the question as to what the ostensible purchasers at the executing sale is himself a benamidar for another person in respect of the decrees. Such enquiry, it seems to us, is altogether outside the purview of the different clauses of section 6(2).

The respondent company instituted a suit against the appellant for recovery of Rs. 7,113 7 0 with interest at 6 per cent. per annum on the ground that the decree was not in existence at the date of the document and therefore the equitable principle came into play and that as soon as the decree passed there would be no transfer of the decree to the respondent company by any assignment in writing executed after the decree became a complete equitable assignment of the debt. The appellant contended that the deed of assignment fell within the principle of those two decisions, that it constituted an equitable assignment and that the application for execution was maintainable under Order XXI, rule 16 and dismissed the appeal. Held, that the respondent could not claim to be a transferee of the suit decree which was subsequently obtained by Habib & Sons, by an assignment in his favour and could therefore claim to execute the decree as transferee under Order 21, r. 16. The transfer in writing of a property which is the subject matter of a suit without in terms transferring the decree or to transfer it to be passed in future would not entitle the intending transferee to claim the beneficial interest in the decree after it was passed and that while a transfer of or an agreement to transfer a decree that may be passed, in equity, entitle the transferee to get the beneficial interests in the suit after it is passed, such equitable transfer does not render the transferee a transferee a transferor of the judgment debtor by assignment in pursuance of the assignment in the writing executed before the decree came into existence and the only way in which the transferee could claim that the judgment was transferred to him by assignment. Kangati Mahanandi Reddi vs Panikalapati Venkatappa & another, A.I.R. , Bhagwant Balajirao & Ors. vs Rajaram Sajnaji & Others, A I. R. , and Bhagwant Balrajirao and Ors. v Pandurang Rajaram Sajjnaji and Others, [1939] 2 Calcutta 325, distinguished.

The respondent carried on the business of fabricating steel doors, windows, sashes and other goods. On April 20, 1957, the respondent submitted in pursuance of an invitation by the Executive Engineer, Ajmer Central Division, its tender for providing and fixing "S.H. Windows"W ' Type", "T.H., Window" and "Composite Winds" of certain sizes "in accordance with the specifications, designs, drawing and instructions in writing referred to in Rule 1 hereof and in Class 11 of the conditions of contract and with such materials as are provided for by and in all other respects in accordance with such conditions so far as applicable". The Sales Tax Officer included in the taxable turnover of the respondent Rs. 23,480/ received under the contract. He held that the contract was one of sale of goods and the amount received by the respondent was not taxable. He accordingly remanded the case with a direction to assess tax on the price for sale of materials only. The Board of Revenue exercising revisional power confirmed the order passed by the Deputy Commissioner observing that the contracts undertaken by the Respondent were not a contract of service. The High Court held that from the acceptance of the tender, two contracts resulted : one for providing doors and windows and another for "fixing" those doors and window leaves and sasps etc. and entered into a contract for "sale of goods". In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State of Rajasthan that the respondent carried out the contract and that the amount paid by the appellant was not 'taxable ', and that in undertaking to install or fix these units or articles the sellers did not enter into a works contract merely because they undertook to install and for the articles sold so as to make them fit for immediate service. HELD : The object of the Respondent was to enter into an agreement with the Government of India under the terms of the contact as window leaves, and only on the fixing of the windows as stipulated, the contract could be fully executed and the property in the windows passed on the completion of the work and not before. It was only upon the "fixation" of the window leaves that the property was to pass to the War Office under the head contract. The service was not rendered under a separate contract nor is the service shown to be rendered customarily or normally as incidental to the sale by the person who supplies window leaves. [510 C] In the present case, the specifications of the doors were set out in the contract, and the primary undertaking of the appellant that the "Fixing" of windows in the manner stipulated required special technical skill. If the windows were not properly fixed", the contract would not be complete, and so the respondent could not claim the amount agreed to be paid to it. [511 E] The object was to entering into a work contract. That clearly appears from the terms Of the tender and its acceptance. The windows were to be fabricated according to the specifications with glass plain or ground as decided by the Engineer in Charge, and were to "fixed" within six months from the date of its acceptance 'to the building with rawl plugs in cut stone work. " The rate quoted by the respondents was based on the current price of mild steel billets, and, the price was to be revised in the light of cost revision of the controlled price of steel supplied to the respondent. The contract undertaken by it was to prepare the window leaf leaves according to specifications and to fix them to the building.

The appellant was a broker of foreign machinery parts went to Ram Avtar Prasad complainant and told him that he (Shanker Lal) could arrange for a transaction of sale of foreign goods which would result in good profit to the complainant. The complainant agreed to the proposal and wanted to see the seller of the foreign goods in question. On November 16, 1967, Shanker Lal handed over the formal order to Ram L and stated that the goods would be supplied on the following day. Shankar Lal handedover the formal orders to Ram lyer 's agent. On the same day, he lodged a report with the police against Shankar Lal after his suspicion had been aroused. Later on that day Shanker Lal and Raj Kumar Agarwalla came to the shop of Ram Avtar. The police did not submit any charge sheet on the basis of the report which had been lodged by the complainant and the accused were discharged. Thereafter, the proceedings were set in motion against Raj Kumar Aggarwalla, Shankar Lal and Saheb Jaman Khan. Charge under sections 420, 468 and 471 Indian Penal Code read with section 120B I.P.C. was framed against all the three accused. The charges were quashed by the Presidency Magistrate on the ground that so far as Raj Kumar Agawalla was concerned no case had been made out against him. Charges were accordingly quashed. On appeal by the State, the High Court allowed the revision petition and quashed the charge. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that there was no cogent ground for interference with the judgment of the High court. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The report which was lodged by Ram Avtar in the very nature of things made no mention of the name of Raj Kumar. [ 279C] 2. There is no infirmity in the judgment and order of the Calcutta High Court as might induce us to interfere. The appeal fails and is dismissed.

The petitioner, an Allopathic doctor by profession had himself drafted and filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the reports of the two accidents from 1970 onwards and for several other directions to the Union Government and the instrumentalities connected with the administration of the Railways. The petitioner alleged that the Railways in this country are owned by the Central Government and on account of failure to fulfil the constitutional, statutory and commercial obligations by the Railways adequate safety protection to the passengers and their properties is not available. The Indian Railways Act, 1890 (Act ' for short) has prescribed several safety measures; based upon experience, the Railway Board through which apex body the administration is run and controlled has also prescribed rules and issued instructions which are not being properly implemented. The Union Government had appointed three high powered Committees in the post independence period, namely, the Kunzru, Wanchoo and Sikri Committees to investigate into the affairs of the Railway with particular reference to accidents and though detailed and useful recommendations have been made by these committees, there has been no adequate implementation thereof. Particular reference has been made to the unmanned level crossings, increasing human error as a contributing factor to accidents, non allocation of adequate funds for improvements, improper utilisation of the assets and facilities, inefficiency in the administration at different levels, prevalence and increase of indiscipline, frequency of thefts,ftsmanship, barbaric checking and supervisory system, want of replacement equipment and repairs to bridges as also non provision of adequate facilities to passengers. The Joint Director (Safety) has filed a counter affidavit in answer to the Rule on behalf of the respondents. It has been averred that the recommendations of the Accidents Enquiry Committee were examined and implemented within the limits of financial and material resources. So far as manned level Crossings are concerned there were as many as 14471 of them as on March 1, 1982; unmanning level crosses with a volume of traffic more than 6000 train vehicle units or poor approach visibility are being manned in a phased manner at the cost of the railways and control at the gate is also being improved. As on June 1,1982 there were about as manyas 27233 unmaned level cross remarks on the Railways and if all of them are to be manned, a capital expenditure of 330 crore rupees would be necessary and similarly an annual recurring expenditure of Rs. 44 crores will have to be met. Most of the States have framed rules under the making it obligatory for drivers of motor vehicles to stop short of unmannerned level crossing crossings and observe and then proceed. With a view to educating the users of the roads wide publicity is given through newspapers, cinema slides, commercial broadcasting and the television about hazards involved while negotiating unmanred level crossing of new level cross ingings in consultation with appropriate State Governments. The rules and instructions issued by these Committees are not properly implemented and there is no necessity of rebuilding a bridge when its codal life is over. There has been considerable delay in the filing of this writ petition. It was also alleged that unmanaged level cross complaints were provided mostly on roads where the volume of road and train traffic was low. The Railways had appointed 3 high poweresed Committees to enquire into the matter and report about the numerous train accidents from1970 onwards and to take action for ensuring safety measures. The joint Director (s) has also filed a Counter affidavit in reply to the rule on behalf the respondents contending that the recommendation of the Accident Enquiry Committee was examined and enforced within the limit of financial, material resources and resources. It is further stated that there were nearly 120000 bridges on the Railway out of which 195 are important bridges and almost 9400 are major bridges. It had been alleged that several unmanunmanned Level crossings were being replaced by manned ones and improved technical gadgets are being provided for efficient operation.

The appellants applied for compensation to the Jagir Abolition Officer under section 13 of the Bombay Merged Territories and Areas (Jagirs Abolition) Act, 1953 in respect of their proprietary jagirs. The applications were dismissed by the Revenue Tribunal on the ground that they were barred under article 168 of the Limitation Act read with Regulation 55 and 041, rr. 17 and 19 of the Civil Procedure Code. The High Court dismissed the applications holding that the applications for restoration should have been made within 30 days from the date of the order of dismissal. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that since the orders passed dismissing the appeals were received by them on April 9 and April 20, 1961, they were within 30 months of the receipt of the said order of dismiss ment and hence the applications were made in time under Regulation 21 of the Act. HELD: The language of Regulation 20 applies not only to a case where the appeal has been decided on merits but also to a cases where the appellant does not appear either in person or through his agent or lawyer when the appeal or application is called for hearing, the Tribunal may decide the same on merits. If an appeal is dismissed for want of prosecution it cannot be said that the Tribunal has decided the appeal and 'recorded its decision within the meaning of section 17 of the Jagirs Abolition Act. [144 H] The language used in Regulation 20, on its true interpretation, applies not to a particular case where an appeal has already been decided but also merely to a ease where the Appeal has been dismissed for non prosecution under Regulation 19(1).

The appellants, two descendants of the original plaintiff, brought a suit under section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure for removal of the respondent Kamal Narayan, another descendant of Dinanath Sao from the office of trustee of the God Shri Ramchandraji Swamy for the village of Telibandha and for accounts. The appellant 's case in the plaint was that Telivancore fell to the share of Sarjoo Prasad 's four sons, who were up till that time living jointly, all the coshares not only re affirmed the dedication made by Dinanath, Sao himself but also dedicated the village Teli misconstru to the deities in this temple by accepting the award made by the Panchas. The Trial Court held that there had been a valid dedication in respect of the village and it was a public religious trust, as the respondent had committed breach of trust by transferring trust properties and appropriating its proceeds and finally by his express repudiation of the trust and was therefore liable to be removed. On appeal the High Court agreed with the Trial Court that the dedication had been made by one Dinanath for the temple of Shri Ramchandra Swamy temple or whether the village was given in full proprietary ownership to Ramsaran Lal with only a charge on it to meet the expenses of the temple, and that the respondent 's suit was therefore maintainable. Held, that the High court 's decision that the plaintiff 's claim of absolute dedication had not been established is not correct and the High COurt was right in holding that the appellant was not entitled to succeed must be set aside. The language used in the original clearly shows anabsolute dedication of the property to Shri Ramchandra Swami temple, which was maintained for the general expenses of a family or that he made certain alienations of the properties of the deity and as owners had full rights to make a valid gift to the deity the dedication as made in para. 2 of the Panch Faisla Award of 1896. The use of the words "at that time" in the opening clause of this Panch Faishil" in section 2 of 'the Act meant "from the profits and income of Mouza Teli Oriya". It is not necessary to examine the oral or documentary evidence as to how the property or the income of the defendant was dealt with. The document then proceeds to say that none of the co sharers and Ramsaren Lal had any right over it, nor the prohibition against the alienations in the following clause, nor "Telibandha has been reserved for ever for the aforesaid purposes and it shall continue to be so only" can,it is argued, limit the amplitude of what is given to Ram sarkar by the opening cl. The words "in that year" mean "from profits and ' income of mouza Telabandha". It was not correct to say, that these words as used in section 3(1) of the Act meant the time of the partition in 1896, but they were intended to be held to be void. The intention was not to make Ramsar an absolute owner of the land but give him possession and management of the same for the benefit of Shri Ramachandra Swamy and Ramrani Lal was merely a presumption which can well be displaced by what follows in the same document as regards this very property. When all these different provisions are considered it is clear beyond any shadow of doubt that the intention was to make ' Ramsarhanlal the absolute owner Of the village but give he possession and manage of the estate just as it has continued to be done from ever.

The two appellants were the President of the Avadh Bar Association and the Chairman, Action Committee of the Lucknow Bar Association. There were three charges against the appellants. The first charge was that they had met and resolved that the Chief Justice was acting in a most partisan manner under the influence of the Allahabad Bar quite unbecoming of the office which he held. The second charge was also that they were responsible for the passing of the resolution. The High Court discharged the notices. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants: (1) The language used by them was unfortunate; (2) the members of the Bar did not act with dignity in regard to the resolu tion; and (3) the language used was unfortunate. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The language employed by them is unfortunate. Counsel for the appellants rightly said that was not proper and it should not have been passed in that manner. [603C] 2.1 In view of the fact that the notices were discharged, the appeal is disposed of with the aforesaid observations. [ 603D E] 2:2 The language of the Resolution was unfortunate and unfortunate. It is true that the High Court referred to the contumacious conduct of the appel lant but the High court did not wish to proceed against the appellant. [ 604E F] 3.1 The language in question was unfortunate, and counsel for the appellent rightly said, on that aspect as follows: 603 "It is a matter of regret that the contem ners who are prominent members of Avadh Bar should have themselves embarked on the path of vilifying the Chief Judge of this Court and that we do not want to be over sensitive in the matter, keeping in mind the surrounding circumstances in which the contu macious act was committed by them.

The appellants Nos. 1 to 4 and their eldest brother, respondent No. 1 were entered into a joint family with the object of partition of joint movable and immovable properties and the same were referred to three arbitrators. The disputes related to certain properties among the brothers in Chinsurah district of Hooghly in the State of West Bengal. The three arbitrators took the assistance of appellant No. 8 and he functioned and acted as one of the arbitrators. On or about November 28, 1977 the arbitrators explained their award to the parties and made signed the award. On behalf of the appellants Nos 1 to4 it was contended that during the subsistence of the interim injunction order on the arbitrators to maintain status quo the arbitrators could not take back the award for presenting the same for registration. The learned Munsif rejected the contention and ordered return of the award holding that it was the Registrar and not the Sub Judge who could determine the question of limitation for the purpose of registration of the Award. The High Court in Civil Rule No. 621 of 1980 on 19th September, 1983 set aside the order of the Sub judge holding that during subsistence of interim injunction orders on the Arbitrators to maintain the status quo, the arbitrators had to keep the award in the custody of the court and there was ample evidence as it would appear from the narration of events hereinbefore made that the arbitrators have tried to obtain the custody for registration and that the award was presented within time as the period during which the judicial proceedings were pending. The appellants Nos., I to 4 filed an application under Section 14 of the Act before the learned Sub Judge praying for a direction on the arbitrator to file the award, but the same was not done. On 2nd September, 1978 the arbitrators made an application before the sub Judge praying that the court be directed to return back the Award to the arbitrators holding that the limitation for registration of award had already expired. The Sub Judge dismissed the application and did not direct return of it holding that limitation for filing the award had expired. In the appeal by special leave, it was urged on behalf of appellants Nos, I to4 that an award affecting immovable properties as in the instant case should be registered. It was further contended that an injunction affecting immovable property as in this case should he registered. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 The limitation period for registration is four months from the date of its execution. [121C] 1.2 In the instant cases indisputably during the period from 26th July, 1978 to 24th November, 1983 there was subsisting injunction preventing the arbitrators from taking any steps. Furthermore, as noted before the award were in the court of the learned Munsif from 28th January, 1978 till the return of award to arbitrators on 24th of November,1983, the award is filed in the Court pursuant to the order dated the Court. It is therefore not necessary to discuss in detail the ratio of A decision of the Full Bench of the Andhra Pradesh High Court which has been upheld by this Court in Nityananda M. Joshi and others vs Life Insurance Corporation of India and Ors., [1982] 2 S.C.R. 891, followed. 1.3 The principles enunciated by this court in Nithial M. Shah and others v Life Insurance Corpn. of India & Ors., ; would have no application to the facts of this case.

The appellant was a tenant for about 20 years in the premises known as " Fida Ali Villa" in Kalyan. The respondent gave notice to the appellant to vacate the premises on the ground of non payment of rent and sub letting which it was alleged had resulted in the termination of the tenancy. The trial court held that subletting was lawful in spite of section 15 of the Bombay Hotel and Lodging Houses Rates Control Act, 1947 (Bom. 57 of 1947). He also passed a decree for Rs. 445 on account of rent remaining due and dismissed the respondent 's suit for ejectment. On appeal the Assistant Judge reversed the order of eviction holding that section 15 was not confined to any other law and therefore sections 13(1)(e) and 15 of that Act did not apply. The appellant came to this Court by special leave. Held, that the plea of waiver cannot be raised because as a result of giving effect to that plea the court would be enforcing an agreement which is prohibited and made illegal. The plea of estoppel was unsustainable. In the present case the question was not merely of waiver of statutory rights enacted for the benefit of an individual but whether the Court would aid the appellant in enforcing a term of the agreement which section 15 Of the Act declares to be illegal. By enforcing the contract the consequence will be the enforcement of an illegality and infraction of a statutory provision which cannot be condoned by any conduct or agreement of parties. Surajmull Nargoremull vs Triton Insurance Co. (1947) L.R. 52 I.A. 126, P. D. Aswani vs Kavashah Mulla ([1945] 1 K.B. 65, 72, 72. 29 226 Oscanyan vs Winchester Arms Company (I.L.R , referred to.

The appellant Board conducted secondary examinations in the month of March 1990, whereat the marks awarded, after the formalities of valuation by the examiners of the answer sheets in each subject, were found tampered with, the appellant. The respondent Board conducted Secondary Examination in the months of March, 1990, whereinat the mark sheets awarded, without the approval of the Divisional Board, Moderators ' mark sheets sent to Pune for feeding the computer to declare the results were found tampering with the appellant and also indicated the proposed punishment, if in the enquiry it would be found that marks were tampered with the knowledge or connivance or at the instance of the candidates or parents or guardians. The appellant Board, by its notification dated August 31, 1990 cancelled the said notification and directed the Board to take expeditious action to declare results of the examination within the specified time. Show cause notices were issued to the students on July 30, 1990 informing them of the nature of tampering, the subjects in which the marks were found compared with the marks initially obtained and the marks increased due to tampering, and also stated the proposed penalty, if any, in the inquiry it would he found that the marks are tampered with. The respondents challenged the said cancellation by filing a writ petition in the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the Standing Committee had no power under the Act and Regulations to enquire into the use of unfair means committed at the final examination conducted under the act, and that the fabrication was done at their behest. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Examination Committee of the Regional Board itself a statutory body acted on behalf of the State Board and is not a delegate of the District Board. Truely, it is regulatory in character and the powers were exercised by the Committee and recommended to the State Govt. to compulsarily retire the respondent and it amounts to taking a decision on behalf thereof. When the enquiry was conducted by some members and the Standing committee was taking the decision thereon, it was acting on behalf or of the Board as its agent. When an enquiry was held by some member and the standing Committee was taking decision thereon it is acting on for behalf of that State Board as their agent.

The appellants were charged under section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code for criminal conspiracy to cause the offence of criminal misconduct punishable under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The Special Judge found the appellants guilty under both heads of charges and sentenced them to three months ' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 500. On appeal by special leave: Held, that before it can be made applicable there must be proof, it was said, that the public servant adopted corrupt or illegal means and thereby obtained for himself or for any other person any valuable thing or pecuniary advantage. The word "obtains" is used in sections 161 and 165 of the Penal Code. The words "corrupt or illegal" are not to eliminate the idea of acceptance of what is given or offered to be given, though it connotes also an element of effort on the part of the receiver. One class of cases might arise where corrupt or unlawful means are adopted or pursued by the public servants to gain for himself a pecuniary advantage; and if a man obtains a pecuniary benefit by the abuse of his position, he will be guilty under sub clause (d). Sections 161, 162 and 163 refer to a motive or reward for doing or forbearing to do something, showing favour or disfavour to any person, or for inducing such con duct by the exercise of personal influence. The offence is of four kinds or categories. Bribery as defined in section 161 of the Code if it is habitual, falls within clause (a). Bribery of the kind specified in section 165, if it was habitual, fell within clause(b) contemplates criminal breach of trust by a public servant and the wording takes us to section 405 of the code. It is with clause (c) that the offence as defined therein does not come with. In one sense this is no doubt true but it does not follow that there is no overlapping of offences. The definition of "corruption" in section 5 of the Act does not bring about any difference between offences.

Consequently, any act of the debtor interfering with or impairing that right will, to the effect, at all events, of any loss inflicted, relieve the surety from liability, and, if it has the effect of altering or purporting to alter the contract Of suretyship, discharge him altogether. [924A B] 1.2. The expression 'Court which passed the decree or order ' would be deemed to include where the decree/order has been varied or reversed in exercise of appellate or revisional jurisdiction, the Court of first instance. [936C D] 2.1 In an almost identical situation with regard to an identical clause in Amrit Lal Goverdhan Lalan vs State Bank of Travancore and Ors., this Court after referring to clause 5 in the letter of guarantee which is in pari materia with clause 7 of the letter dated guarantee under discussion, held as under: "On behalf of the respondent Bank reference was made to cl. It was not a case of granting time or indulgence to the principal defendant or variation of the credit or taking one set of security in substitution of some other security or release of any security.

The appellant was the son of a member of a family. The lands in suit were comprised in six survey numbers, one relating to village Nawabag and the other relating to the estate of the appellant. In 1923 there was a partition between the appellant and respondent No. 1. The appellant claimed that as a result of this partition the " patelki inam" lands were divided and the lands in dispute were allotted to the share of the family. He claimed that the Government had no jurisdiction or authority to resume and regrant the lands to him. The trial court held that the lands were granted by the then sovereign authority by way of remuneration or emoluments for services rendered by the patel and the grant was recognised as a service inam by the British Government, and that it was open to the revenue authorities to resume the lands. On appeal the High Court held that (1) the lands had been given by way Of remuneration or wages for services to be rendered by them by the Patels and Patwaris Law, 1900 in force in Berar and section 190 of the Berar Land Revenue Code, 1928; (2) the grant made was a service Inam by the sovereign authority which the Nazim confirmed in accordance with old judicial usage; and (3) the order of Government did not confer any new right nor did they deprive anybody of any subsisting right in respect of the "patelki Inam lands and Government had any right to resume them. Held, that under section 3 of the Pates and Patwarais Law the emoluments appertaining to the office of the patels or patwari shall be enjoyed solely by the person for the time being holding the office; even a substitute shall receive the whole of the emoluments belonging to the Office unless the Deputy Commissioner otherwise directs. The settlement will be made with the head member of the Family holding the offices or enjoying the inam and who will be held alone responsible to Government, in no case will the Government interfere to compel the actual incumbent of an office to make over any portion of his regulated service grant to other branches of the families, as service grants cannot be divided according to the orders of Government. The provisions clearly indicate that the " Pateki inam " lands are subject to orders passed by the revenue courts in respect Of matters mentioned therein and no right is given to a member or a member to claim a share in the emoluments. He has submitted that the High court had relied on the decision of the Privy Council in Venkata Jagannadha vs Veerabadrayya, (1923) L.R. 75 I.A. 225, which held that co sharers have a right to a share of service grants in Berar. The case of the appellants was that these two plots ceased to be inam lands when they fell in the resumed portion and survey numbers 22 to 39 were included in the jagir portion. Held further, that the grant did not create any new rights nor did it deprive anybody Of any subsisting rights in respect thereof. The fact that the p Patelki inams were treated on the same basis in the resumption proceedings of 1917, and by the order dated August 28, 1922, Government excluded the "Patelki inams" lands from the resumption proceeding relating to jagir on the footing that they were separate from and independent of the jagir of Nawabag. The grant was not a service grant but no question of a share arose in the pay of the produce of the Patel 's office arose there.

The respondents claimed that the family properties were treated as joint family properties and that they had settled down first in Madras and then in Bangalore sometime between 1928 and 1930, and as a large part of the State was situate in Madras, he should prefer the Madras as against the Bombay view. The Deputy Controller held that neither the said evidence nor the fact of their having paid succession duty on one third of the said estate only concluded the issue before him viz., that the rules of Hindu law were consistently acquiesced in and applied to their family and the other Cutchi Memons settled in Madras. He rejected their contention that as there was only one solitary decision of the High Court of Bombay which limited the application of Hindu Law to matters of succession and inheritance, the Bombay decision was correct one. The High Court held that the Khojas who had settled in Bombay were converted as a caste to Islam some three or four hundred years ago, but retained on their conversion the Hindu law as to inheritance and succession. In appeal by certificate to this Court it was contended for the appellant (i) that the doctrine of sons acquiring interest by birth in ancestral properties did not apply to Cutchi memons; and (ii) that in any case there was no scope for raising any such contention after the enactment of the Indian Shariat Act, 1937 and thereafter of the . The respondents ' family was in Madras till about 1930 when its members partly shifted their activities to Bangalore, and therefore, they were governed by Hindu Law. HELD : (i)(a) The High Courts have rightly held that there was a partition between Haji Aboo Bucker Sait 's case and that the ancestral property absolutely vested in Haji Abo Buckers Sait vs Ebrahim Hajee AbooBucker, Sait, and that therefore when a Cutchi had settled among Hindus, according to Hindu law not only in matters of inheritance but also in matters relating to matters other than those specified in section 2 of the Act. [234 D] (b) The question as to which personal law, sects among the Muslims, such as the Khoja and Memons would be subject to in matters Of property succession and succession is a matter of property, succession and devolution. [235 E F] (c) In matters of simple succession and intestate inheritance, it was open to objection, since such a rule could rest only upon proved customs, that no custom of that kind had ever been proved and that Scott, C.J., had based his conclusion only on the case law. The conclusion which the High Courts arrived at on consideration of the decisions referred to above is that the accountable persons having been born lone before 1948, had already acquired a right by birth, in the property held by their father, a right expressly saved by section 3 of the , Act. There was no question of any such interest passing to them on the death of their father as envisaged by section 2. [236 G] (d) The rule of Hindu laws applicable to the Khoias applied only to matters Of inheritance and inheritance and not to maintenance under Hindu law which applied to the Cutchi, Memons, but that the concept of joint family property also governed them, was open for objection, as such a r. could rest merely upon proved custom, that any custom of the kind had never been proved; and that it lay upon a party setting up a custom in derogation of that law to prove it strictly, and (e) that there is no question Of its having to decide whether the Bombay High Court was right in its view that the said view was correct. [237 A C] (2) The contention expressly raised was that the Mitakshara doctrine of son acquiring interest in ancestral property did not arise to Cutch Memons and therefore the rule of 'he sons having a right to demand partition of it did not be applicable.

The appellants are manufacturers of different types of fabrics. In order to manufacture the said fabrics, yarn is obtained at an intermediate stage. The yarn so obtained is further processed in an integrated process in the said composite mill of the appellant No. 1 for weaving the same into fabrics. The appellants do not dispute that the different kinds of fabrics which are manufactured in the mill are liable to payment of excise duty on their removal from the factory. They also do not disputes that the various kinds of fabric which are produced or manufactured at an intermediary stage and consumed or utilised (i) as such or after subjection to any process or processes; or (ii) for the manufacture of any other commodity in or outside such place, until the excise duty leviable thereon has been paid at such place and in such manner as is prescribed in these Rules or as the Collector may require. The Central Excise officers issued a circular dated September 24, 1980 purporting to interpret rules 9 and 49 of the Central Excise Rules 1944 and directing the subordinate excise authorities to levy and collect duty of excise in accordance therewith. In the said circular, the Board directed the subordinate Excise Authorities that "use of goods in manufacture of another commodity even within the place/premises that have been specified in this behalf by the Central excise officers in terms of the powers conferred under rule 9 of the Rules will attract duty". As the said Circular was being implemented to the prejudice of the appellants, they filed a writ petition before the Delhi High Court challenging the validity of the circular. During the pendency of the writ petition in the Delhi high Court, the Central Government by a Notification No. 20/82 C dated 20.2.1982 amended rules 9 & 49 of Rules and also introduced Rule 49 which required that "place of removal" as defined therein, does not contemplate any deemed removal, but a physical and actual removal of the goods from a factory or any other place or premises of production or manufacture or a warehouse etc. Under the definition "place" may be a factory/any other place/ premises of Production or manufacture of excisable goods etc. The Explanation to rule 173A and the proviso to rule 17G, inter alia provides that "for the purposes of this rule, excisable goods produced, cured or manufactured in any place and consumed/ utilised (1) shall be deemed to have been removed from such place or Premises immediately before such consumption or utilisation". The appellants did not dispute their liability in respect of yarn which is also removed from the Factory. They filed a Writ Petition before the High Court inter alia challenging the vires of the Circular. During pendency of that writ petition, the Delhi and the High Courts by its judgment dated October 16, 1980 held that yarn obtained and further processed within the factory for the purpose of weaving the said same into fabric will be liable to pay excise duty in view of the amended provisions of rules 9, and 49. The appeals filed by the appellants were dismissed by a Division Bench of the Delhi. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Rule 9 and rule 49 are ultra vires the provision of clause (b) of sub section (4) of section 4 of the Act inasmuch as "place or of removal", as defined in the Explanation to sub rule (2) of rule 173 A and in the proviso thereto, respectively, does contemplate collection of duty levied on the production of a commodity at an inter unit stage which again is utilised in such continuous process for the manufacturing end product. The explanation to rule 9 and Rule 49 are not ultra vires. [707C] 1.2 In the instant case, the appellants are liable under excise duty to pay any excise duty.

The appellant was charged under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and section 161 Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that Miss Eylene (P.W. 2) used to live in 1962 with her father at Fazilka. She developed illicit connection with someone and became pregnant. In April 1963 Miss Eyar along with her newly born son came to the house of Russel Nathaniel in police uniform and accused Russel n Nathan Lai and his wife expressed their reluctance to make arrangement for the bringing up of the child. Russel Mnen was then instructed to pass on the money to the appellant who put them in the left pocket of his trousers. Ruscy Nathan mature and his daughter Eylene went to Ambala to her maternal uncle, who was employed as a sister in the Ambala Air Force Hospital, and gave birth to a son there in July 1963. In August 1963 MissEylene along with his newly born child came to Delhi to the residence of Rusia N. K. Lal, P.W 11 and stayed there with her sister. It is alleged that on August 29, 1963 at about 9.30 or 10 p.m. the appellant went to the place of Rusrosel N.K. Lal and his brother in law N. Kumar Lal went to Delhi and stayed with her in police custody. On September 4, 1963 the appellant asked Russel to come to the village of N. k. K . Lal at about 7.30 p. m. The appellant told the D.S.P. Mukatdhari Singh turned up and recovered the currency notes from the pocket of the appellant. On being questioned the appellant told him that he never asked for bribe and that the money was paid to him in repayment of the loan by him to RusselNathaniel, it was stated that he had never asked him for bribe. The Special Judge accepted the prosecution case as correct and convicted the appellant under section 161 I.P .C. and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for two years and to pay a fine of Rs. 5001 or in default to undergo simple imprisonment for a further period of six months under section 4(2). On appeal, the High Court maintained the conviction of the appel lant under section S 5(1)(d) of Prevention of corruption Act and section I.C. The High Court also set aside the order with regard to payment of fine or imprisonment in default. In support of this appeal it was contended that the concealment of the birth of an illegitimate child was not an offence under the Indian Penal code or any other criminal statute and if the appellant had obtained money from Russel, it cannot be said that the appellant has obtained a gratification for doing or forbearing to do any official act, or for showing or forbearing to show in the exercise of his official functions, favour or disfavour to any per son. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. When a public servant is charged under s. 161 I P.C., and it is alleged, that the illegal grati fication was taken by him for doing an official act it is not necessary for the Court to consider whether or not the accused public servant was capable of doing or intended to do such an act. [186 E] 2. When the public servant charged under S. 161, I. P. C., and the charge against the appellant is also under s . 5(i)(d), of the Act which states "5.(1) A public servant who commits criminal misconduct shall be punishable with imprisonment for one term which shall not be less than one year but which may extend to seven years and shall also be liable to fine X X : Provided that the court may, for any special reasons recorded in writing impose a sentence of imprisonment of less than two years.

The appellant was charged with having accepted Rs. 100 by corrupt or illegal means or by otherwise abusing his position as a public servant to obtain pecuniary advantage for himself punishable under section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. The charge framed against him related to the same transaction and stated that he had accepted the sum as bribe from the appellant. The Special judge convicted the appellant and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for three months and to pay a fine of Rs. 500 in default to suffer further rigorous imprisonment. No separate sentence was passed under section 6(2). On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The sanction accorded in this case was a valid sanction. The sanction was a validly sanctioned one. The only point which had been argued before the High Court and which was the expressed reason for the granting of the certificate having failed, the appeal must be dismissed and the decision of the High court in upholding the conviction and sentence must be upheld. Gokulchand Dwarkadas Morarka vs The King, (1948) L.R 75 I.A. 30, referred to. (ii)The sanction accorded was a proper sanction. It was not for the appellant to contend that the sanction accorded by him was not a valid one. In order that there may be no misunderstanding it would be necessary to decide whether the sanction granted in this ease was a invalid sanction. Gokul Chand Dwarkadalas Mormarka vs King, , followed. (iii)The sanctioning authority had applied his mind and was of the opinion that in the interests of justice the appellant should be prosecuted. The sanctioning authority did not call for any record in connection with the matter from his office nor did he call for the connected claim cases or find out as to how they stood. It is not for him to judge the truth of the allegations made against the appellant by calling for the records of the connected claims or other records in connection therewith from his official office. The papers placed before him apparently gave him the necessary material upon which he decided that it was necessary in the ends of justice to accord his sanction.

The respondent landlord filed a petition under section 14(1)(b) of the Madras Buildings (Lease and Rent Control) Act, 1960 against the appellant tenant for eviction on the ground that the building was bona fide required by the landlord for demolition and for reconstruction. The Rent Controller held that the requirement of the landlords bona fide and ordered for eviction of the tenants. The High Court dismissed the revision petition filed by the tenants against the orders of eviction. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant tenants that the landlord had only a life interest in the premises in question and that it was inherent in such a lifeinterest that it is not permissible for the landlord to invoke section 14 (1) (b) as grounds for eviction by demolition of the property for the purpose of reconstruction. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The rights between section M. Gopalakrishna and the remainder man with regard to the terms of the Deed of Settlement win have to be worked out in appropriate proceedings, if necessary and the general law win govern the matter if any occasion arises. [276C] 2. When the objection on the score of the landlord being a holder of life interest and hence incapable of invoking section 14 of the Act fails the suit must be decreed. It was contended by the tenant that a tenant with a life Interest cannot be allowed to demolish the property in order to reconstruct it as that action would, per se, be not bona fide. [277D E] 3.

The respondent decree holder in the execution proceed ings in this very case between the same parties which came to this Court on an earlier occasion. The appellant contended that after the coming into force of the U.P. Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act, 1950 (hereinafter referred to as the Act) which vested in the State free from all encumbrances, the respondent 's grove was not included in the 34 grove land, which under section 6(a)(i) of the Act, read with section 73 of the , so that nothing more than the compensation awarded to the intermediary could be proceeded against by the mortgagee. The executing court held that after vesting of all the rights mentioned in section 6 of the said Act in the respondent State, new bhumidhari rights came into existence under section 18 of the . It also held that the only way in which a mortgagee could enforce his right against the mortgage or after the Act came into force was provided in section 4(h) of Act read with s. 73 of Act, so that no more than compensation awarded by the executing court to the respondent could be proceed ing against trees in groves and the view taken by the execution court, that there was a distinction between trees and a grove and grove land and that after such vesting of the rights of the respondents mentioned in. section 6 (h) in the case of trees of groves as these contin ued to vest in the intermediary, the appellant could be pro cuted against the mortgagee by the respondent. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by certificate under article 133(1)(c) of Constitution. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The position taken by this Court in the instant case is well settled that trees before they are cut form parts of 'land '. And an inseparable part is always included in 'the whole. In view of this very clear legal position, it is not necessary even to consider previous definitions or to make out specious or unrealistic distinctions between standing uncut trees, which are parts of grovees and grove lands. The proposition is well established that trees, before they were cut, form parts parts of the 'land. And, an inseparable portion is always excluded in the whole. [34C D] 2. Under the general law, trees, after they clear words of the enactment, are part of bhumidhari right.
