The six accused persons were charged with offences punishable under Sections 143, 147, 148, 341, 323, 324 and 302 read with Section 149 IPC. The prosecution case was sought to be proved by the ocular testimony of PW4 Biju (PW5) and Anil (PW6). At the trial however four eye witnesses, PWs 6 and 7 salesman and his assistant in the arrack shop and PW8 Unni @ Velayudhan turned hostile and did not support the prosecution case. The Trial Court on the basis of prosecution evidence found accused No. 1 guilty of an offence punishable under Section 302 IPC and sentenced him to suffer rigorous imprisonment for life. Accused Nos. 2 to 6, namely, Rajan Preman, Viswan, Sura and Shajan were found guilty of offences under Sections 147, 149, 148 and 149 IPC but no separate sentences were awarded on any of those counts. On an appeal before the High Court, the conviction and sentence recorded against them by the Trial Court was set aside. In view of the limited notice issued by this Court, it is directed that the two accused persons, namely Rajan Premen, Viswan and Sura Surendran, appellant 4, no separate sentence were awarded for the other offences. The High Court acquitted all the six accused and convicted the remaining four only. The appellants preferred an appeal to this Court against the judgment of the High court. Allowing the appeals, this Court HELD: 1.1 In a case like this to determine as to which of the accused is guilty of a particular offence, it must be shown that the assembly was unlawful within the meaning of Section 141 and cannot, therefore, form the basis for conviction for an offence with the aid of Section 149. [92G] 1.2 The existence of an unlawful assembly is a necessary postulate for invoking Section 149 I.P.C. Where the existence of such an unlawful com mitted assembly is not proved, the convicted with the help of Section 34 IPC cannot be recorded or sustained. The failure of the prosecution to show that the con stitution was unlawful must necessarily result in the failure of charge under Section 149 Cr. [93A] 1:3 In a trial like this, it can be said to have been called upon to meet that charge and he could very well have considered it unnecessary to concentrate on that part of the Prosecution case during the cross examination of the witnesses. Therefore, the appellants would be liable for the offence com mitt individually by each one of them.

The assessee, Standard Triumph Motor Co. Ltd., is a non resident company having its place of business at Coventry in the United Kingdom. It entered into a collaboration agreement with the Standard Motor Products of India Ltd. (Indian Company) in November 1939 whereunder the assessee was entitled to royalty of five per cent on all sales effected by the Indian Company. This amount of 5 per cent less the Indian tax had to be remitted to the assessee in the Sterling currency. The assessee 's accounting year was the year ending 30th September, 1966. For the assessment years 1967 68 and 1968 69, it disclosed a royalty income of Rs. 1,600 and Rs. 4,57,311 respectively. When it came to filing of the return for the assessment year 1969 70 (year ending 30.9.1966), the assessee admitted a royalty of Rs 925,257 but filed a nil return saving that it was maintaining its accounts on cash basis and not on mercantile basis, that no part of the royalty amount had been received by it and, therefore, nothing is taxable. The I.T.O. completed the assessment for the first two assessment years on the basis of the returns. For these assessment years, 1969 70 and 1970 71, however, he refused to accept the assessee ' plea that it be maintaining its account on cash account basis. He held that it had maintained its accounts in respect of royalty amount disclosed. In these appeals by the asses see against the order of the I.I.T., the High Court answered the question in the negative i.e., in favour of the revenue and against the assessee. The Revenue contended before this Court that the question of method of accounting adopted by the assessee must be examined afresh and for that purpose allowed the appeals and remanded the matters to the Income Tax Officer. It was further contended that since the IL.R. did not dispute its liability to assessment, it had committed a mistake in filing the returns for the years 196768 and 196869. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in answering the question against the assesee. [102D] 1.2 In the instant case, the assessee has been filing its income tax returns in India through the Indian company. It is true that the agreement contemplated royalty amount being remitted in Sterling Currency to U.K., but it cannot be said that until it is so remitted to and received in the U. K., the assessee had not received the income. The practice evidently was that the Indian Co. was maintaining an account pertaining to the asses sees in its books. After it made up its accounts at the end of the calendar year and determined the royalty money payable to the assesses, the Indian co company was crediting the said amount to the account of the assessee In its returns, the I .T.Os assessed the amounts credited in the accounts of the assesse as the income of the non resident Company. The contention of the appellant that it did not actually receive the amount from the Indian CO. is untenable and unacceptable.

The appellant was convicted of murder and sentenced to death. The third accused was acquitted and the fourth accused was convicted under section 302 read with section 34 for the murder of one Lahu Vithu Patil on the night between May 23, and 24, 1960 at village Pasarde. Two persons Rama Krishna Patil accused No. 1 Bhiva Doulu Patil accused Nos. 2 (now appellant before us) were alleged to have taken part in murder of LahuVithu P.W.7 who was convicted as above stated and sentenced under section 34 I.P.C. read with s 34 for murder of two persons, Rama Krishna Hegde accused No . 1 Bhiviva Douru Patil accused 2 (the appellant before this Court) on the testimony of the approver and found corroboration for the approver 's testimony in the statement of Nanu Sintu Sutar, P. W. 7 who had prepared the knife alleged to be used for the offence on March 17, 1960, and hi, motive to commit the murder because of the suspicion he had about his wife having a liaison with the deceased. The High Court on appeal found corroboration in material particulars; from the evidence of Santu 1W. 6 brother of Deoba to whom Deoba had made a confession of his participation in the offence the discovery of the knife at the instance of accused No 1 and the knife being found blood stained and the unusual character of the weapon which fitted in with the dimensions of the injurious caused to the deceased, and that from these facts the learned Judges came to the conclusion that the approver Deoba was giving a true version of the occurrence. With great respect to the High Court it held that without corroboration of the accomplice qua the appellant the conviction is unsustainable, the law being that there should be corroboration of his approver in material details and qua each accused. 834 Held, further, that though the conviction of an accused on the evidence testimony of an accomplice cannot be said to be illegal yet the courts will, as a matter of practice, not accept the evidence Of such a witness without corroboration in materials particulars. The law may be stated in the words of Lord Reading C. J., in Bhuboni Sahu vs The King (1949) L.R. 76 I.A. Mad. 308, 836 position in which he can hardly fail to have a strong bias in favour of the prosecution ; the real danger is that he is telling a story which in its general outline is true, and it is easy for him to work into the story which is untrue.

The appellant was a public servant within the meaning of section 5(2) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. On or about December 11, 1962, the appellant was charged in the Court of Special Judge for an offence under section 5 (2), read with section 5, (1) (d) of Prevention of corruption Act and section 161 of the Indian Penal Code. The case of the prosecution was that on July 8, 1961, the Electrical Executive Engineer accompanied by his Head Clerk, the appel lant paid a visit to Janta Oil Mills situated at Fatuhas. Ramprit Singh P.W. 2 in the mill premises and told him that the outer seal of the meter, technically called the body seal, was in a tampered condition. The Executive Engineer and the appellant thereafter left the mill Premises. At about 10 a.m. on the same day the appellant had gone again to the mill and informed P. W. 2 that the inner seal of it, technically known as the loop seal, of the machine, was not tampered but on a threat by the Executive Engineer, P.Ws. 2 was compelled to give a written statement that 684 the outer sealed seal was tampered with. Thereafter the Executive Officer cut the inner lock and fixed two fresh seals on the meter one in the terminal 'and the other in the body of the Electricity Board. The appellant denied the charges and pleaded that the entire case had been fabricated against him by Raghuraj, P,W. 16, the proprietor of the mill should meet him at his office at Patna within two days and get the matter settled, otherwise they would be put to a big loss. Thereafter, P was charged with offences under section 161 and 409 I.P.C. and section 5 of the Act. The Special Judge accepted the prosecution case as true and convicted the appellant under section 4(2), I.e., (1)(d) read with s.5(1)(D) of Act and sentenced him to undergo rigorous imprisonment for five years. On appeal, the High Court dismissed the appeal and affirmed the judgment of the Special Judge. In appeal to this Court it was contended that on the findings recorded by the High court the appellant could not be convicted of the charges because he was not a "public servant" within the language of section 2(2). HELD: (i) The appellant was an officer in the service or pay of the Corporation as defined in section 21, cl. (12), Indian Penal code and therefore a "Public servant" under section 21 of the . [687 E] (ii) The word 'officer ' used in the section means some person employed to exercise, to some extent, and in certain circumstances, a delegated function of Government. He is either himselfarmed with some authority or representative character, or his duties are immediately auxiliary to those of some one who is so armed. [687 G] (iii) The words "public servants" include every officer in tho service or paid of a local authority or of a corporation engaged in any trade or industry which is established by a Central, Provincial or State Act or of the Government company as defined by section 617 of the '. In view of Explanation 4 to section 21 the Indian penal Code is one who was appointed to some office for the performance of some public duty. [688 G] The word "officer" in the context of Explanation (4) means a person employed in any business or pay ment of a Government company and includes a banking, insurance or financial corporation, a river valley Corporation and a corporation for supplying power, light or water to the public.

The appellant was tried and convicted under r. 125(9) Defence of India Rules, 1962 for contravening cl. 4(b) of the Maharashtra Jowar (Restriction on Purchase 'and Sale and Control of Movement) Order, 1964, and sentenced to rigorous imprisonment for six months and fine of Rs. 500/ , in default further rigorous imprisonment. He was also convicted under section 3 of the Bombay Prevention of Gambling Act, 1960, and was sentenced to undergo rigorous imprisonment of six months. The sentences were directed to run concurrently. On appeal by special leave it was contended that r. 141(2) of Defence ofIndia Rules,1962, is ultra vires because it lays down a rule of evidence contrary to the law contained in section 114 of the Indian Evidence Act. HELD: Rule 141 (2) falls within section 3 because it is essential to the scheme of the Defence of india Rules. The Rules must necessarily provide for the publication of orders made under the Rules and they must also provide for proof in judicial proceedings of the fact of publication. [273 H] In the instant case, r. 142(2), which deals with forfeiture to the Government of packages, coverings or receptacles in which any stocks of jowar are found, does not enable the Court to order forfeiture of the juar seized from the house of the appellant because, he says, the Maharashtra State Jowarsar ( Restriction on purchase 'and sale and Control) Order 1965, it is true, authorises the Collector to seize stocks but does not empower the court to forfeit the juwar.

The appellant was convicted under section 302, Penal Code and sentenced to death. The incident took place at about 5 p.m. on October 20, 1970. The deceased Kunwar Singh was a practising lawyer and after finishing his work for the day he left the Fatehgarh court along with the brother lawyers, Brijendra Singh Yadav and Om Prakash Dubey. They were proceeding on their bicycles and as they reached a spot near Barhpur Block, Violet, Vitolet, is alleged to have shouted "the Vakil has come". Sia Ram fired a shot from his gun as a result of which Kunwar Singh fell down. All the accused thereafter ran away. The other lawyer Om Prakash Pandey, Om Prakash, Dubey, who stated in his evidence that he knew Shri Ram and was therefore able to identify him. The Sessions Court and the High Court accepted the evidence that Violets did give the particular shout and in accordance with its usual practice, it would not like to take a different view of these simple facts. The question which then arises for consideration is whether the only inference which arises from the fact that violet gave the particular Shout was that by so doing she intended to facilitate the murder of Kunwar Singh, section 107 of the Penal Code which defines abetment provides to the extent material that a person abets the doing of a thing who "intentionally aides, by any act or illegal omission, the doing thereof. " The High Court rejected it was inconsequential by observing that the oral testimony of witnesses even if not tested by holding an identification parade can be made the basis of conviction if the request made by the accused is groundless and the witnesses knew the accused prior to the occurrence. It was also held that the evidence of Om Prakash Singh could be made a basis of his conviction if he had been aware that the accused persons were lying in wait on the other side of the road and it was necessary to inform them so that they might accomplish their aim. The High court further found fault with Vioad for not having offered any explanation during the trial as to why she uttered the particular words. This approach is impermeable. The burden was on the prosecution to establish its case and no adverse inference could be raised against Viovir for her failure to explain her utterance. Besides, an accused cannot while being examined under section 342 of the Code of Criminal Procedure be subjected to cross examination and a bald assertion to explain a piece of conduct almost always fails to convince. The accused cannot be allowed to raise one assumption on another to give, to Vioaclet 's conduct a meaning which it does not naturally bear. The words of Vioomlet are at best in the nature of a circumstance and they do not, without more, necessarily justify the inference that she was a party to the murderous design.

The appellant was charged with committing the murder of one D and others. The charge against him was that they, in view of their common grudge against the deceased combined together and did away with the deceased. The Sessions judge found that the prosecution witnesses were not speaking the truth and that the version given by accused 2 was the probable one. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that when three of the four named accused, who were charged under section 302 read with section 34, of the Indian Penal Code, were acquitted, their conviction under section302 read with s.34 could not be sustained. HELD : (i) The judgment of the High Court cannot stand. [683 E] (ii) In the first illustration the court certainly can convict two or more of the named accused if it accepts the evidence that they acted conjointly in committing the offence. But what is the position if the Court acquits 3 of the 4 accused either because it rejects the prosecution evidence or because it gives the benefit of doubt to the said accused ? Can it hold, in the absence of a charge as well as evidence, that though the three accused are acquitted, some other unidentified persons acted conjointaneously with one of the said named persons ? [683 G H] (iii) The High Court gave conflicting findings. While it acquitted accused 1, 3 and 4 under section 148 read with sections 149 and 147, it convicted accused 2 under section 307 read with 34. [684 B C] Mohan Singh vs State of Punjab, ; , followed.

The petitioner, a manufacturer of MSCR defective sheets or coils, imported certain goods and the goods arrived at the Bombay Port on 12th June, 1984. The clearing agent of the petitioner filed bills of entry for ex bond clearance. However, the bills were returned with the remark that "please obtain no objection from the income tax". This was endorsed on 24th August, 1984, and the petitioner 's clearing agent filed six bills of Entry for ex penses clearance. But, the bill of entry was returned with remark that 'please obtained no objection certificate from the Income Tax Department. The petitioner asserted that he was ever ready and willing, rather was anxious to get the material on payment of the then prevailing customs duty. However due to circumstances beyond the control of the peti tioner, that it to say, by the order of the Income tax Authorities, the goods could not be released. This factor was not of the Petitioner 's making, according to the petitioner. The Customs authorities imposed ban under section 132(1) of the Act, 1961. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed under Article 32 of the Constitution on 16th April, 1988 and on 22nd April, 1989, this Court passed the following order: "Pending notice, there will be limited stay to the extent that the goods name, "MSCR defective Sheets/coils" which have arrived at Bombay Port per S.S. 'SEA PRIMR JUSTICE ' will be released forthwith on petitioner ' paying customs and other duties as leviable on 21.8.84. In addition to the above payment the petitioner will deposit Rs.5 lakhs and for the balance amount petitioner will furnish surety (which may consist of ITC bond but excluding cash/ bank guarantee/NSC/FDR) to the satisfaction of the Collector of Customs. " The notice should be given to the revenue authority to appear before this Court. Learned Attorney General had appeared pursuant to the notice on behalf of the respond ents. It was contended on behalf for the respondents that for the payment of duty, the liability of the petitioners to pay the duty is the duty at the time of clearance of the goods. Our attention was drawn to section 15(1)(b) of Income Tax Act which postulates that the rate of duty and tariff valuation, if any, applicable to any imported goods, shall be the rate and valuation in force on the date on which the goods are actually removed from the ware house.

The appellants were the Managing Director of a bank. The sale was fixed for February 2, 1943 and on January 16, 1943, the sale was confirmed on June 23, 1943. On January 16. 1943, M. B. Jakati sold the property to defendants 8 to 10 who are respondents 2 to 4. The following pedigree table will assist in understanding the case: Madhavarao Balakrishan Jakli Deft. 1 (a) daughter Deft., No. 3 Deft.; No. 4 Deft; No. 5 Deft, No. 6 Deft and No. 7 (b) Deft No. 8 (c) De ft. No. 9 (d) De Mrs. Bakati, defendant No. 1 brought a suit for partition of the joint family property and possession of his separate share alleging inter alia that the purchase by him was not binding on the joint Family as it was not liable to be sold for the illegal and immoral acts on the part of defendants No. I which were characterised as misfeasance " The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court in appeal held that the debt was avyavaharika and therefore in an auction sale the S.C.R. (2) that even if the debt had been not avyvaharika the institution of the suit for Partition operated as severance of status between the members of the family and therefore the father 's power of disposition over the son 's share had come to an end and consequently in the auction sale, the share of the sons did not pass to the auction purchaser. Held, that the liability of the appellants to discharge the debts of the father which are not tainted with immorality or illegality is based on the pious obligation of the members to discharge their father ' s debts not tainted by immority or illegality and the pious duty imposed on the sons under the Mitakshara law would be sufficient to sustain the sale and defeat the sons ' suit in the same way and on the same grounds as in the case of execution proceedings. The liability of a father, who is a managing director and who draws a salary or a remuneration, incurred as a result of negligence in the discharge of his duties is not an avy avyavaaraya debt as it cannot be termed as " repugnant to good morals". The right of the son to make an (i) (1934) L.R,. 44 I.A. 1. 1394 to the suit against the sons obtained by him on partition and by the mere device of entering into partition with their father, the sons cannot get rid of this pious obligation or their shares of their liability to be sale or be a means of reducing the efficacy of the attachment or impair the rights of the creditor. There is no doubt that what was put up for auction sale was the whole bungalow 2,0.6 (1)1934 L. R. 44 I A. 178 (2), and the description of the property in the sale certificate are conclusive to shew that the entire corpus of the estate was sold. The binding nature of the decree passed on the father "s debts not vitiated by immors or illegality, which lays open the whole estate to be seized for the payment of such debts.

The petitioners who are seven in number, challenged the Act on the grounds (1) that the tax was not laid upon "passengers and goods" as authorised by Entry No. 56 but upon "fares and freights", which are different entities, and in support of their contention that there is a difference, reference is made to Entry No, 89 of the Union List where power is conferred to tax "faff and freight 's". The petitioners contended (1 ) that the Act was not ultra vires the legislature; (2) that by making tax payable even though the route between two intra State point passes outside the State, the Act has an extra territorial operation which is ultra vires, the legislature. Held, that the levy of tax cannot be said to offend articles 301 and 304 of the Constitution. The word "accept" shows that the incidence of the tax is upon passengers and goods, though the amount varies in the case of passenger according to the distance travelled, and, in the present case, the tax, however, is still on passengers and Goods, though what it is to be is determined by the amount of fare or freight. The tax is for purposes of State, and falls upon passengers, and goods carried by motor vehicles within the State. No discrimination between operators of public motor vehicles using roads has been pointed out, and all operators are equally affected by the Act. Coutts Trotter, C. Now, Rules 8 and 8 A and the notification only lay down what lump sum payment has to be in each case, if a lump sum is being paid. The mandatory language of the Rules and the Notification still retains the permissive character of the section, but only lays down what the amount must be, if lump sum pay is made in lieu of payment of the Tax calculated on actual fares and freight charges. If the two Rules and notification are read harmoniously, it is plain that the apparent mandatory language is limited to the prescribing of the lump sum rates. Rule 8 and the notifications cannot be held to overreach the section to which they are subordinate and from which they must take their colour and meaning. The Act and the Rules must be read harmoniously and reading them so, it was plain that apparent mandatory words of the rules and the Notifications still retains their permissive character, but merely lays down certain what the amounts of the lumpsum payment must be. If these two Rules are read in this way, the mandatory language would be limited to prescribing of lump sum rate rates.

% The appellant company served notice of retrenchment on 56 workmen alleging non availability or raw material to utilise the full installed capacity, power shedding limiting the working of the unit to 5 days a week, and the mounting loss. Subsequently negotiations took place between the Union and the appellant leading to an agreement dated 1st April 1974 whereby the workmen who were sought to be retrenched were taken back in service with continuity of service by the appellant and the workmen on their part agreed to co operate with the management in implementing certain economy measures and in increasing the productivity so as to make the undertaking economically viable. Simultaneously, the workmen demanded a revision of the wage scales and the Labour Court directed that all the workmen shall be reinstated in service from 1st August 1974 with full back wages, permitting the appellant to deduct any amount paid as retrenchment compensation from the amount payable to the workmen as back wages. The appellant challenged the award in this appeal. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The relief of reinstatement with continuity in service can be granted where termination of service is found to be invalid. It would mean that the employer has taken away illegally the right to the work of the workman contrary to the relevant law or in breach of contract and simultaneously deprived deprived workman of his earnings. If the services were not terminated the workmen ordinarily would have continued to work and would have earned their wages. When it was held that the termination of services was neither proper nor justified, it would not only show that the workman were always willing to serve but if they rendered service they would legitimately be entitled to the wages for the same. If they were always ready to work but they were kept away therefrom on account of invalid act of the employer, there is no justification for not awarding them full back Wages which were very legitimately due to them. [567F G] 1.2. The award has been implemented and the retrenched workmen have been reinstated in serv ice. The only limited question is whether the Labour court in the facts and circumstances of this case was justified in awarding full backwages or some sacrifice is expected of him. [568C D] 2.1 In appropriate cases the Court may, in the spirit of labour and management being partners in the industry direct scaling scaling down of back wages with some sacrifice on management 's part too. [569E F] 2:2. It is not to be arbitrary, vague and fanciful but legal and regular (See Susannah Sharm v.Workfild(4). It is a common venture in the pursuit of desired goal. Now if a Sacrifice is necessary in the overall interest of the industry D or a particular undertaking, it will be both unfair and iniquitous to expect only one partner of the Industry to make tile sacrifice.

The plaintiff 's father Tarak Lall, who was the mortgagee sued in 1938 for a sum of Rs. 89,485 12 plus costs. The mortgage was exe cuted on the 12th June 1936 in favour of one Mst. Gyarsi for a consideration of Rs 80,000. For convenience I will call this suit the mortgage deed though this is not a suit on the mortgage. The mortgagee sued for the recovery of the amount due and costs from the defendants. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court held that it was not necessary to set out the decision of this Court regarding the de tails but only giving an overall picture. On appeal by special leave: Held, that section 82 must exclude section 43 because when there is a general law and a special law dealing with a particular matter, the special excludes the general. In the present case the plaintiff had in substance asked for a mortgage decree up to a limit of Rs 40,253 11 10 with interest against each defendant. The amount which went towards satisfaction of the defendants ' liability was only Rs. 40, 253 11 10 and not Rs. 15,000 as claimed by him. The suit was therefore maintainable under section 92 of the Transfer of Property Act read with section 82. The plaintiff had also asked for the declaration of charge and for a decree under Order XXXIV, Civil Procedure Code. The declaration of charges standing by itself is superfluous although Order XXXIV rule 2(1) does require that the decree in a mortgage suit shall (1) A.I.R. 192 "declare the amount so due" at the date of the decree. But reading the two reliefs together, I am of opinion that though the claim is inartistically worded the plaintiff has in substance requested for a mort gage decree up upto a limit Of Rs.40,253 II 10 with interests against each defendants. Therefore, though he has not used the word "subrogation" he has asked in substance for the relief to which a subrogee would be entitled under the Transfer Of Property Act.

% The appellant No. 1 is a Bachelor of Engineering (Civil) having secured first class with distinction getting 69.96% marks from Karnataka Univer sity. Shri Rajendra appellant No 2 is a B.M. degree holder of Engineering. Appellant No. 2 is the Bachelor of Engi neering (Mech.) from Karnataka University and secured 66.40 marks in the qualifying examination thus in all 99.46 marks out of 150. Both the appellants were not selected in merit as the last candidate selected for the above posts secured higher marks than the appellants. The appellants filed a petition before the Karnataka Administrative Tribunal challenging the Rules on the ground that the percentage of marks for viva voce as 33.3 were excessive and in violation of the decision of this Court. The Tribunal dismissed the petitions and the appellants aggrieved against the aforesaid decision have approached this Court by grant of special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In view of the fact that appointments under the impugned Rules were made as back as in 1987 and only the present appellants had approached the Tribunal for relief, the case of other candidates cannot be considered as they never approached for redress within reasonable time. [495C] Ashok Kumar Yadav & Ors. vs State of Haryana & Ors., ; , followed. 1.2 In view thereof the result of the impugned selections was declared in 1987, and the selected candidates have already joined the posts, it is an admitted position that if the marks for interview were kept even at 15% of the total marks and merit list is prepared according ly then both the appellants are bound to be selected and a large number of selected candidates would have gone much lower in the merit list than the appel lant. [596D E] Ashok kumar Yadav & ors. vs state of Karnata ka pointed out that there are many other candidates who had secured much higher marks, than the appellant in case the above criteria is applied for selection.

The appellants were convicted under section 302 read with section 120 B of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution alleged that the accused had supplied the bombs to him and that he had committed the ghastly murder at the behest of the appellant. The trial court accepted the evidence of 14 witnesses who were examined for the prose cution. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction as also sentence awarded by the trial court and confirmed by the High court. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In a case involving the killing of the District Magistrate in his office, better investigation was expected and the State should have taken great care to ensure that every loophole in the investigation was plugged at the fight time in ac cordance with law. It is unfortunate that lapses have oc curred. P.S. Appeals dis posed of. [415C] 1.2 In a ease involving the murder of the district Magistrate in the office, more so, there is no direct evidence of his involvement and he had also confessed to his guilt. [413D E] 2.1 The confession of a co accused person cannot be treated as substantive evidence and can be pressed into service only when the court is inclined to accept other evidence and feels the necessity of seeking for an assurance in support of its conclusion deducible from the said evidence. [414E F] 3. In a criminal case involving murder, the Court cannot start with the con fession of a person; it must begin with other evidence adduced by the prosecution and after it has formed its opinion with regard to the quality and effect of the said evi dence, then it is permissible to turn to the confession in order to receive assurance to the conclusion of guilt which the judicial mind is about to reach on the said other evidence. The confession must have been the common reaction of all the ashramites including Yadav and Sadiq. Thus, this could not be a feature to supply the link for establishing conspiracy. Prosecution also relied upon a feature, which if accept ed, could provide some link between the two for the commis sion of the offence. According to the prosecution, Yadav was beaten up badly after being apprehended by the mob soon after the bomb burst. Several prosecution witnesses have spoken about Yadav being assaulted by the angry mob soon before them. There is clear material that Yadav was man handled. P.,W.3 has stated: "He was held by me and other persons chasing him. I have killed the Collector by bombs at the orders of Guru Sant Gyaneshwar and one bomb has been left in the Jhola". P.W.10 stated: 'The people who caught of him started to assault him and began to ask him why he had killed the collector under the orders Of Baba. Several other prosecution witnesses had spoken about the confession before them, but there is clear evidence that Yadav made this statement, he appears to have made the statement following assault on him. Even accepting the prosecution story that Yadav has made the statements as alleged, can the same be utilised against Sadanand is the next aspect for consid eration.

The appellants were the workmen of a manufacturing concern known as Crompton Parkinson (Works) India Limited and its main business was to invest money in manufacturing concerns. The first company was New York, which is in the main concern of Cromapton Parkin (Work) India Ltd., and service and repair to the said products at its workshop. The third company was Konyon Greaves Private Limited and Its main business being distribution of the products of a manufacture concern known "Cromptonson Park Inson Park (Workedks)India Limited and service repair to its factory. The fourth company was Ruston and Hornsby (India) Private Limited, and its principal business was distribution of products of the manufacturing concern in Crompson Park wayson Parkndergpur, Bombay. The last three companies were controlled by the first company, namely Greaves Cotton and Co., in one way or the other and that is how the main dispute relating to wages and dearness allowance was dealt with together by the Tribunal. There were nine awards, though the main award dealing with the main controversy relating to wage and dearness allowances was common. It was contended on behalf of the appellants that the Tribunal had gone wrong in applying the industry cum region formula which was the basis for fixing wages and Dearness allowance and had made comparison with concerns which were not comparable; that the tribunal had ignored the wages prevalent for these categories in comparable concerns, and that the award should have been passed as far as the clerical and subordinate staff were concerned. Held: (i) The Tribunal has not specifically considered what the total wage packet would be on the basis of the scales of wages and the dearness allowance fixed by it as it should have done; but considering that wage scales fixed are less than the highest in the comparable concerns though more than the lowest, it cannot be said that the total Wage packet in the case of the appellant would 'be necessarily higher than in the cases of other comparable concerns. (ii) The principle which emerges from these two decisions is that in applying industry cum unit formula for fixing wage scales the Tribunal should lay stress on the industry part of the formula if there are a large number of industrial concerns in the same region carrying on the same industry; in such a case, in order that production cost may not be unequal and there may be equal competition, wages should generally be fixed on the principle of comparable industries, namely, industries of the same kind. The Tribunal had to take into consideration the total pay packet in fixing wages, dearness allowance and adjustment, the employees of the appel lant ' concerns from 1950 that pay scales were not high as compared to pay scales in comparable concern. (iii) In the present case, the Tribunal has relied on a number of cases in which the maximum was higher than fifteen months wages. The reason given by it for doing so is that incongruity in the payment of dearness allowance between clerical and other subordinate staff should be removed. It appears that on account of different scales of dearness allowances for subordinate and clerical staff, a member of 'the subordinate staff drawing the same wages would get less dearness allowance than a member belonging to clerical and subordi nate staff as well as factory workmen on the similar scale, for the need for neutralisation was uniformly felt by all kinds of employees. It is true that in these concerns, subordinate staff was getting dearness allowance on different scales based on the old textile scale of dearness Allowance.

The appellants who are the legal representatives of one Annappa and against whom the present appeal is directed, have not entered appearance in this appeal. The respondents filed a suit for redemption of certain mortgaged property and possession thereof free from encumbrances and for other ancillary reliefs. The trial court held that by the Rajinama, Shiddappa intended to convey the title in the suit land to the mortgagees and hence the appellants could not claim redemption of the mortgages. On appeal the District Court held that the Raj inama passed by Shiddhappa did not extinguish the title of the mortgagors in the mortgaged property, that the plaintiffs were agriculturists, that they were bound to pay the amount also under the simple mortgage and that on taking accounts the mortgages had redeemed themselves. The High Court dismissed both the appeals. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellants that under section 74 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code as it stood at all material times, the Rajnama passed a relinquishment in favour of more persons than one, and that in spite of the opposition of Tukaram, Letters of Administration with a copy of the will annexed was granted to Krishna Kallappa. Held: (i) The contention that an unregistered relinquishment may be in favour Of more persons only than one is correct. It is true that no specific reference was made in the judgment to section 74 but the actual decision in that case, quite clearly indicates the court 's understanding of the law applicable to those facts and that law was nothing but the provisions of section 74. In view of the observation of the Judicial Committee in Khiarajmal vs Daim (1904) L. R. 32 Ind App. App. No. 22 of 1945 which is a case of no specific mention was made, it is clear that so far as the revenue authorities are concerned, it was the registered occupant who represented the entire occupancy and the fact that the notice of relinquishment must necessarily be a notice on behalf of all occupants or any particular occupant other than the registered owner. (ii) The position of registration of one of them as the registered tenant attracts the operation of the Code and confers certain rights or imposes certain obligations on the registered occupants as laid down in the Code but does not take away the rights of other occupants. It was true that the principal one of such persons must enter into a written agreement to become the registered occupancy occupant. This is for facilitating the purpose of the code but it does not mean that the other persons in whose favour the occupancy is relinquished cease to have any right. That their right as occupants remains is clearly recognised by the opening paragraph of the section which gives an occupant a right to relinquish his occupancy either absolutely or in favour or of a specified person. This right is given to all occupants, if there are more than one for the singular includes the plural.

The respondent company, a company incor pated under the Indian Companies Act dealing in carbon paper, typewriter, ribbon, stepler machines and steplers, despatches the said goods from its head office at Bombay to its branch office at Kanpur wherefrom sales there of these goods were effected in the State of Uttar Pradesh. During the course of the assessment proceedings for the assessment year 1956 57, the respondent claimed that carbon paper not being paper falling within the ambit of Entry No. 2 of the Schedule to the Notification but a specialised article used for copying purposes, its turnover had to be assessed at the rate of 2 per cent prescribed for unclassi fied goods and not at the rates of 6 paise per rupee i.e. 6% prescribed in the aforesaid Notification. The Sales Tax Officer taxed the turnover of carbon paper for the period commencing from July 1, 1966 to June 30, 1966 at 2%. The validity and correctness of this order in so far as it related to the levy of tax on carbon paper at 6% and ribbon at 10% was challenged by the respondent by means of a writ petition before the High Court. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the levy. Hence this appeal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) A word which is not defined in an enactment has to be understood in its popular and commer cial sense with reference to the context in which it occurs. In popular parlance, the word 'paper ' is understood as meaning a sub stance which is used for bearing, writing, or printing, or for packing, orfor drawing on, or on, for decorating, or cover ing the walls. [838E F] (2) The word ' Paper ' in the common parlance means paper which is use ed for printing, writing or packing purposes. [889F G] (3) A perusal of the Notification shows that carbon Paper is not paper as envisaged by Entry 2 of Notification No. ST 3124/X 1012(4) dated 1st July 1966. [876G H; 841A B] (4) The mere fact that the word "paper ' forms part of the denomination of a specialised Article is not decisive of the question whether the article is paper as generally understood.

The respondents were employed by the appellant Mills at the Sugar Mill in the district of Nainital. In 1951, the partners of the appellant ' Mills purchased the building machinery and other equipment of another sugar mill at Kiccha in the District of Nainital, but they closed it at Bulandshahr. The new factory was named Pannijee Sugar & General Mills, Bulandshahr. On January 19, 1955, the General Manager of the Appellant Mills ordered the transfer of the respondents I to 4 from the appellant Mill to the new mill at Bulandshahr, and the said respondents through their representative, the fifth respondent, protested to the General manager against the transfer. But the General Managers by his letter dated January 22, 1955 denied the charges. On February 2, 1955 the General managers served a notice on the respondents stating that they had disobeyed his order of transfer and thereby committed misconduct under Standing Order No. L(a). They were asked to submit their explanation as to why action should not be taken against them under the Standing Order. The Labour Union thereafter raised an industrial dispute which was referred by the State Industrial Tribunal for adjudication, but the Government of U.P. by its order dated February 6, 1956, made its award holding that the management was within its rights and that as the respondents 1 to 4 had disobey ed the order of the management they were properly dismissed by the management. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court which held that the respondents had disobeying the order passed by the Management, they were proper dismissed.

The appellant company which was formed in 1965 and went into production the same year, was exempted from the provisions of Chapter V A of the . The scheme could not be implemented straight away by the stages. It became necessary for Parliament to make certain transitory provisions, which it did by the introduction of Chapter VI A by Act 53 of 1951. The Statement of objects and reasons of the Act 53 may be usefully extracted here: "The , was passed by the Dominion Legislature in April 1948. It provides for certain benefits to industrial employees in case of sickness maternity and employment injury and to make provisions for certain other matters in relation thereto. It is an obvious social welfare legislation in tune with the Directive Principles of State Policy contained in Articles 41, 42 and 43 of the Constitution. It was a legislation which comes directly under entries 23 and 24 of List III of the Vlth Schedule of the constitution, which are "social security and social insurance; employment and unemployment", and "welfare of labour including conditions of work, provident funds, employers ' liability, workmen 's compensation, invalidity and old age pensions and maternity benefits". The Act extends to the whole of India and comes into force on such date or dates as the Central Government may appoint, different dates being permissible for different provisions of the , Act and other necessary provisions have been made in this Chapter. The Central Government is empowered to give directions or provide for such matters as may be necessary for the removal of any difficulty. The Chapter can be withdrawn from operation by the Central Govern ment after giving three months ' notice. "Appropriate Government" under section 2(1) means in respect of establishments under the control of the Central government or a Railway administration or a major port or a mine or oil field(i, the Central Govt. and in all other cases, the State Government. Thus it is clear that when extending the Act to different establishments, the relevant provisions (1) ; 6 SCR 1092 Government is given the power to constitute a Corporation for the administration of the scheme of Employees ' State Insurance. The course adopted by modern legislatures in dealing with welfare schemes has uniformly conformed to the same pattern. The legislature evolves a scheme of socioeconomic welfare, makes elaborate provisions in respect thereof and leaves it to the Government concerned to decide when, how and in what manner the scheme should be introduced. " Appropriate Govern ment" under Section 2(i) means "in respect of establishment under the Control of the central Government or a railway administration or any major port, or a company or oil (i) the Central Gov ernment, and in All other cases the State Govt.

The petitioners demand regularisation of their services claiming to be daily rated workmen for a long time in the mines of the Diamond Mining Project, Panna of the National Mineral Development Corporation Ltd. Their demands are of regularisation and "equal pay for equal work" on the ground that they were discharging the same duties as the regular workers. The management has throughout denied the petition ers ' claim and alleged that, in fact, the petitioners have been continued on rolls on humanitarian grounds for several years, even though there was no work for them; and as such, there is no question of regularising the petitioners and giving them the pay of regular workers when in fact they are not doing any work for a continuous long time. The High Court rejected the petitioners ' claim. Dismissing the petition, this Court, HELD: 1. The principle of regularisation of a daily rated workman and payment 'to him of the pay equal to that of a regular workman arises only when the daily rated worker is doing the same work as the normal workman and there being a vacancy available for him, he is not absorbed against it or not even paid the equal pay for the period during which the same worked from him. [610C] 2. The principles of regularisation are not the position. This principle has been reiterated at the hearing before this Court in view of the clear findings supported by evidence that there are no vacancies or work available in the establishment for absorption of the petitioners, and that for quite some time they have been continuing on rolls and paid in spite of there being no work available for them.

The appellants were the owners of a tea estate in Touzi No. 911 of Darjeeling Collectors. The suit out of which the appeal arises was brought by the appellants claiming title to and recovery of possession of a property known as the Azambad Tea Estate which comprised about 378 acres of land in Taizi No, 911. The contesting defendants were the Azamabad Tea Co., who also claim the entire property as transferees from the National Agency Co. Ltd. who too had been impleaded as defendants. The National Agency Company Ltd. claimed to have purchased the entire 16 as. interest in the property at a Court sale in pursuance of a decree obtained by them against Kazi Mohammed Ismail, the eldest son of Azam Ali. The plaintiffs ' claim was that by virtue of the renewal of the lease in 1928 in the name of Ismail and the entry of his name as sole lessee in the revenue records, the leasehold became his sole property. The trial court dismissed the suit but on appeal the High Court confirmed the decree of the trial court as regards the rest. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the lease granted in 1928 by the Government expired in 1928 and a renewed lease was granted in the names of Ismail alone; (2) the sale in execution of the mortgage decree obtained in pursuance thereof and of the court sale in execute of that decree, being confined at the most to 2 1/2 as share belonging to Mohd. Ismail, there was no element of fraud or collusion between the plaintiffs and the defendants; and (3) the suit was liable to be dismissed by reason of the provisions of 0. r. 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure. Held:(1) The High Court was right in holding that the sale deed exhibit 12(i) was executed on April 18, 1931, without adverting to the sale, a piece of conduct certainly not consistent with the sale being real and intended to pass title; (3 ) though in the plaint the necessary averments were made regarding their obtaining the share of Ashfaq through Pir Baksh, the claim under this head was not pressed before the trial Court; and the suit had been filed on 28th November, 1931 without adverting as to the nature and quantum of the title intended to be conferred on or obtained by Ismail and, second, the provisions Of 0. 9 applied equally to the plaintiff in the first suit and those claiming under him, the allegations regarding transmission of title to the plaintiffs in the present suit ceased to be material. (4) The sale deed was not a sham and nominal transaction and therefore inoperative to pass the title. (5) Though the plaintiffs did not agitate or press before the courts below any special right based on the purchase of Ashfaq 's share through P.ir B Laksh, they did not raise any specific ground touching their right to this share nor were any argument addressed to the High court on this point; and in view of these features, it was not possible to entertain or give effect to this claim, because several circumstances throw grave suspicion on the reality of the transaction and that in any event the claim could not be accepted without careful scrutiny of the facts. (6) The mere fact that the plaintiffs had filed an appeal to the Supreme Court from the total dismissal of the suit, did not preclude them from challenging the validity of the sale.

The appellant was tried by the Sessions Judge of Karimnagar in what used to be the State of Hyderabad (now part of the State) under section 302, read with sections 34 and 109 of the Indian Penal Code. The trial court convicted the appellant on the ground that there had been a rivalry between the two brothers which had led to arbitration proceedings. On appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that the omission had the effect of vitiating the entire proceedings ending in the trial of the accused, and that therefore, ipso facto a fresh trial became necessary irrespective of whether or not the accused had shown any prejudice. Held, that the failure to comply with section 360 of the Code of Criminal Procedure by the police officer to fully comply with the provisions of section 173(4) of the code of Criminal procedure was not mandatory but only directory and since no case of prejudice has been made out, the omission complained of in the instant case should not have a more farreaching effect than the omission to carry out the provisions Of section 162 or section 360. Abdul Rahman vs The King Emperor (A.I.R. , followed. In cases exclusively triable by a court of Session it is the duty of the magistrate while holding a preliminary inquiry to satisfy himself that the documents referred in section 173 had been furnished to the accused and if he found that the police Officer concerned had not carried out his duty in that behalf, the magistrate should see to it that is done. The omission complained Of in the present case should have a greater effect than that which was intended by the amending Act of 1955, as indicated above, and there was no scope for variations in their statements during police investigation and those before the court. Abdul Rahim vs The State of Punjab ([1955] 2 S.C.R., 869), referred to.

The respondent Municipality was a chemical works discharged effluent in very large quantities of calcium, sodium and other salts through Katcha Channels thereby corrupting potable water of the wells in the surrounding area so as to render it unfit for use and also prejudicially affecting the fertility of the soil in the adjoining areas by percolation. The respondent Municipality after having obtained the approval of the Government issued a notice under section 153A(1) of the Bombay District Municipal Act, 1901, as adapted and applied to the State of Saurashtra and as amended by Act XI of 1955 (hereinafter referred to as the Act), to show cause why it should not be directed to arrange within a period of nine months from the date of such direction for the discharge of the effluent through a covered pucca drainage and for pumping it over a distance of about 8 miles in the Ran ' area of Cutch near Kuda, as shown in the plan annexed to the notice. The appellant replied that the effluent was being discharged until 1943 through a Katcha channel running parallel to the railway line in the direction of Halvad. In 1944 it was felt that as the water of some of the well in the areas known as Harijanvas and Kolivas close to the vicinity of the channel might be affected another channel was constructed for discharging the effluent, which was at a considerable distance away from Kolivas and Harijanvas, still further away from the city which lies on the western side of the railway lines. The water of certain wells in these areas had been taken by the appellant and these tests had shown that the water was not in any way polluted by reason of the effluents being discharged through the existing channels, that all the papers and reports relating to the tests carried out periodically by the respondent were available for inspection by the Municipality and that they could be inspected by appointment. The Special Officer decided issues No. 4 in the affirmative and held that the question whether the discharge was mala fide, arbitrary, capricious and that the same had been issued without the respondent Municipality sufficiently applying its mind, the Special Officer was of the opinion that it wag out of the purview of the present enquiry. He accordingly directed the Municipality to arrange for the discharged of the drain through a specified pucca drainage, and for taking it over within three months from that date. The Municipality appealed to the High Court by special leave. Held: (i) The scheme under section 154A is to leave it to the subjective satisfaction of the Municipality as to the existence of a nuisance before a notice is issued to the party concerned. Under sub section (3), however, the appointment of a Special Officer is considered necessary because the dispute between the Municipality & the partyconcerned required investigation and report from the Officer. The order of the Special officer declining to go into the question as to whether a particular state of fact exists and on finding that it does exist to proceed further and do something more, then the fact in question is not collateral but a part of the very issue which the Municipality has to enquire into and that ceases to be justiciable. (ii) The satisfaction here is the subjective satis faction of the municipality and no other authority could question the action of the respondent in issuing the notice on the ground that it should have been so satisfied.

The appellant was found in possession of railway stores which were being used or intended to be used for the construction, operation or maintenance of a railway. The search which took place in the presence of witnesses was gone through. One Jaswant Singh described as an expert of Railway machinery parts and Foreman and Chief Inspector of N.E. Kotwali Chowk, Lucknow examined the goods said to be railway stores and kept in 11 bags and made a report to the effect that they were all railway stores being parts of a Railway engine. The usual formality of preparing a recovery memo and the sealing of goods in bags in the absence of witnesses, was gone by. One J.P.S. Appeal allowed. The appellant challenged his conviction under section 3 of the Railway Stores (Unlawful Possession) Act, 1955 on the ground that he had purchased the property in open market where goods of this kind were usually sold or that he has bought them from someone bona fide in the belief that the vendor had lawfully obtained the facts in this case. The Sessions Judge accepted his contention and convicted him under section 2 of the Act. On appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) In order to prove that the articles belong to any particular railway administration it has to establish that the goods conformed to the Railway Standards standards they held that they belonged to any of the railways in India. [189E] (2) The burden of proof in this respect may be discharged by leading evidence about the identifying marks on the goods or some, peculiarity of the goods not to be found in cases of non railway goods. Again the mere description of the articles as new would not fulfil the requirements of section 2(b).

The appellants had leased out the demised premises for 11 months from May 1, 1964 on payment of monthly rent of Rs. 18 which expired on March 31, 1965. The respondent landlord terminated the lease by a notice under section 106 of Transfer of Property Act but she remained in possession and enjoyment of the shop carrying on small kirana business. She died in September 1966. The demised premises were governed by the Rajasthan Premises (Control of Rent and Eviction) Act, 1950 for short the 'Act '). Section 13(1) thereof postulates that "notwithstanding anything contained in any law or contract no court shall pass any decree or make any order in favour of the landlord whether in execution of a decree or otherwise evicting the tenant so long as he is ready and willing to pay rent thereof to the full extent allowable by the Act" unless the landlord proves to the satisfaction of the Court any one of the grounds enumerated in clauses 'a ' to 'k ' thereof. The action for ejectment was initiated by the respondent on the premise that on the death of the tenant, the appellants have no right to continue in occupation of the demised shop. The Trial Court dismissed the suit on the ground that Smt. Anandi paid and the respondent accepted the rent after determination of the lease. So she was a tenant holding over. During the pendency of the appeal, the Act was amended through Rajasthan Premes (Control) Act 26 of 1975 which was replaced by Act 14 of 1976. The definition of 'Tenant ' in section 3(vii)(b) of the Act is amended by section 3 (ii) of Amendment Act introducing to Section 3 Clause (vii), thus: "tenant" means a person by whom or on whose account or behalf rent is, or but for a contract express or implied would be payable for any premises to his landlord including the person who is continuing in its possession after the termi nation of his tenancy otherwise than by a decree for evic tion passed under the provisions of this Act; and 10 (b) In the event of death of a person as is referred to in sub clause (a), his surviving spouse, son, daughter and other heir in accordance with the personal law as applica ble to him, who had been, in the case of premises leased out for commercial or business purposes, ordinarily has been carrying on business with him/her in such premises as member of his family upto his death. The appellants contended that the lease hold right is an heritable estate and on death of her tenant in September, 1966, the tenancy rights held by Smt. A. Anand i was a personal right to the tenant. The respondents contended that during her life time she had not carried on the business with her till date of her death. They also did not carry on the businesses with her until date of his death and that the tenancy came to a terminus with its determination by issuance of notice under Section 106 of the Transfer of property Act. The trial court dismissed the suits on the grounds that Smt Anandi was the tenant holding 7.

The appellant Board maintains a Contributory Provident Fund where the contribution is on the basis of basic wage, the Board and the employees contributing equally. The workmen claimed that all workmen of the Board should have the same and similar benefits and that therefore there should be no distinction between the Board 's Contributory Provident fund scheme and the scheme under the Employees Provident Fund Act. The Industrial Tribunal accepted this contention and ordered that the contribution should be 6.25 per cent but not on the basic wages but on the total wages. On appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellant Board that the State Government is the financier of the Electricity Board which charges interest now at the rate of 6.26 per cent as against the previous 4% per annum and that the services of the workmen of Board are liable to be transferred from one establishment to another both which may not he covered by the same scheme under Act and therefore it will bring about serious injustice if they are deprived of their benefits under the Act, and such anomalies will be removed by making the benefits under both the schemes similar. HELD: The Tribunal had dealt with the matter in a perfunctory way. It should be directed to dispose of the matter afresh in the light of the observations made in this judgment. [44E] Gramophone Co. vs Its Workmen, ; and Gramophonone Co., vs Its Workers, [1964] II L. J. 131, referred to. The Tribunal was not right in holding that the interest should No. be taken into account in working out the profits is not borne out by the provisions of the statute. Indeed the Tribunal did not look into the Act at all. Whether in view of the statutory obligations laid on the Board under various sections just now referred to in analysing the capacity of the board to bear any additional burden in the matter of provident fund or other amenities the same considerations that applied in the case of private commercial concerns could be applied is a rather difficult question. [45F G] Gramphone Co operative Society vs Its workmen, ; , followed.

The respondent wife filed an application before the Magistrate under section 125 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973 for grant of maintenance by the appellant on the ground that her husband was guilty of wilful neglect and was unable to fulfil his primary responsibility of discharging his marital obligations. The Magistrate rejected the application holding that the husband having been found to be impotent, this should be a just ground for the wife to refuse to live with the husband and hence she was entitled to the grant of Maintenance. The respondent filed an appeal before the High Court which differed from the view taken by the Magistrate and held that the appellant was not entitled to maintenance if he refused to live alongwith her husband merely because her husband had been impotently impotant. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that it is now well settled by a long course of decisions of various High Courts that impotency is no good ground or reason for the husband to refuse live with her husband and, therefore, the wife is not entitled under section 488 of the Criminal Procedure Code. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The decision in Velayudhan vs Sukmari a Single Judge of the High Courts was purely obiter. It would appear that there was a clear finding cf fact by the Magis trate which had been accepted by the High court, that the wife failed to prove by convincing evidence that her father was impotable and unable to discharge his marital obligation, that she should suffer that predicament without demur and be satisfied with a grab to bite and some rags to clothe her and a roof over her head. [707C] 1.2 In view of this finding of fact, the question of law posed and decided by the learned Judge did not fall for decision at all because if the wife fails to prove that her deceased husband was impecotent and unable, to discharge her marital obligations, how could he fulfil the main object of marriage, more particularly under the Mahomedan Law where marriage is a sacrosanct contract and not a purely religious ceremony as in the case of Hindu law. [700D] 1:3 In the instant case, there was no dispute and the case will have to be decided on the point of law that arises on the contentions raised by the parties before the courts below as also in this Court. Both the High courts and the Metropolitan Magistrate clearly found that the appel lant was impetent and was, therefore unable to discharging his matrimonial obligations.

The suit property described in two parts of the schedule to the plaint was a large extent of vacant land which was referred to in these proceedings as Parade Ground. The second part of the property covered by Survey Nos. 162, 163, 164 and 165 on which structures of old Lancer 's lines were standing and certain evacuees were Occupying at the time of the suit. This second part was described as Lancers quarters and also sometimes as Rasala Lines. The plaintiffs ' case was that by Resolution No. 37 dated 19th January, 1984 published in the Bhavnagar Darbar Gazette dated 24th January 1948: "The Bhavnagar State bestowed the rights of the State of Bhavnagar to effect sales of land in the Municipal area of Bhavnager and by a further order No. 77 of dated 29th February, 1948 the State vested the said lands except four plots of land mentioned therein in the survey numbers referred to above in the said proceedings as parade Ground. " The plaintiffs case was: (i) By Resolution No 37 dated January,1984 published in Bhavnagar Gazette dated 25th January. 1948, the entire suit lands mentioned in part 2 of the Schedule to the Plaint were vested in the Defence Ministry and (ii) by virtue of these orders the entire suits lands mentioned therein had: "vested in and belongs to the plaintiff who entered into and remained in possession thereof till recently." And that subsequent to the erstwhile State of Saurashtra merging in the United States of Kathiawar which was subse quently known as the State Government of Saurashtra, the Government of India recognised the aforesaid Resolutions dated 19.1.1984 and 29th Febru ary 1948. The further case of the plaintiff was that By Resolution Nos. 37 and 165 dated 19nd January, 1948, vested in and belonged to the plaintiffs who entered on and remained In possession thereof until recently. And that consequent upon the Bombay Merged States (Laws) Act, 1950, the State vest ed the said land except four items of land covered by the Survey numbers referred t o in part 1 of the schedules to the suit property. The defendants also denied that they were trespassers or liable to pay damages and rent in respect of the said suit property and claimed damages for wrongful occupation in respect thereof. The Trial Court held that the plaintiff had proved its title to the land and that they had proved their title to it and that the plaintiffs were in possession in the suit land till 7th July, 1952 when physical posses sion was handed over by the military engineers of the Government to the State Public Works Department of the state of Saurashtra. However, on the ground that in respect off par tial lands which were in occupation of the erstwhile state military had been taken over and remained under the control of the Defence Minister of India to the Government, the Board of Officers consisting of six members including Executive Engineer, Public Works Depart ment as representative of the Union of India was constituted and the buildings known as infantry lines and Lan cercer ' 's Lines were taken over on 7th June, 195 1 by the Government. The High Court also held that since the plaintiff has not shown possession of the building within 12 years prior to 3rd March, 1964 when the suit was filed, the suit is liable to be dismissed as barred by limitation, and that therefore it was not necessary either to deal with the argument of the defendants that the vesting that was contem plated in the Resolution 37 dated19th January was not intended to be vesting in its full amplitude but was meant only to appoint the Municipality as agent of the Govern ment.

The appellant was a class III servant employed as a metal examiner in the Railway Carriage Workshops at Ajmer. He was charged under section 161 Indian Penal Code with having accepted from one Nanak Singh currency notes of the value of Rs. 150 by dishonest representation that he could secure a job for the said Kallu. The Special judge convicted him of the offence under section 5(1)(d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 and sentenced him to suffer rigorous imprisonment for six months and one year respectively in regard to the same, both the sentences to run concurrently. In appeal by certificate the appellant contended that he was an "officer" within the meaning of section 21(9), Indian Penal code and therefore a public servant be fell within the definition of a public Servant contained in section 2 of the Act. Held, that the appellant was an officer within the expression of section 2(1) (d) Of the Prevention Of Corruption Act and being such public servant he fell within section 21 of the Indian Penal. Ram Krishan vs Delhi State, A.I.R. 1918 Cal. 918, distinguished. The question for consideration before the learned judges of the Lahore High Court was whether a quarter Master 's clerk as such was a public service or pay of the Government and was therefore an "office" within section 2 Of the Act II of 1947. Ram Krishna vs Delhi, A I. R. 1918 Mad. 921, distinguished and applied. The appellant was not an officer but a mere contractor bound by his engagement but not by the terms of his office or employment to pay a certain proportion to the Government. There was no delegation to him of any authority for coercion or interference nor was he an assistant appointed to help any one who was vested with such authority. The duties which he performed were contractual duties owed to him by the Government, and were therefore, "an officer" within that meaning of the section.

The respondent along with one Gora Lal and Sat Pal, had been granted a liquor vending licence for the year 1968 69. The licences paid a sum of Rs. 86,450 leaving the balance unpaid in spite of repeated reminders. Ultimately recovery proceedings under the said Act were started by the department and the Collector. Excise and Taxation Department, Patiala issued a proclamation prohibiting the transfer or creation of a charge by the respondent of his half share in an immovable property consisting of a plot of land bearing Khewat No. 374, Khatuni NO. 511. Khasra No. 39710 19 situate in village Ghagga with a building constructed thereon. The auction in respect of the said share of the respondent in the said property was notified for June 14, 1977. Just a day prior to the holding of the auction sale the Respondent filed a suit in the Court of Sub Judge, 1st Class, Patiala C, being Suit No. 472/13 6 77 against the State of Punjab and the collector cum Deputy Excise andTaxation Commissioner, Patiala Division, for a permanent injunction restraining the State and the Collec tor from auctioning his said half share. The contention of the Respondent was that a part of the building standing on the said plot of Land was being used by him for his residence and he had no other residential house and therefore his half portion was exempt from attachment under clause (ccc) of the proviso to sub section (1) of Section 60 of the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908. The Trial Court upheld both these contentions and dismissed the suit with costs. The Respondent then filed a second appeal before the District Judge, Patiala, being Civil Appeal No. 554 of 5.9.79. The Additional District Judge dismissed it with costs but allowed the second appeal holding that the portion of the property used for residence was exempt under clause(ccc)(c) and that the said portion in which the liquor shop was situated was liable to be attached, and accordingly issued a permanent order restraining the state and Collector from auction ing his said one half share, while that portion in that portion was in which it was being use by him was for his own residence and that he had not any other residential building and therefore, his halfshare was exempt. The Respondents then filed an appeal to the District judge, Patiala being Civil Appeals No. 556 of 5 979.79 and the Additional District judge dismissed it. The High Court allowed the Second Appeal holding that since the conclusion arrived at by the trial court on facts was per verse whereas the appellate court applied totally a wrong law in deciding the appeal, the second appeals were not maintainable. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal and setting aside the Judgment and decree of the High Court, this Court, HELD: 1. The provisions of Section 59 of the Civil Procedure Code do not apply to an attachment and sale under any of her statute made expressly applicable thereto. So far as the said section is concerned it contains a complete code providing for the modes and machinery for recovery of arrears of revenue. The attachment in a question was levied under the provisions of the Act and the sale which was notified was also under the provi sions of the aforesaid Act. [847C] 2.1 In the instant case, the properties, if my, which are exempt from attached and sale in revenue recovery proceedings, under the Act would be only such properties as are so exempted by the said act. There is no provision in the Act corresponding to cl.

The respondent was the owner of certain agricultural land. The lands were acquired by the Government under the Land Acquisition Act, 1894 and the compensation was paid to him in April, 1963 and by two separate awards both made on January 31, 1963 the Special Deputy Collector awarded a total compensation of Rs. 4,29,360. This compensation was received in April '955 by the heirs of Rashid, who were his widow Mrs. Freny Chenai and son Shapoor Rashid Chenai on whom the estate of Rashid devolved in equal shares. On the death of Rashid on November 4, 1963, Mrs.Freny chenai (the appellant in C.A. No. In making this assessment also the respondent as well as the High Court had proceeded on the wrong assumption that the acquired lands formed part of the estate and passed on his death for, it was on such basis that the High 's decision upholding the issuance of such notice on the erroneous basis was liable to be set aside. The Revenue preferred appeals before this Court contending: (i) that the accountable person had only a claim lo get an extra compensation which was an inchoate right which could not be called 'property ' and whether that claim amounted to a right to property capable of sale in open market was a highly debatable question and a mistake which had to be discovered after lengthy discussion and debate could not he said to be a mistake apparent on the record, (ii) that land acquisition proceedings and land references in Civil Court not being part of assessment record a mistake discovered by reference to such other record was not a mistake detected from the record of the case and (iii) that even assuming that any asset or property chargeable to estate duty had escaped assessment the notice was illegal and without jurisdiction because such escapement was not due to any omission or failure on the part of accountable person to disclose fully and truly material facts necessary for making the assessment. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The very issuance of the notice under section 59(a) which was done on a basis clearly unsustainable in law is liable to he quashed on this ground. [330G] 2.1 In the instant case since the wards made by the Special Dy Collector were not accepted by the representatives of the deceased and Land References were sought by them and the same were pending in Civil court at the relevant date (being the date of ShapUn 's death) the notice issued under section59(a), would have been valid if the same had been issued on the basis that such right to compensation had been undervalued on the earlier occasion and required to be properly valued as on 328 the date when the death, but what we find is that the said notice was issued by the respondent on the correct assumption that it had been given on the incorrect assumption that there had been escapement of assessment to duty because the lands in the original assessment had been valued at an enhanced figure in the probate proceedings and as such the same bad escaped assessment to tax.

The appellant filed his nomination papers in July 1986 and he was elected on 18.8.1986 as one of the Directors of the Bank from the Brehmapuri Agricultral Sales and Purchase Society. His election was not called in question according to the procedure prescribed by the Maharashtra Cooperative Societies Act, 1960. On 8.1.1987, the District Deputy Registrar issued a notice to the appellant under section 78(1) of the Act to show cause within 15 days as to why he should not be removed from the Board of Directors as per the provisions of section 73FF and directed him to remain present on 2.2.1987 at 11 A.M. in the Deputy Director 's office. The notice stated that the appellant had borrowed a loan of Rs. 10,000 (Rs. 7,000) from the Bank and he kept the loan constant in arrears till 21.10.1986, and being elected as Director of the bank on 18 8.12.1987.
