Till then he was working as the Director of respondent Bank. The appellant 's appeal against that order was dismissed by the Divisional Joint Registrar of the Cooperative Societies, Nagpur on 15.2 1988 holding that section 73F(1)(b) of Maharashtra State Co operative Societies Act 1960 came into force on 12.5.1986 and the appellant could be treated as a defaulter under that section; and the mere making of payment on 21. 10.86 did not mean that the disqualification on account of his being defaulter which continued from 18. 8.1986 to 21.11. 1986 was extinguished and hence the appellant was not at all eligible to contest the election. The order of the Assistant Registrar dated 7.12 1987 was served on the appellant on 8. 12.87. The Assistant Registrar, Cooperative Societies by his order dated 7th December 1987 removed the appellant from the Committee of Directors holding that appellant was defaulter on 31.1 .86 and he became defaulter under the provisions Of section 73 F(1). The order was served upon the appellant by the appellant after removing him from the committee of Directors of respondent bank holding that he was defaulter under section 73 E(2) of that Act. The appeal against this order was also dismissed on 30.8 .89 holding that the dues calculated on 31st January, 1986 became recurring dues every following day and on 12th May, 1986 when section 73FA came into operation the outstanding dues continued even on 18th August, 1986, when the appellant contested the election; and that the question of giving retrospective effect to the section did not arise because the appellant ' was a defaulter when he contested the Election and though he paid all the debts on 21st October, 1986 yet he could not be "absolved of the disqualification. The Divisional Joint Commissioner dismissed the appeal holding that since the dues computed on 31th January,86 became recurring due every following days and on December 12, 1987 when section 74F(I) came into existence the outstanding amount continued even after 18th July, 1986 he could be deemed as a " defaulter" under that Section; and since the appellant having repaid the entire loan before the impugned notice under section78(1), he was not a defaulter in presenti on the date of the notice and the provisions thereof were not attracted. The revision petition filed by the Appellant against this Order was dismissed on 10th February, 1988 holding inter alia that section 74FF became applicable from 6.81986 as per Government Notification issued on 18 4.4.86 and that as he had accepted that he paid the dues on 21 10.6.86 when he was declared elected as Directors he was still defaulter under Section 73 F (1).

The respondent was in the service of the State as Supply Inspector and he retired from service on attaining the age of superannuation on September 1, 1977. After his retirement the respondent was served with a charge sheet on October 16, 1978 containing allegations of misconduct and negligence against him for the period he was in service. Enquiry was held and the respondent 's explanation was found to have been established while charge No. 2 was partially proved. In his report to the State Government the Collector of Kolhapur held that the respondent had already retired from Service on September l, 1977 and reduced the amount of pension payable to him by 50 per cent permanently under Rule 188 of the Bombay Civil Services Rules. The respondent challenged the validity of the Government 's order by means of a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court. A Division Bench allowed the writ petition and quashed the State 's orders dated December 4, 1982 on the ground that the State had no authority in law to take any disciplinary proceedings against the respondent as he had already been retired from serv ice. Placing reliance on a decision of this Court in B.J. Shelet vs State of Gujarat & Ors., [1987] 2 SCC 179 and State of Uttar Pradesh vs Brahm Datt Sharma & Anr., [ 1987] 2 SCR 179, it was held that merely because a Government servant retired from the service on reaching the age Of superannuation he could not escape the liability for misconduct and fault and negligence or financial irregularities which he may have committed during the period of his service and the Government was entitled to withhold or reduce the pension granted to a Government Servant. The State Government 'S power to reduce or withhold pension by taking proceedings against a Government employee even after his retirement is expressly preserved by the aforesaid Rules. 35 Allowing the appeal partly, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Rule 189 contemplates withholding or withdrawing of a pension or any part of it if the pensioner be convicted of serious crime or be found to having been guilty of grave misconduct while he was In service or after the completion of his Service. Grant of pension and its continuance to a government servant depend upon the good conduct of the Govern ment servant. Rendering satisfactory service maintaining good conduct is a necessary condition for the grant and continuance of pension. Rule 189 expressly confers power on the Government to withhold, or withdraw any part thereof if the pensioners be convicted offi cute of serious crimes or be find to have committed grave misconduct whilst he was not in service or After the completion or his service. Granting of pension & its continuance by 50% would seriously affect his living. Accordingly, it is not a case where the purpose of the enquiry was not to inflict any punishment; instead the proceedings were initiated for determining the respondent "s pension. The proceedings were taken in accordance with Rules 188 and 189 of the Rules. It appears that the attention of the High court was not drawn to these Rules.

The appellants were the tenants of a shop in which they had applied for permission to the District Magistrate under section 3(1) of the U.P. (Temporary) Control of Rent and Eviction Act, 1947, for carrying on their own business in the shop. The application was refused by him whereupon they moved the Commissioner in his revisions jurisdiction under section 33(3) of that Act. The respondents resisted the claim made by the appellants on several grounds. They urged that the suit was bad for non joinder of necessary parties; that the permission to sue granted to the appellants by the Commissioner was not valid in law and so, he came to the conclusion that the appellants ' suit was incompetent. On appeal the District Judge upheld the respondents ' contention that the Commissioner had given them permission to file the suit. The High Court upheld the contention of the appellants that the power conferred on the State Government under section 7 F of the Act is very wide and in other words, whenever it is brought to the notice of the State Govt., either by a party aggrieved by the order passed by the District Magis trate, their decision is final and cannot be questioned in a civil court. The appellants then applied for a certificate from the High Court and it was granted with the said certificate that this appeal has come up before this Court. On behalf of the respondents it was contended that the jurisdiction conferred on Commissioner under section 2(4) read with section 16 of the , is exactly similar to the jurisdiction imposed on the High Courts under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure; and that the words of section 3 (4) are clear and unambiguous, they indicate that the jurisdic tion of the civil courts can be excluded by a statutory provision which expressly provides for it, or which necessarily and inevitably leads to that inference. In other words the jurisdiction of the Civil Courts can be exclusion by the Legislature by special Acts which deal with special subject matters; but the exclusion of the jurisdiction Of the civil court must be made by a statute which expressly provide for it. or which naturally and inevitably lead to that conclusion. [559 C] The power conferred under section 4 F is very wider than that of the Commissioner only to cases where irregularity or illegality bad been committed by the district Magistrate in granting or refusing, to grant permission. It is not easy to conceive of a limitation as to jurisdiction being relevant in section 3 of the .

The President of India, who was alleged to have assaulted her, the Chairman, Punjab Public Service Commission, in exercise of the power conferred by Article 317(1) of the Constitution, referred for consideration of this Court under Article 317 (1) and issued notice of the reference to five members of the Commission including the Member Smt. Santosh Chowdhary and Shri Gopal Krishan Saini who was stated to have attacked her. All of them filed their affidavits in these proceedings. Certain other persons who claim to have knowledge of the incident or of its alleged background had also filed their affidavit, were: Dr. An affidavit has also been filed by Shri Saini 's wife, the purport of which is that Shri Saini has been involved in this false incident since the Chief Minister of Punjab, Shri Darbara Singh was not happy with his appointment as a Member of the Punjab Public Services Commission. It is on the basis of this material that the President made the Reference. The material is of a kind and nature enough to justify the President 's opinion that a prima facie case exists for an inquiry and report by this Court. The question which then arises before this Court was whether Shri Saini, Member of Punjab Public service Commission ought, on the ground of misbehaviour, to be removed from his office of the Member of Commission. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Article 317 provides that, subject to the provisions of clause (3), the Chairman or any other member of a Public Service Com mission can only be removed by the order of the President on the grounds of misbehaviour after the Supreme Court has on inquiry held in accordance with the procedure prescribed in that behalf under Article 145. [646C] 2. The power of the president to make a reference to this Court is not subject to any condition precedent that he must first have the facts examined by some other body or authority. That Article provides that the Chairman may summon such witnesses as it considers necessary. This provision confers the requisite power on this Court to summon and examine witnesses, but nothing contained therein can be read to mean that after deciding which witnesses should be summoned and examined, evidence must be recorded by this court itself. [643D E] 3. The inquiry contemplated by the Article is into the facts themselves and facts also so as to enable this Court, to pronounce upon the question whether the allegations made against the Chairman/ member are proved at all. The purpose of article 317( 1) is to ensure independence of members of Public Service Commissions and to give them protection in the matter of their tenure. [651C] 4. Article 145 provides that an inquiry has to be held by this Supreme Court in accordance With the procedure laid down in that Article, the Supreme court may summon and examined witnesses, and record their evidence. A procedural issue which was debated before us is whether it should permit the parties to cross examine persons who have filed their statements. Considering the nature and gravity of the matter referred to, the importance of this court will be served by expending our own time in recording the evidence of various witnesses except for the advantage of seeing and hearing the witnesses. [631G H] 5. The entire evidence, admissible and relevant shall have to be taken into account for the purpose of deciding whether the allegation against Shri Saini can be held to be proved. [641C D] 6. It will not be conducive to justice to decide the Reference on a consideration of the affidavits only. [661D] 7. The Supreme Court cannot, through the medium of a Reference, be called upon to discharge functions which ordinarily fall within the jurisdiction of a trial court, civil or criminal. The danger of such a procedure is said to be that if this Court hold that the incident is proved, Shri Saini will automatically be held guilty by a criminal court of the charge of assault and he will have to suffer a decree for damages in a civil court.

The appellants plaintiffs instituted a suit under section 62(2) of the Orissa Religious Endowment Act, 1939 (Act 4 of 1939) (the Act) against the respondent temple for setting aside the order dated 4 8 1950 of the respondent defendant by which the temple of the appellants was declared to be a public temple and a trust and the endowment was held to be of a public nature and, therefore, was to be governed by the Act. The Subordinate Judge decreed the suit holding that the deity installed therein being a public endowment fell within the four corners of the Act and the respondent was fully entitled to pass orders for its management. The respondent defendant preferred an appeal in the High Court against the decision of the Subordinate Judge which was heard by the Division Bench referred to above. The High Court reversed the decision and held that the temple and the deity install therein being private endowment fell outside the four boundaries of the statute and the Respondent was fully justified to pass order for its proper management. Hence this appeal by certificate. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. Under the Hindu law what is a public trust is only a form of Charitable Trust. [830C] 1.2. The essential distinction between a private and a public charitable endowment is that whereas in the former the beneficiaries are specified individuals, in the latter they are the general public or class of unascertained people. This being the essential distinction both between a Private and a private trust is that while in the later the beneficiaries were specified individuals the general Public or a section of the same and not a determinate body of individuals as a result of which the remedies for enforcement of charitable trust are somewhat different from those which can be availed of by beneficiaries in a private Trust. The members of the public who worship as a matter of right then the real purpose is to confer benefit on God. [861D E] 1:3. In the former, the beneficiaries in the public trust are thegeneral public or a class thereof. This distinction between the nature of a Public or private endowment is generally called Waqf allal Aulad where the ultimate benefit is reserved to God but the property vests in the beneficiaries and the income from the property is used for the maintenance and support of the family of the founders and their descendants. [862C] 2:1. The object which can he gathered from this document is placed beyond doubt by a later document Ext. 1 which was executed on 17 11 1932 and is in the nature, of a settlement Deed, the relevant portions of which may be quoted thus: "Our forefathers for the good of our family by making the family deity Sri Radhakanta Deb Thakur, erecting a 836 temple befitting.

The appellant Bank entered into certain contracts and executed an irrevocable power of attorney in favour of the appellant on July 13, 1946. The power of Attorney recited: "Whereas we are working as contractors to the Government in its various departments and have entered into various contracts and will in future enter into other contracts and whereas an agreement dated 13 7 1946 has been made between us and the Bharat Bank Ltd., in pursuance of which the attorneys had agreed to finance contracts and to advance moneys to Malhotra against his bills for supplies under the contracts. " The appellant Bank, formerly known as the Bharat bank Ltd., agreed to Finance the contracts and advanced monies to Malhotra on behalf of the Government Departments. On July 19, 1948, the appellant made out a bill on the military authorities for Rs. 49,633/8/7 then due to him in respect of his supplies under contracts during 1945 46 and handed over the bill to the appeLlant for collection. The appellant bank sent the bill for the monies then due under the bill. Before the appellant received the payment, the amount due under it was attached by Takhatmal in execution of a money decree obtained by him against Malhotra. The appel lant 's objections were dismissed. On December 12, 1952, the appelLlant filed a suit in the court of the 1st Additional District Judge, Jabalpur against Malhotra and Takhat Mal asking for a declaration that the appellant was an assignee of the biLl and that Takhat had no right to attach it. The trial Court held that the appe lant was the assignee of that bill and decreed the suit. On appeal by the plaintiff, the High Court allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit on the ground that there was no equitable assignment. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) A document amounts to an equitable assignment of future debts, see Tailby vs vs Official Receiver, ; , Loonkaran Sethiya vs State Bank of Jaipur, [1955] 2 S.C.R. 971, referred to. (ii) The law on the subject admits of no doubt. In Palmer vs Carey, A.I.R., 777, it is necessary to bear in mind that the relationship of the two parties, both, Malhotra and the Bank was that of borrower and lender and that the document was brought into existence in connection with a proposed transaction of financing of Malhotra 's contracts. [705 E F] Palmerv carey, ; Loonkarkaran Sethiyya vs state Bank of Rajasthan, A I. R.

The assessee was the manager of a Tea Estate under the managing agency of M/s. Gillanders Arbuthnot & Co. Ltd. The said company had a Provident Fund scheme for its employees. But that provident fund was not a recognised one. The Income tax Officer assessed this amount as the assessee 's income from other sources. That order was confirmed in appeal by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. But on further appeal to the Tribunal, the tribunal came to the conclusion that the receipt in question being profits 'in lieu of salary ', the same was his salary as defined in section 17 of the Income tax Act, 1961 (to be hereinafter referred to as the Act). The High Court answered that question in the negative and in favour of the assessee. Dismissing the appeal by certificate, HELD: 1. The meaning of section 17(3)(ii) is plain and unambiguous. Hence there is no need to call into aid any of the rules of construction as was sought to be done by the High Court. [440E] 2.1 In view of section 16(1), all receipts of profits in lieu of pay have to be considered as salary. But then the question is what is meant by "profits in lieu ' of salary". [439C D] 2:2 The receipt of Rs. 27,948/ by the assessee in the relevant accounting year cannot be considered 'as salary though undoubtedly that is an income. [414E F] 2 :3 In view Of section 17 (1) (iv), all receipt of profits ' in lieu thereof have to he considered as "income from other source" and brought to tax under section 56.

The Bihar Legislature passed the Bihar Act, 1950, which was later amended by the Bihar and Orissa Acts, 1950. The Bihar Act provided for the preservation and improvement of certain animals in the State of Bihar. Section 1(3) of the Act provided that section shall come into force on such date as the State Government may, by notification appoint and that different dates may be appointed for different provisions and for different areas. It was contended on behalf of the petitioners that (1) the impugned Acts were violative of article 19(1)(g) of 'the Constitution inasmuch as they infringed their fundamental rights under article 19 (1)(f) of India, (2) the Act was not saved by cl. (6) of article 31; and (3) the provisions of section 1(4) of Bihar Act were violative Of articles 14 and 19(5) of that Act. Held: (i) The impugned Acts did not contravene article 19 of the Constitution inasmuch it imposed a total ban on the slaughter of all animals belonging to the species of bovine cattle which included buffaloes (male or female adults or calves) but it was still possible for the Legislature to enact a law imposing such a blanket ban. The restrictions imposed by section 1 (4) were reasonable and valid and was in consonance with the directive principles laid down in article 48 of the Constitu tion. The impugned Act was constitutionally valid in so far as it prohibited the slaughter Of cows of all ages and calves of buffaloes, male and female, but that it was not possible for them to apply the doctrine of severability and uphold the ban on slaughter of she buffaloes, breeding bulls and working bullocks (cattle and buffalo) without prescribing any test or requirement as to their age or usefulness. The provisions of sections 1(5), 2(6) and 2(7) of Act were not violative of articles 14, 19(2)(f), 31 and 31 of the constitution inasmuch as it imposed an unreasonable restriction on the fundamental right guaranteed by article 19. The ban was reasonable but was not reasonable restrictions imposed in the interest of the general public. The imposition of a total prohibition of the rights of the citizens of India under article 21 was not valid. The State of Bombay vs R. M. Sheshadri, ; , followed. (ii)The impugned Acts infringed articles 19(i)(g), 31, 32 and 31 Of the Constitution as they prohibit the slaughter or of buffaloes without prescribing a test or pro ceeding any requirement as regards their age and usefulness, it offended article 14. The Act was therefore constitutionally valid and did not violate article 19 Of the constitution.

The respondent company was a 'workman ' within the meaning of the Central Provinces and Berar Industrial Disputes Settlement Act, 1947. The dispute between the parties related to the question whether the Standing Orders applied to the respondent. Held, that the Standing Order did not apply to the appellant as he was an employee within the terms of Standing Order No. 16. The essential content of the definition of 'employee ' is employment in the Office, Mains Department, eta., of the Company either at Nagpur or at Wardha, and that of a workman the necessary declaration by the company which would entitle him to a ticket under standing order No. 18. Held further, that Standing Order no. 16 was applicable to the case as it applied to employees to Whom tickets had been issued, the respondent who had no ticket was outside their purview, and the result was that the company had committed a breach of the statutory provision in section 30 of the local Act in the sense that no standing Orders had been made in respect of the respondent and employees like him to whom tickets had not been issued. Held also, that there could be no Standing Order in respect Of his conditions of service. The Standing Orders did make a distinction between 'employees ' and ` workmen ' and there may also be employees who have no tickets. Standing Order 18 was applicable only to those employees only to whom ticket had been issue; but such inclusion was not an essential characteristic of an employee.

The appellant company was an undertaking owned, controlled and managed by a Government Company. The workmen claimed bonus at the minimum rate prescribed under the Payment of Bonus Act, 1965 in respect of the year 1965 631 1966 on the plea that this Alloy Steel Project was a separate establishment in respect Of which separate balance sheets and profit and loss accounts were maintained, so that no bonus was payable until either this Project itself earned profits or from the sixth accounting year following the year 1964 65 when this Project went into production. The dispute between the work men and the Company could not be resolved amicably and consequently a reference was made under the which came up before the Ninth Industrial Tribunal, West Bengal. The Tribunal held that alloy Steel project could not he treated as a separate Establishment because under the Act a company is itself an establishment so that all units of a Company like Hindustan Steel Ltd. will constitute one establishment. Since this Project had not been earning any profits the Tribunal directed payment of bonus at 4 per cent of wages prescribed by the Act. The appellant contended before this Court that even the establishment employing less than 20 persons would be a part of the parent establishment consisting of the factory and that the word "establishment" has been used in the Act to indicate a "Company" as called in common parlance. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The Tribunal went entirely wrong in holding that simply because alloy steel Project is owned, managed controlled and run by Hindustan Steel Company Ltd., it has to be treated as one part of Hindustan Steel Limited. [631 E] (2) The proviso to section 3 will apply to establishments consisting of different departments, undertakings or branches which are owned, regulated or managed by the Government company or a corporation. Obviously, the word 'establishment" is intended to indicate something different from a company as defined in the . This is further clarified by the provisions of sub section (3) of section 1 which lays down the applicability of the Act.[632 B] (3)(a) The provisions of section 16(1) are to apply even to new departments, Undertakings or branches set up by existing establishments. Consequently, even if alloy iron Steel Project is treated as an establishment newly set up for purposes of section16(1), the exemption claimed would be fully justified.

The appellant State of Haryana issued a notification under section 3 of the , levying cess on water consumed by persons carrying on certain industries and by the local authorities with a view to augment the resources of the Central Board and the State Boards constituted for the prevention and control of water pollution. The Cess Act was enacted by Parliament under Article 252 of the Constitution with a avowed object to control the pollution of rivers and streams which has assumed considerable importance and urgency in recent years as a result of increasing industrialisation and urbanation, the Act is intended to ensure that the domestic and industrial affluence are not allowed to be discharged into water coars without adequate treatment. This Act was later amended by the Central Act 36 of 1977 with a further provision for levy of cess on electricity consumed by person carrying on the industries specified in the Schedule. The cess levied under the Cess Act is on the person carrying out any specified industry and every local authority and is calculated on the basis of water consumed, by such person or local authority as the case may be for any of the purposes specified in column I of Schedule II to the Act, at such rate not exceeding the rates specified in Schedule I. The appellant challenged the levy before the High Court a writ petition which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that sugar manufacturing industry would come within Entry 15 as "processing vegetable products" and that it could not be given the meaning of vegetables which are kept on the dining tables for dinner purposes, and it had a wider amplitude. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The word "vegetable" has been defined in many ways. In the World Book it is defined as follows: "In the usual sense, the word vegetable is applied to those plants whose leaves, stalks, roots or tubers are used for food, such as lettuce, asparagus, cabbage, turnipan, bean, dandelion etc., also the edible part of such a plant as prepared for market or the table. Vegetables and fruits are some times loosely distinguished by the use of cooking the former or the use by man while the latter may be eaten raw; but the distinc tion often fails, as in the case of quinces, barberries, and other fruit, and lettu, celery, and others. 23, "veetgetable ' is defined to mean: "a general term used as an adjective in refer ring to any kind of plant life or plant product, viz. "vetgetable matter". [529C E] 2. The expression "who processes any goods" in the Bombay Sales Tax was held to refer to the subjecting of any goods to a treatment or process. It is refining, development, preparation or converting of material especially that in a raw state into marketable form. It would be interesting to note that this Act contains a Schedule of the agricultural or processed food products which are to be governed by the Act which reads as follows; " SCHEDULE I (See section 2(i)) 1. Fruits, vegetables and their products. Poultry and poultry products. Dairy products. Confectionary biscuits and bakery products. Honey jaggery and sugar products. Cocoa and its products, chocolates of all kinds.

The respondent an Advocate filed an application before the Rent Controller seeking eviction of the appellant, his tenant from the premises in question on the ground that he required the premises for carrying on his profession as an advocate. The application was contested by the appellant who was carrying on the business of manufacturing art jewellery in the premises. The Appellate Authority passed an order of eviction against the appellant. Before the High Court it was contended by the tenant that there was a clear distinction between 'business ' and 'profession ' and that the practice of a liberal profession like that of an Advocate or Doctor which had nothing commercial about it was not business within the meaning of section 10(3)(a) (iii) of the Andhra Pradesh Buildings (Lease, Rent and Eviction) Control Act 1960. The tenant contended that the expression business was to be given a narrow meaning and was to he confined to activities of a commercial nature. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The expression 'business" occurring in section 10 (3)(A)(iii) is used in a wide sense so as to include the practice which is used cannot be of any assistance in determining its meaning in section10(3) (a) [14C] 1.2. The word must be interpreted in the context of the statute in which it occurs and not in the background of other statutes or in a manner alien to the context in which the term has been understood in the several statutes does not necessarily throw any light on the manner in which, the term should be understood generally generally. [14D] 1:3. The appellant is a member of the legal or medical professions and who requires the premises to carry on the practice as an Advocate and that he pursues a profession which is variously and justifiably described as learned, liberal or noble. [15E F] 2.1 In the context, of Madhya Pradesh Act, the word 'business has to be construed in the light of the statutes in which they occur and not elsewhere.

The respondent deposited a sum of Rs. 4,00,000 with M/s India Supplies which the appellant was the partner on behalf of the firm. The loan was made on 30 December 1942 and therefore the suit was filed within three years from the demand. The respondent contended that Article 60 of the Indian Limitation Act, 1908 was the relevant Article because if was a case of money deposited under an agreement that it was payable on demand and therefore limitation would commence from the date of demand and the suit should be filed within 3 years from that date. The trial court decreed the suit in favour of the respondent. At the trial the issues were first whether the respondent deposit ed the sum of RS. 4 lakhs with the appellant and secondly whether the suit, was barred by time. The entire controversy in the suit is whether it was a ease where money was deposited under agreement and that it Was payable on demands or whether it Was a case where money had been deposited under the agreement that the same would be paid on demand. Held, that the respondent 's contention that the background of the transaction was mercantile loan would be more a conjecture than a conclusion to be arrived at. The financial transactions between the respondent and Lakshmi Ratan Cotton Mills were running accounts. It would be most consistent to hold that by allowing India Supplies a deposit of Rs 4 lakhs would be relieved of the situation of repaying the money immediately. It is precisely because of the then inability of India Supplies to repay Lakshmi Ratan cotton Mills that the parties resorted to the mode of having the use of the money by way of deposit. The transaction was between the appellant, the respondent, and Lakshmi Rattan Cotton Mills. All figured in the transaction. A more loan of Rs, 4 lakhs will not have sufficed the needs of the appellant who were then unable to pay the dues of Lakshmi Ratan Jute Mill. Some of the partners of the appellants and the respondent in the year 1942 were common. It was more explicable and natural course of events that monies would be kept in deposit with the respondent at order to enable them to have financial accommodation without immediate worry of repayment. The mere fact that money in specie was not paid would not be destructive of deposit, and the appellant acted as bankers. The amount was deposited with the appellants.

The petitioner was detained by an order passed under section 3(1) of the COFEPOSA. The grounds of detention served on him were that he had been called by the Customs Authorities for investigation and that he was taken into custody and produced before the Additional Chief Metropolitan Magistrate who ramanded him to custody and directed him to be produced on the following day in the Court. By the time the order of detention came to be made, the petitioner was in jail for at the most one day. Charge sheet had not been submitted against him in the criminal case and he had also been remanded to judicial custody on the 27th February, 1986 with the direction to be produce on the next day in court. The petitioner was arrested at 2.00 p.m. on 27th of February,1986 and was produced before a Magistrate and an order was made requiring him to appear before the Metropolitan Magistrate on the 28th of Febru ary, 1986. In view of the positive case of the respondents that there was no summons and the detenu had been orally directed to attend the office by the authorities concerned, the Court dismissed the writ petition on 22nd April, 1987. The High Court dismissed his writ petition holding that the period of parole had to be excluded in recoking the period under sub section (1)of section 3 of the Act. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that the order passed by the High Court did not find favour with the Court, and that the only point which was argued was on the question of the period parole, that was, from 15th May, 1986 till February 22, 1987 should not be added to the period for detention speci fied in the impugned order under section 2(1). Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The fact remains that only one contention had been raised. There is absolutely no basis for the alle gation in paragraph 2 of the writ peti tion that if the Court had indicated to Mr. Jethmalani in course of arguments that the submission on this limited point did not found favour with it he would have proceeded to argue the other points. It was open to Mr, Jethmalani to make full submissions on all as pects arising in the writ Petition. That having not been done, it was improper on the part of Mr. Desai to raise such allegations in paragraph2, as have been extracted above. [848C D] 2. The facts that the detenu is al ready in detention does not take away the jurisdiction of the detaining authority in making an order of preventive detention. What is necessary in a case of this type is to satisfy the court when detention is challenged on that ground that the detaining authori ty was aware of the fact that the detenue was already in custody and yet he was sub jectively satisfied that his order of deten tion became necessary. [850E F] 3. The mere service of the detention order on the petitioner in jail would not therefore invali date the order. On the basis of antecedent activities of the detenu in the proximate past the detaining Authority could reasonably reach its subjective satisfaction about his tendency or inclination to act in a manner prejudicial to the maintenance of public order after his release on the termination of the security proceedings under the Code. [851C D; 849A B] 4. The detention order is dated 28th February 1986 and it was addressed to the detenu at his residential address at Delhi and not to the jail authorities for service on the detenu. From the facts and circumstances emerging in this case, it is clear that the fact remains, that only two contentions had been urged. There was absolutely no foundation in the submission that there is prejudice to the detenue on account of the authority 's withholding the summons.

The petitioners were not satisfied with the reply received by them. They filed a statement of demands through the Secretary General, BPTEF, New Delhi, of which they were members, claiming regularisation of casual labourers, payment of interim relief, payment Of bonus, supply of dresses, leave and medical facilities etc. They received a reply from the Department on January 10, 1986 which read as under: "Sub Demands of casual labour daily rated workers. Ref: Your letter No. PF/Casual Labour/86 dated 13.12.1985. Please refer to your above cited letter. The position regarding the various demands in your above mentioned letter is as below: (i) Regularisation of Casual Labour. This is being done as per existing instructions of department of Personnel & Training as against the vacancies as and when they arise. (ii) Payment of interim Relief. Revision of wages is done once in a year for casual labourers of category 1 (those who have not completed 720 days of service over a period of three years or more). ^ HELD: The petitioners are entitled to corresponding Dearness Allowance and Addl. Dearness Allowance, if any, payable thereon. Whatever other benefits which are now being enjoyed by the casual labourers shall continue to be extended to them. India is a socialist republic. It implies the existence of certain important obligations which the State has to discharge. [608C D] The right to work, the right to free choice of employment, the rights to just and favourable remuneration ensuring a decent living for himself and for family, the Right to form trade unions.

The assessee, a public notice under section 22(1) of the Income tax Act, 1922, was issued requiring every person whose total income during the previous year exceeded the maximum amount which was not chargeable to income tax to furnish within such period not being less than sixty days. The Income tax Officer included the sum of Rs. 59,026 in the total income of the assessee and assessed him on it for the assessment year 1945 46. 59.026 could not and should not have been included in his income that the amended section 34 of the Act had no retrospective effect, and that the assessment completed on February 26, 1951 was invalid inasmuch as it was completed four years after. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner rejected his contention but the Tribunal on being moved by him raised two questions of law under section 66(1), and (2) whether the notice issued under section 34 could be taken to be a 'best judgment ' assessment. The High Court held that the Department ought to have issued a notice under s.22(2) within the assessment years, and if no return was made within the time fixed by the notice, the Department should have proceeded under section 23(4) to a ' best judgment assessment '. On appeal by certificate, Held: (i) The notice under S.23(1)(a) of Income tax is not invalid because it was filed in response to a notice issued by the assessee, and the assessment thereon were valid in law. (ii) The return in answer to that notice could be filed under section 24(1). The notice was improper, because with the return already filed there was neither an omission nor a failure on the part of the assesses, nor was there any question of assessment 'escaping '. The notice issued thereunder did not amount to a "best judgment" assessment within the meaning of cl. (c) of sub section (1) Of section 28 and could be completed within one year of the date of service of the notice. The assessee might have filed the return on the last day showing income less than the taxable limit, but the return in law was not a mere scrap of paper. It was open to him, if there was sufficient justification for it, to hold that the amount noted in the footnote was really the assessee 's income, in which case an assessable income would have been found and the tax could be charged thereon. If the Income Tax Officer had acted on that return and assessed the assessee (1)[1955] 1 S.C.R. 869), the assessment would have become valid. He chose to ignore the return, and served on the assessee a notice in answer thereto could not be treated as such a return filed under s .24(1); he chose to disregard the return and served a notice on him under section 33(2). (iii) The time limit provided by section 34(3) was not available in this case.

The petitioners, who are the principal office bearers of a nationalised bank, filed a writ petition in this Court challenging the circular dated 23.8.1982 (Annexure A) issued by the Joint Secretary to the Government of India, Ministry of Finance, Department of Economic Affairs, (Banking Division), New Delhi. They contend that Clause 3 of the Scheme in terms of which the circular was purported to have been issued is ultra vires Section 9 of the Act unless the said clause is so read as to be in harmony with the Section, and when so read, the said cl does not justify or support the impugned circu lar. The petitioners contended that the circular is contrary to the mandate of the Banking Companies (Acquisi tion and Transfer of Undertakings) Act, 1970 and the Natio nalised Banks ( Management and Miscellaneous Provisions) Scheme, 1980 (hereinafter referred to as 'thescheme '). They further contend ed that Clause 2 of the scheme in terms whereof the circular has been issued was ultra vires section 9 of that Act unless it is so construed as to render in harmony therewith with the section, and since so read the said Clause does not support or support its circu lative. The Central Government contested the writ petition contending that there is no justification whatsoever to issue any such circular for the very object of the Nitio nal Bank (Bank ing Division) and that the Act postulates both election and nomination of members of the Board of Directors and the choice between the two modes of appointment is left to the Central Government. The Additional Solicitor General, representing the Central Govern ment and Mr. Harish N. Salve, counsel for the Reserve Bank of India contended that there was no justification whatever whatsoever to issuing any such Circular for the said very object. Dismissing the writ petitions, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The object of Section 9 is to nationalise the banks in order to, as stated in the preamble to the Act, "control the heights of the economy and to meet progressively, and serve better, the needs of development of the nation in conformi ty with the national policy and objectives". The very purpose of that legislative exercise is to render the largest good to the largest number of people of this 'sovereign, socialist, secular democratic republic.

The respondent was imposed penalties in respect of the assessment years 1954 55, 1960 61 and 1961 62. The penalty was imposed under section 271(1)(c) read with section 274(2) of the Income tax Act for concealment of particular income and furnishing inaccurate particulars. The assessee preferred appeals to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who rejected the applications. The Tribunal declined to stay the proceedings as also the collection of penalties pending the appeal since that power was incidental and ancillary to its appellate jurisdiction. The High Court held that the Tribunal had the power to stay recovery during the pendency of an appeal, and directed the Income Tax Officer to file an appeal against the order of the Appellate Asstt. Commissioner. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that in the absence of any express provision in sections 254 and 255 of the Act relating to stay of recovery during pendency of the appeal it must be held that no such power can be exercised by the Tribunal, suffers from a fundamental infirmity inasmuch as it assumes and proceeds on the premise that the statute confers such a power on the Income. tax Officer who can give the necessary relief to an assessee. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The Appellate Tribunal must be deemed to have the power of stay as incidental or ancillary to the appellate jurisdiction created by section 64. [69C] 2.1 In the instant case, when section 254 confers appellate jurisdiction, it impliedly grants the powerof doing all such acts, or employing such means, as are essentially necessary to its execution and that the statutory power carries with it the duty in proper cases to make such orders for staying proceedings as will prevent the appeal if successful from being rendered nugatory. [70E] 2:2 The power of staying by the Appellate Tribunal is not likely to be exercised in a routine way or as a matter of course in view of the special nature of taxation and revenue. It has further been observed that "where the legislature invests an Appellate Tribunal with powers to prevent an injustice, it expressly empowers it to stay proceedings which may result in causing further mischief". [70G] 2 :3 The power conferred by section 254 on the Appellate Tribu nal with widest possible amplitude must carry with them by necessary implication all powers and duties incidental and necessary to make the exercise of those powers fully effective. In the present case, the Appellate 'Tribunal must be set aside. [71C] 3:1. When section 254 conferred appellate jurisdiction it impliedly confers grants the powers of doing all those acts, and employing such mean ing, as were essentially necessary for its execution, and that statutory power carry with it, the duty is in proper case to make them for staying the proceedings. [72D E] 2(a) The power to grant stay by treating the assessee as not being in default during the pend of an Appeal has been given to the Income ' tax Officer only when an appeal has been presented under section 246 which will be to the Appel late Assistant Commissioner and not to the Tribunal.

The respondent was appointed a constable in U. P. Police Force on December 1, 1945, he was promoted to the rank of head constable and posted as officer incharge of Police Station, Intiathok District Gonda. Complaints were received by the District Magistrate, Gonda, to the effect that the respondent was receiving bribes in the discharge of his duties. On November 3, 1952, the Sub Divisional Magistrate directed the Sub divisional Magistrate to make an enquiry in respect of the said complaints. The Superintendent of Police, who conducted the trial, examined many witnesses and found that seven out of nine charges had been established. Thereafter he issued a notice to the respondent calling upon him to show cause why he should not be dismissed from the police force. On February 20, 1954, the respondent submitted his explanation on November 29, 1952. The respondent was asked to showcause why he be dismissed and after considering his explanation, dismissed the respondent from service with effect from the said date. The appeal preferred by him to the Deputy Inspector General of Police was dismissed by his order dated June 2, 1954. Thereafter the respondent filed a petition under article 226 of the Constitution before the High Court for quashing the order of dismissal. The High Court allowed the petition and quashed the orders. Held: (i) The departmental inquiry was only a further step in respect Of the misconduct of the respondent in regard whereof the magisterial enquiry was held at an earlier stage; if so, the question is whether para 486 would govern the present inquiry or it would fall out side its scope. The relevant provisions of the Police Regulations read: Paragraph 486: "When the offence alleged against a police officer amounts to an offence only under s 7 of the police Act there can be no magisterial inquiry under the Criminal Procedure Code. In such cases, and in other cases until and unless a magisterial Inquiry is ordered, enquiry will be made under the direction of the Superintendent of police in accordance with the following rules." Paragraph 489(2) does not apply to a case where a mag ministerial inquiry is ordered; and that a police Officer can be departmentally tried under section 7 of Police Act after such a magjudicial inquiry. In this case, the departmental trial was held subsequent to the completion of the magical inquiry and therefore it falls within the express terms of para 489(1). The fact that in the interregnum the police received further complaints or that the C.I.D. made further enquiries do not affect the question, if substantially the subject matter of the Magisterial enquiry and the departmental proceedings is the same. In the circumstances, it would be hypertechnical to hold that there was no magical enquiry in regard of the matter which was the subject of the departmental inquiry.

The appellant, a highly qualified ophthalmic surgeon feeling aggrieved by the promotion of respondents 4 to 24, though convinced that even if the Court were to accede to his request he was in no way likely to be benefited by this bizarre exercise. 51 First to the fact situation. The Union of India framed Central Health Service Rules 1963 ( '1963 Rules ' for short). These Rules envisaged categorisation of personnel manning the Service into five different categories, namely, category I comprising supertime grade I Rs. 1800 2250; super time grade II Rs. 1300 1200 and category III consisting of Specialists ' grade Rs. 1600 2000. The Rules envisaged classification of personnel in the service into five distinct categories, to wit, category 'A ' supertime scale Rs. 1100 2000, category `B ' super time scale Rs,. 1600, category II consists of Specialist ' grade IRs. 1800 2350 and category IV comprises General Duty Officers Grade II Rs., 450 900. On account of various imponderables the Service could not be constituted and 1963 Rules were amended by Central Health Services (Amendment) Rules 1966. The appellant contended that as these 28 posts were in specialists ' grades and the strength of Specialisedists ' Grade posts was reduced by 28, whenever any post out of these 28 vacancies added to supertime Grade II is required to be filled in, it can only be filled by promotion from amongst those originally belonging to specialists grade, i.e. category `C ' under 1963 Rules. The respondent contended that the 19 unspecified Specialists " posts were meant only for promoting category 'C ' clinical Specialists to super time Grade II and that the strength was reduced to 28 whenever any posts out of those 28 posts added to Supertime grade II is needed to be filling in, It could only be made in by promotion and not in any other manner and particularly not by transfer. The contention was rejected by the Government on the ground that the posts were not in Specialists Grade and the number of posts in specialist ' grades was reduced from 28, when a post in supertimely grade II was created at Willingdon Hospital from amongst unspecified specialists. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the 29 posts were really meant only to promoting category `D ' and that promotion of each of them deserved to be quashed. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the 19 unified Specialists" posts in super time grades II could only have been filled in by promotions from amongst the persons who qualify for the same as provided for in rule 8(3); and (2) the promotion was in contravention of rule 8 of 1966 Rules. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appellant being conscious of this position tried to circumvent it by saying that the post at Will ingdon hospital alone must have been filling in the post created at willingd on Hospital alone must be considered eligible for promotion to super lime grade I because he had not put in 8 years of service in the category of specialists " grade officers formed on September 9, 1966.

The Punjab Security of Land Tenures Act, 1953 was enacted to bring about an agrarian re ordering so pivotal to the progress of our rural economy. Haryana, happily a granary of our country is one of the States where land reform laws are likely to generate great changes by banishing big concentration of Natur 's bounty in a few feudal hands creating an enthusiastic sense of distributive justice and exploiting the productive potential of land by the possessive passion of the landless many. So strategic is land reform that special constitutional concern has been shown for this programme. Naturally the State enacted the Act whereby ceiling on land ownership was set; surplus lands were taken over for settling ejected tenants and others, peasant proprietorship created. The scheme of the Act with which we are concerned is fairly simple and somewhat scientific, although its language, what with frequent amendments dovetailed from time to time, has made for ambiguity, obscurity, marginal inconsistency and a rich crop of litigation. Indeed, the conflict of opinion at the High Court level and the bone of contention before us arise from this drafting deficiency Legal Preface: A thumb nail sketch of the Punjab Act is a prefatory necessity. The defines 'small land owner ' as section 2(2) having in mind the optimum ownership in the given conditions. Permissible area ' [section 2(3)] is a cognate concept limiting the maximum permissible extent a person may hold, and so long as he does not have any excess, he is a small landholder. He can evict the tenants from his holding and be in actual enjoyment as provided by the Act. If, however, he has lands beyond the permissible area, he becomes a large land owner and has to cough up the excess. However, he was given the option to choose there best area he desires to keep, called 'reserved area ' ' [Section 2(4)] and then he must make available to the State such excess as called surplus area [section 10A]. This creation of a surplus pool or reservoir is vital to the success of the statutory project since, by distribution of such lands, rehabilitation of ejected tenants, and landless persons is to be "accomplished". Even if a person is a big holder, it is quite on the cards that, by inheritance or other operation of law, or by voluntary transfer he may acquire lands in excess of the permissible limit. In short, the legislative mandate is that every agricultural holder in the State shall hold no more than the permissible Area and the surplus in the hands of large holders, whether acquired by voluntary transactions or involuntary operation of laws will go to feed the surplus pool. With this end in view, the Act has been amended to block all escape routes unearthed by the law makers as often as the High court has upheld certain patterns of alienations and oblique dealings by interpretative process. A study of the history of the legislation suggests an unspoken criticism about judicial approach which we will refer to later. Suffice it to say that the law is interpreted a radical agrarian measure; its basic goals are to cut down large holdings and distribute lands to various landless people according to a design and to foster, according to legislative policy, an agrarian community of peasants proprietors.
