The appellants claimed that the property in suit originally belonged to Gangashah, who had five sons: Hiru Bhakta, Sakru, Kajur and Raju. The branches of Shakru and Bairagi became extferent from among the descendants Of the common ancestor Gangasasthah. The plaintiffs relied upon the following genealogy Gangasadhah Niru Bhakti Kajur Thakur Thakur ThakurThakur Sitaram Tanba Chatturshah Thakur Thakur (dead) Nilkanthah Pratapshah Dawaltshah Ranwirsha (Platff. Shah dead) No. 1) (Deft. No. 2) (dead). Hanmantrao Amarshagh Basu Chandarsha Karbi Angshitheba Dawalsabah (Pliff. No: 1) No 2 (dead), Hanmantabai Amarsahah Basu Nath Basha Basu Chandarath Samanta Basu Chandsha Karbah Nirashgava Dec. 9, (dead.) 1950) Diwakarrao Am Narshah vs The State of Madhya Pradesh and Others, ; , followed.

The respondent landlord terminated the tenancy of the appellants inter alia on the ground that the appellants were in arrears of rent for more than six months. The appellants filed a suit for recovery of possession of a portion of the ground floor of a building on the grounds, (1) that they were in arrear of rent from 1st September 1964 and (2) that the respondent bona fide required possession of the premises in suit. The trial court gave a decree in favour of the respondent for possession of his premises. The appellate Court confirmed the judgment and decree. In an application under article 227 of the Constitution the High Court held that when the respondent paid all arrears and costs of the suit on 23 December 1964 it could not be said that the tenant did not comply with the provisions of section 12(3) (b) of the Act. The High Court also took the view that the dispute as to standard rent was to be raised within one month from the service of the notice on the tenant. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (1)(a) The Bombay High Court in Dattu Subhana Panhalkar vs Gajanan Vithoba Bobhate & Anr., held that the effect of sections 11 and 12 of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act 1947 is to give the tenant a right to dispute the standard rent in the event of a suit and if the tenant raises a dispute in answer to a suit or proceedings for fixing the standard Rent it would be a dispute within the meaning of section 10(3)(a). [632 B] (b). The Bombay view is that disputing within one months of the service notice though subsequent to the date of the notices that would be sufficient to oust the operation of section 11(3), (a) of tho Act, the dispute must be in existence latest within one year after service of notice. [633 C] (c). The provisions in section 11 (3) of Bombay Rents Hotel and lodging House Rates control Act 1947 deal with orders which may be passed by the Court during the pendency of the application disputing the rent. Provisions in section II(4) of that Act deal with order which may have been passed consequent upon dispute as regards standard rent or permitted increases. It is only when an application disputing rent is made within the time contemplated by Explanation I to section 12 of that the provisions in sub section (3), and (4) are attracted. [625 E] (d). The provision in section ll(3 ) of the said Act deals with orders passed by Court during proceedings disputing the standard rents. Provisions dealing with orders made by court during the course of the proceedings disputing rent.

The respondent company was a company incorporated in what was then British India having a capital of Rs. 3,600 divided into 360,000 shares of Rs 10 each. The Aluminium Limited, a company registered under the provisions of the Indian Companies Act, 1913, held 359,790 shares in the chargeable accounting periods ending on December 31, 1939 and December 31,, 1941, and December31, 1943, and January 31, 1943 respectively. In exercise of the power given to it by article 105 of the articles of association of the respondent company, the Aluminium Ltd. appointed three permanent directors on the board of directors of the Company. Two of these directors eventually retired and only one, namely, Mr. L. G. Bash who continued to be a director of the company nominated by the Aluminium Limited. The respondent company thereupon appealed to the Incometax Appellate Tribunal which reversed the decision of the Excess Profits Tax Officer. The Commissioner of Excess Profits tax upheld the decision. On appeal by the respondent Company, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner of excess profits tax upheld that decision. Held, that the shares in question which give the controlling interest are neither held by Mr.L. G., and they cannot be said to have a controlling interest therein, no matter by what machinery or means that result has been effected. The shares being always subject to his will and ordering, the controlling interests which the holder of the majority of shares has never passed to the agent. The controlling interest remains vested in the shareholder. The shareholder may revoke the authority of the agent at any time. In spite of the appointment of the agents the shareholders may himself appear at the meeting and cast his votes personally.

The respondent was serving as an Accountant Grade II in the Electricity Department of the former State of Hyd erabad. On 1st October, 1957, the Mysore State Electricity Board was constituted under the Indian Electricity (Supply) Act. An option was given to the respondent to continue in the Government service or to opt to the Board. On 2nd November, 1972, the respondent opted to the Service under the Board and ceased to be an employee of the Government with effect from that date. In 1960, the Board framed Recruitment and Promo tions Regulations in exercise of its powers conferred on it under section 79(c) of the Act. The Regulations were subsequently amended on 16th December 1966. The amended Rules prescribed that the posts of Accounts Superintendents were to be filled by promotion of I Division Clerks on the basis of seniority cum merit on their having passed Part I and II of the S.A.S. examination. On 30th December, 1966, some persons junior to the respond ent were promoted on their being promoted on the ground that they had not passed the examination. The respondent made several representations one such representation being on 24th December 1970. On 21st November 1972, however, the resolu tion was rejected. The appellant 's writ petition challenging the Resolution was dismissed by the High Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the writ petition ought to be dis missed on the grounds of inordinate delay and laches on the part of the respondent and also on the view that in view of the later resolution of the Board dated 5th January, 1970, it was no longer open to the appellant to rely on the Resolution dated 19th May, 1969. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High Court was in error in construing the relevant provisions of the Regulations and the Resolutions passed by the Board under section79(c).

% The petitioner 's son was taken in police custody on 1.12.1987 by respondent No.6, Sarat Chandra Barik, Assistant Sub Inspector of Police, Jaraikela Police Station, Bisra, District Sundergarh in Orissa State. On the night between the 1st and 2nd December, 1987, he came to know that the dead body of his son was found on the railway track near a bridge at some distance from the Jaraiampur Railway station. There were multiple injuries on the body of Suman Behera when it was found and obviously his death was unnatural, caused by those injuries. The allegation made is that it was a case of custodial death since Suman Behra was died as a result of the multiple injuries inflicted to him while he was in police detention. The petitioner filed a writ petition before the High Court for determining the claim of compensation to the petitioner, the mother of the deceased, for contravention of the fundamental right guaranteed under Article 21 of the Constitution. The State of Orissa and its police officers including Sarat Chander Barik Assistant Sub Inspectors of Police and Constable No.127, Chhabil Kujur of Police Outpost Jeraikela, Police Station Bisra are impleaded as respondents in this petition. The defence of the respondents is that Suman Behara managed to escape from police custody at about 3 a.m. on the night intervening between 1st & 2nd Dec., 1987 and it was likely that he was run over by a passing train after he had escaped from police detention; that the death was due to the multiple injury inflicted to his son, while he is in police possession; and thereafter his dead body was thrown on the Railway track.

The two prisoners have been sentenced to death for an offence under section 302 Indian Penal Code and the petitions filed by them to the President of India for commutation of the sentence are reported to have been rejected by the President recently. Before considering the merits of the application, it would like to observe that the constitutional right to freedom of speech and expression conferred by article 19(1)(a) of the Constitution, which includes freedom of Press is not an absolute right nor indeed does it confer any right on the press to have an unrestricted access to means of information. The Press is entitled to exercise its freedom of freedom of circulation and expression by publishing a matter which does not invade the rights of other citizens and which does neither violate the sovereignty and integrity of India, the security of the State, public order decency and morality. But in the instant case, the right claimed by the petitioner is not the right to express any particular view or opinion but the right asserted by him is not a right to be considered for the purpose of selection for admission for admission to interview. The existence of a free Press does not imply or spell out any legal obligation on the citizens to supply information to the press, such for example, as there is under section 161(2) of Criminal Procedure Code. No data has been made available to us on the basis of which it would be possible for us to say that the two prisoners are ready and willing to be interviewed. The presence of afree Press does no imply or spelt out any right obligation on citizens to supplied information to Press, such as there was under section 162(2). No data had been made in support of this contention.

The respondent mortgaged a tea garden to the appellant Bank. On January 19, 1950 the Bank applied for the appointment of a Receiver. The District Judge directed that the Bank should nominate a Receiver in terms of clause 12 of the mortgage deed first the Secretary of the Bank and later another employee called Adhir Ranjan Dutta was appointed as the Receiver subject to his furnishing security in the sum of Rs. 50,000. The appellant filed an appeal against that order but it was dismissed for default by the Judicial Commissioner on June 29, 1970. On October 4, 1961 respondent filed a suit against the Receiver and the appellant praying that execution do issue against the appellant as directed by the Court. The Subordinate Judge decreed the suit on May 31, 1956 but he allowed the respondent 's cross objections and enhanced the damages to Rs. 4,525. He also ordered that the Receiver should pay the amount within two months failing which the amount should be recovered from the security of Rs 50, 000. The High Court dismissed the appeal filed by the Receiver against that decision. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the bond executed both be the Receiver as well as the appellant in favour of "Sri Ramani Mohan Goswami the District Judge of Agartala his successors, successors in office and assigns; (2) under the terms of the bond the appellant is not answerable for the loss caused to the tea garden by fire. Both these contentions were contested on behalf both sides. HELD: The surety bond was a part of the proceedings pending before the District judge and on the transfer of the suit the entire proceedings including the bond stood validly transferred to the Court of the Subordinate Judge. [359 C] (2)(a) Under section 150 of the Code of Civil Procedure, save as otherwise provided, where the business of any court is transferred to any other Court, the transferee Court has the same powers and is entitled to perform the same duties as those respectively conferred and imposed by the Code upon the transferor Court.

The appellants are dealers in food grains supplied to the Regional Food Controller diverse quantities of wheat. The Sales Tax Officer levied tax under the U.P. Sales Tax Act on the aggregate price of the wheat by the appellants, rejecting the contention raised by the appellant that the wheat supplied was not sold by them to the Controller and that the sales were not made in pursuance of any contract of sale. The order was confirmed by the Additional Judge (Revisions) Sales Tax. The Additional Judge held that the turnover resulting from supplies of wheat was not taxable since there was no "sale" within the meaning of the U .P. Act, 1948. The High Court also held that as the wheat procured or purchased daily by the dealer thereafter it was open to the State Government to say that from any particular date it will not purchase any or all of the specified percentage of wheat and therefore the levy order did not result in a contract of sales. In appeal to this Court, HELD : The expression "sale of goods" in section 2(h) of the Act is restricted by its first sub section (3) of section 3 of the . It contains a bald injunction to supply wheat of the stipulated quantity day after day and enacts that in default of compliance the dealer was liable to be punished. It does not envisage any consensual arrangement. A sale predicates a contract Of sale of goods between persons competent to contract for a price paid or promised : a transaction in which an obligation to supply goods is imposed, and which does not involve an obligationto enter into a contract cannot be called a "sale ' even if the person supplying goods is declared entitled to the value of goods, which is determined or determinable in the manner prescribed. Assuming that between the licensed dealer and the Controller there may be some arrangements about the place and manner of delivery of wheat, and the payment of " controlled price", the operation of cl. 3 of Order and acceptance thereof do not result In a contract for sale of Goods between persons entitled to contract, for a fixed price paid Or promised : in which a obligation to purchase goods is impose, and does not involving an obligation on entering into a bargain cannot be said to be a "Sale" even if it is declared as a sale. [682 H; 681 A B] The expression 'sale of Goods ' in the Constitution must be understood in the same sense in which it is (1) (1969) All L.J. Legislature could therefore legislate for levy of sales tax on a transaction which amounted to a sale within the ambit of the , and not on any other transaction which was deemed by fiction to be, a sale [690 C] Commissioner of Sales Tax, U. P. Lucknow vs Shri Om Prakash & Ors., ; , followed.

The appellant Abdul Latif Wahab Sheikh was in jail from November 12, 1985 onwards awaiting trial on a charge of murder. He was due for release from prison on June 23, 1986. On that day, however, an order for his detention was made under the provisions of the Gujarat Prevention of Anti Social Activities Act, 1985. The mandate of Article 22(4) of the Constitution is that no law providing for preventive detention shall authorise the detention of a person for a longer period than three months unless the Advisory Board has reported within the period of three months that there is in its opinion sufficient cause for such detention. Section 10 stipulates that in every case where a detention order has been made under section 11, the State Government shall, within three weeks from the date of detention of the person under the order, place before the Advisory board the grounds on which the order has be made, the representation, if any, made by the detenu and the report, ifany, of the authorised offi cer. What is important for the purposes of this case is that section 11 stipulates that a detention shall not bar the making of a subsequent detention order under the Act against the same person, subject to the proviso that if there were no fresh facts, the maximum period for which a person may be detained shall not extend beyond the expiry of a period of 12 months from the day of detention under the earlier detention order. The period of 3 weeks stipulated by section 11 of the Act expired on July 14, 1986 and the appellant was entitled to be released on July 19, 1986 as no reference had been made to the Advisory Boards within the time stipulated by Section 11 of that Act. But he was not so released. This state of affairs continued till August 7, 1986 when the order of detention dated June 23. 1986 was revoked and a fresh order of deten tion was made on the same facts on the basis of which the earlier order of his detention had been challenged by filing a writ petition in the High Court. Consequent to the revocation of that order, the appellant filed a writ peti tions challenging the second order of Detention dated August 7 1986. The Advisory Board was constituted on August 18, 1986, and the reference to the Adviso ry Board was made within three months after the detention which commenced on the making thereof. The High Court dismissed the writ petition. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the appellant that there has been a contravention of the constitutional protection afforded by Article 22 (4) and therefore, the appel lant is entitled to have be set at liberty; and that under section 15(2) of that the Gujarat Act the expiry or revocation of an earlier detention ordi n shall not debar the making Of a subsequent deten tion order under section 10 against the said same person. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The procedural requirements are the only safeguards available to a detenu since the court is not expected to go behind the subjective satisfaction of the detaining authority.

The respondent, a father of the respondent, was advanced in age and both the father and son had been fighting between themselves since more than a decade. The High Court found that the petitioner and the respondent had referred their disputes to one Kantibhai Vaidya who had intervened between them with the good intention to bring their dispute to an end. He made an award on 18th January, 1977. Below the award, both the parties and the arbitrator had signed. The endorsement reads, when translated in English, as found by the High Court that the award is agreed to and binding upon both the Parties and that the entire responsibility of the arbitrator will lie on Shri Kantibhai Desai Vaidya and that he has taken the responsibility. Thereafter followed a spell of litigation. The respondent applied for filing the award and sought the judgment in terms of the award under section 17 of the (hereinafter called 'the Act '). A notice consequent upon the filing of the Award was issued to the petitioner. The application was converted into Special Civil Suit No. 84 of 1977. It was stated in the application that the respondent has torn off the award. The petitioner filed his objections to the application but did not file any application within the prescribed limitation of 30 days. The trial Judge rejected the objections filed beyond the period of limitation and for the reasons that (1) the notice was already given to the party concerned about the filing, and (2) the time for making an application to set aside the award had expired and no such application was made. The learned trial Judge held that the First Appeal and Civil Revision Application were withdrawn in pursuance of an agreement reached between the parties on or about 14th August, 1978. A copy of the said agreement was also produced before the Court as Exhibit 40. The award was signed by both the witnesses as well as their respective advocates. The agreement was in the form of a letter addressed to the arbitrator wherein it was stated that both of them had appointed him as an arbitrator to resolve the disputes between them and that they had given an award dated 20th January 1977 in respect of which award, there had been continued objections but now they have agreed that both the petitioner should abide by the award dated 21st January,1977 and that its interpretation should be left to the Arbitrator himself. The judgment of the trial Court was challenged in a civil revision application before the High court. The same was rejected summarily. The main objection to the award was that there was no written agreement signed by the parties to refer the disputes to arbitration. It is clear from the narration of facts that the parties had agreed to refer to the arbitration of the named arbitrator and that it was not relevant according to the Judicial Committee, whether they decided it rightly or wrongly, they had jurisdiction to decide the case; and even if they decided wrongly, there were no such express or implied prohibition nor any inability of the Judge concerned.

The respondent was appointed receiver of the estate in question. On August 10, 1908, the said receiver with the permission mortgaged properties to the said firm as security for the due repayment of the loan advanced by that firm. The said receiver had mortgaged the properties to a firm then carrying on business under the name and style of Laik Banerjee & Company. On the same day the said Receiver with like permission mortgaged these properties to another firm, carrying on the business under name and styled as Laik Ghosh & Co. The respondent was also appointed receiver for the purpose of determining whether or not there was privity of estate between the landlord and the mortgagee. The appellant who was one of the partners of the firm filed a suit in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Asansole, on behalf of Deva Prasanna as the decree holder. Order 22, rule 57, Civil Procedure Code, which purported to dismiss the respondent 's execution case for non prosecution while continuing the attachment already effected terminated the proceeding in execution which had resulted in the attachment. The trial court dismissed the suit but the High Court set aside the order of dismissal and directed that the attachment be made on the execution petition pending before the executing Court. Held, that the order was a final order which brought the Execution Case No. 118 of 1936 to an and the attachment continued not because there was a pend ing execution proceeding but because a special order was made under Order XXI, rule 56, as amended by the Calcutta High Court. Ram Kumar De vs Abhoya Pada Bhattacharjee (I.L.R. , approved.

The appellant was the Karta of a joint family consisting of himself and his four sons. The appellant was his concubine since 1945 until his death on February 22, 1949. By two registered deeds purporting to be sale deeds dated April 15, 1946, (Exbts. A 1 and A 2), he transferred certain properties belonging to the joint family. In 1947 after the execution of exhibit A 1 & A 2 there was a disruption of the joint Hindu family and a severance of the Joint status between the appellant and his sons. In 1954 his widow and sons instituted O.S. No. 12 of 1954 against the appellant for recovery of possession of the properties alleging that the documents dated April, 1946 were executed without consideration or for immoral purposes, and were void. The trial court dis missed the appellant 's suit. On appeal by special leave to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the transfers were made by Venkatacharyulu in favour of the appel lant in view of past illicit cohabitation 45 with her, such past cohabitation was the motive and not the consideration for the transfers under exhibit A I and A2. HELD: The transfers were without consideration and were by way of gifts. The gifts were not hit by section 6(h) of the . But the properties gifted under exhibitA 1 andA 2 were coparcenary properties. Under the Madras school of Mitakshara law by which the appellant was governed, he had no power to make a gift of his undivided interest in the coparcenary property to his concordine. The transfers under Exts. Aland A 2 were not invalid because they were motivated by a desire to compensate the concubines for her past services. In the alternative, the respondents contended that assuming that the transfer was made in consideration of past cohabit ment, they were hit by sec. 6(g) of . But, the properties transferred under exhibit AlandA 2 are coparcenary properties and under the Madras School of Mitakshara Law by which Venkatachallulu was governed he had not power to making a gift for his own property to the appellant but he did not make any such gift. The properties gifted were therefore invalid.

The appellant was the Chief Justice of a High Court in exercise of his original jurisdiction under section 116A of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The respondent filed an appeal against the order of the Election Tribunal under section 98 of the Act before the High Court which held that the appeal presented to them by the respondent was within time if computed after making the deductions permitted by section 12 of the Limitation Act. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the expression "appeal" in article 156(2)(a) of Schedule 11 of the Indian Limitation Act means an appeal governed by the Code of Civil Procedure, 1908; and (ii) the word "appeal under the Code Of Civil Procedure means an order governed by a special or local law. Held: (per Subba Rao J.) that the expression 'appeal" used in article 157(2) (a) to include a suit, appeal or application for which no period of limitation is prescribed in the First Schedule to the Limitation act would be an appeal under the Indian , and therefore it was governed by section 29(2). The word "appellate" in the first limb of sub section (2) of section 29 must be read as including a suit. It is not necessary that the period should have been expressly prescribed by the First schedule for an appeal created by a Special law but the special law prescrib a period of Limitation different from the period prescribed therefor by the first Schedule. The word 'appeal ' in article 154(2), therefore, must be construed as including the suit. The words "appeal " under the , Code of Criminal Procedure, are not intended to take in appeals under the Act. The expression "appeals" in section 29 (2), is wide enough in its ambit to include suits, appeals and applications filed beyond time. The first limb is concerned only with proceedings of this kind, that is, proceedings under special or general law for which a period Of limitation is provided in the Act, and are not excluded by such special or special local law; and the second part of section 30(2 ) would be attracted by reason of the provisions of cl. (a). The expression 'appellate jurisdiction" in that clause means an appellate jurisdiction governed by that Code. It will be noticed that no argument was raised in that case that the appellant was governed under the . [143 E F] In order to deal with the second ground given by his brother it is necessary to reproduce the provisions Of section 29, sub section(2): "Where any special or other local law prescribes for any suit appeal, appeal, application or application a periodof limitation different from that prescribed therefor under the First Scheduled Schedule, the provisions contained in section 4, sections 9 to 18 and section 22 shall apply only in so far as, and to the extent to which, they are not expressly excluded by the special or Local law."

The appellant, a person providing transport service in the District of Mathura, challenged the validity of the order dated May 22, 1986 passed by the District Magis trate declaring Plot Nos. 701 and 703 in the Town Area, Baldev (Mathura) as a bus stand/halting place of Baldev, where the stage carriages were directed to stand for the purpose of allowing the passengers of Baldev to get into and to get down from the stage carriage vehicles in a writ petition, Civil Miscellaneous Writ Petition No. 501 of 1986 filed before the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution of India challenging the said bye laws. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that section 76 of the Act conferred wide powers on the District Magistrate 'to fix the places for the bus stand andhalting places '. It further held that since the impugned order did not specifically state that the bus operators could allow the passengers to get up and pick up the passengers, it could not be construed as an order fixing the area as a Bus stand. The appellant has filed this appeal by special leave against the said decision of the High court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 Section 76 of tho Uttar Pradesh Municipalities Act, 1961 has nothing to do with the fixation or alteration of a bus stands and the power to compel persons in charge of motor buses to stop only at certain places for tho purpose of taking up or setting down passengers was a matter which relating to motor traffic and that there was a specific provision in section 68(2)(r) of the Uttar Pradesh Municipal Act, 1922 for that pur pose. [717C D] 1.2 The Town Area Committee can derive any assistance from this rule. It only authorises the District Transport Officer to exercise the powers under section 76. of the U.P. Motor Vehicles Rules 1940 which is confined to the question of determination of parking places and halting places which are not the same as bus stands which can only be notified by the Regional Transport Author ity as held by this Court in T.B. Ibrahim 's case [supra]. It is open to the Regional transport Authority to take action immediately for determining any convenient place or places within the Town area of Baldev (odar) as bus stand. [ 717E F] T.P Ibrahim vs Regional Transport Authority, Tanjore, ; , followed.

The appellants were prosecuted under section 3(1) of the , and section 7, read with section 5 of the . The trial court convicted all the accused ' but on appeal the Additional Sessions Judge set aside the conviction. In revision to the High Court it was contended that upon the facts found by the lower courts no offence had been committed by the appellants. HELD: (i) There is no provision in the Act which makes a preparation to commit an offence punishable. It follows therefore that the appellants should not have been convicted under section 7 of the. [666 C] (ii) The appellants should be acquitted of this offence if he approaches the stack with the matches in his pocket but, if he bends down near the stacks and lights a match which he extinguishes on perceiving that he is being watched, he may be guilty of an attempt to commit it. [667 D] (iii) The preparation consists in devising or arranging the means or measures necessary for the commission of the offence. On the other hand, an attempt is to commit the offence is a direct movement towards the commission after preparations are made. In order that a person may be convicted of an attempts to commit a crime he must be shown first to have had an intention to commit 'a crime and secondly to have done an act which constitutes the actus reus of a criminal attempt. [665 E F] (iv) The object of section 8 is to prevent the repetition of offences punishable under sections 7 and 7, and to prevent repetition of such offences.

The Sassoons agreed to transfer their Managing Agency of the said companies to Messrs. Agarwal and Company, Chidambaram Textile (Agencies) Ltd., by letters dated the 3rd September, 1943, 16th April, 1943 and 27th April 1943 respectively. The Sassoon executed in favour of Messrs. Agarwala and Company Affairs were transferred by the Sassoffons to the respective transferees with effect from 1st December, 1943. The agreement was duly registered on the 31st December 1943, and the Managing Agency Agreement was signed between the Sassoon and Company Ltd., and all the rights and benefits as such Managing Agents under the said Agreements and no part of the consideration paid by the transferees to the Sascoons could be allocated between them and their transferees. The managing Agency Agreement provided that the Sasiffons would transfer their managing Agency to Messrs Agarwal and Co. and thereafter to the transferees with a view to bring about the result specifically stated in the second portion of that clause (which had been side lined) i.e., that on assignment, the assignee firm shall be entitled to demand and obtain from the principal Company a fresh Managing Agency agreement in its own favour for the residue of the term outstanding and with like powers authorities remuneration and emoluments subject to the like terms and conditions. The transfer was to be given retrospective operation from the commencement of the year in respect of the work so far done. It was also provided that on the assignment, assignment had to be made retrospective effect from the date of the assignment. The Managing Agency Agreements were registered on 31st March 1943 and the Sasifons executed in their favour by Messrs. Jhaveri and Company with effect on the 1st June, 1943 respectively, and all its rights and privileges as such managing Agents under these agreements and no portion of the remuneration paid by them to the said Sassoors could be allotted between them. The Income tax Officer included the Sashions in the taxable income of the Sasassoons ' share of the profits of the company on the ground that they had earned the income by rendering services as Managing Agents to the Companies for the respective periods that they continued to be the Managing Agents and the transferees had rendered the services for the balance of the periods completing the full year of accounting and had earned proportionate commission and therefore the amount of commission which the latter actually received included the share of commission in respect thereof. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Income tax officer but the Tribunal, on a reference made at the instance of the assessee, held that the managing Agency commission was earned for services rendered and therefore it was taxed in the hands of the person who carried on the business of the Managing Agent and not in the hand of the persons to whom it was assigned. The High Court also held that as the Sas Soons had not earned any income for the broken periods, they could not have assigned it to the transferee with the result that when the transferees were paid the commission under the terms of the managing agency Agreements, the transferees received the same in their own right even though they had not rendered the service to the Company for the whole of the calendar year 1943. Held, further, that the mere ownership of Managing Agency cannot as a matter of law be treated as the source of income, as explained above, any term in the Managing agency Agreement between the principal and the agent entitling only the assignee to receive the year 's remuneration and negativing to the assignor any direct recourse to his quondam principal for his share of income.

The appellant was a resident of the District of Gonda. He had two sons, Badri and Kirpa Shanker. The deceased and the accused 's second son, Kirpa Shankar (P.W. 17) slept in the room inside the house; and on the early morning of August 13, 1963, Sunderpatti was found with serious injuries in the rooms of the house where she was sleeping and the appellant was not in the house. The only other inmate of the family was the appellant 's first son, who died in the hospital. The trial court convicted the accused under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced him to death. On appeal a Division Bench confirmed both the conviction and sentence. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the soliloquy of the accused admitting his guilt was not an extra judicial confession as the courts below held it to be. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: (1) The evidence in the case is circumstantial. It certainly corroborates the circumstantial evidence adduced in the ease. [89C] (2) A confessional solilADH Guaranty is a direct piece of evidence. It may be an expression of conflict of emotion; a conscious effort to stifle the pricked conscience; an argument to find excuse or justification for his act; or a penitent or remorseful act of exaggeration of his part in the crime. The tone may be soft and low; the words may be confused; they may be capable of conflicting interpretations depending on witnesses, whether they are biased or honest, intelligent or ignorant, imaginative or prosaic, as the case may be. [90D E] (3) A confession is a substantive piece of Evidence. It can be an express expression of contradiction of emotion. a conscious attempt to stifate the proonked conscience and an argument that such evidence cannot be made the sole ground of conviction. [91E F] (4) The word "statement" in section 157 meant only "something that is stated" and the element of communication was not necessary before "s something that is mentioned" became a statement under that section. If, as it was an extrajudicial confession, it would really partake the character of direct evidence rather than that of circumstantial evidence. [92F G] (5) A retracted solil Guaranty does not depend upon its communication to another, though just like any other piece ofevidence, it can be admitted in evidence only on proof. This proof in the present case is corroborated by the circumstantial circumstantial evidence and in the instant case. [93G H; 94A B] (6) A statement whether communicated or not admitting guilt is a confession of guilt guilt. But there is a clear distinction between the admissibility of an evidence and the weight to be attached to it. A confessional Solil Guarantay is adirect piece of testimony. It might be an act of conflict or emotion; conscious effort may be hard and low, the words might be confused. They may be incapable of conflicting interpretation depending on witness witnesses, if they are bias or honest intelligent or ignorance, imagine or prohibic,asic, or as the ease may be [93D E; 94B C] (7) A confessions are a direct pieces of evidence and it may be either an expression or a conscious endeavour to stifles the prust conscience; but there is no reason why the statement implied in the confession should be given (1).

The appellant was working as Divisional Manager at Delhi, the general insurance business was nationalised and its management was taken over by the Central Government under General Insurance (Emergency Provisions) Ordinance, 1971 replaced by Act 57 of 1972. The appellant was kept under suspension from August 9, 1973 pending investigation into the embezzlement, Explanation was called for on October 16, 1973 in response thereto the appellant submitted his reply on December 7, 1974. While dropping the proceeding, the appellant was served with termination order dated April 17, 1975 issued by the respondent. The services of the appellant and others stood transferred and vested with the custodian. Under the Act, the Board of Directors was empowered to terminate the service of the officer/employee of the insurer. The Central Government framed the New India Assurance Co operative Society Ltd. Merger Scheme 1973 with effect from December 31, 1973. Thereunder by Rule 3, the undertaking was transferred to the respondent; under Rule 5 the existing whole time officer etc. became the officer of the transferee company (New Indian Assurance Co. Ltd.) and could hold his office on the same terms and conditions as would have been admissible to him if there had been no such transfer, as referred to in paragraph 3. He shall continue to remain an officer unless and until his employment in the transferee Company is terminated or the terms and condition are duly altered by any other scheme framed under the Act. By Notification dated April 29, 1976 the Central Govt. also framed the scheme called the General Insurance(Rationalisation of pay scales and other Conditions of Service of Development Step) Scheme 1976 which came into force on May 1, 1976, the details of which are not material for the reason that service of appellant was terminated in terms of the existing rule 5 of the Rules. The respondent also challenged it in a writ petition in Delhi High Court which was dismissed by a learned Single Judge on November 11, 1983 and was confirmed by the Division Bench in Letter Patent Appeal No.351/1984 dated April 23, 1984. Section 7 of the Act provides that every whole time Officer or other employee of an existing insurer employed in connection with his General Insurance business immediately before the appointed day, shall become an officer/ employee of the Indian Insurance Co.

The Collector of Mayurbhanj issued a notice on February 3, 1970 by which he invited tenders for the grant of li cences for establishing 70 outstill shops for 1970 71. Ajodhya Prasad Shah gave the highest bid for a group of seven shops, in one lot, for Rs. 34,000/ per month. His bid was accepted and his name was entered in the prescribed register, and the entry was signed by the successful bidder and the Collector. Ajendra Prasad Shah deposited Rs. 329 of 1970) in the High Court with the allegation that the Collector was not acting according to law as the State Government had issued instructions to him not to issue the licenses. The High Court quashed the said notice on the ground that section 29(2)(a) did not authorise the exercise of "such absolute and naked power" in determining the sum of money as was sought to be done by the order dated August 19, 1970. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the State that (1) the High Courts erred in holding that the sale notice issued by the Collector did not for itself absolute and arbitrary power; (2) the State had no power to interfere with the auction held by the Collec tor after it had "become final in appeal and revision", and (3) the order left it to the uncontrolled discretion of the authority concerned to determine the adequacy of the amount offered in the tender. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.

The appellant was charged with having entered into crimi nal conspiracy with an approver. The prosecution case was that the deceased and his wife were friends and that the appellant had a common intention to kill him. The evidence showed that the murder and the theft formed the same transaction and were committed by the same persons. The High Court found that there was corroboration of the evidence which connected accused No. 2 not only with the offence of theft but also with murder. The appellant contended that there could be no corroboration in regard to accused No, 2 and 3 being guilty of the offence. HELD : (i) It is well settled that an accomplice is competent to depose but as a rule of caution it will be unsafe to convict upon his testimony alone. [620 E] (ii) The warning of the danger of convicting on uncorroborated evidence is given when the evidence is that of an accomplice. [625 G] (iii) It may consist of the testimony of second witness or of circumstances like the conduct of the person against whom it is required. Corroboration must connect or tend to connect the accused with the time. When it is said that the corroborative evidence must implicate the accused in material particulars it means that it is not enough that a piece of evidence tends to confirm the truth of a part of the statement to be corroborated. That evidence must confirm that part of tho testimony which suggests the crime was committed by accused No 2. If a witness says that the accused and he stole the sheep and he put the skins in a certain place, the discovery of the skins would not corroborate the evidence of the witness as against the accused.

The appellant was the lessee of a Town Planning Scheme, Surat. The Town Planning Officer awarded compensation to the appellant at the rate of Rs. 2.40 p. per sq. by his order dated November 4, 1971. Not satisfied with the decision of the Town Planning officer the appellant preferred an appeal before the Board of Appeal. Before the Board the appellant reduced his claim to Rs. 9.50 p. by its order dated December 4, 1972. The appellant challenged the order of the Board before the Gujarat High Court by filing a writ petition in which certain provisions of the Act were also challenged as unconstitutional and it was claimed 85 that the town planning scheme was invalid. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appeal preferred by his client before the board of Appeal was maintainable he would not press the grounds questioning the constitutional validity of the impugned Act at this stage and the matter should then go back to the Board for a decision on the adequacy of the compensation; if however it found that the Board 's appeal was incompetent, he would then urge the grounds challenging the vires of the provisions at this Stage and the matters should then went back to Board of Appeals for a determination on the sufficiency of the Compensation. The question is whether the order determining the amount of compensation payable to the Appellant falls within any of the appealable clauses of section 32(1). Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. Under section 64 (1) of the Land Acquisition Act compensation is determined on the basis of "market value" of the land on the date of the notification under section 4 (1). It is a principle applicable to all cases in which by virtue of the operation of the town Planning Act a person is deprived of his land whether in whole or in part. [90G] 2.

One Viswanatha Iyer died in 1934. He had no male issue but left two daughters surviving him who were minors at the time of his death. He made a will on October 4, 1927, appointing his brother Seetharama as guardian of his minor daughters as well as of his foster son. The appellant was the third son of Seetharamamma. He left the management of his properties to his brother and provided that as soon as his minor daughter attained majority he should give to them per head one veli nanja land and one vela of punja land in vattam No. 149 in village Nagampadi 976 and further provided that the said Seethara shall deliver possession of the remaining properties to the appellant immediately after he attained majority. It was also provided in the will that Seetharams should pay to the minor daughters the income from the properties devised to them after the death of the testator. The two daughters claimed possession of their lands and their claim was that they were entitled in law having regard to the provisions of the will to select their respective one vehi of anja land and another veli land from out of the land in Vattam. The trial court dismissed the suit but the High Court held that the English rule of benevolent construction that a legatee has a right to choose in such circumstances applies to India also and has further held that on the construction of the Will in this case the right to choosing was in the legatees and not in the legatee. On appeal by certificate, Held: (i) The testator appointed Seetharayamma as the guardian of the three children will be in possession so long as the three sons were minor and shall deliver posses sion of the properties to them. The words " he shall deliver Possession" are contrasted with the words "he shall deliver pos session to his son". (ii) The word "shall" used in section 89 is not restricted to a specific area of land but only to a specified area of lands and it can be inferred from the language used in the section. (iii) In the context the words in our opinion mean the same. Therefore, the direction of the Lord is that as long as three children obtain majority the guardian will deliver possession to them of the respective lands bequeathed to them must now be partitioned in the ordinary course. (iv) The rule of beneficial construction evolved in English law is not intended to give effect to wills which are not quite uncertain and which can be made certain should be called an artificial rule. It is only when the uncertainty is so great that there is no way of resolving it and finding out the intention of the executant that section 89 comes into play. But where the uncertainty in the testator 's intention to make a gift was clear, though there may be some difficulty because there is more property of that kind than actually bequeathed, that (1) (1860) 5 N.

The appellant, a co bhumidar, was the widow of one of his brothers. The respondents were in joint possession of the plots in dispute being co bhumidars, because after the abolition of Zamindari by the Uttar Pradesh Zamindari Abolition and Land Reforms Act 1950, the plaintiff appellant lost her title by operation of law. The allegation of the plaintiff that the defendants had committed fraud was stoutly denied. The trial court decreed the suit for joint possession in respect of Chakbandi plot Nos. 201 and 274 only. As regards plot No. 93, the dismissal of the appellant 's suit by the trial Court was upheld. In second appeal, the District Judge decreed the plaintiff 's Suit for joint Possession in respect thereof. Against this order, the defendants preferred an appeal before the High Court which allowed the appeal filed by the respondents and set aside the judgment of the District judge. The High Court proceeded on the basis that there was nothing to show that any fraud was practised upon the consolidation authorities so as to make the order a nullity. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 In view of the clear decision of this Court, referred to above, the High court erred in law in holding that the present suit was barred by section 49 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holdings Act. [868E] 1.2 The High court committed an error of record because the clear evidence of PW, Karbalai Begum, is to the effect that she was not at all informed about the consolidation proceedings and was assured by the defendants that they would take proper care of her share in any proceedings that may be instituted. This was accepted by the District Court and should not have been interfered with by the High Courts in second appeal. [888E] 2. The suit was contested by the defendant mainly on the ground that the respondents were co sharers of the land or plots in question and the plaintiff had absolutely no concern with them. It was further averred that although at some time before, the lands in dispute were joint but during the consolidation operations the plots were entered exclusively in the name of the defendants. The allegations of the plaintiffs that the defendant had practised a fraud on her by giving her an assurance that her share would be properly looked after by them and on this distinct understanding she had left the entire management of the properties to the defendants who also used to manage them. The Trial Court did not fully appreciate this part of the case made out by the plaintiff and the District Judges in clear terms accepted the same.

The petitioner was a Minister of the Union and there was no separate form even for the Prime Minister. The oath register is by the incumbent signed as Prime Minister and all other ministers sign as Ministers. He further indi cates that describing Shri Devi Lal as Deputy Prime Minister, while being sworn into office, he describes himself as Prime Ministers and this practice is in vogue eversince 1950. The petitioner challenged the appointment of Respondent No. 1 as Deputy Chief Prime Minister contending that the oath administered to him as Deputy Minister was not the oath in accordance with the prescrip tion of the Constitution. The High Court dismissed the petition for the reasons indicated above. Allowing the writ petition, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The essential requirement of Article 173 read with Form VII A was that the person taking the oath or making the affirmation would bear true faith and allegiance to the Constitution and uphold the sovereignty and integrity of India. [3H; 4A] 1.2. The words which precede this portion are merely descriptive of the person and of his nomination as a candidate. " In view of the clear statement made by the learned Attorney General that Respondent No 1 is just a Minister like other members of the Council of Ministers though he has been described as Deputy Cabinet Minister but the description of him as the Deputy Prime Ministers does not confer on him any powers of the Prime Ministers, along with his other submis sions, it is the first contention raised by the petitioner that the prescribed oath should be divided into two parts, one which is descriptive and the other which contains the sub stantial part. And according to him, as long as the substantial part is properly followed, a mere mistake or error in the descriptive part would not vitiate the oath. [4B C] 1:3. The requirement of article 173 read along with Form 7 A was clearly con tended and it was rightly held that Respondent 1 was just a minister like other member of the council of Ministers although he has described as the Prime Prime Minister but he has not been described in the affidavit.

The appellant, a carding and spinning department of the Carnatic Mills stopped work some at 4 p.m., some at 5 p. m. The strike ended completely. The apparent cause for the strike was that the management of the Mills had expressed its inability to comply with the request of the workers to declare the forenoon of the 1st November, 1948 as a holiday for solar eclipse. On the 3rd November, the strike ended totally. The appellant contended before the Labour Appellate Tribunal that the action of the 859 workers on the night of the Ist November did not amount to a strike and did not cause any interruption in the workers service. Held, that the decision of the Labour appellate Tribunal was clearly right and the conclusion could be avoided that the workers were acting in concert. That being so, the action by the workers on their night of 1st 11, 1948, fell within the definition of "strike" in section 2(q) of the . The decision of this Appellate Tribunal on this point is set aside. Held further, that in view of the facts and circumstances detailed in the adjudicator 's award this contention cannot be seriously considered. The decision was set aside and the decision was restored. The case remanded to the Industrial Tribunal for deciding whether the action was a strike as not amounting to a dismissal. Held also, that there was no force in the contention that stoppage of work on 1st11, 1948 amounted to a concerted action on the part of the worker and that several workers in their own individual capacity wanted leave on that date.

The respondent complainant, actor, photographer, exhibitor and distributor of that film, was convicted under section 292 I.P.C. for having committed an offence under section 293 I. P.C., by the Magistrate, after examining some witnesses, took cognizance of the offence and issued notice to the accused. Thereupon, the producer, namely, the present petitioner moved the High Court under section 482 Cr. P C. on the score that the criminal proceeding was an abuse of the judicial process and engineered by ulterior considerations and that no prosecution could be legally sustained in the circumstances of the case, the film having been duly certified for public show by the Board of Film Censors, the public exhibition circulation or distribution or the production of the film even if it be obscene, lascivious or tending to deprave or corrupt public morals, cannot be an offence. The High Court dismissed the petition, ignoring the contention that the film had been given 'A ' certificate by the Central Board of film Censorors and finding in the prosecution nothing frivolous or vexatious nor any material to quash the proceedings. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: (1) Section 79 I.p.C is exculpatory when read with section 5A of the Act and section 79 of the Penal Code. The issue is of some importance since the cinema is one of the major mass media with millions of viewers and many millions in investment. [517G] (2) The resolution of the problem raised in this case thus becomes simplified. If the offender can irrefutably establish that he is actually justified by law in doing the act or, alternatively, that he entertained a mistake of fact and in good faith believed that he was justified by Law in committing the act, then, the weapon of section 79 demolishes the prosecution. [511B] (3) The Resolution of the problems raised in the case thus became simplified.[517C D] (4) Section 5A(1A) of the Prevention of Corruption Act is exculpatory while read with Section 5 A of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1952 and Part II of the , relating to certification of films.

The petitioner, a Government Pleader, was appointed as the sole representative of the Government Pleader for Patna District, authorised to represent 'Government in all civil cases. During the currency of his term a plurality of nine Assistant Government Pleaders was appointed and one of them was put in charge of a bunch of land acquisition cases. The petitioner challenged the power of Government, like any other litigant, to appoint any other lawyer except under him and never by excluding him. He went to the extent of writing to the Government: "I am, therefore unable to comply with your instruction in allowing any Assistant Government Pleader to work in this case. I shall myself conduct this case and have enough time for it." " Government wrote back that in future he would not be given such cases. Chagrined by this loss of income and mayhem to his monopoly he rushed to the High Court for the universal panacea of a writ. The chemistry of Article 226 is governed by severe rules, and the High Courts declined to dispense the magic remedy. So he has sought special leave from this Court but Article 136 has its own conditions and limitations. Sans substantial question of law of public importance which deserves to be decided by the Supreme Court or at least flaw in law which is fraught with manifest injustice, there is no other open sea for this House of Justice. That password has not been uttered here despite exercise in professional martyrdom the petitioner claims to have suffered and so he has prayed for special leave. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in ordering about a Government pleader is obnoxious but nothing savouring of such conduct is made out although we must enter a caveat that Governments under our Constitution shall not play with law offices on political or other impertinent considerations as it may affect the legality of the action and subvert the rule of law itself. [766C] 2. The essential criteria are, source of the office, the tenure and the duties. I have applied that test and am of opinion that the conclusion that the office is a public office is irresistible. In this view, ordering about the Government pleader was obnoxious but something savouring or of such act is made clear although we cannot subscribe to the U.S. Chief Justice Burger) Law Reform includes any officer appointed by the State Government to perform all or any of the functions expressly imposed by this Code on the Government Advocate and also any pleader acting under the directions of the government Pleader. [764E F] 3. The duties of the Govern ment Pleader, Madras are duties of a public nature. Besides as already stated the public are genuinely concerned with the manner in which he discharges his duties. [774G H] 4. The State is expected to fight and win its cases and sheer patronage is misuse of power. One effective method of achieving this object is to act on the advice of the District Judge regarding the choice of Government pleaders. When there were several thousand cases in the Patna courts and hundreds of cases before a plurality Of tribunals, it was but right that Government did not sacrifice the speedy conduct of cases by not appointing a number of lawyers on its behalf, for the sake of the lucrative practice of a single Government Pleader. It is inconceivable how he would have discharged his duties to the court and to his client if this crowd of land Acquisition cases were posted in several courts more or less at the same time. adjourn to suit advocates ' convenience becomes a bane when it is used only for augmentation of counsel 's income, resisting democratisation and distributial justice within the profession. These principles make poor appeal to, those who count, which is a pity. [754C E] 5.

The appellants held out of a total issue of 800 shares of the Navjivan Mills Ltd., Kalol, a public limited company. The shares were issued at a premium of Rs. 50. The shareholders had to pay Rs. 100 for each new share. The Mills as the holder of 5,000 shares became entitled to receive 1,6662 shares of that Bank at the rate of Rs 100 per share. In the assessment of the seven appellants and other shareholders of the Mills was reopened under section 34(1)(a) of the Indian Income Tax Act by the Income tax Officer on the footing that the release by the Mills amounted to a distribution of "dividend" within the meaning of section 2(6A). The order of the Income Tax Officer reassessing the income of the 7 appellants was confirmed in appeal by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and by the Tribunal. At the instance of the appellants, the i following question was referred by the High Court at Bombay under section 66(1) of Income tax Act: "Whether on the facts and circumstances of the case the distribution of the right to apply for the shares of Bank of India by Navjivivan Mills Limited in favour of the assessees amounted to distribution of dividend within the expression of section2(6 A) of Indian Income tax, 1922. " Held, that the High court was right in holding that the distribution Of the right of the Bank to apply to and obtain two shares of its Bank ofIndia amounted to 'distribution of dividend". The resolution did not purport to distribute the right amongst the shareholders as dividend. It took the form of distribution of a right which had a monetary value. But by the form sanctioning the distribution, the true character of the resolution could not be altered.

The appellant, who was the returned candidate, challenged the election of the 1st respondent to Haryana Legislative Assembly from Jind Legislative Assembly constituency. The petition was contested by the returned candidates. After going through the pleadings of the parties, the Court ascertained the points on which parties were at variance and framed appropriate issues. The election petition reached the stage of recording evidence. It appears an application was filed by the appellant seeking permission to produce and examine witnesses whose names were set out in the application. It was averred in the petition that the names of the witnesses whom he desired to produce were already mentioned in the appropriate paragraphs of the election petition and that the petitioner would keep the witnesses present. The learned Judge to whom the election petitions were assigned made an order on November 29, 1982 that as and when witnesses are produced, appropriate orders will be passed determining whether the witnesses could or could not be produced. In the meantime, the evidence of election petitioner was being recorded. It appeared that again on January 11, 1983, petitioner submitted a list of witnesses intimating to the Court that he desires to examine them. This was objected to by the respondent. The Judge after hearing the parties made an Order upholding the objection raised by the election petitioner that the purpose for which the witnesses were offered is not mentioned in his list and therefore, the election Petitioner could not he permitted to examine more witnesses whose name had not been mentioned in accordance with the relevant provisions of the Code of Civil Procedure and the rules framed by the High Court. The appellant challenged this order before the High court. The High Court allowed the petition holding that except Bahre son of Sher Singh no other witness could be examined and that as soon as the evidence was recorded, the court would proceed to record the evidence on behalf of the returned petitioner; and thereafter the matter will be set down for hearing oral arguments of the learned counsel of either side. It also held that except H.L.C. appeal, the High Courts have introduced a proviso to sub section (4) of Rule 1 of order XVI. The scheme is that after the Court framed issues which gives notice to the parties what facts they have to prove for succeeding in the matter which notice would enable the parties to determine what evidence oral and documentary it would like to lead, the party should file a list Of witnesses with the gist of evidence of each witness in the court within the time prescribed by sub rule (1). This advance filing of list is necessary because summoning the witnesses by the Court is a time consuming process and to avoid the avoidable delay an obligation is cast on the party to file a List of witnesses whose presence the party desires to procure with the assistance of the Court.

% The appellant, a double M.A. and holding a Doctorate applied in response to an advertisement that appeared in Hindi Daily Bhirgu A Chetna and Dainik Jagran on May 18, 1980 for the post of Principal. Pursuant to this decision of the Selection Committee, the Manager of the College issued an appointment order dated April 27, 1981 to the appellant informing him that the Committee of Management had appointed the appellant as Principal on one year probation in the scale of 550 1200 at initial pay alongwith DA admissible under the rules. The appellant was required to present himself before the Manager and take over charge within 10 days of the receipt of the order failing which the appointment would be void. On receipt of this letter, the appellant wrote to the Manager that as permitted by him he has assumed charge of the post and he has convened an urgent meeting of the staff to be held on the same day after college hours in the teachers ' room. The Committee of management of the college issued an order dated May 1, 1981 communicated by a radiogram to the various authorities. It reads as under: "From Secretary to Government of U.P. Education Department No. 1701/l5 7 FI 1 (27)/81 dated 1.4.1981 Stop all fresh selections and appointments of Principals Headmasters and teachers including recruitment by promotion in all non government aided secondary schools except minority institutions pending further orders(.) District Inspectors to ensure non drawal of pay of teachers appointed after his date(.) Detailed instructions follow(.)" Pursuant to the receipt, the District Inspector of Schools, Ballia had sent a copy of it to the College. There was some dispute between the parties as to whether this copy of radiograms was received by the Management of the Colleges but there is a letter dated May I, 1981 addressed by the District Superintendent of Schools to the college. The Manager replied that as per the radiogam had suspended or withdrawn its power. The State Government issued an Order dated April 7, 1981 stopping all fresh selection and appointments and of Principals etc. in all Non government aided schools except non minority institutions. The order was challenged before the High Court under Article 226 of the Constitution praying for a writ of mandamus directing the 5th respondent, the Committee, of Management of which had been impleaded as respondent No. 5, the Principal of the institution, not to interfere with the work of the appellant discharging his duties as Principal of that College and also to pay salary. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The appointment was otherwise valid though ineffective and if appellant under the orders of the High court functioned as Principal, discharged his duties and was paid, no question of recovery of amount paid to him could arise and neither the Government nor the Committee would be entitled to recover any salary paid to the Appellant. [978G] 1.2 The appointment of the appel lant was otherwise invalid though ineffective. If appellant under orders of High Court functioned in contravention of the provisions of the Act, the State Government was bound to hear the appellant before making any consequential order.

The appellants, manufacturers of tyres to whom the fabric is supplied "impregnate the fabric with rubber and weave it into a fabric in the same way as is being done by the first appellant. The goods were sold by the Delhi Cloth & General Mills Co. Ltd., to manufacturers of tyre cord fabric. After indicating the manner in which and substance out of which "rayon tyre cord fabrics" was made and its composition, the petition sets out item 22 of the first schedule of the Central Excises and Salt Act, 1944 as the applicable entry covering the goods manufactured by the appellants. This item reads as follows: "18. All cotton fabrics, rayon or artificial silk fabrics shall have the meanings respectively assigned to them in Items Nos. 1, 4, 19, 20, 21 and 22 of First Schedule to the Central Excise and Salt (Central) Act,1944." The petitioners state that the manufacturers of goods to whom they the fabric was supplied " Impregnating the fabric" with rubber fall under entry 18 of the Schedule of the Rajasthan Sales Tax Act, 1954. They further contended that, from years 1966 to 1969, the respondent Commercial Tax officer was not subjecting the goods of this description to sales tax and accepted the case of the petitioners that they were exempt from taxation. The reasoning of the Commercial Tax Officer, in exempting these goods, is also mentioned. It is then stated that as some questions were put in the Rajasthan State Legislative Assembly on or about 20th April 1971 asking for the reason why this particular type of goods of the appellants were exempted from Sales tax, the Commissioner of Commercial Tax issued a letter to the Commercial Taxes Officer to levy Sales tax on the "ray on cord fabric" manufactured by it. Thereafter, notices under the proviso to section 12(1) of the Act were issued for the years 1965 to 1969 with a view to reopening the assessments on the ground that the sales of these goods had wrongly escaped assessment. The petitioners contended that they are exempt from tax and that they should first resort to alternative remedies provided under the Act so that the appellate authority under section 13 of the said Act may go into the whole evidence and decide disputed questions of fact. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Court was right in not interfering with the decisions of the taxing authorities at this stage. [501C] 2. It was not a case on which two views seem possible on apparent facts. And, neither of the two views can be rejected outright as untenable. It requires careful consideration of the technical processes of manufacturing, of the composition of the "tyre cord fabric". and an evaluation of opinion of experts on the subject, to be able to decide the question satisfactorily may also require some examination of commercial usage and terminology or the language of the market in goods of that type. [500D] 2:1 The word "textile" has a wide meaning. Its first meaning given in the Oxford English Dictionary is: "A product of skilled workmanship". The first example of such a product is: 'An edifice, a building." The fourth example of the First meaning is: (I) manufactured material; now only a 'textiles ' as fabrics.

The appellant company was engaged in construction of coal. The management held domestic enquiry into the incident and found him guilty of committing theft. He was dismissed from service. The dispute arising therefrom was referred under Section 10(1)(c) of the Act to Labour Court Dhanbad for adjudication. The Labour Court registered the case as refer ence case No. 4 of 1988 and issued notice to the parties. The parties entered appearance and filed their respective pleadings. When the matter was thus pending consideration, the respondent seems to have written to the Government stating that it would be difficult for him to attend the Labour Court, Dhanbad since he has been residing at Hajipur and it would he convenient for him if the case is trans ferred to Labour court Patna. That application was made without intimation to the management. The Government acceded to the request of the respondent and without opportunity to the Management transferred the case to Labour Appellate Court Patna. The Notification issued in that regard reads as follows: " NOTIFICATION Patna dated 8th August 1988 S.O. In exercise of powers conferred by sub section (1) of Section 33 B of the , the Governor of Bihar after careful consideration of the application of the petitioner Shri Shivajee Prasad Sinha wherein he has prayed for the transfer of adjudication proceedings to Patna keeping in view the difficulties expressed by him to attending the labour court, Dhanbad regu larly due to his residence at Hajapur is pleased to withdraw the proceeding shown in Annexure 'A ' pending before Labour Court. " The management moved the High Court by way of writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution to have the Notification quashed. The High Court did not agree and summarily dismissed the writ petition with an observation: "Since no prejudice is being caused to the petitioner and no allegation of mala fide has been made against the presiding officer, Patna, we are not inclined to interfere with the order under challenge. This application is dismissed". Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Government was misled by the representation of the workman. [295C] 1.2 In the instant case, the State has withdrawn the pending refe rence from the Labour court, Patna and transferred it to another Labour Court at the distant District of Patna on the representation af ters of the workmen without getting it veri fied from the management, without getting them verified by giving an opportunity to manage which is a party to the pending reference. Denial of that opportunity is a fatal flaw to the decision of the Government.

The appellant, the manager of a hotel, was dismissed by an Industrial Tribunal on the ground that it did not specify how many of the 480 workers of thirty different categories working in the hotel were involved in the dispute. The High Court dismissed the writ application holding that the reference was incompetent and two grounds had been urged in support of it. Held, further, that the appeal must be dismissed with costs to respondent No. 3. (i) The question whether a particular workman is entitled to be represented by an officer of a trade union of which he is a member is essentially a technicality upon technicality for the union not being a living person can only be served through some officer, such as its president or secretary and it is that officer who will really represent the workmen before the tribunal. (ii) The fact that in the order of reference the word "as represented by the Hotel Workers ' Union, Katra Shahanshahi Chandni Chowk, Delhi " has been added for the sake of convenience so that the Tribunal may know to whom it should send a notice on behalf of the workmen whose number is generally very large. (iii) The nature of the dispute is also specified in the terms of reference. It was entirely unnecessary to mention in the judgment of reference as to who were the workmen who were responsible for the dispute, and the nature of that dispute is further specified in, the terms thereof. State of Madras vs C. P. Sarathy, [1953] S.C.R. 334, followed.

The appellant, a motor carhings and bearings imported by the appellant, was entitled to the benefit of the Notification No. 281 Cus/76 granting part exemption from payment of Customs duty in respect of the rod bushes and camshaft bushes imported by it. The appellant claimed that the bushings were the same and as the bearings came under the Heading No. 84.63 and not under Heading 84.06, they are not entitled to benefit of exemption under the said Notification. The Customs, Excise and Gold (Control) Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal of the appellant and affirmed the orders of the Customs authorities. According to the Appellate Tribunal, the busiings and the bear ings were the identical goods and as held by the Appellate Tribu nal and, as borneings have been provided for under Heading No 84.6, they were parts of the engines referred to in Heading No . 84. The Notification also exempted parts of engines mentioned under Heading Nos. 8406 and 84. In appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appel lant that even assuming that Heading No, 84.05 also contemplates parts of engine, such parts must be all the parts of tile engine and not a few parts thereof. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The intention of the notification is clear enough to provide that the parts in respect o fences specified under Heading no. 84,06 will get the benefit under the Notification and in the absence of any provision to the contrary, we are unable to hold that the part of the engine or engines mentioned in Heading 84,6 are excluded from the benefit Of the Notification. [226C D] 2. The Notifications do not mention 'parts ' of such engines.

The appellants and their counsel were the contesting parties in the suit filed by them as defendants. The Trial Court decreed the suit and in the operative part held that the plaintiffs were entitled to manage the Dargah for 27 days in February, 1972 (viz. from February 1 to February 27) and to 19 filed appeals aggrieved against the Judgment of the Trial Court while 7th defendant in the Suit filed cross objections in respect of a particular portion of the decree. The High Court allowed the second appeal and set aside the judgments and decrees of the Courts below dismissing the suit. Hence this appeal by the plaintiffs. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 A perusal of the Judgment in the above case goes to show that there was no ouster in the facts of the present case. The defendants were carrying a mistaken impression all along that females under the Muslim Law were not entitled to any right or management of the offerings in the Dargah and on that account they were pleading an ouster of Fathima Bee as well as the plaintiffs, [529C] 1.2 A perusal thereof shows that neither in the written statement nor in reply to the notice of the plain tiffs any stand was taken that the right of Fthima Bee or plaintiffs was specifically denied on any particular occa sion so as to put them on notice that from that date the possession of the defendants would be adverse to the inter est or rights of the plaintiffs of Fafima Bee. [530D] 1:3 There is no dispute now as regards the period of 27 days falling to the share of the appellants and on the question that females are also entitled in the right and management of Dargah according to Muslim Law. Thus the only controversy now left to be determined is whether the High Court was right in holding that the rights of F Thathima Sai Bee had become barred by ouster and as such the plaintiffs who were also claiming through Fathiman Bee had lost their right by ouster? It would first be necessary to make it clear as to what is the impact of the judgment decree dated 11.8.1910 passed in Civil Suit No. 116 of 1909, so far as the present litigation is concerned.

The first respondent was a gangman in the employ of the Central Railway. At that time his wages were Rs. 18 per month plus dearness allowance.
