With effect from 1st November 1947, the Railway Board introduced a scheme of grant of compensatory (city) allowance and house rent allowance at rates specified in their memorandum No. E47 CPC/14 dated 1st December 1947. The 1st respondent thus became entitled to the allowance of Rs. 10 per month. This allowance was however stopped with effect from the 19th August 1948. On the 8th June 1951, the 1st Respondent put in his claim before the Authority for Rs. 290 on the ground that the house rent allowances which were subject matter of the claim was not "wages" within the meaning of section 2(vi) of the Act. The Authority condoned the delay and condoned the same. On appeal by special leave to this Court, HELD: (i) The rules which must be included in the terms of contract between the employer and the employee contemplate that an employee posted at one 173 1352 of the specified places would be entitled to house rent Allowance; but that as soon as he is offered Government quarters for his accommodation he ceases to be so entitled. [1350 C] (ii) The house rent in the first instance is not admissible to all the employees of a particular class. It is admissible only to such railway employees as are posted at specified places in order "to compensate railway servants in certain costlier cities for excessive rents paid by them over and above what they might normally be expected to pay". [1351 E F] (iii) The definition of "wages ' under the Act cannot include the value of any house accommodation supplied by the employer to the employee; otherwise it would not be a legally permissible deduction from wages. It Is equally clear that house rent grant which may in certain circumstances as aforesaid be included In "wages", is not the same thing as the value Of any house accommoda tion referred to in the Act, because it is no more payable under the terms Of the contract.

The detenu was one Indru 's Ramchand Bharvani; while in Writ Petition 435/80, the detenu was carrying on business in diamonds and precious stones in partnership under the style of "M/s. Gems Impex Corporation". 35, New Marine Lines, Bombay since 1971. On November 16, 1979, the Customs Officers raided the residential premises of the son Indru"s son Indu 's son, Indru Ramchand, Bharvani, and seized two cameras and three wrist watches worth about Rs. 55 lakhs and also some jewellery and Rs. 1,40,000 in Indian currency and two gold sovereign coins. On the following day, the customs officers raided the premises of M/s Gemsimpex Corporation. The detenu were arrested on November 23, 1979 and interrogated. During interrogation, the detenus claimed that the gems and other articles seized were not smuggled goods but were local materials locally acquired. They also gave the names of four persons from whom these gems had been acquired. Both the father and son were arrested and were produced before a Magistrate. The detention order was authenticated by the Under Secretary to the State Government, who advised the State Govt. to furnish the detenus with the material relied upon by the detaining authority in the grounds of detention. On March 25, 1980, the wife of the detenu addressed a letter to the first respondent (Under Secretary to Government of Maharashtra), requesting him to furnish them with the materials relied upon in the ground of detention and on March 24, 1980 the detenu also made a representation to the Central Government which, according to the information furnished at the Bar by the detenu, was declined. The State Government informed the detenu that the copies had been refused in exercise of its power under Article 22(6) of the Constitution, but the request for revocation had been rejected. On April 3, 1980 copies were received by the detenus from the State government under their covering letter dated March 31, 1980. On February 18, 1980 an order of detention was authenticated and authenticated by Under Secretary, to the Government of India, Home Department, in reply to the latter 's letter, dated March 14, 1980 was served on the detenu alongwith the order of Detention on February 16, 1980 purporting to have been made under Section 3(1) of COFEPOSA. The grounds of deten tion were also served on them along with the order dated March 25. On May 18,1980, the husband of the detenue addressed a communication to the Collector of Customs (Preventive), Bombay requesting him not to supply copies of the necessary documents. The detenus were arrested by a Magistrate and released on heavy bail subject to the condition that they would attend daily before the Customs officers and cooperate in the investigation. This condition was later on related. On June 18, 1981, an order purporting to be made under section 3(2) of detention Act by the State Govern ment was served upon the detenus alongwith the grounds and documents relied upon. The first respondent filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the detention mainly on the ground that (1) the detaining authori ty had no authority to pass the order, (2) the detenu had got a right to be afforded a fair and full opportunity of making an effective representation against his detention; and (3) there was non application of mind on the part of the detaining Authority. The High Court allowed the writ petition and directed the release of the detention. Allowing the appeal by special leave, ^ HELD: 1.1. The constitutional imperatives enacted in Article 22 (5) are two fold: (i) the Detaining authority must, as soon as may be, that is, as expeditiously as practicable after the detention communicate to the detenu the grounds on which the order has been made; and and (ii) the detention authority must afford the detenu earliest opportunity of being making a representation against the detention order. [352A B] 1.2.

The Gujarat High Court in its order referred to ss 258, 410, 417 and 423 of the Code and came to the conclusion that the scheme of Chapter XXXI of the code as disclosed by these sections and particularly by section 419 is against the maintainability of a joint appeal by the State against an order acquitting several accused persons tried jointly. The High Court also recorded the main judgment only in Criminal Appeal No. 60 of 1965. The question which arose for determination was whether, several accused person jointly tried have been acquitted by the trial court, the state can prefer one appeal against the acquittal of all them. The Gujarat High court in its Order referred to SS 258, 418 and 423 Cr. P.C. and came ting to the conclu sion that the Scheme of Chapter XXVIII of the Bombay High Court Appellate Side Rules, 1960 was inconsistent with Chapter XXXI Of the Code of Criminal Procedure, with the result that a joint appeals by several accused against them are not maintainable under section 482 Cr.P.C., and so holding rejected the appeal by it without going into the merits. The Division Bench of the High Court held that r. 6 in Chapter XXVI of the Act as disclosed in these sections is against its maintainability, and in summarily rejecting the same. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) A joint appeal must be sustained. [879 E] (2) The power to frame this rule is specifically conferred on the High court by section 554(2)(c) Cr.

The appellant was a firm carrying on money lending business in India and in the former Federated Malaya States and it was assessed under the Indian Income tax Act, 1918. The family which consisted of Meyyappa Chettiar and his two brothers carried on money lent business in the latter FederatedMalaya States. In the course of assessment for the year 1939 40 it was claimed by M that having regard to the severance of joint family status, the income from April 13, 1938 to June 2, 1938 was not liable to be taxed by reason of the provisions of section 25(3) and (4). The Income tax Officer accepted the fact of partition amongst the members of the family but rejected the contention that the family was not entitled to claim relief under section 25 (3) of the 1922 Act. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, allowed the appeal of the assessee in part. Both the assessee and the Department applied to the appellate Tribunal for reference of the questions of law to the High Court. The High Court held that the foreign business of the appellant was at any time charged under the provisions Of the 1918 Act within the meaning of section 2(3), and accordingly answered both the questions in favour of the Department. In appeal by certificate, HELD: (1) The assessee received the entire profits of the foreign company in British India and the entire income were assessed to income tax in the hands of the asses see under the 1918 act. [908 B] (2) The High ' Court was in error in holding that the Indian business of M was not charged under section 3 Of the 1922Act because what was taxed was the remittances received by the assessee from the foreign source and not the foreign income itself. [ 909 C D] Commissioner of Income tax, Madras vs section V.R.M Palaniappa Chettiar and Others, ; , followed. (3)(a) The words "on which" in section 25 of the Indian 1922 Act cannot be interpreted as meaning "with reference to which" and that in order to claim and avail the benefit under section 5(4), the tax clearly should be charged on the business as such under the 1922 act.

The respondent entered into a contract with the Public Works Department of the Government of Gujarat on September 6, 1965 for manufacture and supply of kiln burnt bricks to the said department for construction of Capital Project, Ghandhinagar. Large quantities of bricks were manufactured and supplied under the contract and the applicant received payment for the same in accordance with the agreed rates. The assessee made an application under section 52 of the Bombay Sales lax Act, 1959 on November 19, 1967 to the Deputy Commissioner of Sales Tax to determine the question whether the said supplies of bricks by the respondent to the Public works Department were sales or works contract. The Deputy Commissioner held that the supply of bricks was sales and that at the instance of the assessee, the Tribunal referred the following question of law to the High Court: "Whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case the transaction envisaged by the contract entered into by the applicant with the public Works Department for the manufacture and sale of kiln burning bricks to it Department and the supply thereof to the aforesaid department in terms of their running Bill No. XI dated 28th October 1967 is a sale or a works contract ? The High Court answered the question in favour of the respondent holding that the transaction was a works Contract. In coming to this conclusion, the High court held as follows: (1) The decision of the Supreme Court in Chandra Bhan Gosain vs The State of Orissa and others, [1971] 2 S.C.R. 879 is clearly distinguishable on facts; (2) The contract in that case was a contract of sale and not a works contracts. The question will depend upon the intention of the parties executing the contract. As it has observed in Chandra Nath Gosain 's case, this Court would completely govern the facts of this case. [162H; 163A] State of Gujarat vs Variety Body Builders (I) Ltd., ; and Chandra Bhan Maha Gosain`s case (supra). The question is not always easy and has for all time vexed jurists all over. The distinction between a contract for sale of goods and a contract to work and labour is often a fine one. A contract of Sale is contract whose main object is the transfer of the property in and the delivery of possession of a chattel as a chatte to the buyer. (Halsbury 's Laws of England Third Edition Volume 34 page 6.) The contract with which we are concerned in this appeal is found in a tender for the supply Of materials containing a memorandum of the conditions. The nature of work is described as manufacturing and supplying kiln burn bricks for constructionof Gandhinagar . The question would depend upon its true construction of the tender which on acceptance is treated here as the contract containing all the terms and conditions agreed upon between the two parties. In the tender, the assessee stated that he had earnest money for the purchase of materials described in the Schedule attached therewith subject to the condition annexed. The schedule described materials as bricks, and also stated quantities to be delivered, and "rate at which materials are to be supplied". The tender is described by "Supply of Materials Tender" which is described "Supply Of Material Tender". Although the above nomenclature, by itself is not decisive, it cannot be said that the same is justified by the principal terms governing the contract to which we will presently refer. "Clause 6:The contractor shall give notice to the Executive Engineer or his Assistant of his intention of making delivery of materials and on the materials being approved, receipt shall be granted to him by the Executive Engineers or his Assistants and no materials which is not so approved shall be considered to have been delivered. Clause 7: on the completion of the delivery, of materials, the contractor shall be furnished with a certificate to that effect, but the delivery shall not be considered complete until the contractor has removed all rejected materials, and shall have the approved materials, stacked or placed in such position as may be pointed out to him.

The petitioner, an assessee under the Income tax Act and Wealth Tax Act during the assessment year 1976 77, was assessed to income tax and wealth tax in accordance with the rates prescribed by the Finance Act, 1976 which was passed by the Lok Sabha during its extended period. The petitioner challenged the validity of the Proclamation of Emergency issued on 3rd December, 1971 by the President of India under Article 352 of the Constitution on the ground that the proclamation of Emergency had ceased to be in operation on 4th February, 1972 and the Proclamation had ceased not been published in the official Gazette of the Government of India. The contentions raised were (i) that the two Proclamations of Emergency dated 3rd Dec., 1971 and 25th June 1975 were either ultra vires the Constitution or had ceased by the time the House of the People (Extension of Duration) Act,1976; (ii) that even though the said Proclimations had been validly issued, the Proclamation ceased to operate in force on 3st February,1972 and the proclamation was revoked by him by the Proclamation dated 21st March, 1977. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1. The two Pro Clamations dated 3th Dec.,1971 and 25rd June 1975 are both in operation. [436C] 2.1 The resolution of the Lok Assembly approving the two resolutions have been duly published in two newspapers. The newspapers, radio and television are also the other modern means which give publicity to all Acts and resolutions of Parliament and the Legislatures of the States. The publication in the Parliamentary Debates though after 455 some short delay is adequate publication of the resolutions of the Parliament as there is no rule which requires that the resolutions should be published in official Gazette. [441E] 2:2. The production of the Rajya Sabha Debates and of theLok Sabha containing the proceedings of the two Houses of Parliament relating to the period between the time when the resolutions were moved in each of the Two Houses of parliament and the time, when the resolution was duly adopted amounts to proof of the said resolutions. [442G] 2 :3. The reports of the proceedings are widely circulated. The newspaper, radio & television are the journals or the reports of two Houses.

The appellant filed an application in the District Court for a declaration that the said premises were private property and for an order setting aside the said decision. The District Judge decreed the suit in favour of the appellant holding that the premises constituted a temple within the meaning of Madras Act 19 of 1951. On appeal, the High Court reversed the judgment and decree passed by the Trial Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the respondents that the property belonged to the Thogulu family and he was in management thereof for and on behalf thereof. HELD: (i) The suit in the first instance was filed by him in the form of an application, being O.P. No. 37 of 1950 under section 84(2) of Madras Hindu Religious and Charitable Endowments Act, Madras 11 of 1927. Under that Act only a fixed court fee was payable. That being so, the appellant did not have to pay court fees as it would in the case of an ordinary suit on a valuation made by him therefor. The application was subsequently converted into a suit by an order of the High court. He was therefore entitled to contend at the time of the leave application that the properties in dispute were of the value of not less than Rs. 20,000/ . [157 C] (ii) The appellant 's case was accepted by the trial Court but was rejected by the High 'High Court and the High Courts held that the subject matter of the dispute had to be ascertained with reference to the claim made by the plaintiff in his plaint and since according to the respondents the property was the private property of the said family capable of alienation, the District Judge ought to have valued the property accordingly though according to them the property is inalienable and was a public temple.

The appellant company, which had given rise to the present appeal centered round two items of claim made by the respondents. The respondents claimed that they should be given cash allowance in lieu of tiffin arrangements at present made by them and they urged that the practice started by the appellant of employing retired persons should be discontinued. The Tribunal held that the appellant was under an obligation to provide some cash allowance for tiff in lieu thereof, because he argued that it is not obligatory on the part of the appellant to make any provision for the tiffsin of its employees. Held, that the question posed by the respondent ' demand must be considered. The fact that the re employed persons have made an affidavit supporting the practice adopted by the appel lant can have no material bearing in dealing with the point; in the very nature of things, the said re employed person are bound to support the appellant. Chandi Charan Banerjee vs Union of India, ; , referred to. The question posed was whether the limited direction issued by the award is either improper or unjustified. The facts that the employ ers have made a representation supporting the practices adopted by them can have any material bearing on dealing with tiffing employees and, in fact, when after the award was pronounced in the proceedings of 1956 and this question was taken up for further negotiations between the parties, the appellant agreed to consider the claim sympathetically and make suitable provision in that behalf. Chandii Charan Banerjee 's case, , referred only to the facts of the case.

The respondent was an employee of the East India Railway and was a subscriber to the State Railway Provident Fund. He elected to be governed by the Provident Fund Sterling Accounts Rules, whereunder payment of the provident fund credited in his account in rupees was on retirement to be made in sterling. On August 26, 1947, Browne addressed a letter to the Financial Adviser and Chief Accounts Officer, East India Railways requesting that the amount standing to his credit in the Provident Funds Account be remitted to him by Bank Draft on the District Bank Water Street, Liverpool. After Browne retired from service, the Deputy General Manager, Eastern Railway, wrote a letter on July 27, 1955, to the Chief Accounts officer, communicating the sanction of the General Manager for payment of special contribution to provident fund to Browne in sterling in terms of r. 1410(1) of the Railway Establishment Code. Another communication was received from Browne (who had apparently by then migrated to the United Kingdom) on February 22, 1956, by which he requested that the amounts standing to their credit in his Provident Fund Account be sent to him through Bank Draft. The respondent thereupon filed a suit for attachment of the money lying in the executing court in the execution case which had been struck off. The Union of India resisted the suit contending that the money represented provident fund money and was immune from attachment under the law and that the attachment was "illegal and without jurisdiction". The trial Court overruled the objection observing that the seizure issued by the Court on December 8, 1956 was perfectly in order. The High Court confirmed the order passed by the executing Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the Union of india that by sending the two cheques to the Reserve Bank of India in performance of the manner of Payment prescribed by Browne, the debt was discharged and the money must be deemed to have been paid out to the subscriber Browne. HELD: The High court was in error in holding that the moneys in the hands of the Reserve bank had ceased to be provident fund and was liable to be attached. [31E] In order to carry out that obligation, the Accounts Officer of the railway made out two cheques in the name of Browne and sent them to the Bank for conversion of the amount into sterling. The Reserve Bank was the only authority which could permit such conversion in view of the 31 currency restrictions imposed by the Government of India.

The appellant, a Regional Manager of the respondent 's factory, was terminated by an order dated September 2, 1970. The management challenged the termination as illegal and/or unjustified on the ground that the action being a simple termination without a sting process and consequence of a disciplinary action were not attracted. The Labour Court held that the punishment was not a disguise or cloak for dismissing the employee but merely bid him good bye. On appeal, the High Court set aside the order of the Labour Court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (1) the workman was being entrusted with stores worth several lakhs of rupees, some goods were lost from the stores and the Union was informed by the management that it had lost confidence in the employee; (2) the action was bona fide and the overall unsuitability led to a loss of confidence in him; and (3) the punishment imposed was not one of dismissal as and by way of punishment. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The workman in his statement before the Labour court was that although he was efficient, appreciated and awarded merit increments, the management was antagonized by his active part in the formation of an Employees ' Union especially because oral warnings by the Regional Manager against his Unionist proclivity were ignored. As such, this letter may be treated as a notice for the termination of his services with immediate effect. [490C] 2. The termination simpliciter may be bow fide, not colourable, and loss of faith may be evidentiary of good faith of the employer. Some testimony of unseemly attempts by the workman to get at secrets outside his orbit, some indication of the source of suspicion, some proof of the sensitive or strategic role of the employee should and would have been forthcoming had the case been bona fide. [495E F] 3. The loss of interest was often a subjective feeling or individual reaction to an objective set facts and motivations. The Court is concerned with the latter and not with the former, although circumstances may exist which justify a genuine exercise of the power of simple termination. In a reasonable case of a confidential or responsible post being misused or a sensitive or sensitive oristic position being abused, it may be a high risk to keep the employee, once suspicion has started and a disciplinary en quiry cannot be forced on the master. There, a termination simpliciter might be bow bonafide, not fraudulent, but ingeniously passes an innocent looking order of termination simpliciter, such action is bad and is liable to be set aside. Loss of confidence is no new Armour for the management; otherwise security of tenure ensured by the new industrial Jurisprudence and authenticated by a catena of cases of this Court, can be subverted by this neo formula. [596C E] 4. The law is simply this : The Tribunal has the power land, indeed, the duty to X ray the order and discover its true nature, ifhe object and effect, if the attendant circumstances and the ulterior purpose be to dismiss the employee because he is an evil to be eliminated. But if the management, to cover up the inability to establish by an enquiry, illegitimately but ingenlessly passes an innocuous looking order, of termination simplicitor, such act is bad, and is not liable to suffer any punishment. [498E F; 499A] 5. The power of the Court to go behind the form of the order, look at the substance and set aside what may masquerade as termination simpliciter if in reality it cloaked a dismissal for misconduct 'as a colourable exercise of power by the Management. The court is concerned only with the later and notwith the former. [500G] 6.

The petitioners, who were the State of U.P., and the Lions Club of Pottery Town in Uttar Pradesh, invited Dr. R.M. Sahay of the Sahay Hospital, Jaipur and his team of doctors to offer surgical services. The Camp was arranged in 'Aggarwal Dharamshala ' at Novelty Road, Khurja. Dr. Sahay returned on the 24th April and undertook himself some ameliorative treatment. But the operated eyes had been damaged completely. Similar mishap, but on lesser scale affecting some patients, repeated itself at Moradabad. Some of the victims were later sent to and treated at Dr. V.P. Sharma, who had himself brought all medicines and surgical instruments for use at the Camp claims to have purchased the Saline from a certain M/s Mehtaad Company, Jaipur on 22.3.1986 under Invoice No. 1533. Originally, the four respondents were the state of U .P., Dr.R.M., Sahay, the Chief Medical Officer, Buland Sahar District (U.P.) and the 'Lions Club ' of Potteries Town, Khurja; but this Court by its order dated 26.9.1986 directed the Indian Medical Council and the Union of India to be impleaded as parties to the proceedings. In the Writ Petition, the petitioners have made serious allegations about the very bona fides of, and the intention behind, the sponsoring of the iII fated 'eye camp ' and have alleged that motives of monetary gains by way of State and International subsidies. The prayers in the writ petition are that: (1) the victims of this medical misha p be given expert rehabilitatory treatment and appro priate compensation; (2) the Government do conduct a thorough investigation as to the conditions which rendered a medical misadventure of such a scale possible and evolve proper guide lines which will prevent recurrence of such tragedies; and (3) appropriate legal action be instituted against Dr. RP. RM. PATHAK and his staff also against officers of the Government who, according to allegations committed serious breaches of duty in sanctioning permission for the conduct of the 'eya camp ' without ensuring a strict compliance with the conditions prescribed in the guidelines prescribed by the Government in that behalf and in not effectively dis charging the duties enjoined upon them to over see the satisfactory and safe functioning of the camp. At the directions of the Govern ment, the Deputy Director (Eye Treatment) conducted an inquiry into the happenings and his report and recommendations submitted to the Government are produced in the proceedings, and that, indeed, a criminal case has been regis tered against Dr R. M. Sahay and his commis sioner Dr. S.RM.Prasad, who granted permis sions for the eye camp and who, allegedly, did not discharge their duties implicit in the guideline issued by Government. One of the points brought out in the petition is that the propaganda scruction published by the Les t Club in relation to the camp was that allurements prohibited by medical ethics were held out to the patients with attrac tive slogans such as 'Get Operated and go home ', 'No re striction of food ', `No bed rest ' and No stitches to be removed etc. It is now undisputed that this terrible medical mishp was due to common contaminating source. The suggestion in the Report of the 245 enquiries that ensued is that, in all probability, the source of the infection, referred to as E coli cation of the intra ocular cavity, was the "normal saline" used on the eyes at the time of surgery.

The petitioner Society was a registered society under the Indian Registration Act, 1908. The Society had its registered office at Gauhati and its head office at Shillong. It is a literary body and under Section 4 of the Bidban the objects of the Samiti have been stated thus: (a) To propogate and promote Hindi as a na tional language in Assam Meghalaya, Meghalaya, Mizoram, Nagaland, Manipur Tripura and Arunachal Pradesh as provided in Article 351 of the Constitution of India. It was also alleged that the Samiti from the very inception had acquired assets and properties and the assets and property at the time of filing of the petition were stated to be: (i) To expel Hindi as na tural language in the Assam, Meghalaya; Mizoram, Manipur Nagaland, Tripura and Sikkim as provided for in Article351 of the Constitu tion of India; (ii) To impris on and promote the Hindi as the a na lional language In Assam, the petitioner Society had a membership of about 164 22,000 persons scattered all over the States and Union Territories of North Eastern part of India and in 1934 it was established in Madras City in the name of Sikkim Hindi Prachar Samiti. The Samiti also has two affiliated bodies namely Manipur Hindi Pra char Samiti, Imphal and the Asom Rashtrabhasha Sewak Sangh. This Samiti has a sole constitution known as Bidhan which is also regis tered with the Registrar of Societies Assam at Gauhati. It has a principal constitution known by its members having elected Byabasthapika Sabha (meaning the General Council) and the Karyapalika (mean ing the Executive Committee), the term of each body is 5 years from the date of holding of their first meeting. According to the petitioner, the first meeting of this last Byabra ri Sabha was held on 10.8.82 wherein the petitioner society had a share of about 16,000 person scatted all over its States and union Territories of South Eastern part India and with a view to promote national integrity and in pursuance of this resolution institutions for the spread and prachar of Hindi in the non Hindi areas were established. The first meeting was held by the Board on 10th August 1982 wherein the peti tioner Society had two affiliated body namely Manipur Rashtraba Prachar Sabha, Impul and the asom Raka Samity was formed with its head Office at Gauhati, with a direction to promote the national integrity & in pursuance thereof, the institution for the development and spread of Hindi. In the meeting of the last Bya chyth er held on 17.7.83 passed a resolution for 167 amendment of the provisions of the bidhan (constitution of the Society) as it stood in 1982, the Chief Minister of Assam under the 1935 Act as its President. The petitioner challenged the action taken by the respondent State Government under Clause 1 of Article 230 of the Consti tution which provided that the Ordinance shall extend to all areas over which the Asam Rashtra bhasha Prachar Samity Samiti had its jurisdiction immediately before the commence ment of the Ordinance by a Notification No.

The appellants were the sons of one Ram Kishori Lal Sao, a resident of Asansol in Bengal. They were the wives of Sumitra Devi and Kamala Devi. The marriage was settled at Deoghar on Shivratri day in 1938 and the plaintiffs respondents before us had no concern with the negotiation. It was alleged that the terms of the marriage included a promise by Sumitra Devi of a gift of four houses at Asansole, worth about Rs. 20,000 to Kamala Devi, though the evidence led on behalf of the appellants did not make it absolutely clear or specific that the promise related to the four particular houses which were the subjectmatter of the subsequent gift. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court affirmed the decree. Held, that the gift was made after the father 's death and subsequent to the marriage. It could not be said that the gifts were made at the time of the execution of the deed of gift. There was no consideration nor any discussion of the texts bearing on the question whether a particular gift is reasonable or not will have to be judged according to the state of the family at the date of the gift, the extent of the property, the indebtedness of the families and the paramount charges which the family was under an obligation to provide for. The evidence of this witness supported the evidence of Sumitra ' with regard to the promise made regarding the gift of 4 houses at Dehuiyan ceremony on the occasion of the marriages at Deori. It did not show that the possession of the houses in question was made over to Kamala after the Sampradan ceremony on her marriage. The gift was not made at a time of marriage and it was made at an earlier stage. There is no consideration, nor any discuss ence of the text bearing on this question and the learned Judges of the High Courts were right in holding that there was no " sankalpa" or promise of a gowna ceremony. The mere fact that one of the sons had become indebted cannot take away the power of the father to make such a gift. But in this case the gift made by the widow was not binding on the reversioners.

The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the allegations of corrupt practice indulged in by Tej Singh have been clearly proved. Allowing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 In view of the very narrow margin of votes (123) between Tej Singh and Avtar Singh, a strong presumption and possibility that the votes polled in favour of section Tej Singh will have gone to the appellant (Avtar Singh) and, therefore, the result of the election would have been materially altered. [419D] 1.2 In view Of the very limited margin of vote (123), between Tej singh and Avtar singh, a firm presumption and possibilities that the voters who would have voted for Ruplal would now cast their votes in favour to vote and elect Shri Tej Singh. [416E F] 2.1 The appellant has proved beyond reasonable doubt that Tej Singh had indulged in corrupt practices particularly when the printing of the posters by Tej. Singh has been clearly admitted by him as indicated above. It is also clear to us that in view of this very narrow limit of votes, (123). between Tejinder Singh and R.W. 2) which contained the appeal purporting to be of Ruplar were in fact printed at the instance of Tej Singh, had no connection with the same. In these circumstances, it is clear that the appellant has , proved beyond doubt that the payment of vouchers .(Ex. P 5 and P 6) was made by him and the vouchers were appended by him along with the return of expenses incurred during his election campaign which was verified by him to be a true and correct statement.

The appellant, a Forest Minister in the Council of Ministers headed by Shri Bhajan Lal, was personally keen on giving him an office of profit. In order to achieve this objective, he got an Ordinance being Ordinance No. 44 of 1982 promulgated by the Governor. The Ordinance inter alia provided that the constitution of a Forest Development Board shall be with a view to appointing the said Devinder Sharma as its Chairman. It was alleged by the appellant that after having failed to threaten and demoralise the appellant through indirect means, the respondent, Bhajan Lal called him to his official residence on July 26, 1983 through the Acting Chief Conservator of Forests and criminally intimidated him to withdraw the writ petition and pursuant thereto eleven officers withdrew from the petition. It is alleged by him that after getting failed to convince and demororalise, the appellant, through indirect ways, called him, called himself to his office on July 27, 1983, through the acting Chief Conservator Forests and Penalally intimidating him to withdrawing the writ Petition and pursuant to that, eleven officers withdrawn from the writ petitioner. It further alleged that after the failure of threaten and terrorizing the appellant by indirect means the respondent Bhajan Lal calling him to the official residence, on July 28, 1983 along with eleven officers, withdrew from his petition. The further allegation of the appellant was that after knowing fully well that the constitutional validity of the Ordinance was challenged by twelve Indian Forest Officers including the appellant in the High Court complaining of interference by the respondent with due course of judicial proceedings. The application was admitted and a rule nisi was issued upon the respondent. The respondent appeared in the rule and opposed the same by filing an affidavit denying all the allegations made against him by the appel lant. The learned Single Judge of the High COurt took the view that there were circumstances to indicate that it was not a fit case in which the Court should exercise its jurisdiction under the Act. In that view, the learned Judge dismissed the application and discharged the rule niisi. It also held that there was no violation of any provision of law or contempt by the High court in exercising its jurisdiction to punish for contempt. The appeal filed by the State against the order of the Single Judge was dismissed. Hence this appeal under section 19(1) of the Contempt of Courts Act, 1984. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.

The respondent was the daughter and grand sons of the original plaintiff Vinayakbhat. His father paid a premium of Rs. 999 for the lease, and also agreed to pay a yearly rent of Rs 80 to Dattatraya during her lifetime and after her death a yearly amount equal to the assessment of the two lands to the heirs of expires. The lease provided that in default of payment of rent the tenant 's rights would come to an end. On 18th August, 1870, Ladha Ibrahim sold his tenancy rights to one Girdhari Balaram Lodhi for Rs. 7,999. The sale deed provided that the tenant would have no right whatsoever left over the property and that on the same day the purchaser passed a rent note in favour of Dattatraya. The rent note provided for payment of the agreed rent in the month of Pousb every year and stated that in case of default the tenant or his heirs would have any rights whatsoever leftover the property. On the same date the purchaser obtained a rent Note in favour Of Basappa. The landlord claimed that he was entitled to the whole compensation money as the tenants rights had ceased by forfeiture for non payment of rents, and that the lease was therefore determined under section 111(b) and not under section III(g) of the . The trial court rejected the claim but the High Court in second appeal confirmed the decree. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant tenant that (i) the High Courts erred in refusing relief against forfeiture because no rent was fixed in respect of the suit property and also because it was for the plaintiff to approach the defendants and not for the defendants to go to the plaintiff, and (ii) the mere fact that the defendant had disentitled themselves to relief by contumacious conduct on their part, that even this paltry rent had never been paid in time during the last twenty years at any rate, and therefore, the High court erred in interfering with the discretion of the trial judge in refusing to grant relief against Controller. Held: (i)(a) The requirement of a notice in writing as a preliminary to a suit for ejectment based on forfeiture of a lease is not based on any principle of justice, equity or good conscience and cannot govern leases made prior to 1929 or even prior to the coming into force of the , or to leases executed prior to 1930. (b) The rule laid down in section 111 (g) that in cases where non payment for rent was not a part of the English law, the insistence therein that the notice should be given in writing is intrinsic evidence of the fact that formality is merely statutory and it cannot trace its origin to any rule of equity. If the purpose of the rule as to notice is to indicate the intention of the lessor to determine the lease and to avail himself of the tenant, 's breach of covenant it could as effectively be achieved by an oral intimation as by a written one without in any way disturbing the mind of a chancery judge. That it was not so was apparent from the circumstance that the requirement of notice in a writing to complete a forfeiture has been dispensed with by the legislature in respect to leases made before 1st April, 1930. The law in India and England on this subject is not the same and it could not be said that this sub section enacts or enunciates any general principle of equity and good conscience. (c) The High Court was right in holding that the rule applicable for the exercise of the discretion in such cases and that in general they reflect the point of view from which judges would regard (1) (2) A.I.R. , referred to. (ii)(a).

The Associated Cement Companies Limited (the Appellant ') has quarries worked by its department called Kymore & Bamangaon Lime stone Mines at Ky More, District Jabalpur M.P. Workers employed in the said quarries have a union called Koymore Quarry Karamchari Sangh and the four concerned workmen Rama Shankar Barmapradhan, Emmanual and Mohd. Rauf (fourth charge) were also at the material time the office bearers in the union. In connection with the implementation of the Recommendations of Second Central Wage Board for cement industry, after serving a strike notice on the management of the Appellant on 13th September 1968, the Karamchari Sangh & all its members went on a strike for 24 hours commencing from the mid night of 19th September, 1968 which was accompanied by acts of intimidation, threats, ghearoes and unlawful obstruction. According to the management before the commencement of the strike two meetings were organized by the Respondents, one at 4 P.M. and the other at 11 P. M. on 19th Sept., 1968 at which fiery speeches were made by them wherein they not only instigated the quarry workers to resort to strike but intimidated and prevented the willing workers from going to their work and threatened the supervisory staff and officers with dire consequences if they tried to work the quarries and what is more from the middle of August till 4.30 A.M on 20th September and inciting others to gherao the said staff and forcibly and illegally occupying the area near the quarry between 4 P .M. on the night of 20th Sept. and incited others to go on strike, (c) ghe Raoing the Quarry Manager and other supervisory staff between mid night and 4. 30 A. M., on 20.9.1968, on the ground that the Quar Factory Agent should be examined first which was not being done, whereupon the enquiry proceeded ex parte and on a consideration of the entire evidence led before him the Enquiry Officer came to the conclusion that the first three charges were fully proved and the fourth charge was partly proved against all the Respondents while the additional charges against Emmanianual and Md. Rahaf (third charge) being held not to have been proved, the punishment of dismissal in respect of Emmanulual and Rs. 1,000/ was confirmed but set aside the dismissal order in respect thereof. The Appellant challenged the award in the High Court by means of a Writ Petition ( Misc. Petition No. 129 of 1970) contending that the Arbitrator had misconstrued Standing Order No. 17 and that no second opportunity was required to be given to the Respondents and that in the alternative the interference with the punishment in respect Of Rama Shankar and BarmaPradhan was erroneous while another writ petition (Misc. Petition NO. 129/70) was filed by the respondents against the punishments that were awarded to each one of them, the High court by its judgment dated 27th July 1972 confirmed the award of the Arbitrator by dismissing both the Writ Petitions. The appellant contended that the learned Arbitrator as well as the High Courts have erroneously construed the certified Standing Order 17 as requiring a second opportunity being given to a workman at the conclusion of the enquiry into his mis conduct and before inflicting upon him the punishment was not so harsh as to smack of victimisation. On behalf of the Respondents it was urged that once the enquiry got vitiated the entire field of determining the mis conduct as also the punishment therefor became open and the Arbitrator could not have entered into merits of the case or interfered with the award passed by dismissing the Writ Petition.

Section 7D of the Kerala Land Reforms Act, 1963 as amended by Act 35 of 1969 provided that certain persons occupying land for not less than ten years to be deemed tenants notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in section 52 or any other provision of the , or any law, custom or usage, or in any judgment, decree or order of court, shall be deemed to be a tenant if he or his predecessor in interest was in occupation of such land on the 11th day of April, 1957. The appellant 's plea before the Courts below was that he was himself the owner of the area having acquired title to it by adverse possession. In such circumstances the High Court held that the appellant was not entitled to the protection of section 7D. Dismissing the appeal and Special Leave Petitions, ^ HELD: 1.1 Section 7D must be construed as meaning "in lawful occupation". [114A] 1.2 The intention of the legisla ture was to grant protection only to persons whose posses sion had a lawful origin in the sense that they had either bona fide believed the lands to be Government 's lands of which they could later seek assignment or had taken the lands on lease from persons whom they bona fide believing to be competent to grant such leases or had come into possession with the intention of attorning to the lawful owners or on the basis of arrangements like varam etc. which were only in the nature of licences and fell short of a leasehold right. [114B] 1:3 The intention was to confer the benefit of protection on persons who had wilfully trespassed upon lands belonging to others and whose occupation was unlawful in its origin. The expression "in occupation" occurring in section 7 D must be interpreted as meaning 'in lawful possession '. In the present case, the finding of fact entered by the High court is that the appel lant had come to posses tion of the lands by trespass. His plea before courts below was not that he himself the owners of the areas having acquired the title to them by adverse Possession. [115C] 2:4 The appellant had come in possession of the land by trespass and his plea before Courts below is that he had come within the contemplation of the Act to confer benefit of the protection on person who had willfully trespassed on lands belonging t o others and their occupation was illegal in its trict tion. [116E] 2.5 The High Court was in error in holding that the appellants were not entitled tO the protection under section 7FD.

The appellants were the President of a registered Association formed for carrying on a business which had for its object the acquisition of gain by the individual members thereof and further because it was not registered as a company under the Rewa State Companies Act, 1935. The Association functioned through a President and a pioneer worker; they kept accounts and distributed the profits. Respondent No. 1, who was President of the Association from January 1946 to June 26, 1946, had given an account of income and expenditure for the months of January, February and March, 1946 but had given no accounts for the month of April, May and June, 1946. The appellants filed a suit in the Court of Additional District Judge, Umaria, for accounts of the Cloth Association at Budhar from April 1, 1946 to July 26, 1945, and for accounts on the sale thereof. The trial court decreed the suit but the High Court reversed the finding of the trial court and came to the conclusion that the other members of the association were not entitled to participate in the profits made on the sales of 284 bales of Gwalior cloth and inasmuch as Nagar Mal had rendered accounts with regard to all other transactions, the suit for accounts must fail. The question was whether by reason of section 4(2) of the Rewa state Companies Act 1935, the purpose of the partnership was not illegal and a suit for account lay at the instance of the plaintiffs appellants, who were also members of an unlawful Association, could be instituted on the ground of illegality. Held, that the preliminary objection must succeed. The provisions of section 72 of the Indian Contract Act are mandatory in nature and cannot be excluded from consideration even though the bar of that provision has been raised at this late stage. Surajmull Nargoremull vs Triton Insurance Company Ltd., , relied on.

The respondents, who were accused in a complaint filed by the appellant, were prosecuted for offences under sections 447, 429 and 379 IPC read with section 54 and 39 of the Wild Life Protection Act, 1972. The Magistrate took cognisance of the offence and ordered issue of process to the accused. It would appear that at the Police Station, a case had been registered under sections 448, 429, 429 IPC read With section 54, and 39, of the wild Life Protection (Amendment) Act, 1986. The respondents moved the High Court under section 482 Cr. P.C. or quashing of the order of the Magistrate taking cognizance on the complaint. The High Court quashed the proceedings against the respondents. From the orders under appeal it would appear, that two grounds commended themselves for acceptance to the High court. The first was that the learned Magistrate acted contrary to the provisions of section 210 Cr.P.C., 1973 and ordered issuance of process against the accused; and that the second ground on which the High 'Court quashed the proceeding against the other respondents was unsustainable in law. It was contended by the appellants, that the Magistrate acted without jurisdiction in taking cognizance of the offences and ordering issue of summons; and, that as an investigation by the Police was in progress in relation to the same offence, the learned magistrate would be required to stay the proceedings on the complaints and call for a report in the matter from the police; and (ii) that the allegations in the complaint taken on their face value would not amount in law to any offence against the 'Act '. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The policy and object of the ' Wild Life laws have a long history and are the result of an increasing awareness of the compelling need to restore the serious ecological imbalances introduced by the depradations inflicted on nature by man. [465C] 1.2 In order that the prohibition is attracted the same act must constitute an offence under more than one Act. If there two distinct and separate offences with different ingredients under two different enactments, a double punishment is not barred. In order to that the Prohibition is attracted, the same acts must constitute offences under two or more enactments. [467D] 1:3 The prohibition is applicable the same Act i.e., they should be identical. If, however, the two offences are distinct, then notwithstanding that the allegation of facts in the two complaints might be substantially similar, the benefit of the ban cannot be invoked. It is, therefore, necessary to analyse and compare not the allegations In the two complaint but the ingredients of the two offence and see whether their identity is made out. [468E F] 1 :4 The prohibition under section 9(1) read with sec. 50(1), in its ingredients and content, is the same or substantially the same as Sec. 429, IPC and that after due investigation and police had filed a final report that no offence was made out and that initiation of any fresh proceedings against respondents would be impermissible.

The petitioner was convicted for offences under sections 302 and 307 IPC. He was released on bail in his favour "to the satisfaction of the Chief Judicial Magistrate". The direction of this Court did not spell out the details of bail, and so the magistrate ordered that a surety hl a sum of Rs. 10,000/ be produced which, in actual impact, was a double denial of the bail benefit. For one thing the miserable mason. the petitioner could not afford to procure that huge sum or manage manage a surety of sufficient prosperity. Affluents do not hefriend indigents. For another, the magistrate made an odd order refusing to accept the suretyship of the petitioner 's brother because he and his assets were in another district. If mason and millionaire were treated alike, egregious inegality is an increditability. Likewise geographic allergy at the judicial level makes mockery of equal protection of the laws within the territory of India. India is one and not a conglomeration of districts, untouchably apart. When this Court 's order for release was thus frustrated by magisterial intransigence the prisoner moved this Court again to modify the original order "to that extent that petitioner be released on furnishing surety to the tune of Rs 2,000 or on executing a personal bond or pass any other order or direction as this Hon 'ble Court may deem fit and proper". From this factual matrix three legal issues arise ( 1 ) Can the court under the Code of Criminal Procedure enlarge, on his own bond without sureties, a person undergoing incarceration for a non bailable offence either as undertrial or convict who has appealed or sought special leave ? (2) If the Court decides to grant bail with sureties, what criteria should guide it in quantifying the amount of bail and (3) Is it within the power of the court to reject a surety because he or his estate is situate in a different district or State ? This formulation turns the focus on an aspect of liberty bearing on bail jurisprudence. The victims, when suretyship is insisted on or heavy sums are demanded by way of bail or local bailors alone are presona grata, may well be the weaker segments of society like the proletariat, the linguistic and other minorities and distant denizens from the far corners or our country with its vast diversity. In fact, the grant of bail can be stultified or made unreasonibly inconvenient and expensive if the court is powerless to dispense with surety or to receive an Indian bailor across the district borders as good or the sum is so excessive that to procure a wealthy surety may be both exasperating and expensive. The problem is plainly one of the human rights, especially freedom vis a vis the lowly. This poignant import of the problem persuaded the Chamber Judge to invite the Supreme Court Bar Association and the Citizens for Democracy to assist the court in decoding the Code and its provisions regarding bail. There is already a direction for grant of an bail by this Court in favour of the Petitioner and so, the merits of that matter do not have to be examined now. That is why we have decided to examine the question from a wider perspective bearing in mind prisoner 's rights in an * Justice V. Social justice is the signature tune of our Constitution and the little man in peril of losing his liberty is the consumer of social justice. There was no definition of bail in the Code although offences are classified as bailable and non bailable. (1) Before this Court, the law in its majestic equality, forbids the rich as well as the poor to sleep under bridges, to beg in the streets and to steal bread", lampooned Anatole France.

The assessee company had advanced Rs. 3,21,460 to another concern, the Bombay Fine Worsted Manufacturers ' Castle Mills. In the assessment year 1951 52, the assessee claimed under section 15C of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, exemption from tax in respect of 6% of the capital employed in 'Eldee ' as a newly established undertaking and sought to include in the computation of the Capital so employed Rs.3,21460 advanced to 'Castle '. The Income tax Officer rejected the claim but the Appellate Assistant Commissioner modified the assessment and directed in clusion of the amount advanced to the assessee in the calculation of capital invested for the purpose of 429 section 15 C. An application submitted under section 66(1) of the Act to the Tribunal to refer a question which it was contended by the Commissioner arose out of the order of the Tribunal was rejected and the petition of the Commissioner under section66(2) for an order directing the Tribunal, to state the case and refer it to the High Court was also dismissed. The assessee appealed to this Court. Held: (i) Under the Income tax law it is for the Tribunal in deciding all questions of fact that the High court has the power merely to advise the Tribunal on questions of law arising out of an order of a Tribunal. But the refusal of the tribunal to state a case for the opinion of the High ' Court on the view that a question of law does not arise out of such order is not conclusive. The High Court had the power to call upon the Tribunal 'to state the Case if in its view a question was of law arises out of tho order of Tribunal.

The Minister concerned, heard the parties and made a speaking order on February 18, 1975 affirming the earlier seniority list. The writ petition was thereafter amended and 97 in the amended petition, Duggal respondent also challenged the validity of the later order of February 18.1975. At the hearing of the appeal before this Court, the Advocate General for the State of Punjab has contended that looking to the facts of the case if the High Court came to the conclusion that the Minister was a necessary or proper party, this Court should not interfere in the matter. Allowing the appeal partly, HELD: The direction for impleading of the Minister as a party is given by the High court with a view to apprise the Minister of the allegations made in the petition and thus to afford him an opportunity of controverting those allegations, if he so deemed proper. Taking the totality of the facts and circumstances of the ease, this court does not feel persuaded to interfere with the order of the High Courts adding the Minister to the writ petition. [97C D] The direction of the high Court in so far as it has directed that the Secretary be impleaded as a Party is set aside. [98E F] The appeal shall stand disposed of accordingly. [99G] The parties in the circumstances shall bear their own costs. [1005D] The order whereby the Minister concerned was directed to file his personal affidavit is set down aside. The appeal will stand disposed accordingly. The parties are directed to bear their respective costs. M.R.

The respondent was a tenant of the appellant. An application was made by the Cantonment Executive Officer, Ambala, for realisation of arrears of rent due under a lease in favour of the respondent. The Magistrate held that he had jurisdiction and issued warrants for attachment of movable property of the Respondent on June 13, 1961. Thereupon the respondent went in revision to the Sessions Judge, Ambala contending that the magistrate had no jurisdiction to realise the arrears of rents due under the lease. The Sessions Judge accepted the view of the Sessions judge and set aside the order of the Magistrate dated June 13. 1961. The High Court having refused the certificate the appellant obtained special leave from this Court. HELD : (i) The section provides for recovery by suit also and as such it wilI not be possible for the Board to recover rent of land and buildings by suit for such rents are entirely outside the section and the right of the Board under the general law of the land is not taken away by the section. [344 C] (ii) The words "rent on land and building" which appear between the words "any tax" and "any other money" must equally be governed by the words 'recoverable by a Board etc." Therefore, in respect of rent of lands or buildings under the management of the Cantonment Board neither remedy would be available though the claim for the rent is ultimately traceable to those provisions of the Act and 'the Rules which empower the Boardto let out the land or buildings upon the ground that it cannot be said to be claimable or recoverable under any express provision of the Rent Acts and the Rules. [345 E F] (iii) The word "rent" in section 259 must be given a restricted meaning that word itself would be rendered otiose because there is no provision whatsoever in the Act which expressly makes rent claimable nor recoverable by either of the two authorities specified therein. [346 G H] (iv) Section 259 does not bar the right to the Board as an owner or holder of land & buildings to take action for recovery of rent thereof by suit under the General law of India, 1950, and the rules made thereunder. Therefore, section 259 does no bar the rights of the board as an 'owner or holder ' of land ' and buildings to recover it by suit against a tenant who was liable under an express provision Of the Act or the Rules to pay rent to the board.

The appellant was appointed as a section salesman and his services were controlled by the head office through its territory office situated in Delhi. The various correspondence and other evidence produced before the Labour Court showed that the appellant was employed for canvassing and pushing and promoting the sales of the company 's product in his area. The Tribunal also found that the appel lant is required to send reports about the publicity and advertisement of placing posters, holders, cinema slides and suggest means to canvass the sale in this area. Some of the documents relate to matters of publicity in melas, some relate to the existing position of the stock of the goods of the Company in the area and the action taken to ameliorate stocks. It was not the duty of the appellant to procure orders for the company. None of the salesmen were employed to sell the product of the companies in any particular area or collecting the sale proceeds and depositing the same with the company, but the Tribunal noted that the salesman neither sells nor collects any money from the wholesaler or retail dealers. The appellant was required to supervise the work of the local sales salesmen and local travelling salesmen appointed in the areas of his operation as well but it was only incidental to his main function of canvassing and promoting sale of the product in the four districts allotted to him. On these facts found, the Tribunal came to the conclusion that the termination of the appe lant from service was illegal, but dismissed the application only on the ground that the was not applica ble. The Labour Court held that the ap pointment itself was illegal and dismissed the appli cation only on ground that it was not appli dable. In appeal to this Court, it was contended for the appellant that a long period of over 16 years had passed it would be unjust to leave the appellant without any remedy at this stage. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The object of the enactment and the employees covered by the enactment also go to show that persons employed for sales promotion normally would not come within the definition of workmen under the Industrial Disputes Act as it stood in the year 1973 when the appellant 's service was terminated, in addition to whatever amount they were paying during the pendency of the appeal under orders of this Court. [475C] 2. The purpose of the Act and the employ ers covered by enactments also go t to show hat persons employedfor sales promotion generally would not coming within the defined definition of workman under the Act. The Act is to apply in the first instance to every establishment engaged in pharmaceuticals industry. It enables the Central Government by notification to apply the provisions to any other establishment engaged In any notified industry. If an industry is notified under this Act then the provisions of the would also be attracted to these types of workmen. This is a subsequent enactment and it is not applicable to the termination in the instant case which was long prior to the enactment of this Act. [476D E] Burmah Shell Oil Storage & Distribution Company vs Burmah Oil Storage and Distribution Co. ; , D.S. Nagraj vs Labour Officer, Kamal and others, 1973 F.J. (42) P. 440, J.M. Dechane Distributor vs State 476 of Kerala and others; , ; D. S. Nagaraj vs Labour Commis sioner, Kamal & Ors., 1973 FLR (42), P. 441, J J. Decane Distributor vs state 476 ofKerala and others ; , ; Burmah Mahan Oil Storage Corporation Ltd. vs Burmath Shell Management and Staff; ; ; D G.S Nagraj V Labour Officer Kamal and Others, 1973F.JR. (43) P 440, referred to.

The respondent No. 1, a Government lessee under section 181 of the M.P. Land Revenue Code, 1959, initiated proceedings against the 3rd respondent, the Gwalior Dairy Limited (the Company) under Section 182(2)(i) of the Madhya Pradesh Land Revenue Act, 1959 for eviction of the Company from the land in question. The Additional Collector held that the land was held by the Company in terms of the lease granted by the State and the Company was not a `pakka ' tenant and did not enjoy the status of a " Gair Maurusi" tenant. The High Court, however, held that since the Company failed to pay the agreed rents and thus contravened the conditions of the leasedeed, proceedings were initiated by the Additional Collector by his Order dated 1.10.1977 for eviction. In the appeal before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant Company that (i) the land under the lease was neither Zamindari nor ryotwari land; (ii) the Company had not become an ordinary tenant earlier in Madhya Bharat under Act No. 66 of 1950 and, therefore, it was not liable to be proceeded against in terms thereof; and (iii) the High Court had found in the earlier proceeding that the Company did not possess the status as a "pakta" tenant and that it had never become an 'pakki ' tenant under Section 54(vii) of Part II of Act 177. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The finding of the Additional District Collector is a finding of fact based on evidence and is not liable tO be questioned in these proceedings. His finding shows that large amounts are due and payable by the company as rent and that the rents have remained unpaid for a period far in excess of three months from the dates on which they became due. In either event, the Company has been holding the land from the State Government and it has never been an ordinary terms as defined in the Madhya Bharat Act No 66 of 1960. [179G] 2.

The Orissa Land Reforms Act 16 of 1960 received the assent of the President on October 17, 1960. By section 1(3) of the principal Act it was provided that the Act shall come into force in whole or in part on such date or dates as the Government may from time to time by notification appoint and different dates may be appointed for different provisions of the Act. By a notification issued on September 25, 1968 certain provisions of which were brought into force were brought in the principal Acts : (1) No person shall hold after the commencement of this Act lands as landholder or raiyat under personal cultivation in excess of the ceiling area determined in the manner hereinafter provided; (2) no person shall acquire any portion of such land as is within the ceiling limit applicable to him under any law for the time being in force. By virtue of section 37 it was further provided that where any law makes any provision for the acquisition by the State of any estate and where any land comprised therein is held by a person under his personal cultivation, it shall not be lawful for the State to acquire any part of such lands as is outside the ceiling limits applicable to the holder under any laws for the period being in operation. The Orissa Land Reform Act 16 Of 1960 received assent of President on September 17,1960. By that notification certain provisions were brought to into force. But Ch. IV (sections 24 to 37 dealing with resumption for personal cultivation of any land held by the a tenant and related matters) was brought into operation. By the amendment made in the Constitution by the 17th Amendment Act the principal ' Act was incorporated in the Ninth Schedule to the Constitution with effect from July 1, 1964. The Act is not liable to be attacked on the plea that it is inconsistent with or takes away or abridges any of the fundamental rights conferred by Part III of the Constitution. But the power to repeal or amend the Act incorporated in tho Ninth Schedule is not thereby taken away. the enactment of the of the competent Legislature to amending Act passed after the (Seventeenth Amendment) Act, 1964 does not therefore qualify for the protection of article 31 B. The contention that section 47 incorporated by Act 13 of 1965 which provided for payment of compensation at a rate which is less than the market value of the land falling within the Ceiling limit as originally fixed under 1960 and the guarantee of the second proviso to article 31 A of the Constitu tion is on that account infringed.

The appellants, who were the reversioners of a Hindu widow 's estate, filed a suit for possession of the properties during the lifetime of her husband. The trial judge dismissed the suit on the ground that there was a severance of joint status by an informal partition between Mathurbhai and Kashibhai but he dismissed the suits on the grounds that a suit of this character was not maintainable in law. On appeal, the High Court held that the surrender was valid for the period of the widow 'S life. The appellants came to this Court by special leave. Held: (i) A surrender may and in the majority of cases does take the form of transfer, e.g., when the widow conveys the entire estate of her deceased husband without consideration and not as a mere device to share the estate with the reversioner, in favour of the latter. The true nature and effect of a surrender by a Hindu wife of her late husband 's property have been thus summoned up and in our opinion quite correctly by a Division Bench of the Madras High Court (3) A transfer may and even though such alienations might not be binding on the reversions as not being made for a proper or necessary purpose, they are binding on her. In the case before this Court no equitable considerations at all arise. The widow 'of her husband 'S estate can, if she likes, stipulate for a right to be maintained out of the property for her lifetime; but reservation of such small benefit absolutely necessary for her maintenance does not invalidate a surrender as has been held by the Privy Council in more cases than one. (ii) A person who has acquired by adverse possession the limited interest of a widow by adverse Possession against her, occupies, according to the Madras decisions, as stated above, the same position as an alienee from the widow. The reversionary right to challenge it is no part of the estate which he has herself made; but as has already been held, surrender is not an alienation and as the reversioner does not derive his title from her, there is no principle of law under which the acts of the widows could bind him. (iii) A gift by a widow of her stridhana property without any justifying necessity or in the case of a stranger acquiring title by adverse posses sion against her the interest created is to be deemed to be severed from the inheritance and if a surrender is made subsequently by the widow, the surrender must take it subject to such prior interest. (iv) A transferee who has paid valuable and substantial consideration for a property on the expectation of enjoying it so long as the widow would remain alive and his expectations have been cut short by a surrender on the part of her widow which no doubt benefits the reversioner in the sense that he gets the inheritance even during the widow lifetime. (v) A surrendered is not a transfer and as such the reversioners do not derive their title from the reversion, there was no principle Of law under Which the acts could bind them.
