The petitioners were plaintiffs. They instituted a suit in a representative capacity under Order 1 rule 8 of the Code of Civil Procedure in the Court of the Additional Senior Sub Judge, Barnala for a declaration that they were the owners in posses sion of the suit land along with some others, that the Gram Panchayat Mehal Kalan, Tehsil Barnala District Sangrur in the State of Punjab (the Panchayat) had no sort of right in the suit lands and that the suit property had been wrongly shown as belonging to the Panchayat by the entries made in the revenue records which were not binding on the plaintiffs and for an injunction restraining the Panchayat from interfering with their possession. The Panchayat filed a revision petition before the High Court of Punjab and Haryana in Civil Revision Petition No. 571 of 1986. The learned Judge who heard the Revision Petition came to the conclusion that the issues involved in the case were not triable by a civil court by virtue of section 11 read with section 13 of the Act and accordingly he held that the Suit was not maintainable before the civil Court. Aggrieved by the said finding recorded by the trial court, the Panchayat filed revision petition in the High court which came to be dismissed. The petitioners have preferred this petition under Article 136 of the Constitution of India praying for grant leave to prefer an appeal against the decision of the High Courts. Dismissing the petition, ^ HELD: 1.1. The suit had been filed against the Panchayat and the Panchayat had expressly claimed that the land in question belonged to it as shamlat deh. It will not be possible in the circumstances for the civil court to make a declaration in favour of the plaintiffs without deciding the question whether the property in question was shamlatted or not and whether it belonged to the Gram Panchayats or not. Reliance was also placed by the counsel for the petitioners on a decision of this Court in Bhagu and Ors., vs Ram Sarup and Ors. [1985] Punjab Law Journal Page 366 in which the suit had already been held to be maintainable in a civil Court even though the defendant had contended that the plaintiff had only stated in the plaint that the lands in question were 'Gali Sheh re aam ' or a throughfare belonging to it for about 30 years and had prayed for an order injunction restraining him from interfering in his right. [835E F] 1.2. The High Court found that plaintiff in that case had only mentioned in the Plaint that the property was 'Gati Sheh ' or ' throughfare ' belonging to 'the Gram Panchayat which was being used by the plaintiff as an approach to his house for about 40 years and has prayed for injunction restraining it from interfering, with his right, and the Gram Gram Panchayat in question had not been impleaded as a defendant. The plaintiffs cannot by drawing their plaint cleverly by not claiming a declaration of that the said land was not shamlat mallat deh confer jurisdiction on the civil courts when by virtue section 13 read with sections 13A and 13B of the Punjab Village Common Lands (Regulation) Act, 1961 which had been inserted by the Haryana Legislature into the Act. [ 835F G] Bhagu & Ors.,v Ram Sarup & Ors. ; , referred to.

The appellant Board had to pay the consumption charges for electricity supplied by it. The Electricity Board had also to borrow and make payment of interest. This was a condition of supply. Under clause 28.6 of the terms and conditions, in the event of delay in payment of consumption or additional consumption deposit within the stipulated period, the consumer is obliged to pay surcharge at 18%. The appellant Board was required to pay interest on such deposits. The appellant company had to borrow, and make payments of interest, which were to be conducted in such a manner as to ensure a surplus. The consumers were also required to deposit with the Electricity Board a sum in cash equivalent to estimated three months consumption charges. Under cl. 28.1, the appellant was obliged to deposit surcharge at 12% per annum. The Board had power to demand additional security but the average consumption of three months should be taken as the basis for calculating the amount of such security. The respondent Electricity Board levied penal interest at 2% per month for non payment of bills within the specified period. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the appellant company was not obliged to make payment interest on the security deposit, and that the Board had no power to charge penal interest on a deposit made by the consumer with the Board in terms of clause 20(a) & (c) of the General Conditions of Supply. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The true nature of the transaction in these cases is one of advance payment of charges for consumption of electricity estimated for a period of approximately three months. In one sense, the consumption security deposit represents only a part of the money which is payable to the Board on the bill being raised against the consumer. (2) The Electricity Act clearly indicates that the Electricity Act and the regulations are not arbitrary or violative of Article 14 of the Constitution. [262C] 1.2 The true character of the transactions in these case is one one of loan payment of electricity charges for use of energy estimated for more than three months, and in one sense the consumption deposit represents merely a part thereof of the amount which is paid to the Electricity board on the Bill being raised by the consumers. (3) The Board 's interest requires that there should be some protection by way of security of advance payments in respect of the consumption of this three months period. [263D] 1:4 In the case of daily supply of electricity, there is a consequential liability to pay for each day 's consumption of Electricity. Therefore, it is contended that the amount does not contemplate appropriation is not correct because in the nature of contract it is liable to be appropriated for the satisfaction of any amount liable to he paid by the appellant to the respondent Electricity board for violation of any conditions of supply in the context of wide scale theft of energy, tampering with the meters and such other methods adopted by the customers. [264E] 1 :5 The Board has fixed the period of security deposit equal to the amount payable to it on the bills being raised. It also requires to be noticed under clause (6) of Schedule II of 252 the Electricity Supply Act that the requisition for supply of energy by the Board is to be made under proviso (a) after a written contract is duly executed with sufficient security.

The petitioners are working as officers in the Telecommunication Research Centre. They are being paid Special Pay of Rs. 300, Rs. 200 and Rs. 150 per month in addition to their pay scales in the grades of Deputy Director, Assistant Director and Scientific and Technical Officers Grade I respectively with effect from 1.1.1973. The direct recruits to which category the petitioners belong and the transferred Field Officers Group A working in the P&T Board of the Ministry of Communications, Government of India, there were in all 21 officers who had been recruited at the entry level of Junior Class I posts of S & T.Os Grade I. They were recruited in four batches in 1965, 1967, 1970 and 1973. The Class I post in the telecommuni cation Research Centre consists of the following posts: 1. Director (Senior Adminstrative Grade Level I) 2. Additional Director (Junior Administrative Grade Level II 3. Deputy Directors (Senior Administrative Grade) 4. Assistant Directors (Junior Class I). The Posts of Deputy Directors, Assistant Directors and S.T.Os. Grade I are filled by the following methods: 1010 (a) by direct recruitment through the Union Public Service Commission, (the petitioners belong to this category; (b) by transfer of Group A Field Officers recruited through the union Public Service Commis sioner by written examination followed by an interview, (These officers belong to the Indian Telecommunications Service Group B) and (c) by transfers of Group B Field Officers who are Posts and Telegraphs departmental promotees belonging to the P &T Board on relevant technical matters relating to the introduction of new equipment and technology in the existing public communication net work. The recruitment to the different cadres in the Telephone Research Centre is now being made under the Scientific and Technical Officer Grade I (Telecommunications Reve ntration Centre) is now be made under Stitu tional Service Rules, 1962 framed by the President under the provisions of the . During the period between 1956 and 1962 and further till 1965 all the Class I Posts of the Scientific and technical ary Officers Grade 1 namely Assistant Director & Deputy Director were manned by the transferred field Field Officers belonging to Indian Telecommunication Service Group A and Group B. For the first time, the Union Government Public Service commission advertised for the recruitment of 10 Scientific andTechnical Officers Grade II in the Telegraph Research Centre under the Recruitment Rules. These were General Central Service Class I Post and they continue to be so till today. In response to the said advertisement petitioners 2,3 and 4 applied for recruitment and they were selected for appointment to the posts of Assistant Directors or Deputy Directors since 1975. Direct recruitment to these posts was discontinued.) The direct recruit recruits to whom category the peti tioners belong and transferred Field Officer Group A who are Post and Telegraph Officers Class I and Group. For this first time the UnionPublic Service Commission advertised for recruitment of 11 Scientific & Technical Officers in the Posts Research Centre, discharge same functions as the petitioners. In reply to the advertisement petitioners 1,3,4 and 4 they applied for ap pation and they had been selected for appoint ment to the post of Assistant Director or Deputy Director since 1975, but all in vain. The Writ Petitions were contested by the petitioners contending that the offi cers who are likely to be affected by the decision are not impleaded as parties by name to these petitions, and that the petitioners are not enti tled to any Special Pay but the transferred officers from the Indian Telephone Research Centres which are not in their general line. Dismissing the Writ Petitions, this Court, HELD: 1(a) The first question relating to denial of promotional opportunities to the petitioners according to the Recruitment rules is left open to be decided by the Central Administrative Tribunal. No opinion on the said question. [1010C] (b).

The appellant, who was employed as a munshi in the appellant 's Bidi factor at Bhandara, framed a charge sheet against him in respect of certain acts of misconduct, gross negligence of duty insubordination etc. on May 13, 1965. An enquiry in respect thereof was held on May 15, after receipt of written statement from Nathu. Holding that the charges levelled against him were proved, the employer dismissed the third respondent with effect from August 1, 1965 and the said respondent filed an application challenging the order of dismissal before the Labour Court under section 78 of the Bombay Industrial Relations Act 1946, on the 5th August. His complaint was that the charge sheet was not proper, that the Head Office of the appellant had no authority to deal with his case under the Standing Orders, that no evidence was allowed or filed on behalf of the employer and that the finding was based only on his statement and in particular his cross examination. He had been forced to append his signature to a certain paper without the same having been read over to him. The Labour Court after holding an enquiry took the view that the findings of the enquiry officer were perverse, that he ordered reinstatement of the third Respondent with all back wages. The appellant preferred an appeal before the State Industrial Court contending inter alia, that (i) the third respond ent had failed to comply with the provisions of law in that he did not make an application under section 42(4) of the Act which was a condition precedent to approaching the Labour court and prayed that the order should be set aside on that ground alone; (ii) the finding of the Enquiry Officer were perverse and that, therefore, the order passed by the Labour Appellate Court should be quashed on that grounds alone. The State Industrial Tribunal confirmed the order. The High Court also held that it was not necessary for an employee first to approach the employer or to follow the procedure laid down in section 42 (4) including the proviso before he could apply to the Labour Courts for relief under section 7 8(1) D.P.C.; and (iii) the findings were perverse. In appeal by certificate, HELD: (i)(a) The scheme of Chapter VIII seems to be that in regard to any "change" in an industrial matter there must be compliance with the provision of that chapter. [737 A] (b) The object of which was to make numerous changes in the Act shows in its Statement of Objects and Reasons that clause 31 of the Bill was meant to "enlarge the powers of the Labour ' Court under s.78". According to this clause "the Labour Court is empowered (by paragraph D) to direct temporary withdrawal of any change the legality of which is a matter of issue in any proceeding before it, pending its final decision." [738 B] (c) The procedure for attraction of such jurisdiction is as laid down by section 79. It will be noted that no mention is made in section 84 of paragraph D of section 78(1). but inasmuch as orders of dismissal, discharge, removal, retrenchment, termination of service or suspension of an employee would come under section78(1), para A, the legislature felt it unnecessary to make any mention of an order under paragraph D in section 83.

The contesting respondents, who were the successors in interest of the lessor company, filed a suit for eviction against the appellants on the ground that they had formed a partnership firm and as a result of which a new month to month tenancy was created. The trial court accepted the appellants ' case that they were the heirs and successors of the original lessor and the lessee respectively. The respondents then moved the Patna High Court in its revisional jurisdiction, inter alia, contending that the application under section 12 of the Bihar Buildings (Lease, Rent and Evic tion) Control Act, 1947 before the Munsif was not maintain able. The plea was accepted by the Judicial Commissioner, Ranchi. The appellants ' revision petition was dismissed by the Patna high Court. The High Court held that in absence of a month 's notice under section 10(1) from the tenant, the application of the appellants was not maintainable before the Munsiff and the entire proceeding was mis conceived. It was pointed out that in the circumstances the appropriate remedy of the appel lants was to file a suit under section 11 of the Act. Before proceeding further it would be helpful to examine the provisions of the section 12 which is quoted below: "12. Extension of period limited by lease. (1) If a tenant in possession of any building held on a lease for a specified period, in tends to extend the period limited thereby he may give the landlord at least one month before the expiry of the period extended by the lease, a written notice of his intention to do so; and upon the delivery of such notice the said time shall, subject to the provisions Of section 11, be deemed to have been extended by double the period covered by the original lease subject to a maximum of one year. (2) Where the landlord to whom notice has been given under sub section (1), wishes to object to the extension demanded by the tenant on one or more of the grounds mentioned in sub section(1), he may, within fifty days of the delivery, appeal to the court in that behalf and the Court after hearing the parties may termi nate the lease or extend the same for such period as it deems proper in the circum stances. Provided that the tenant shall not in any case be allowed to remain in possession beyond the period permissible under sub sec.(1). (3) If the tenant fails to vacate the building on the termination of the lease Or as the case may be, on the expiry Of the period fixed by the Court under sub s.(2), the court shall, on an application by the land lord pass an order for ejectment which shall be executed as a decree and may further order that the tenants shall pay to the landlord such amount as may be determined by it as daily compensation. It has been contended on behalf of the respondents that in view of the findings of fact in the case, it was not necessary to deal with this aspect now. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.

The appellant a registered Society filed the suit out of which this appeal arises in the court of the District Judge, Jaipur City. The counsel engaged by the appellant were Sri Satya Narain Sharma and Sri Shyam Bihari Agarwal. The suit was later transferred to the Court of Additional Dis trict Judge No. 1, Jaipur city where it was renumbered as Suit No. 116 of 1974. After the institution of the suit, an election of the office bearers of the Society was held on 1.6.1973 and according to the appellant 's case one Sri Laxman Das Swami was elected as the Secretary. On 4.9.74 a prayer for withdrawing the suit was made by one Hari Narain Swami through another lawyer claiming to have been elected as Secretary of the society. In support of his claim, having been elected, none of them had any knowledge of the order passed by the Court. Later in the next election another Secretary named Jeeva Nand Swami was nominated and when he learnt about the fate of the Suit, an application was filed for recalling the order of withdrawal and restoring the suit to its file. The prayer was contested and the trial court rejected the application. The High Court agreed with the trial Court that the application under section 15 1 of the Code of Civil Proce dure, was not maintainable. While agreeing with the argument of the appellant that the trial com plaint had been wrongly decided by the trial Judge on merits of the case, the High Court observed that the mistake could not be corrected in the present situation. It accordingly dismissed the appellant appeal. Allowing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The case has to go back to the trial courts for reconsideration of the evidence on this point, and it is the inherent power of every court to correct its own proceedings when it is satisfied that in passing a particular order it was misled by one of the parties. [237B] Sadho Saran Rai and Others vs Anant Rai and Ors., AIR 1923 Patna 483; Basangowda Hanmantgowda Patil and Others v Churchigirigowda Yogangowda and Another, I.L.R. 34 Bombay 408, the defendant applied to the court to set aside a compromise decree on the ground that he had not engaged the lawyer claiming that to be representing him and had not authorised him to compromise the suit. The Court accepted his plea and ruled that it is inherent power vested in every court of justice to correct their own proceedings whenever it is satis fied that in passa particular order, it was deceived by one party. [236C] 2. If a party makes an application before the Court for setting aside the decree on ground that the plaintiff did not give his consent, the court has the power and duty to investigate the matter and to set t aside the deci sion if it is found satisfied that the consent as a fact was lacking and the court was induced to pass the decree. [238D] 3.

The appellant was charged along with the co accused of an offence punishable under section 7 read with section 4 thereof, and with having on or about July 11, 1953 transferred by sale 10 High Denomination Bank Notes of the Denomination of Rs. 1,000 each to one Velji Lakhamshi Joshi for Rs. 180 per note and thus contravened the provisions of section 4 of the Ordinance read with sections 109 and 109 Of the Indian Penal Code. The appellant contended that Ordinance promulgated under the emergency powers vested in the Governor General under section 72 of the 9th Sch. of the Government of India Act, 1935, was in operation during the period of emergency but would cease to be in operation after the emergency was declared to have ended on April 1, 1946, by the Indian Legislature and therefore the prosecution was not maintainable. Held, that Ordinance No. III of 1946 which was promulgated during the periods between June 27, 1940 and April 1 1946, was perpetual in duration and continued in force until it was repealed. The Ordinance having been promulgated during that period, the said notes continued to be ineffective as legal tender in India though the position in Jammu and Kashmir in regard to the same could not be affected by reason of the expiration on the 1st April, 1946. King Emperor vs Sibnath Banerjee, (1924) L.R. 51 I.A. 206, referred to. Held further, that the Ordinance having continued in operation even after April 1. 1946, and was in force on July 11. 1953, the date on which the offence in question was committed by the appellant and the appellant was rightly convicted by both the courts below.

The appellants were charged with murder and the trial court convicted them under section 302 I.P.C. and sentenced them to death. The High Court confirmed their convictions. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the sentence of death awarded to each of the appellants by the trial Court was not 'erroneous in principle nor was 'arbitrary or excessive ', or 'indicative of an improper exercise of discretion ' and that the court had no power to impose a lesser sentence. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The determination of public opinion on this difficult an(l complex question was essentially a legislative function not a judicial function. [1069C] 2.1 In the instant case, the High Court was justified in confirming the death sentences passed under section 368(a) Cr. P.C., 1973 being satisfied that there were "special reasons" within the meaning of section 354(3) Cr P. C. The award of death sentence to the two appellants was neither 'errorally wrong nor excessive ' or 'Indicative ' of an ' improper exercise ' of discretion". Nor was it constitutionally permissible for this Court while hearing such an appeal to lay down that on grounds of compassion and humanism the sentence awarded to them by the learned Additional Sessions Judge is also not liable to be reduced to life imprisonment. [ 1069C E] 2:2 The High Courts were bound thereby. [1000G] Rajendra Prasad vs State of Bihar, ; , applied. In the present case, it was neither feasible to define nor legally permissible for the Court to limit or circumscribe the connotation of the expression 'special reasons ' occurring in section 354 (3) of the Code so as to bind all Courts within the territory of India. [1007C] 3:1 The assessment of public and opinion on the difficult an (l complex questions was essentially legislative, not a Judicial function. The deliberate extinguishment of human life by the State for an offence of murder, they reasoned on metaphysical theories of punishment, was a denial of human dignity. They concluded by stating that the death penalty was usually inflicted only on a few, i.e., the poor and down trodden who are outcastes of a society which led to the irresistible inference that the punishment was not fairly applied. This may be a 'progressive ' stance, which is out of place in a judicial pronouncement, which ought to be based on the facts and circumstance of the case and the law applicable. But the professed view does not stem from a firm belief in dignity of human lives for they themselves advocate the death sentence for certain classes of offenders, (I) R. On the facts before them they commuted the sentence to a sentence of imprisonment for life, and the decision cannot, therefore, be construed as laying down a ratio decidendi. [1017E F] 3.2 The assessment on this score was essentially one legislative, no judicial function, not 'a judicial function '. The mere fact that the appellants were convicted under section 307 I. P C.C.; but the High Courts felt that he might have been caught between the cross fire which subsequently ensued after the three had fallen.

The appellant was in service upto 30th April 1958 when he was prematurely retired. The appellant also claimed arrears of salary but he reduced this claim to Rs. 16,561.29. The Commissioner of Income tax, U.P., Lucknow, on the basis of a preliminary enquiry held by him, recommended that the appellant should be given a reasonable opportunity to lead evidence and to be heard or not was largely a question of fact. The second charge was that he had made various investments in the name of various members of his family far in excess of and disproportionate to the known sources of his income. His high standard of living and expenditure were also mentioned there. The third and last charge gave particulars of thirteen assessment cases in which the appellant was alleged to be either "grossly negligent, careless, inefficient, and/or corrupt in the performance of his duties as Income tax Officer". The appellant 's defences included confused nature of charges characterised by him as "vague, over lapping, intermingled" and wrongly joined together. He also pleaded that there had been an enquiry in 1949 by Shri A. K. Bose, Deputy Director Investigation, or against the punishing authority. No mala fides were alleged against either the Inquiring Officer, Shri A, K. R. T. Rangachari vs Secretary of State, do not help the appellant. If an inquiry is held at a particular stage, possibly to determine whether regular proceedings should be drawn up or started, it does not debar a departmental trial. That was the nature of the previous enquiries. It appears that it is only after the appellant ' his activities had become more than notorious that further enquiry was undertaken and regular charges framed. It was possible that the appel lant may have been emboldened by the failure of officers to report earlier that charges should be framed and tried. In any case, this could not stand in the way of the first regular enquiry in the course of which charges were actually framed and fully enquired into by Officers whose integrity and sense of justice was not challenged. The question whether the appellant is given a "reasonable opportunity" to lead additional evidence and also to be hear or not is largely a matter of fact, and it is for the appellant to satisfy the Departmental authorities, which had looked into the case upto its final stage, that he suffered some injustice which could have affected the final decision.

The appellants were the last purchasers of manganese ore within the State of Andhra Pradesh. The appellants contended before the Sales Tax authorities that their sales of manga nese ore to the Mines and Minerals Trading Corporation in short called the M.M.T.C. were complete within the state of Andhra pradesh, that they were not the last purchaser but the M M.T.,C. was the last buyer within the Sate, and therefore, the M .M. T.C., was liable to pay the tax. The High Court held that the contracts between the appellants and the M/s. M. Mec.T.(C) were similar, and that there should be examination of five other contracts. In appeal by special leave it was contended for the State that there were six contracts and it had been the case of the appel lants that the contract was different, and, therefore, there should have been examination of 5 other contracts, and the High Court also considered only one contract. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1. The contracts between M/Mec. T.(C.) on board the ship are pursuant to the contracts of sale between the merchants and the Corporation. These directions are not in the course of export, because the export sale is an independent one between the Corporation and their foreign buyers. [444E F] 2.1 In the instant case, there was no privity of contract between the Mec trate and the foreign buyers from the S.T .C. The privity of the contract had been between the S .T. C. and the Foreign buyers.

The appellant was employed with the respondent M/s Bharat Electronics Limited as Salesman at its Delhi Sales Depot on a salary of Rs. 520 per month from 8th December, 1973. His service was abruptly terminated by letter dated 12th October 1974 with effect from 19th October, 1974. Consequent upon this termination an industrial dispute was raised and the Delhi Administration referred the following dispute to the Labour Court for adjudication: "Whether the termination of services of Shri Mohan Lal is illegal and/or unjustified and if so, to what relief is he entitled and what directions are necessary in this respect?" As the respondent management at one stage failed to participate in the proceedings, the reference was heard ex parte and the Labour court made an award on 2nd May, 1977 directing reinstatement of the appellant with continuity of service and full back wages at the rate of Rs 520 per mensem from the date of termination till reinstatement. Subsequently, respondent moved for setting aside the ex parte award and seeking permission to participate In the proceedings which motion was granted. The respondent inter alia contended that the appellant was a salesman appointed on probation for six months and subsequently on the expiry of the initial period, the period of probation was extended upto 8th Sept., 1974 and on the expiration of this extended period of probationary period, his service was terminated by letters dated 12st October, 1975, as he was not found suitable for the post to which he was appointed. The Labour Court held that the termination was neither illegal nor improper nor unjustified and therefore the claim of the respondent was negatived. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The termination would constitute retrenchment and by a catena of decisions it is well settled that where pre requisite for valid retrenchment as laid down in section 25F has not been complied with, retrenchment bringing about termination of service is ab initio void. In other words, it does not bring about a cessation of service of the workman and the workman continues to be in service. According to him unless the workman has put in continuous service for not less than one year his case would not be governed by section 25 F. [532C D] 1.2. The conditions are that commencing the date with reference to which calculation is to be made, in case of retrenchment the date Of termination of the service which is complained of as retrenchment. After that date is ascertained, move backward to a period of 12 months just preceding such date the workman had rendered service for a periodof 240 days. If these three facts are affirmatively answered in favour of the workmen pursuant to the deeming fiction enacted in sub section 2(a) it will have to be assumed that the workman is in continuous continuous service within the meaning of sub section (1) and his case need not be covered by sub section(2). And sub section.(2) provides for a fiction to treat a workman in continuous Service for a periods of one year despite the fact that he has not rendered uninterrupted service for 240 days within the period Of 12 calendar months commencing and counting backwards from the relevant date, i.e., the date when the retrenchment is complained off as retrenchment.[532D E] 1:3.

The appellant was appointed an Inspector of Consolidation by order dated October 5, 1953 of the Settlement Commissioner of Patiala and East Punjab States Union. The appointment was on temporary basis and terminable with one month 's notice. On February 5, 1955, the appellant was served with a charge sheet setting out his mis demeanour, an enquiry was held in respect of the alleged misdemeanour and his employment was terminated because in the view of the settlement Officer with which view the Deputy Commissioner agreed. The appellant challenged the authority of the Deputy Commis sioner or the Settlement Commis missioner to hold the enquiry and submitted that the procedure followed by that Officer in making the enquiry was irregular. Held, that the protection of article 311 (2) of the Constitution applies as much to a temporary public servant. By virtue of article 310 of the Constitu tion the appellant is not liable to be dismissed or removed from service until he had been given reasonable opportunity against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him. The fact of holding of an enquiry is not decisive of the question. What is decisive is whether the order is by way of punishment, in the light of the tests laid down in Parshotam Lal Dhingra case ; , referred to. State of Orissa vs Ram Narayan Das, A.I.R. 1960 S.C. 689, distinguished. State Of Bihar vs Gopi Kishore Prasad, A I. R. 1960 section C. 689 and State of Bihar vs Ram Narain, [1958] S.

The appellant State Government issued a notification on November 15, 1968 for selections to be made to posts of Professors in the colleges. By Notification No. SRO 161 dated March 25, 1969 those rules were replaced by the rules made by the Governor specifically for the appointment of Professors which were called the "Jammu and Kashmir Professors of Colleges (Selection) Rules, 1969". The appellant challenged the validity of this notification on the ground that it was not at all attracted in the matters of making promotions in the same service. The High Court allowed the writ petition and quashed the State Government 's order No. 643 HTE dated July 25,1969 in regard to the appointments of respondents Nos. 3 to 46 and directed that it would be open to the State Govt to make a fresh selection of Professors. In appeal by certificate to this Court, HELD: (1) The question whether the requirement for consulting the Commission is mandatory or not does not arise in this case because it was neither disputed nor was in fact the case of the appellant State, that the Commission was consulted in regard lo the principles to be followed in making the promotions in question. [873 E] (2) It is not necessary for the Commission to carry out a plea to the contrary. The State Government has stated in its reply that it consulted the Commission under section 133 of the Constitution and as the writ petitioners have not ventured to take a plea which was not taken by the appellant, the High Court erred in holding that the selection made by it was invalid for that reason.

The petitioner was the Chief Minister of Bihar. The Assembly of Commons passed a resolution on May 30, 1957, to the effect that a portion of the speech was objectionable and ordered it to be struck off and expunged. The petitioner challenged the validity of the said resolutions by a petition under article 32 of the Constitution. It was contended for the petitioner (i) that the privilege conferred on the Legislature of a State is subject to the freedom conferred on a citizen under article 19(1)(a); (ii) that even if the privilege was not expressly made subject to article 19, having regard to the nature of the fundamental right and the rules of interpretation, this Court should so construe the provisions as to give force to both the provisions; (iii) that in view of the fact that it infringes the fundamental rights of a citizen, the Legislature has no power to take any action in respect of the publication by or under the authority of the House of Commons and even if it did, by reason of article 212(1), the validity Of its proceedings cannot be questioned on the ground of any alleged irregularity of the procedure. Held: (i)(a) The right conferred on Parliament by article 19 (1) (a) is subject only to reasonable restrictions made under clause (2) of the Article and, therefore, if the House or Houses of Parliament makes a law under entry 74 in List I to the Seventh Schedule defining the powers, privileges and immunities enjoyed by the House, of Commons of the British Parliament of the United Kingdom, at the commencement of the constitution, i.e., January 26, 1950, and the House Of Commons on that date had no privilege to prevent the publication of its proceedings or portion expunged by the Speaker in respect thereof of the proceedings. (b) The provisions of clauses (1), (2), and (3) shall apply in relation to persons who are not members of the Assembly but who, by virtue of this Constitution have the right to speak in, and otherwise to take part in the proceedings of a House of the Legislature or any committee thereof as they apply in respect Of members of that Assembly. The provisions Of clauses (2)(3) and (4) shall be subject to reasonable restriction made under cl. (2). (c) In other respects, the powers privileges and immunity of a house of Commons conferred by the latter part of article 194(3) on each House of Parliament and of its members and committees thereof are a reproduction mutatis mutandis of article 105 which applies to both Houses of parliament and the members and committee thereof. The common law rights of the citizen were threatened by the said resolution. (d) The privilege conferred upon the Legislature is subject, to reasonable limitations made under cls. (1)(2), (3), (4), (5) and section 19(2). The provisions in clauses (i), (ii), (iii), (iv) and, (v) of article 195 do not import into India the law of a foreign country; (e) The power, privileges, immunities and immunities of a Houses or Houses and the Members and committees of a Legislature of the State and of the members of a committee thereof are such as may from time to time be defined by the Legislature by law. (f) The restrictions imposed on the freedom of speech and expression which include the freedom to vote in any House of a legislature of a state and of members and com mittees of a Legislative Assembly of a Province, would be void to the extent the law contravened the provisions of article 19.(1)(c).

The Respondent was a private college known by the name of Khallikote College. This is an institution which grew out of a school established in 1856. The management had to meet with financial crisis in the past and obtained financial help in the shape of liberal endowment under a trust deed from the then zamindar of Kullikote. The institution, it was stated, became one of the premier colleges in the town of Behrampur, Ganjam District, Orissa. The College was taken over by the Government in pursuance of the unanimous resolution of the managing committee of February 18, 1970 and the transfer to the Government was of all the assets of the college but without any liability. The Managing Committee continued to be liable for the outstanding liabilities, if any, of the College for which Government was not liable. The college after taking over the management of the Colleges continued to remain liable for outstanding liabilities. If any, the College after takingover the management had been administered as a Government College, it is not merely taking over its land and buildings, tables and chairs. It is also contended that since the Respond ents have not completed eight years of service in the college they are not entitled to be considered by the Public Service Commission for appointment as Readers. Dismissing the appeals, HELD: 1.1 The requirement of eight years ' teaching experience, as mentioned above, which is needed for appoint ment as a Reader is more than amply fulfilled by each of the Respondents. [780A] 1.2 In the instant case, the Respondents answering the test of educational qualifications, as well as, experience of teach ing in a recognised private college are discriminated amongst the very category of Readers on an irrational and illusory consideration. Denial of an opportunity to these Respondents even for being considered for the post of Reader is clearly violative of Article 16 of the Constitution. [781C] 1:3 The requirement that eight years teaching experience as mentioned in the circular of March 23, 1971 alone, was in controversy in the High Court, as much later than the four of the Res pond ents (Nos. 9 and 10) in Annexure I.

The appellants applied for temporary permits under section 68 F(1 C) for plying the passenger vehicles on the route. The U.P. State Road Transport Corporation (Corporation for short) also made an application for grant of three temporary permits for the same purpose and the application was granted while the application made by each of the appellants was rejected on the ground that once a scheme had been published in view of the provision contained in section 68 C, the Corporation alone to the exclusion of others is entitled to apply for temporary permit and if such an application is made by the Corporation and granted no one else is entitled under section 69 F( 1C) to obtain a temporary permit. This decision was upheld both by the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and the High Court. The appellants applied to the State Government for grant or renew any temporary permits during the period intervening between the date of publication of the scheme and the date on which the scheme had already been published. The State Transport Authority rejected the applications on the grounds that once the scheme has been published, it is open to the Corporation or the Regional Transport Authority as the case may be to fix or increase the number of vehicles that may operate on the routes. But the power to increase strength of fleet operating on the road is conferred and has to be exercised in public interest meaning transport facility to travelling public. The expression 'any person ' would comprehend any person even other than the Corporation. One has to read section 68F(1 A) and section 68 E (1 C). If the Corporation applies for all the permits but only for some, the inescapable conclusion is that for the remaining strength the Corporation has made no application for the temporary permits and section 69F( 1 C) would be squarely attracted. In view of this raising of the strength, 7 temporary permits could be granted.

The appellant, who was the son of a Hindu governed by the customary law prevailing in the Punjab, succeeded to his maternal grandfather 's estate. On March 22, 1927 he executed a registered mortgage deed in respect of the said properties in favour of the ancestor of respondents I to 9 for Rs. 5,000. Subsequently on April 12, 1929, he sold the equity of redemption to the said mortgagee for Rs 11,000 and in suit No. 145 of 1946 filed by the appellant in the Court of the Sub Judge, Panipat, from which the present appeal arose, the appellant had claimed a declaration that the two transactions of mortgage and sale in question did not bind his own reversionary rights, because the impugned alienations were without consideration and were not supported by any legal necessity. The trial judge held that the property in dispute was ancestral qua the appellant 1101 and that the impugned alienation were not effected for consideration or for legal necessity and dismissed the suit on the ground that they were not based on any legal con tention. On appeal, the District Judge held that it was not necessary to decide whether the property inherited from maternal grandfather was ancestral property or that such property in the hands of a grandson can be given that description. The High Court also held that in view of the fact that the question about the character of such property even under the Hindu law was not free from doubt, the High Court ordered that parties should bear their own costs throughout. Held, that the decision of the first Full Bench must be affirmed. It would now be necessary to consider the two Privy Council decisions on which reliance has been placed by the learned counsel for the appellant. The question as to whether the suit in question attracted the provisions of article 2 of the Punjab Limitation (Custom) Act, 1920, was not a decision on the proof of custom as such and that raised the same old question whether property from maternal grand father in the favour of a sonless proprietor can be described as ancestral property. The doctrine of stare decisis is not so imperative or inflexible as to preclude a departure therefrom in any case, but its application must be determined in each case by the discretion of the court, and previous decisions should not be followed to the extent that error may be perpetuated and grievous wrong may result.

The appellants were tried by the Additional Sessions Judge, Birbhum, on charges under section 449 and 307/34 of the Indian Penal Code. The prosecution case was that on the night of 14th November 1950 when Haji Ebrar Ali was sleeping on the Verandah of his hut, these appellants came there and while one of them armed with a dagger while the other three held him down. Fortunately, the injury inflicted on Ebrahim Ali did not prove fatal. The jury returned an unanimous verdict of guilt against all the appellants on both charges. The Sessions Judge accepted that verdict and convicted the appellants under sections 449 and 302 read with section 34 of the Penal Code and sentenced them to rigorous imprisonment for four years under section 307/149 and to rigorous imprison ment for two years under s.447 of the Act. He sentenced the other two appellants to rigorous fines, for four months under section 147 and to undergo rigorous imprisonment. The High Court dismissed their appeal. Held: (i) There can be no doubt that the words "in order to" have been used in section 449 of the Code of Criminal Procedure are quite inde pendent of the question whether the offence "inorder to" the commission of which house trespass was committed has been actually committed or not. In the present case, when it is found that the four appellants attacked Haji E brar Ali in furtherance of the common intention of all of them to kill him and some of them held him up while one used the dagger on him each of the four is in law considered to have done the entire act of holding Eb Varnnnninini. Each of the other accused who did not use the dagger must in law be considered to had done this act of using the dagger; and so, each of them becomes punishable under section 302 of the I.P.C. for injuring Ebshad Ali with the dagger was guilty of murder, except in some special circumstances as mentioned in section 300 of the IPC. (ii) The fact that the murder was not actually committed will not affect the applicability of section 449 I. P.C., because the murder is not actually actually committed would not affect its application.

The appellant filed a suit for a declaration of his title as collateral within four degrees of Gurdial, who was a Sarswat Brahmin. The respondent contested the suit mainly on the grounds (i) that the suit for declaration of title to the lands was maintainable; and (ii) that there was no custom whereunder the collaterals of the father who was the last male holder excluded the daughter from succession to the self acquired property of her father. Held, that the appellant had failed to discharge the onus that was initially on him by producing in evidence the Riwaj i am of 1913 and, consequently, the appellant must succeed. The appellant had discharged this initial onus in two ways, namely (1) by producing the Rwiwaji am of the Gurdaspur district prepared by Mr. Kennaway himself in 1913 and (2) by adducing evidence showing that the collateral 's of one Harnam Singh who was also a Sates of the same family of Gurdial succeeded in preference to his daughter. The High Court was right in holding that the evidence as to the succession to self acquired properties of her deceased father had been discredited in judicial proceedings and held to be incorrect. The general custom of the Punjab being that a daughter excludes the collateral from inheritance to the ancestral property of their father, the initial onus, there fore must be on him to displace the general custom recorded in Rattigan 's Digest of Customary Law. The question whether there is a custom in the Gurdaspore district in so far as they purport to record the local custom as to right of succession of daughters to the property of his respective father are reliable and trustworthy documents.

The respondent was the Managing Director of a number of companies registered under the Indian Companies Act. He was also a Director of another company and had on occasions acted as liquidator of some companies, as executor or administrator of estates of deceased persons and as trustees of various estates. On 4 7 1949 he applied to the Collector of Calcutta under section 31 of the Stamp Act for adjudication of duty payable on a power of attorney marked as exhibit A in the proceedings which he proposed to execute. By that power he empowered Messrs Douglas Chisholm Fairbairn and John James Brims Sutherland jointly and severally to act for him in his individual capacity and also as executor, administrator, trustee, managing agent, liquidator and all other capacities. The Collector referred the matter under section 56(2) of the Act to the High Court of Calcutta stating his own opinion that the stamp duty was payable on the power "for as many respective capacities as the principal executes the power". The reference was heard by a Bench consisting of the Chief Justice Das, Das, J. and section R. Das Gupta, J., who differed in their opinion. The learned Chief Justice with whom Das, jj agreed held that the different capacities of the executant did not constitute distinct matters for purposes of section 5 of the Indian Stamp Act as amended by section 13 of Bengal Act III of 1922. On appeal by special leave: Held, that when two persons join in executing a power in respect of all the matters in which he could act, it should be held to comprise distinct matters and thus requiring to be stamped with the aggregate amount of the duties with which separate instruments each comprising or relating to one of such matters would be chargeable under the Act within the meaning of section 6. The transaction is a single transaction whereby the donor constitutes the donees jointly and separately his attorneys for him and in his name and on his behalf to act as for him, in his personal capacity and in the capacity as managing director, director, managing agency agent, secretary or liquidator of any company in which the donor is or may at any time thereafter be in terested in any such capacity as aforesaid and also in his capacity as Managing Director, director or in any capacity whatsoever as occasion shall require. The fact that the donor of the power of Attorney executes it in different capacities is not sufficient to constitute the instrument one comprising distinct matters. There is no provision in the statute law of this country similar to the above, and it is significant that it assumes that a powerof attorney might consist of distinct matters by reason of the fact that there are (1) Mad. 849 (2) Mad., 849, 849; 849 and 849 respectively, and (3) Mad, 851 952 953, 954, 955, 956, 957, 958, 959, 961, 962, 963, 964, 965, 966, 967, 968, 969, 971, 972, 973, 974, 975, 976, 977, 979, 981, 984, 987, 988, 986, 989, 990, 991, 992, 993, 994, 999, 997, 998, 996, 995, 985, 983, 982, 978, 980, 948, 949, 953 and 987. The question whether a power is related to distinct matters is one that will have to be decided on a consideration of the terms of the instrument and the nature and extent of the authority conferred thereby.

The assessee was carrying on business in Bhavnagar which was formerly an Indian State. In 1948, the Raj Pramukh of this newly formed State instituted the Saurashtra Income tax Ordinance, 1949. This Ordinance was in force for one year only the assessment year 1949 50. In assessing the profits of business by the two appellant companies for the years 1949 50 the Income tax Officer had to proceed in accordance with the provisions of the Ordinance. For the purpose of calculating the depreciation allowance to which the assessee was entitled in computing the profits or gains of the business, the written down value had to be computed by deduction from the actual cost of depreciation allowance which was allowable under the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, even though not claimed. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner as also the Income Tax Tribunal took a different view and held that this expression "or which would have been allowed to him if the Indian income tax Act 1922 was in operation in the past" did not permit the Income 8 tax Officer to make any deduction under this head. In appeal by the assessee, the High Court held that the words actually used were not sufficient to express and give effect to this intention. The question of law which was referred to the High court under section 66(1) of the Indian Incometax Act on the application of the Commissioner of Income tax had therefore been framed thus: "Whether on the facts and circumstances of the case and upon a proper construction of the expression " or which would be allowed to he assessee if theIndian Income tax (Act, 1922), was in law in force in the previous year" in section 13(5)(b) of Saurashtra Income Tax Ordinance,1949, the write down value has to be determined by deduction of from the original cost of deprecia tion allowance which could have been claimed under the Act even though no claim had been made or could be made for such allowance, was rejected by the Income. tax Officer. The High Court also held that it was not necessary in order to give effect thereto an intention that the word "actually allowed" means "allowable" under the law in operation. In appeals to this Court, HELD: (1) The words "actally allowed" in para 2 of the Removal of Difficulties Order must be applied according to its terms. [226 B] (2) The expression "actly allowed" meant "allow able". The word "depreciation" is not used in the clause as meaning "all depreciation actually allowed under any laws or rules of a Part B State relating to income tax and super tax or any law relating to tax on profits of Business which was law of a part B State. If the omission had been by way of ellipsis, as argued by Mr. Kolah, it would be reasonable to think that the expression 'actually allow able" means 'allowable".

The petitioner, an instrumentality of the State of Karnataka in favour of the Mysore Construction Co. (M.C.) was a party to the contract. He invited tenders from registered contractors of appropriate class. Paragraph I of the notifi cation listed three "Minimum qualifying requirements" viz., that the intending tenderers should have executed civil and architectural works including insulation in a power plant/industrial complex, preferably in power plant; (2) should have an annual turnover of atleast 1 crore for each of the preceding three years. Paragraph V required the intending tenderer to furnish the following information "along with the application for issue of blank tender books", namely: (a) Audited Balance Sheet/Certificate from Chartered Ac countant for preceding three year; (b) Latest income tax clearance Certificate; The issue of the blank tender book was to be between 23rd January to 27th January, 1989 and the completed tender books had to be submitted by 3.00 p.m. on 6.2.89. These were scrutinised with reference to the prequal qualifying requirements and data on experience, work done etc. as furnished by each of them. The petitioner was found to have fulfilled certain preliminary requirements which, under the Notification Inviting Tenders (N.I.T.) had to he verified by reference to audited balance sheets called for under clause (a), of para V, and that the details called for in para V could be supplied at any time before the final award of the contract, and the pre qualifying requirements were only the three conditions set out in para I of this notice. The tender was to contain a description of the work estimated cost of the works, period of completion and minimum prequalifying/eligibility condi tions required and other general requirements such as the value/ fashion of C.M.D. to be furnished latest certificates works, and furnishing of audited balance sheet etc. duly indicating the dates for issuing and receipt of tenders. The Petitioner was also found to fulfil certain preliminary requirement which, according to him, had to have been complied with before the tender books could be submitted. The Tender Committee considered the petitioner 's application for tender forms and after making necessary adjustments it was found that the tender of M.C.C., was Rs. 1.8 crores. The High Court dismissed the writ petition filed by the petitioner. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the petitioner that (i) the K.P.C.; should not at all have entertained the tender; and (ii) the extension of time given to M. C.C; to submit the tender with requisite clarifications were not warranted. Dismissing the Appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The High Courts were in error in holding that it was only para I that stipulates the pre conditions and that all the documents referred to in the other paras can be supplied along with the applica tion for tender form. [234C] 1.2 In order to satisfy itself that the requirements of para I(1) and (2), are fulfilled, the KP. C call for the certifi cates mentioned in para VI. It is clear that apart from para I there are some other requirements in the N.I.,T. which have to be complied with at anytime before the contract can be supply ed, an intending ten derer should satisfy the K P.C, by supplying such of the documents called for In para V as are material in assessing the fulfilment of the condition in para 1, that he fulfills the three prequali tying conditions set forth in para l.

The appellant was the owner of a house. On October 10, 1947, in pursuance of an exchange under section 5 A of the East Punjab Evacuees ' (Administration of Property) Act, 1947 as amended in 1948 and applied to the State of Delhi, such a transaction required confirmation by the Custodian. In compliance with this section the appellant made an application on the 23rd February, 1948, to the Additional Custodian of Evacuee Property for confirmation of the above transaction of exchange and of the consequent transfer to her of the property in agricultural land. The application was not disposed of until the 20th March, 1952. On that date he passed an order confirming the exchange. After the order confirming it was passed by the Additional Deputy Custodian on the 20nd March,1952, the appellant filed an amended application dated the 14th August, 1948 stating that the application was to be in a set form furnishing certain particulars, and that the appellant had been put in possession of the agricultural lands in Punjab Khore presumably by way of attornment 1120 of tenants who were in actual cultivating possession of them. The Custodian General rejected this application on his own merits. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the order under appeal was one passed by virtue of the wide powers of revision vested in the Custodian General under section 27 of the Act. But with respect to the learned Custodian General, his order was such that it was difficult to maintain it. The revisional power cannot be exercised when there was an appeal provided but no appeal was filed, that it Was open to the Assistant Custodian who appeared before the Custodian in support of the notice for revision or to the allottees of the properties in whose interest the revisional order appears to have been passed, to file an appeal under the Act as persons aggrieved. Nor could the scope of revisional powers be confined only to matters of jurisdiction or illegality as is contended, because under section 58(3) of the Central Act XXXI of 1950 which repealed the prior Ordinance was understood with reference to the scheme, there was no reason to confine the operation of the second portion of section 58 (3) to administrative action as suggested by counsel for the appellant.

The appellant company was a manufacturer of hardware merchants. The company had its factory in Bombay and its factory was located at the relevant time. Its factory was situated in the city of Bombay, studded with small hardware businesses where pipes and fittings, nuts and bolts, tools and other small products were made and sold. These establishments, well over a thousand, employ a considerable number of workmen in the neighbourhood of 5,000 although each unit had (barring four), less than the statutory minimum of 20 workmen. The appellant company claimed bonus for the relevant four years prior to 1965, when trouble began. Although rooted in goodness and grace, the annual repetition of these payments ripened, in the consciousness of the workers into a sort of right nothing surprising when we see in our towns and temples a trek of charity seekers claiming benevolence as of right from shop keepers and pilgrims especially when this kindly disposition has been kept up long years. The compassion of yesterday crystallises as the claim of today, and legal right begins as that which is humanistically right. Anyway, the hardwareliers merchants of Nag Devi made of sterner stuff, in their year 1965 abruptly declined to pay the goodwill sums of the spread out past and the frustrated workmen frowned on this stoppage by setting up a right to bonus averring considerable profits for the Industry (if one may conveniently use that expression for a collective coverage of the conglomeration of hard ware establishments). The defiant denial and the consequent dispute resulted in the appointment of a Board of Arbitrators under section 10A of the Industrial Disputes Act to arbitrate upon twelve demands put forward by the company. The Tribunal did not enter the merits of the claim but dismissed it in limine on the score that the demand for bonus was barred by res judicata, the arbitral board 's decision negativing the bonus for 1965 being the basis of this holding. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The plea that only a profit based bonus has been claimed by the workers must fail. [501 C] (2) The Tribunal 's award is not vitiated on any ground. It was not open to the Tribunal to try the dispute referred to it. [602 D E] (3) The main question about the policy of the Parliament that was agitated in that case turned on the availability of the as an independent method of claiming profit bonus de hors the Bonus Act and the Court took the view that it would be subversive of the scheme of the Act to allow an invasion from the flank in that manner. [613 A] (4) The Industrial Tribunal has no jurisdiction to try a dispute referred by it. It is true that if the Bonus Acts are a complete Code, on a true decoding of its scheme and spirit, the industrial Court cannot take off the ground with any other forms of bonus yes, that is the implication of 'a complete code '. The story of 'war bonus ', the Full Bench formula and this Court 's view that 'bonus is not a gratuitous payment made by the employer to his workmen, nor a deferred wage, and that where wages fall short of the living standard and the industry makes profit part of which is due to the contribution of labour, a claim for bonus may be legitimately made by tile workmen ' are set out in that decision. [625 E G] (5) The object and reasons of the Bonus act indicate that the subject matter of the statute is 'the question of payment of bonus based on profits and to recommend principles for computation of such bonus and methods of payment .

The petitioners were direct recruits to the Superior Judicial Services of Punjab and Haryana. The State Government in consultation with the High Court, made the Punjab Superior Judicial Service (Second Amendment) Rules, 1976, which was amended by clause 6 in the same manner as in Punjab, that is to say, 1038 by providing that the seniority of the members of the service, whether direct recruits or promoted officers shall be determined by the length of continuous service (in a post in the service irrespective of the date of confirmation) and that the length Of continuous officiation in a post is the true test of seniority. The amendments made in Punjab on December 3, 1966 with retrospective effect from April 9, 1976 including the amendment to rule 12 governing seniority were made in the teeth of opposition of the High court and indeed, in so far as the retrospective effect of the rules i concerned, the amendment was made without consulting the High Courts. The petitioners who were officiating continuously in the Superior judicial Service of Punjab as Additional District and Sessions Judges for two or three years prior to the appointment of Respondent 3 directly to that service lost their seniority over him by being allotted a date of confirmed which was one day later than the date on which he completed his probationary period. These rules were originally framed by the Governor of Punjab in consultation With the High, Court of Punjab, in exercise of the powers conferred on the Governor by the proviso to article 309 of the Constitution. Rule 12 as it stood originally was revived with effect from 4th April, 1970 with retrospective operation from April 1, 1970.

The appellant was the owner of a Gadi Sirampur and he executed a simple mortgage of Gadi Shirampur in favour of the Chota Nagpur Banking Association Limited. In 1920 the Bank filed a suit against his son Wazir Narain Singh to enforce the mortgage security and obtained a mortgage decree. The suit was decreed by the trial court but the High Court on appeal reversed this decision. Held, that the question whether the mortgagor in possession has power to lease the mortgaged property has got to be determined with reference to the authority of the mortgagor as the bailiff or agent for the mortgagee to deal with the property in the usual course of management. The true position has been stated in the following terms by Mukherjee, in Madan Mohan Singh vs Baj Kishore Kumar (I.L.R. , and Madan Mohan Singha vs Raj Kishore Kumari (I L.R . , referred to. Held further, that section 66 of the Transfer of Property Act has nothing to do with the mortgagor 's power to leases the mortgaged properties. The mortgagor in Possession may make a lease conformable to usage in the ordinary course of administration of management but he is not competent to grant a lease unusual terms or to alter the character of the land or to authorise its use in a manner or for a purpose different from the mode in which he himself had used it before he granted the mortgage. The only relevant consideration is whether, the mortgagor has power either to lease or to modify the character or to restrict the character Of the land and to authorise his use in such manner or to limit the nature of the property or to limits the limits of the limits prescribed by the law.

The petitioner, who was a contractor in respect of the work entrusted to him by the respondent, sent bills on July 12, 1979 but payment was not made. For the first time he sent notice on Nov. 28, 1989 to the respondent for reference to arbitration. On receipt thereof, the respondent filed an arbitration suits in the Calcutta High Court under sections 5 and 12 and 33 of the for short the Act. The learned Single Judge held that the claim was hopelessly barred by limitation. In appeal, the division bench set aside the award and directed the parties to approach the Court for appropriate remedy under section 8 of the Arbitration Act for appointment of an arbitrator. On further appeals, the Division Bench reversed the order of the learned Single judge. The petitioner contended that clause 68 of the Contract provides for appointment by arbitration of all or any of the disputes or differences enumerated therein that have arisen between the parties at the instance of either party to the contract. It was also contended that section 5 has no application to the facts of this case. On behalf of the respondent it was submitted that clause68 of the contract provides for appointing an arbitrator and when the petitioner had legally invoked clause 68 and issued notice to the Respondent, the Respondent is duty bound to appoint an arbitrator; on its failure it is open to him to approach a Civil Court for reference under section 9 of the Act for appointing arbitrator. The question was whether the High Court was justified in permitting the respondent to rescind the contract of Arbitration provided in clause 68. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The provisions of the Limitation Act would apply to arbitrations as they apply to the proceedings in court. Sub section (2) of section 12 accords consequential power which postulates that the power of the Court where Arbitrator is removed or his authority revoked. Where the Court grants such authority consequentially arbitration agreement shall cease to have effect with respect to the difference or dispute. It flows therefrom that there exist implied power vested in the court permitting a party to avail the remedy under sections5 and 12 to rescind, the arbitration agreement. [362C D] 1.2 The provisions Of the Limitation Acts would apply only to arbitrations and notwithstanding any term in the contract to the contrary, cause of arbitration for the purpose of limitation shall be deemed to have accrued to the party in respect thereof at the time when it should have accrued but for that term in an agreement. Sub sections (4) and (5) are omitted as being not material.

The appellants obtained a preliminary decree on June 26, 1947 on the basis of a mortgage. The property mortgaged was an Estate within the meaning of the Bihar Land Reforms Act, 1950. That property included both Bakasht lands as well as other lands. The Act came into force after the passing of the aforesaid preliminary decree. Thereafter the mortgagees applied under section 14 of the Act and got determined the compensation to which they were entitled under the Act. The appellants resisted that execution by filing an application under section 47, Civil Procedure Code (Misc. Case No. 94 of 1959) on the ground that the decree could not be executed in view of the provisions of the said Act. That application was dismissed for default of the judgment debtors on September 12, 1959. A second application raising the same ground of objection ( Misc. Case Nos. 94 and 110 of 1959), was filed by the judgment debtor on September 8, 1960. The executing court came to the conclusion that the objection raised by the Judgment debtors is barred by the principles of res judicata and further on July 23, 1960 for default in the judgment debt. A third application raising it the same plea of resjudicata was dismissed on January 4, 1962 after examining the contentions of the parties. In second appeal by the appellants, the High Court reversed the decision of the executing court but reversed in second appeal. The two questions that arise for decision in this appeal were (1) whether the objection as regards executability of the decree pleaded by the judgement debtors is not barred by principles of Res judicata and (2) whether a mortgage decree has become unexecutable in view Of the provisions Of the Act, and (3) whether it is 'so barred whereas according to the appellants as the Bakashts lands which form part of the mortgaged property had, not vested in the State. HELD : The decision of this Court in Sidheshwar Prasad Singh vs Ram Saroop Singh, [1962] Supp. 3 S.C.R. 564 was not correct. The true effect of the decisions of this court in the Full Bench decision in Sidheswar Prasad 's case is as explained by Kamla Sahai, J. In that case, the whole of the property mortgaged is an estate, there can be no doubt that the procedure prescribed by Chapter IV has to be followed, in order that the amount due to the creditor should be determined by the claims officer and the decision or the Board has been made final by the Act.[914 B] In construing section 4(d) it would not be right to assume that the interests of the debtors affected by the provisions do not fall within the protection of the ,of the Act ' and again at page 578 "Having regard to the said scheme, it is difficult to confine the application of section 4 (d) only to execution proceedings in which the decree holder seeks to proceed against the estate of the debtor.
