The appellant was detained under section 3(1)(i) of the (COFEPOSA for short) by filing a writ petition before the High Court and that application, had been dismissed. The appellant challenged his order of detention on the ground that he was not very much acquainted with them and that he had sought the assistance of a friend at the hearing and for the reasons and in the manner indicated in the counter affidavit, the request was turned down. In the writ petition, the High court held that on 25th November, 1986 while the detaining authority was assisted by a Deputy Collector and a Superintendent of Central Excise, the detenu was denied the assistance and that the detention order was confirmed. The appeal to this Court was filed in this Court. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In matters like the proceedings of Advisory Boards, whosoever assist or advises on facts of law must be deemed to be in the position of a legal adviser. [792C] 1.2 In matters such as the proceedings in Advisory Boards and whosoever assist it with a view to justifying the detention orders. If that be so, the authorities should not permit the authorities to do indirectly what they cannot do directly; and no one should be enabled to take shelter behind the excuse that such officers are not "legal practitioners" or legal advisers. [788E] 1:3 The rule in A. K. Roy 's case (supra) made it clear that the detenu had no right to appear through a legal practitioner in the proceedings before the Advisory Board, but it did not preclude the Board to allow such assistance to the detenu when it allowed the State to be represented by an array of lawyers. [789E] 2:1 The rule was applicable to the facts of this case. [781C] 2.2 The refusal by the Advisory board to permit the appellant to be assisted by Sundararajan as a friend was bad and continued detention of the appellant became vitiated. Accordingly, this appeal is allowed and the order of his detention is quashed. [784E F] 2 :3 In the instant case, on 25.11.1986 while the detenu 's detaining authority is assisted by the Deputy Collector of Central excise and a superintendent of Central Excises, the detenue was denied assistance of the Deputy Commissioner of Central Revenue. The rule made it explicit that the detenue had no legal right to be heard by counsel.

The Government of India issued a notice under sub r. (2) of r. 75 A(2) Of the Defence of India Rules, 1939, to acquire the requisitioned goods and acquired movable property under the rules made under the Defence Of India Act, 1939. The owners of the jute mills were in possession of the Mills and therefore the proper persons to be served with the orders of requisition in this case were the mills. The Government of india issued a notification on September 30, 1946, under sub rule (2), of r . The owner of the property was served with a notice on the same managing agents. The appellants contended that the order of requisition was not valid and binding as it did not comply with the provisions of r, 75 A (2). Held, that the service of the notices of acquisition in this ease having been admittedly served on the managing agents of the mills it was effected on one of the principal officers of the company and 835 would be a good service under O. 2(11) of the Rules. The notice of acquisition was properly served on all the managing directors of the textile mills through the managing agent and therefore these orders were validly and duly served on them through the Managing Agents and therefore they were not valid. Held, further, that as the Government of lndia was claiming under the Mills, it would also be estopped from denying the title of the holders of pucca delivery orders in the same way as the mills through whom it was claiming. The word " service" in section 18 of the Act means service on the owner and not on the person who can place the goods in question at the disposal of the requisitioning authority and until that is done there cannot be any valid and effective requisition. Held further, also, that when the service in this present case was effected by the managing agency of the mill it was affected on one or the other of the directors of a company and not by the appellants. The order of the requisition was properly made and duly executed on the Managing agents of those mills through them and therefore there could be no valid requisition of the goods mentioned in the notice of requisition.

The assessee is a Private Limited Company. The assessment year concerned is 1963 64. Sometime in 1955 56, a notice was issued to the assessee under Section 23A of the Income Tax Act, 1922. Apprehending that it may become liable to pay additional tax under the said provision, the assessee set apart a sum of Rs. 6,52,000 in its books for the year ending March 31, 1956. Out of this amount an amount of Rs 2,02,000 was transferred to the profit and loss account during the year 1958 59 with the result that a sum continued to remain and was shown as a provision set apart to meet the taxation liability which the assessee called a contingent liability. At the same time, the Income tax Officer did not agree and the matter was ultimately taken to the IncomeTax Appellate Tribunal. The Tribunal held that no action could be taken against the assessee. In appeal by the Revenue, it was contended on behalf of the assessee that inasmuch as no order levying additional tax was made on or before the date relevant to the assessment year 1963 64, the said amount cannot be treated as a 'provision '. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The High Court was right in holding it to be a provision and not a reserve. [113C] 2. In Metal Box Company of India Limited vs Their Workmen, , the distinction between a provision & reserve is stated in the following words: "The distinction between the provisions and reserve is that whereas a provision is a charge against the profits to be taken into account against gross receipts in the P.& L account, a reserve is in appropriation of profits, the asset or assets by which it is represented being retained to form part of the capital employed in the business. Bearing in mind the aforesaid broad distinction, this will indicate how the two concepts are defined and dealt with by the " Applying the said test it must be held that the provision made by the assessee in its Books for meeting the anticipated liability of tax (under Section 23 A) was indeed a provision. [ 113D E] 3. The assessee itself called it a provision, and did not call it a reserve nor was it set apart or appropriated as a reserve, [113E F] 4.

The petitioners, who were direct recruits to the Indian Railway Service of Engineers (Class 1) (hereafter referred to as 'the 'Engineers ' at places), were appointed by the Railway Board through the Union Public Service Commission. The appointments were due for different courses of training earmarked separately. There were a host of other factors which distinguished the quality and character of the personnel of the two parallel services as elaborately detailed in Katyani Dayal 's case, (supra). Between the years 1955 and 1964, as many as officers (temporary Assistant Engineers) were appointed on the basis of selection by the Union Government. The petitioners, describing themselves as members of the Federation of Temporary Officers Association, Indian Railways joining with them, their President Vice President and Secretary of the said Federation as writ petitioners approached this Court in a representative capacity to seek relief in their seniority status. The principal claim of the writ petitioners was that officers were appointed to temporary posts on the cadre of Engineers and that their seniority had to be reckoned on the date of their absorption into the Indian Railways Service of engineers (Class I) ( hereinafter referred to, as 'Engineer ' at place). While the President was the appointing authority of the Engineers, the Railway board was theappointing authority of officers. Both the members of these services were due to different courses and training earmarked differently. There was a host Of other factors, which distinguished their quality and nature of the work of the staff of the three parallel services, as elaborately in Katakyani 's Case, examining the question afresh in the light of Raghunandan Prasad Singh vs Secretary, Home (Police) Department, Government of Bihar & Ors., [1988] Supp. SCC 519, Dr. O.Z Hussain vs Union of India, [1990] Supp SCC 691 and Direct Recruit Class II Engineering of officers Association vs State of Maharashtra & Ors. ; and 1025 other cases. The Court while dismissing the writ petitions held that the classification of temporary Assistant Officers separately from the Indian railway Service of Engineer Class I was neither discriminatory nor violative of Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution, for the reason that it had nexus to the object sought to be achieved, which mainly was efficiency of service, and that both the services had started separately and never became one. This Court further observed that the object of recruitment being different, the methods of recruitment dissimilar, the appointing author being not the same, the training imparted to the two unlike, the tenure of temporary Assistants being precarious, and their maximum aspiration being only to be absorbed into the Iona wait by giving them weightage of half of the length of service as temporary Assistant officers subject to the maximum of five years. And lastly this Court rejected the claim of temporary Officers asking for "equal status for equal pay and equal work" leaving a ray of hope that such goal might be achieved in the not too distant future. The instant batch of matters is virtually on the same lines as of Katyni Dayal ' 's cases claiming the same relief and this time by the Temporary Assistant Officers through a body styled as the Federation Of Directly Appointed Officers (Suppressed) of Indian Railways and a few others, in a Representative capacity across which stand arrayed the Union of india and the Railway Boards as respondents. When this matter came up for hearing on 15th March, 1990 before a three Judge Bench in which one of us (Punchhi, J.) was a member, it was contended that principles of constructive res judicata would bar the re agitation of the issues decided in Kattani Dayal"s case justifying demolition of the demarcation between the two services made as it was in Katalani Dayal vs Secretary Home ( Police) Department Government ofBihar & Ors [1988], Supp.

The appellant State of West Bengal vs Anwar Ali Sarkar, ; , followed. The Bombay Special Courts Act, 1949, which was in identical terms with section 11 of the Ordinance of 1948, provided that "all offences under the Indian Penal Code shall be investigated, inquired into, tried and otherwise dealt with according to the provisions hereinafter contained", and that the procedure applicable to the trial of such offences. The appellant contended that sections 9 and 11 by empowering the State Government to constitute Special Courts for any area or for the whole of the State of Saurashtra contravened article 14 Of the Constitution and was void as offending against the equal protection clause in article 14 of the Constitu tion. Held, that section 11 was not discriminatory and did not offend article 14. The classification implied in this part of the sub section had no reference to, and was not directed towards, the singling out of any particular person as an object of hostile State action but was concerned only with the grouping of "offences", "classes of offences" and "cl classes of cases". The Legislature had left it to the State Govern ment to classify offences or classes of offences or class of cases for the purpose of the ordinance, for the State Gov ernment was in a better position to judge the needs and exigencies of the state and the Court would not lightly interfere with the decision of the Government. Benoarilal 's case, , referred to. The object of the Act was to provide for public safety, maintenance of public order and preservation of peace and tranquillity in the State. It was not correct to say that section II of the Saurashtra Ordinance which authorised the State Govt. to direct "offenses" to be tried by Special Courts was discriminatory and violative of article 14 as it conferred a power on the State Legislature to make a classifi cation of " offences", 'classes or classes thereof to be try ed by the Special Court, offended against the provisions of article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution.

P.Ws. 2,7 and 8 who was sleeping in their house in the western kotha and PW 2 and her children in the eastern kotkha of the house were sleeping in a tin shed situate west of the western wall of the northern kothakha where there is a barotha. The appellants attacked P.W 2 with lathis, spears and lathis on the ground that he had been murdered in his house and property had been looted from his house by dacoits and that his brother and certain other persons had gone to the police station for lodging a report. In that incident P. Ws. 2 and 8 were injured and P. W.2 who was sitting on the eastern wall of his house while PW 2 was sleeping earlier to the western Kotha where he was sleeping later to the northern wall of a tin storeyed west of his eastern kutha, saw the other appellants from behind the door of the eastern store and the lantern material Exh. P 18 issued by that Doctor in respect of P. PWs. 2 7 and 8 had been proved by the Compounder Vishamber Nath (P). The trial Court acquitted nine of them. On appeal by the convicted accused persons, the High Court set aside their conviction and sentence and confirmed the convictions of the appellants for the offence under section 396 I.P.C. and the sentences awarded to them by the Sessions Judge and confirmed by the High Courts. In the appeals before this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the evidence of P PWs 1, 7 and 9 is not convincing; (ii) the prosecution has failed to prove the presence of PW 2 in the tin shed of the houses of the accused at the time of occurrence; (iii) the appellants were in the northern Kothaka together at the same time at the place of occurrence and it was not improbable that these appellants were seen by P.w. 2 or 3 minutes after the accused persons went away, My Dewar (husband 's brother) Baijnath (P.[574A] HELD: 1.

The respondent employer terminated the services of some of its employees during the initial period of probation and of some others during the extended period on the ground of unsatisfactory service. Thereupon an industrial dispute was raised questioning the legality of their termination and the State Government referred the dispute to the Labour Court for adjudication under section 10 of the . The Labour Court held that section 25F had no application, to the effect that the discharge was invalid. The employer Corporation came before the High Court challenging the Award. A learned single Judge dismissed the writ petition holding that the order of discharge amounted to retrenchment as defined in section 2(oo) of the and those orders were bad for non compliance with the provisions of section 25 FF. The appellant Corporation challenged the decision of the Single Judge before a Division Bench and the Division Bench upheld the decision. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The question whether the discharge of the employees from service amounted to 'retrenchment ' or not was not relevant for consideration in these cases. [787G] 1.2 In the instant case, the requirements of section 2 (oo) are satisfied. The termination of the service of a workman on the transfer or closure of an undertaking was treated by Parliament as 'deemed retrenchment '. The effect was that every case of termination of service by act of employer even if such termination involved was a consequence of transfer or cancellation of the undertaking was to be treated as 'ret retrenchment ' for the purposes of notice, compensation etc. [788A] 1:3 In the present case, there is no dispute that as a condition precedent to discharge the requirements under section 25 EF had not been complied with in these matters. The requirement of section 26F had never been complied. If the discharge had been grounded upon unsatisfactory service during the period of Probation, it has been argued that such termination was not due to discharge of surplus labour force and, therefore, did not amount to retrenchment. [789B] 1 :4 In the circumstances, the order passed by the Labour court which set aside those orders and gave appropriate relief is set aside.

The assessee South Eastern Railway disposed of unclaimed and unconnected goods for money consideration. On 1 April, 1952 the assessee applied to the Commercial Tax Officer for cancellation of the registration of the assessee as a "dealer" under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. The Commercial Tax officer examined the case and did not accept the contention that the assessee was not a " dealer". On 6 June 1959 he made an order rejecting the application on the basis that the disposal of unclaimed goods for valuable consideration was a regular feature of the asses see 's activities, and that therefore the assessee fell within the scope of the Act. The assessee applied in revision before the Assistant Commis sioner of Commercial Taxes. The Board held that a transfer of property was involved in the auction held by the assessee and that consequently a sale of goods took place. The High Court also dismissed the revision application on merits. In these appeals, it was contended for the appellant that the activity of so disposing of the goods did not indicate that the Railway concerned was carrying on business as a dealer liable to assessment under the Act, and therefore the assesee fell within its scope of section 2(c) of the Bengal Reve nue (Sales tax) Act. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The activity of disposing of goods was adjunctive to the principal activity of the carriage of goods by the Railway. It is an activity which may be regarded as necessarily incidental or ancillary to its business as carrier of the Goods. [781C] 2. In the instant case, the assessee Eastern Railway was a "business" for the purposes of the Indian Reve tue ( Sales Tax) act, 1941, and it was engaged in selling scrap and unserviceable material lying with it. The case is covered directly by the decision of this Court in the District Controller of Stores, Northern Railway, Jodhpur vs The Assistant Commercial Taxation Officer and Another, [1976] 37 S.T.C. 423. In C.A. No. 1069 of 1975 the facts and circumstances in the case out of which Civil Appeal No.1069 of l0 arises are substantially similar to those narrated in the earlier case, except that the assesse was the Eastern Railway and it is engaged in sale scrap and waste unserviceable materials lying with It. The Case is covered by directly by this decision of the Court in District Controller 's Stores, Southern Railway, Jaipur vs The Asstt.

The appellants were convicted of certain offences arising out of the overt acts committed by them. The main statement on which the prosecution relied was that the moneys of the Insurance Company were diverted to Union Agencies by the transactions proved by the prosecution, and that the balance in the account of the Union Agencies with the United Bank of India and Rs. 35,00,000 on behalf of the said Insurance Company had been passed on to the Union agencies. The appellants contended that they were not delivered to the Insurance company by Bhagwati Trading Company and yet Chokhani made payment of the purchase price from out of its funds to the union Agencies when funds were needed and also providing funds in the Insurance Companies ' account with the Chartered Bank, Bombay, in case the balance was not sufficient to meet the losses. Held, that the appellants were rightly convicted under section 120 read with section 409 I.P.C., and they could be convicted under sections 477A, I. P. C. The charge under section 409 was framed against the appellants on the basis of the statement made by Bhagwati trading Company in its books of account and not on his own. The prosecution had failed to lead direct evidence about Gurha 's knowledge with respect to the full working of the scheme to provide for the losses of the company from the funds of the insurance company to the said Union Agencies, and therefore the falsification of the journal vouchers related back to the original diversion of the Bank 's moneys to the Defence Agencies and was with a view to deceive any such person in future who be tracing the source of money received by the Union Agency. The mere fact that the funds were diverted from the Reserve Bank of lndia in contravention of the manner in which he was to deal with that money, did not make it possible for the prosecution to lead further evidence about the appellants ' knowledge with regard to the true state of affairs and the desirability of falsifying the accounts and papers of the office. The fact that funds of a company were diverted by the said transactions to Union agencies by the dealings proved by it was not challenged by Dalmia, because he was a Director of the latter as he never issued instructions regarding the activities of the union agencies, had no knowledge of passing money from the Bank to the Bank.

The appellants were holding permanent posts in the ministerial service of the Secretariat Service of the State of Gujarat. By virtue of section 8 of the States Reorganization Act 37 of 1956, the new State of Bombay which included the territories of the states of Saurashtra and Kutch was formed. Under section 81(1) of the Bombay Reorganisation Act, the States of Saurashtra were carved out of the territory of the new state of Bombay. Under the provisions relating to services other than All India Services were made and by section 82 of the Act, it was provided that conditions of service applicable immediately before November 1, 1956 to the case of any person allotted to another State shall not be varied to his disadvantage except with the previous approval of the Central Government. Section 116 provided for the continuance of officers in the same posts. By section 117 power was conferred upon the Central Govern ment to give directions to the States. Those provisions were substantially the same as the provisions of sections 115, 116 and 117 of the . The appellants were allotted to serve in connection with the affairs of the former State of Saurashtra under section 81 of the Gujarat Reorganisation Act. Under that section, the conditions of services applicable immediately prior to November 1 1956 were 'a list of 90 persons designating the departments in which they were posted, posts to which appointed and the dates from which they are appointed. The officers of the secretariat who before the date of the order constituted the ministerial Service then filed a petition out of which this appeal arises challenging the validity of the orders of the Government. The High Court held that since the impugned order purported to amalgamate the former Saurashtra and Saurashtra States personnel with the Gujarat Secretariat Service contrary to the terms of r. 138 of the Recruitment Rules, 1957, and the Government had no authority to vary the method of recruitment provided by the statutory rules framed under article 309 of the Constitution, it could not operate as absorption under the Allocated Government Servants ' (Absorption, Seniority, Pay & Allowances) Rules,1957. The appellants came to this Court by special leave. HELD: (i) The order dated August 19, 1966 was contrary to r.138 of the recruitment rules framed by the State Government in 1957. [519 E] (ii) The expression "absorption" has not been used in the order but that will not justify an inference that there was no intention to absorb the former and Kutch States personnel in the Secretariat. In the absence of determination of equivalent posts under the orders, of the central Government, the State was competent as a matter of provisional arrangement to absorb absorption the former de fendants and Kutch states which they acquired under the , to hold posts in tho 'new State which were equivalent and on terms which were not, unless the previous sanction of the Chief Government was obtained. [525 G] (iii) The State has the authority to transfer, subject to the Constitution and the rules made under article 311 any public servant to render service which by his training and aptitude he was competent to do. [500 E F] N. Raghavendra Rao vs Deputy Commissioner, South Kanara, Mangalore ; , followed.

The petitioners of the second category purchase oil seeds for use in manufacture of edible oils. The surplus oil seeds were sold to other dealers, registered or unregistered, inside and outside the State. Both these commodities are essential commodities to which the Central Sales Tax Act applies. Certain provisions of these Amending Acts were challenged on the ground that they offend section 15 of the Central Act and are also unconstitutional being in violation of Articles 14 and 19. The Punjab General Sales Tax (Amendment and Validation) Act, 1967 was passed in 1948. The petitioners contended that there was a possibility of tax being levied at more than one stage, the provisions of the first proviso notwithstanding. The contention was negatived by this Court on the grounds: (i) that section 2(ff), 5(1)(a)(vi) and (2)(a) were in conflict with section 15; (ii) that there is a delegated legislation in that the maximum has been provided without indication of the circumstances under which the tax is to be levied. HELD : (i). The question as to how far a party can ask for refund, without the order of assessment being set aside by appropriate proceedings is highly doubtful because at the time when the actual order of assess ment is passed, in certain eases, it may not be possible for a party to say whether he was entitled to exemption or not, under sub cl. (vi) of section 5(2)(A), negatives the assumption that the normal rule under the Act, in respect of declared goods, is to levy the tax on the first purchaser. It will be absolutely difficult if not impossible, for persons like the appellant, to collect materials in this behalf, because there is no provision, contained either in the Act or the rules, on the basis of which it will be entitled to be supplied with all the material information relevant, relevant for sustaining a request for refund. If the Central Legislature makes it mandatory that the tax can be collected only at one stage in our opinion, it is not enough for the State to say that a person, who is not liable to pay tax must nevertheless pay it in the first instance and then claim refund, at a later stage. [550 G H] (ii). The matter is now in the hands of the dealer. If he knows that he is not the last dealer having parted with the goods to another dealer or he knows what he is going to use the goods or sell them to consumers, he knows when he is no liable to tax and when he was. as the last purchase or sale by a dealer liable to payment of the tax makes the stage quite clear and by giving an option to him not to include such transactions in his return saves him from the liability to pay the tax till he is the dealer liable. [553 C D] (iii). The point as to what should be the rate of tax same in every case. Nataraja Mudaliar, [1969] S.C.R. 557, followed.

The appellants, who were the representatives of three original plaintiffs, instituted a suit against the respondent for enforcement of a mortgage. The suit was contested by all the defendants except defendant No. 1 against whom it proceeded ex parte and there was a preliminary decree passed on May 15,1937, by which a sum of RS. 1,08,098 was directed to be paid by defendant No 1 and defendants 3 to 7 in default of which the plaintiffs were declared entitled to apply for a final decree for sale of the mortgaged properties and the suit was dismissed against defendant No 2. Against this decree two appeals were taken to the High Court, one by defendants 3 and 6 being Appeal No. 48 of 1938 who contended that the mortgage debt was one and indivisible and even though different amounts were mentioned as payable by two groups of defendants in the decree, the decree holders were bound under the terms of the decree to release the entire mortgaged property even on payment of the amount directed to he paid by them under the decree. The High Court accepted the finding of the District Judge but held that defendant No . 1 was entitled to have the debt scaled down and set aside the ex parte decree. On appeal by special leave, Held: (i) The High court 's approach to the case has not been a proper one and the conclusion it has reached cannot be supported in law. The learned Judges appear to have overlooked the fact that they were sitting only as an executing court and their duty was to give effect to the terms Of the decree that was already passed and beyond which they could not go. It is enough to say that the ratio decidendi in all these cases is not applicable to the present case. Rainier vs Srinivasiah, [1940] 2 M. 39 300 decisions referred to. (ii) The Madras Agriculturists ' Relief Act is a special statute which aims at giving relief not to debtors in general but only to a specified class of debtors viz., those who are agriculturists as defined in the Act. To this extent it trenches upon the general law and section 7 of the Act expressly provides that notwithstanding any law, custom, contract or decree of court to the contrary all debts payable by an agriculturist at the commencement of this Act shall be scaled up in accordance with the provi sions of this chapter. [301 E] (iii) The principle of unity and solemnity of a mort gagor decree is that a mortgage decree is one and cum indivisible and exception to this rule are admitted in special circumstances where the integrity of the mortgage has been disrupted at the instance of the mortgagee himself; e.g., when there is severance of the interests of the mort gawalli with the consent of the mortgagor or a portion of the equity of redemption is vested in the latter. It was not necessary for purposes of this case to express any opinion as to the correctness or otherwise of these deci sions.

The City Civil Court had no jurisdiction to entertain the suit. The City Civil court had no juris diction to entertain a suit in the City Civil Courts, Bombay, and the City civil Court was called upon to decide whether the first plaintiff was a tenant of the premises within the meaning of the Act and whether he had lawfully sublet the same to the second and third plaintiffs. The High Court agreed with the view of the Judge of the City Court that he had jurisdiction to try the suit but did not record any decision on the merits of the appellants ' case. Held, that the City Curt had no power to entertain an application in the city Civil Courts for trying the title thereto. The provisions of section 28 and 29A of the Bombay Rents, Hotel and Lodging House Rates Control Act, 1947, clearly indicate that all claims or questions arising out of the provi sions of Part 11 of the said Act, even though they may be in the nature of a title to the premises, were to be determined by the courts specified in section 28. The suit was not one between a landlord and a tenant merely because the defendants denied the claim of the plaintiffs. Whether the plaintiffs were tenants would be a claim or question arising out o the Act or any of its provisions, even although they may not be in tho nature of title to tile premises, was that a title which section 29A permits a party to establish in a competent court other than that specified in s.28 and no other. The suits were essentially a suit between a landlords and a tenants. The claim of defendants was one which arose out of a Act or some of its provi tions.

The respondent was a private company. The appellant was the managing director of the Company in respect of its business under the name and style of Oriental Metal Pressing Works Ltd., hereafter called the Company, which had been transferred to it by the respondent. On July 7, 1955, the respondent filed a suit against the appellant for the declaration that he ceased to be a director on account of his failure to attend the directors ' meetings. The trial court accepted all the contentions of the respondent and made the declarations claimed. The High Court held that the appointment of the appellant as managing director by the will of Dadoba was void in view of section 312 of the . Held, that the word "assignment" in section 312 included "appointment". The word "resign" in the section included "appointments". The proviso to section 86B did not prevent a director from appointing his successor. The power to appoint alternate directors was not given by the old Act but had to be given by articles, such an appointment would also be void under the section. Held further, that section 312 was not applicable to the case as the appellant had been lawfully appointed the managing directors of the company and set aside the decision of the courts below. The word 'assignment ' in section 313 meant "appointment" and did not include "appointment." The word was used in the sense of a term which would indicate that the office contemplated was one held by the director at the time of assignment. An appointment to an office can be made only if the office is vacant. It is legitimate, therefore, to infer that by using the word 'his" the Legislature indicated that an appointment by a director to the office which he previously held but did not hold at the date of the appointment was not to be included within the word`assignment". The section was intended to prevent this result and would not have used the word `assign ' in it, as was done in the High Court.

The appellants are a partnership firm and carry on business in the name and style of M/s. Adeshwar Glass Mart, which carried on business there. The respondent filed an eviction petition against the appellants and one other partnership firm, carrying on business at the said premises and that firm was also joined by the respondent herein as respondents in the eviction petition on the ground that they were unlawful sub tenants. The Trial Court held this ground established and passed a decree for eviction as sought by the respond ent. The appel lants preferred an appeal against this decision to the Appellate Authority under Section 23 of the Rent Act, being the Court of Small Causes at Madras. The said appeal was numbered as H.R.A. 156 of 1979. The Appellate Authority dismissed the said appeal upholding the finding of unlawful subletting by the appellants. The appellants then moved a Civil Revision Petition in the High Court against the aforesaid decision. This revision petition was dismissed by the then Chief Justice of the Madras High Court. In the appeal before this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appel tants that the impugned judgment must be set aside as the eviction peti tion was filed against the appellant firm and one partnership firm M/S. Adieswar Glass Mart without joining any of the partners of the said firms as respondents or serving them as partners and hence, the eviction Petition was not maintainable at all. It was further contended that there was no evidence in the case to come to the conclusion that the appellants had sublet the shop to M/ s. Adarseshwar Glass Shop Mart without join ing any of their partners as respondents. Dismissing the appeal, this Court HELD: 1. The partners of a firm are before the Court though in a wrong name. [420B] 2. In cases where no such objection has been raised at all till the stage of Special Leave and it is surely not open to the appellants to raise such an objection at a very late stage and thereby delay matters for a number of years. This contention must, therefore, be negatived. [ 420C] Chhotelal Pyarelal, the partnership firm & Ors. vs Shikharchand, ; , relied upon by Mr. Nayar, the objection to the main tainability of the petition was raised at the earliest stage and was wrongly negatived by the Trial Court. [421D E] 3. In view of this, there is no substance in this contention.

The Andhra Pradesh (Andhra Area) Act, 1976 was enacted to provide for the imposition of a ceiling on urban immovable property and for matters connected therewith, with a view to preventing the concentration of urban land in the hands of a few persons and speculation and profiteering therein and with a direction to prevent the concentration Of urban land into the hands or to make it an equitable distribution of land in urban agglomerations to sub serve the common good. The Andhra Pradesh Act was enacted by Parliament alone was competent to legislate with respect to ceiling on Urban immovable property, and acquisition of such property in excess of the ceiling limit and all matters connected thereto, ancillary or incidental thereto should be regulated in the State of Andhra Pradesh by law. Section 2(a) (i) defines "vacant land" by providing that if the extent of the holding of a person is in excess Of the ceiling area, the person shall be liable to surrender the land held in excess. If therefore an individual or a family unit holds land in excess thereof of the Ceiling Area, the excess would have to be surrendered to the State Government. The Explanation thereto requires that the lands held by all the members of the family unit shall be aggregated for the purpose of computing, the holding for the family units. Where, therefore, there is no master plan or where the master plan does not refer to any land as urban agglomeration at the date of the enactment of the Andhra Pradesh Urban Land (Ceiling and Regulation) Bill 1976 in Parliament, the Andhra Act would apply in relation to land situate within such area, but until that happens the Andhra State Act would continue to be applicable to determine the ceiling on holding of land falling within the definition in section 3(j) of that Act and situate within the said area. The expression "vacent land" is defined in section 2(f) to mean "land which A is used or is capable of being used for purposes ancillary thereto, including horticulture, forest land, pasture land, waste land plantation and tope; and includes land deemed to be agricultural land under this Act". Section 10 is the key section which imposes ceiling on the holding Of land by providing for that if extent of holding of any person isin excess of ceiling area the person would be liable liable to surrendered the land hold in excess, but if the family Unit consists of father, mother and three minor sons or daughters, the lands hold by all these persons would have been clubbed together and then the ceiling areas applied to the aggregate holding. Both stand on the same footing and a divided minor son is as much a member of the Family unit as an undivided minor son and consequently the lands holding held by a divided major son would have had to be included in the holding. The land obtained by the divided minor sons on partition would be subject to the maximum limit of 2 standard holdings. When the ceiling was applied to, the holdings of a family units consisting of father mother and 3 minor sons were notified as an urban agglemy under section 2 (n) (A)(ii) of the Central Act but until it was so notified it would not be an urbanisable agglomeration and the Andhra pradesh Legislature would have legislative competence to provide that for imposition of ceiling on land situate in such area even though it is not an urban commuterative at the time of enactment of Andhra Act. The question whether a particular land is within the meaning of section 2 of the Act or not, was answered by this Court in Union of India vs V.

The workmen of the appellant company were dismissed from service by the Company on account of misconduct. The workmen 's case was that on a particular date between July 5, 1953 and July 10, 1953 they were taken in custody by the police and remained in custody for some time; they applied for leave when in custody but leave was refused. The Union could take up the case on merits with the management of the company. The Tribunal dismissed both the appeals of the workmen on the ground that it did not involve any substantial question of law. Held, that the two Tribunals below had misdirect ed themselves as to the true scope and effect of the Standing Orders in question and their decision with regard to the seven workmen mentioned above cannot be supported. It was well settled that if a large number of workmen are arrested by the authorities in charge of law and order by reason of their questionable activities in connection with a labour dispute, as in this case, the work of the Company will be paralysed if the company is forced to give leave to all them for a " more more or less indefinite period. It may be readily accepted that if the workmen are apprehended at the instance of the companies for the purpose of victimisation and in order to get rid of them on the ostensible pretext of continued absence, the position will be different. Held further, that when the words used in the notices sufficiently bring out the intention of the parties, it is necessary to refer to other evidence in the record. The two Tribunals had mis direct themselves as regards the true nature of the strike declared by the workmen and also as to their legality of the lock out declared by them. Held also, that though the Tribunal found that the company scrutinised the conduct of the workman to find out how far they were associated with the Action Committee, how far he took part in the meetings etc., and on that basis some workmen were taken back and some were not taken back, it was for the Company to decide whether the charges had been proved and the Industrial Tribunal should not have interfered with the decision of the Tribunal unless it found that it was mala fide or amounted to victimisation. The finding of the Industrial tribunal that the charge sheet on which Chattoraj was suspended had not been proved could not be supported as a result of any exceptional or special circumstances or of grave injustice, and the Tribunal did not act as a Court of appeal and substitute its own judgment for that of the management.

The University of Rajas than invited applications for the post of Professor in the department of Botany. The Selection Committee constituted under section 5 of the Rajasthan University Teachers and Offi cers (Selection for Appointment) Act, 1974 held interviews on 20th June, 1989 and selected Dr. Nathawat for the said post. Dr. Urea Kant was appointed as Professor in a Department of Bast ery. Dr Shiv Sharma, Dr. Sudhakar Mishra and Dr. T.N. Bhardwaj who were not selected filed a writ petition in the High Court initially challeng ing the appointment of Dr. Uma Kant as well as the University of Rajasthan tiled special appeal before this Court. The Division Bench of the High COurt held that once a person selected by the Selection Committee has joined, that post is filled and some vacancy is caused thereafter a fresh and de novo selection committee has to be started because that will be a case of future vacancy aris ing after the post had been filled up on the recommendations of the Selection Commit tee. The High Court further held that the constitution of the Committee was valid but as regards the appointment from the reserve list it was held that since 1978 not only in the University but all other universities in the State of Rajasthan but all others in the state of Rajasthan reserve lists are prepared and appointments are being made from the re serve list against future vacancies arising on account of resignation, retirement or promotion. The appointment of Mr. Usi Kant was held illegal and it was directed that Dr. Laxmi Kant be removed from the said posts of Professor of Btany. Both Dr.Urea Kant as also the University have come in appeal by grant of special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The High court committed a clear error in restricting the scope of reserve list only against the post for which the selec tion was made and which according to the High court could only be available to the incumbent in the reserve List if the person recommended in the main list did not join such post. Such interpretation is not borne out from any of the provisions of section 3(1), Section 5 or sub section (4) of section 6 of the Act of 1974.

The petitioners were owners of plots of land in areas round about Bombay, commonly known as Greater Bombay. They had all similar but separate grievances with respect to the development plan prepared and published under the Act. In Writ Petition No. 228 of 1966 the petitioners ' complaint was that their lands were needed for the public purpose of a park in the Development Plan prepared under the Bombay Town Planning Act, 1954, and that they had written a letter to the Municipal Commissioner of Bombay for approval and such approval was given on July 2, 1964. The authority responsible for drawing up the plan had to have regard to the wishes and suggestions of the public and in particular, architects, engineers, industrialists and public bodies. Chapter II containing sections 3 to 17 related to development plans generally. Section 21 showed that such a scheme may be made in accordance with the provisions of the Act in respect of land which is in the course of development or is likely to be used for building purposes, or has already been built upon. section 22 empowered the local authority to make rules for carrying out the purposes of the said Act. The petitioners ' grievance was that the list of sites reserved for public purposes was for the first time submitted by the second respondent to the Development Committee on February 8, 1964 showing for the second time that a major portion of the petitioners lands were earmarked for a recreation centre and green belt in the development Plan prepared by the Municipal Corporation of Bombay. The respondents contended that the said plots were earmarked in the plan published on January 9, 1964 by green colour without assigning any purpose and the reservation and re designation of these lands for recreation centre should be removed, that their land should be redesignated as earmarked for industrial purpose, that the order of the Assistant Engineer rejecting the petitioners proposal for construction of two factory buildings and lavatory blocks was illegal and ultra vires the Constitution of India. The High Court dismissed the petition on the ground that there were no principles in the Act itself to guide the competent authority in the exercise of his will and pleasure to refuse permission to execute a decree for eviction violated the right to hold property under article 19(1)(f) of the Constitution, on the grounds: (i) that by the combined operation of sections 4 and 11(3) the local author ity could easily delay the acquisition of any land designated for public purpose under section 7 of the Bombay City Town Planning act, 1954; (ii) that the power vested in the competent autho rity at its sweet will and discretion to refuse to execute such a decree was unguided, arbitrary and uncontrolled as such infringed the fundamental rights of the peti tioners under articles 14, 19(i)(f), 31 and 31 of the Constitu tion. The Court also held that the provisions regarding the levy of contribution towards the cost of the scheme and all other matters relating to the working of the Scheme were unauthorised and unreasonable and that the powers vested in tho Town Planning Officer and other authorities under the said Acts were unguided, uncontrolled and uncontrolled and as such violated the fundamental right of the Petitioners under articles 19( 1)(f). The Court further held that sections 4 to 16 would also be operative with the result that the acquisition might be delayed for a further period of ten years. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellants: (1) that section 11(1) empowers the local autho rie to acquire any land described in the Plan for a purpose specified in cls. (a), (b) or (e) of section 7 and if such land does not vest in the local Authority, the State Government could validly pass the Act as it was not covered by any of the entries in List 11 or List 111, of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution; and (2) that even assuming that the State Legislature could pass the impugned Act, nevertheless its provisions regarding levy of contributions towards the costs of the schemes were unauthorised.

The petitioners who were five writ petitions under article 32 of the Constitution and three appeals against the decisions of the High Courts of Gujarat and Delhi, claiming that there was no territorial dispute as there was a well established boundary running roughly along the northern edge of the Rann of Kutch as shown in the pre partition maps which needs to be demarcated on the ground. The petitioners contended that the territory in this sector belonged to the Kutch State and that claim was supported by survey maps, correspondence between the officials of Kutch State, and the British Adminis tration, assertions made in the annual Administration Reports for 75 years before 1947 Statistical abstracts relating to British India, Bombay Administration Reports Gazetteers, Memorandum on Indian States and a number of official publications, and by the Resolution of the Government of Bombay, dated 305 February 24, 1914. The respondents urged that the area was in different state at different seasons in the year, for part of the year it was water and for the remaining part it was land. It was further contended that there were no clear evidence of demarcation of a boundary acceptable to the parties now or in the past, (e) that the claim of the respondents was supported on survey maps and correspondence between them, and (f) that there could be a cession of Indian territory and the rule earlier laid down by this Court applied. HELD : The dispute related to the boundary between the two States. It is not evidence of the fact that it was territory over which the Maharao of Kutch exercised sovereign rights and which by merger of the territory became Indian territory. [301 C] In the present case, the area in question was a part of Kutch state but there was an extension of the mainland of Sind, and apart from the survey maps there is no evidence that it is part of Great Rann or that it has been part of India.

The mortgagor borrowed Rs. 5,500 from one Rabindra Nath Chakravarty and executed a deed of mortgage whereby he agreed to repay the amount and encum bered his share in Mauzas Bansjora and Simitanr Bahaldih for repayment of the amount borrowed with interest at the rate of Rs. 1/8 per mensem. The mortgagor also agreed that the mortgagee do receive the amount due as royalty from the tenants under mining leases in Mauza Bahaldhih in the month of Aswin of the Vikram year and the second in the months of Chaitra. On June 14, 1922, the mortgagor assigned his interest in Mauza Bansjor to one Mahendra Nath Rai and on October 2, 1927 he assigned his share of the coal mines in Mauza Arshidpur to one Narendra Nath Chakrabarty and on that date he assigned the said interest in village Simitanar and Sim Karnr Bahadih. By another deed dated August 27, 1922 the mortgagor created a mortgage in favour of Sasindranath Chakravartity and Indra Nath Chakrawartyto secure payment of Rs 5,000 advanced to him and interest thereon. The covenants of this mortgage deed were substantially the same as the covenants of the earlier mortgage deed dated June 14.1923 and it was agreed that in default of payment by the tenants, competent to realise the full amount due to him together with interest and costs by selling Mauzhatas Bans jora and simitanr. By paragraph 13 the mortgagor undertook to pay interest at 9% per annum from April 1, 1937 till the date of payment was made. The plaintiff relied upon part payments evidenced by these endorsements to extend the period of limitation in respect of the two mortgages.

The appellants employ as many as 7.000 workmen in those factories. In order to provide transport facilities to their employees to come to the factories from their respective villages, the appellants provided transport which would pick up passengers from Pune or Khed or Vadgaon or Alandi or places enroute to TELCO Factory at Pimpri and back. For this journey a nominal charge of Rs. 10 per month was realised by the appellants from the employees. Similarly, for the transport facilities provided to the employees from Pimpri Railway Crossing and onwards to TLCO factory, they were charged at the rate of Rs 5 per month. A charge of RS. 2 per month levied for the transported of employees from Chinchvad Village to TALCO Factory was levied for transport of employees of Chinchwad Village toTELCo factory at Pimgra and back and the appellants further averred that these amounts were realised by them only from a particular category of employees and no charges were levied in respect of those employees who were in supervisory grades. In the course of arguments, it was pointed out that when the company was prepared to grant free transport facilities, there was no reason why the same amenities should not be extended to the other employees and Mr. Nariman contended that even if a nominalcharge is realised from the appellants that would not make the transport a public service vehicle carrying passenger; so as to attract the provisions of section 3 which is the charging section of the Act. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The tax levied on all passengers by road in stage carriages falls squarely within the ambit of the aforesaid definition Moreover, in the instant case, it is not disputed that the transport provided to employees by the company would be a public services vehicle. [362C D] 2.1 In view of what we have already said, it cannot be said that the Transport vehicle provided to tho employees by appellants could be a Public service vehicle in any sense of the term.

The appellants, who were residents of the locality and had objected to the grant/renewal of a licence for a temporary cinema to respondent No. 3 Prem Narayan son of Ganpatlal Chouksey, proprietor Chitra Talkies, Lalbagh, Burhanpur (M.P.) against which a petition under Article 226 of the Constitution by the appellants was dismissed in limine by a speaking order dated 27th December 1977. The second respondent made an application on 5th December 1975 for grant of a "no objection certificate" for a period of six months. This licence was renewed upto 30th June 1976 and there was a further renewal up to 30th September 1976. A subsequent application for renewal was turned down by the Distt. Magistrate by his order dated 29th June 1977 on the ground that Paras Talkia with permanent cinema licence which was closed, has now been functioning in the locality, and therefore a renewal of the licence for the temporary cinema in the same locality would not be proper. The appellants filed a writ petition under article 226 questioning the validity of the order of the State Government conceding inter alia that they were the residents of tho locality and that they had objected thereto to the granting/renewal or renewal of licence on the grounds that there was mosque a madrasa and a temple in the vicinity or the place where the cinema house is to be constructed, and even though their objections were upheld by the licensing authority, the District Magistrate, they were not heard in the appeal preferred by the third respondent and therefore the order granting the no objection certificate was violative of the principles of natural justice. The High Court dismissed the writ petition holding that the District Magis trate was not influenced by the fact that there is a mosque and a Temple in the nearby vicinity of the place, where the proposed cinema house was to be built but he was influenced by an extraneous consideration that a cinema having a permanent cinema license having been re opened in the area there was no need for a cinema house with a "temporary" licence and that it being a matter left to the subjective satisfaction of the Government, the State Govt. on being satisfied that there had no impediment to the grants of such a licence, was perfectly justified in granting the same and therefore it was not a fit case for interference of the High Court. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the appellants: (1) that if before the grant of an "no objections certificate" is granted there ends the matter subject, of course, to any properly constituted legal proceedings, conceivably a writ Petition under Article 32; and (2) that the appellants were not acting bona fide in vindication of their own rights but they are a fence or a cloak for the owners of Paras Cinema, the holders of permanent cinema licen ties in the localities and the appellants thus being proxies for such a trade rival, they have no locus standi to file the objections. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The rules envisage issuance of a license for a permanent or quasi permanent cinema as well as a touring cinema. Rule 3 envisages construction of a cinema houses and as a first step, selection of a site where the Cinema house is To be located.

The plaintiff instituted a suit against the defendant alleging that by a contract dated August 3, 1957, the defendant agreed to assign to the plaintiffs his leasehold interest under a mining lease in respect of 184 acres of land in Kudrekanave Kaval, Hosadurga Taluk and claiming specific performance of the contract. The Trial Court decreed the suit. On appeal the High Court allowed the appeal and dismissed the suit on the ground that there was no concluded contract between the parties. In appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that there could be no con tract in the plaint, nor was it usual to communicate an acceptance by serving a copy of the plaint through the medium of the court. HELD: The plaint in O.S. No. 46 of 1957 was not an acceptance. There was no other acceptance either oral or in writing. Mere mental assent of the plaintiffs to the defendants proposal is not sufficient. [585 C] In re: Pellatt 's Case, , referred to. In re : Pell Attoxam 's case turned on its own special facts. Bloxam could be regarded as having dispensed with the necessity of the communication of the acceptance. [58 E F] In the present case there was nothing in the pleadings to show that the plaintiffs had made an offer to assign a mining leases. No acceptance was made or communicated to the defendant before hi withdrew the offer. There were no concluded contracts and the appeal must fail on this ground.

The appellants were office bearers of M/s. S.K.G Sugar Ltd., Ltd. (Lauriya). A complaint was registered against them under sub rule (3) of Rule 3 of the Order read with section 7 of the , on the ground that they had failed to pay the sellers the price of sugarcane purchased by them, within the time prescribed. The said complaint was investigated and the appellants were objecting to that investigation on various grounds. They unsuccessfully sought intervention of the High Court under article 226 of the Constitution in Cr. W.I.C. No. 11 of 1966. The High Court dismissed the petition. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the regulation of price of sugar is expressly dealt with by the Bihar Sugar Factories Control Act, 1937 and therefore the power conferred on the Government under section 3 of that Act cannot be challenged as invalid. HELD: (i) The power that is sought to be exercised in the instant case is an implied one. [677 E] (ii) The authority altered or amended that law is a competent one. The next contention of the appellants was that the Parliament had no competence to enact any law relating to the control of sugarcane as that subject is within the exclusive legislative jurisdiction of the State, the same being a part of agriculture. This contention was also unsustainable in view of Entry 33 of List III of the constitution which empowers the Parliament to legislate in respect of production, supply and distribution of foodstuffs. [67 G H] (iii) The question whether the cultivation and sale of sugarcane can be regulated under section 2(a) of the Act came up for consideration for this Court in Ch. Tika Ramji & Ors. vs The State of U.P., ; , followed.

The Government of Karnataka decided to adopt a policy to encourage rapid industrialisation. An order No. CI 58 FMI 69 dated 30th June, 1969 was issued which recited that the Government, namely, the Government of the State was committed to a policy of rapid industrialization and that, in pursuance thereof, the Govern ment had on 30th November 1966, issued directions indicating the incentives that would be given to entrepreneurs starting new industries in the Mysore State. The material part of the said order ran thus: "Consequently, the Governor of Mysore is pleased to sanction the following incentives and concessions to the entrepreneurs for starting new industrial units in the State: (1) Sales Tax A cash refund will be allowed on all sales tax paid by a new industry on raw materials purchased by it for the first five years from the date the industry goes into production, eligibility to the concession being determined on the basis of a certificate to be issued by the Department of Industries and Commerce. " By an order dated 11th August 1975, the procedure was prescribed for obtaining the concessions given under the orders referred to earlier. On 12th January 1977, the State Government issued another order which recited: "the reasons for making the said Order of 12th Jan, 1977 were that the scheme of concessions adopted by the Government earlier had given room for many types of misuse and the earlier orders had not prescribed any ceiling limits or restrictions on the quantum of refund of sales tax or concession to be granted. The said order dated 12th December, 1977 inter alia provided as under: " (i) The concession of refund will he limited to 10 per cent of the cost of fixed assets per year, thus not exceeding the total of 50% over a period of five years for which the concession is available. Where the annual sales tax payable on raw material is less than 10 per capa ble of the costs of the fixed assets according to the original value, the concession will be limited to the actual sales tax pay paid. " The said Order dated 12st January, 1977 was challenged by the appellants before the High Court contending that the doctrine of Promissory Estoppel was not applicable in the present case because it was found by the Govern ing of Karnataka that the concessions granted under the order dated 30.6.1969 were being misused and undue advantage was being taken of the same. The learned Single Judge allowed the writ petitions and granted relief on the ground that the said grant of concession constituted a promissory estoppel against the Government on the principle of Prom promissory Estoppel. On appeal by the Assistant Commissioner of Commercial Taxes, Dharwar, Deputy Commissioner of Sales Tax and the Government Of Karnataka before a Division Bench of the Karnataka High Court, the learned Single judge held that the State had no authority to provide for the grant of refunds. The appellants contended that the concept of Prom statuto estoppel was applicable in this case because the benefit given was called a refund, it could not be said to be an exemption or reduction as permitted by section 8A. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 An Assistant Commissioner or Deputy Commissioner who are functionaries of a State can say that a concession granted by the State itself was beyond the powers of the state or how the State can add either. Moreover, if the said argument of learned counsel is correct, the result would be that even the second order of 12. January,1977 would be equally invalid as it also grants concessions by way of refunds, although in a more limited manner and that is not even the case of the appellants.

The appellants were tried for the offences under Sections 147, 148, 323, 379 and 302 read with Section 149 I.P.C. on the allegations that they caused the death of Madda Laksha mandas of village Ramaraogudem on November 1, 1980 near the Tobacco garden of A 1. The Trial Court acquitted A 7 of all the charges. A 1 to A 6 were however found guilty for the offence punishable under Sections 148 and 302 I. P.C., but convicted them under Section 148 and sentenced them to imprisonment for life. On appeal, the High Court confirmed the conviction and sentence of A 4 to A 3. The appellants contended that after the acquittal of four accused persons by the courts below the conviction of the appellants under Section 149 and on applying 149 I 1.P .C. cannot be sustained. It was argued that the appellants being three in number, there was no question of their forming an unlawful assembly within the meaning of Section 141 I.p.C.; that apart from the seven accused persons there were some other unidentified persons who were involved in the crime; and that the High court clearly fell into error in confirming the conviction under Sections 302 readwith Section 34 I.I.P., on the ground that they formed an unlawful com mission alongwith some unidentified person. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The appellants acted in the furtherance of their common intention of murdering the de ceased. [8G] 1.2 There is force in the contention of the learned counsel for the appel lants that after acquittal of 4 accused persons, by the Courts below, the conviction cannot be sustain. It is not the prosecution case that apartfrom the seven appellants there were other unified persons who are involved in t he crime. The High Court clearly fell in error in confirmed the convic tion and sentence.

The assessee was the owner of a house situated in Ernakulam which he had purchased in 1958 for the price of Rs. 16,500. On 25th December 1965 the assessee sold the house for the same price of RS. 16500 to his daughter in law and five of his children. The assessment of the assessee for the assessment year 1966 67 for which the relevant accounting year was the calendar year 1965 was completed in the normal course and in this assessment no amount was included by way of capital gains in respect of the transfer of the house since the house was sold by the assessee at the same prices at which it was purchased and no capital gains accrued or arose to him as a result of the sale. On 4th April 1968 however, the Income tax officer issued a notice under section 148 of the Income Tax Act seeking to reopen the assessment of assessee for for the year 196667 and requiring the assessee to submit a return of income within 30 days of the service of the notice. 48,500 to tax because there was admittedly no under statement A of consideration in respect thereof of the transferred house and it was not possible to say that the transfer was effected by the assesee with the object of avoidance or reduction of his liability under section 45. The Income Tax officer issued notice under Section 148 of Act seeking reopening the assessment for the reason that there was a admittedly nounder statement A consideration in regard to the transfer and it had been enough to attract the applicability of the sub section if the fair market value of the property as on the date of the trans action. 48 The assessee submitted a return disclosing his income from the said house at the rate of Rs 16,000 shown by him as capital gains. The assessing authority rejected the contention of the asses see that there were no under statements A of considerations in respect to the transferred property and it did not require as a condition precedent that there should be under statement of consideration. On appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the assessing authority.

The appellant was charged with an offence under section 16(1)(a) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954. The two witnesses produced to support this charge were D. P. Tambe and section P. Gaydhani. D.P. Tambbe (P.W. 1), a businessman, said that he had gone to "a shop to make purchases", without giving either the name of the shop or approximate date or time of his visit. Under cross examination, he stated that he did not know whether it was a foodgrain shop. He said that there was some talk between the complainant and the accused. The appellant denied the presence of D.W., but asserted that the Food Inspector had clearly told him that the black Tils in his shop were only meant for pooja and not for human consumption. The trial court convicted the appellant under section 8(1) (a)(i) of Act, and sentenced him to rigorous imprisonment for two months and fine of Rs. 1,000/ . On appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) It is a matter of common knowledge that black Til seeds are not used as food. Even if this be true, it is not so widely known a fact that we could take judicial notice of it. [334 C] Bhagwan Das vs Delhi Administration ; , followed. (2) The appellant must get the benefit of that doubt. As already indicated above, the prosecution has to prove beyond reasonable doubt that what Was stored or sold was `food '. [330 E G] Bhagwan Dass vs Delhi Admn., ; , distinguished.

The plaintiff, a Government servant of Madhya Pradesh was dismissed from service by the Collector on 13th January 1966. He preferred an appeal to the Divisional Commissioner and that appeal was dismissed on 31st August 1966. The order of dismissal was communicated to him on 19th September, 1960. The plaintiff gave notice under section 80 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 17.6.1969 asking for a declaration that the order of dismiss ment was inoperative and he continued to be in service. This suit was dismissed in the Courts below on acceptance of the defence plea that it had not been filed within three years from the date when cause of action first arose, as required under Article 58 of the First Schedule of the . When this appeal came up for hearing before a Division Bench, reliance was placed on the decision of this Court in Sita Ram Goel vs The Municipal Board, Kanpur & Ors., ; , in support of the contention that the suit was barred by limitation. The Division Bench dismissed the second appeal holding that it would not be correct to say that the dismissal having taken place in 1948 could not be the subject matter of an application under Article 226 of the Constitu tion for that would be giving retro spective effect to that Article. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The cause of actions shall be taken to arise not from the dates of the original adverse order but on the date When the remedy availed of has not been provided by law. It is proper that the position in such cases should be uniform. [54D E] 1.2 In all these three cases after the appellate authori ty has disposed of the appeal the operative order is the order passed of the appel late authority whether it has reversed the original order or modified it or confirmed it. [55E F] 2.1 It is not disputed that in the first two cases where the order was either reversed or modified, it is the orders of the appellate authority whether they have reversed the order or modify it or confirm it. In law, the appellate order of confirmation is quite as efficacious as an operative order as an appel l late order of reversal or modification.

The appellant filed a suit in forma pauperis in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Chittoor for his half share in the properties which once belonged to the joint family consisting of himself and his father and to this suit he impleaded his father as his son and several alienees from him. His case was that the alienations effected by his father were not binding on him and so his share in all the said properties covered by the said alienations was not affected by them. The trial court rejected his contention that the alienation did not bind him, upheld all the alienations and dismissed his suit. On appeal the High Court reversed the trial court 's decree in respect of alienations which covered items 2, 10 and 14 in Schedule A as well as item 5 in Schedule B. Held, that the decision of the Privy Council in Annapurnabai 's case was not a part of the decision or the grounds stated for it but the decision on that part of tile controversy between the parties which is brought to this Court in appeal must be considered as a whole and decide whether the appellate decree passed by the High court affirmed the decision. The word "decision" in article 133(1) should mean not a whole of the decisions but the judgment of the trial Court must be regarded as a part and must be confined to the said explanation. The words "judgment, decree or final order" occurring in article133(1)(a) are intended to be interpreted on the basis that every decree passed in a suit should be held to be a composite decree made up of several decrees in respect thereof. If the judgment or decree of the High ' Court varies the decision in respect Of a matter in controversy in the proposed appeal to this court, then there is a right of appeal not only to the person against whom the variation has been made but even to the party in whose favour the variation had been made.

Section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure, read with section 115 of Civil Proce dure Act, provides that no revision petition shall lie to the High Court against a revisional order passed by the District Judge under section 25. The proviso to section 115 was without prejudice to the generality of the provisions of section 6, and in consequence, the entire sphere of revisional jurisdiction was restored to the high Court, no such power being now vested in the District Court. In 1970, the U.P. Civil Laws (Amendment) Act, 1972 was enacted by Parliament and amended section 115 with effect from 20th September, 1972. Section 97(2) provided that section 115 as originally amended by the Amendment Act, 1976 would not apply to nor affect any proceeding for revision which had been admitted after 37 preliminary hearing, before 1st February, 1977 and every such proceeding for Revision would be disposed of as if section 43 had not come into force. The U. P. Civil Courts Laws ( amendments) Act was amended by successive State amendments, each attempting to close the gap left by its predecessor. Civil laws (Amendment), 1970 section 115 were amended and the result was that : (i) The High Court possessed exclusive jurisdiction under section 115 in a case arising out of an original suit of the value of Rs. 20,000/ and above; and 36 (ii) The District Court possessed concurrent jurisdiction under Section 115 in cases arising out o f the original suits of the values of Rs 20, 000/ and Rs. 10,000. The High ' Court held that no such revision petition was maintainable before the High court. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that: (1) the High Courts possesses revisional jurisdiction under s 115 in respect of cases arising from original suits or other proceedings of any valuation, decided by the district Court; and (2) the District Courts had exclusive jurisdiction u/s 115 in the case arising in which a District Court would exercise revisional power under section 5 of the Act. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The scheme embodied in the bifurcation of the revisional jurisdiction is to relieve the High 's burden of exercising revisional jurisdiction in respect o matters decided under the Provincial Small Cause Courts Act. [39C] 2.1 In determining whether the Legislature intended a further revision petition to the District court, regard must be had to the principle that the construction given to a statute should be such as would advance the object of the legislation and suppress the mischief sought to be cured by it.

The respondents were the owners of certain lands situated at Jaipur on outskirts of Jaipur city. On June 25, 1975 the Special Officer , Town Planning Department, Jaipur issued a notice under section 52 (2) of the Rajasthan Urban Improvement Act, 1959 stating that it was proposed by the State Government to acquire the said land admeasuring more or less 44,770 square yards under section 53 (1) of that Act for a public purpose namely, for implementation of a development scheme at public expense viz. the Civil Lines Extension Scheme. The said notice was duly served on the respondents and they in compliance therewith appeared before the Special officer, Town Planning department, Jaipur and filed their reply dated September 8, 1975. In the reply, the respondents while denying the existence of a public pur posation for acquisition of the lands under section52 (1), asserted that they needed the said property to start new businesses in the State , to open a branch office at Jaipur and to construct residential quarters for their Director and other Senior Executives but at a later stage they alleged that they wanted to construct a Three Star Hotel on the said lands. The Special Officer by his order dated March 13, 1984 held that the alleged need of the respondents was just a pretence and he was satisfied on the material on record that the land was really not needed by them bona fide and their real object was just to get the land released from acquisition. The State Government in its special leave petition have explained that the notification under section 51 (2), 52(1) or the Act could not be issued till February 8, 1984 because the Government were primarily thinking of making the land available for construction of residential houses before making provisions for construction ,of a Three star hotel but nothing came out of the said proposal as there was no response from the respondents. Allowing the appeal by special leave, the Court ^ HELD: 1. The cause of action culminating in the acquisition of land under section 50 (5) of ' the Act arose within the State of Rajasthan i.e. within the territorial jurisdiction of the High Court at Jaipur Bench. [605C D] 2.1 In the instant case, the cause of actions neither wholly nor in part arose within tho territorial limits of the Calcutta High Court and therefore the learned Single Judge had no jurisdiction to issue a rule nisi on the petition filed by the respondents under article 226 of the Constitution or to make the ad interim exparte prohibitory order restraining the appellants from taking any steps to take possession of the land acquired.

The respondent filed a suit for eviction and arrears of rent and damages for use and occupation pendent lite on the allegation that the appellant was inducted as a tenant of the premises in suit on a monthly rent of Rs. 250 on 7th February, 1972, that the building in question was constructed substantially out of funds obtained from the sources mentioned in the proviso to section 2(2) of the U.P. Urban Buildings (Regulation of letting, Rent and Eviction) Act, 1972 for which the Bank advanced loan. The building in suit was assessed to house and water tax on 1st October 1971 and as such the building was not covered by the U .P. urban Buildings ( Regulation of letting Rent and eviction) Act. The respondent terminated the tenancy of the appellant.
