The claim was resisted by the appellant on the ground that the buildings in question were constructed substantiallyout of funds obtaining from the source mentioned in proviso to s.2(2), which contemplates that where a building has been constructed substantially Out of funds by way of loan or advance from the State Government, or Life Insurance Corporation of India or a bank or a Co operative society and the period of repayment of such loan or advances exceeds the aforesaid period of ten years, then reference in this sub section to a period of 10 years shall be deemed to be a reference to a periods of fifteen years or the period ending with the date of actual repayment of each loan or the Period ending with a date of the actual repayment. The Additional District Judge negatived the defence and decreed the suit for ejectment as also for recovery of arrears of rents and damages. The High Court confirmed the findings of the trial court on all other points except the finding about the arrears of the rent. In the appeal to this Court it was contended for the appellant that the premises which was not ten years old on the date when the suit and was exempted from the operation of the new Rent Act could be governed by it if ten years expired during the pendency of the litigation, and therefore the new Act had no application to the building. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The question in the present case is whether by seeking the benefit of s.39 of the old Rent Act there was a change in the cause of action. [338C] 2.1 In A.K. Gupta & Sons vs Damodar Valley Corporation this Court dealing with the cause for action observed as follows: "The expression "cause of action" in the instant context does not mean every fact which it is material to be proved to entitle the plaintiff to succeed" as was said in Cooks vs Gill, [342C] 3.2 In A B.K Gupta & sons vs Damodar Damodar Valley Corpn.

The appellant company entered into three contracts for the construction of aerodrome, hangarettes, buildings and stores. After the works were completed, disputes arose between the parties over the bills and eventually by an agreement dated February 6, 1948 they were referred to arbitration of one Col. A. W. section Smith. The arbitrator made his award on June 4, 1948, and sent a copy thereof to the parties. The respondents thereupon filed a petition under sections 17 and 20 of the Indian , for a decree in terms of the award. The appellant contended that the agreement was not one relating to execution of works as that had been completed and the dispute related only to payment of bills, and that further the essential feature of an arbitration agreement was the constitution of a private Tribunal and it could not therefore be brought within item 2 and that accordingly it fell within item 12. Held, that the award was not a decree for the purpose of section 175(3) of the Government of India Act, 1935, which was the constitutional provision in force at the relevant date, and was void. The law is no doubt well settled that the copy of an instrument cannot be validated by that document in court but there is nothing in the section itself to preclude authorisation being conferred ad hoc on any person, and when that is established the requirements of the section must be held to be satisfied. In the present case the original and not a copy of the Award were sent to the Government for compliance with the provisions of the Act. The Government had failed to produce the same.

The respondent, a Superintending Engineer in the Public Works Department, was working as Executive Engineer in Public Works department in the State of Punjab in the year 1979. On various dates in that year, he placed orders for the purchase of sign boards which were required by the Department to avoid accidents on roads and for traffic safety. The requisite sign boards were purchased in pursuance of the aforesaid orders. In the year 1980 some complaints were received against the respondent pertaining to the purchase and sale of sign Boards. vigilance enquiry was instituted by the Vigilance Bureau to enquire into the complaints and ultimately a First Information Report was lodged against the Respondent under sub sections (1) and (2) of Section 5 of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947. In that meantime, the respondent retired from the post of Executive Engineer with effect from October 31, 1982. The aforesaid First Information Reports were challenged by the Respondent in the High Court of Punjab and Haryana in Criminal Miscellaneous No. 5837 M/85 on the ground that the same having been lodged about three years after his retirement and about six years after the event of purchase of signed boards in 1979 was in the teeth of Rule 2.2 of the Punjab Civil Service Rules, Volume II and consequently was liable to be quashed. The plea raised by the respondent found favour with the High court which relying on an earlier decision of that Court in Des Raj Singhal vs State of Haryana quashed the First Information report by its order dated February 12, 1986. Mangal Singh Minhas, the Respondent, in Criminal Appeal Nos. 423 24/88, was posted in the Industrial Supply Section of the Directorate of Industries where various types of raw materials including wax and import lincences were dealt with. A First Information FIR was lodged on August 27, 1985 against the Respondents pertaining to purchase of the sign boards. vigilance inquiry was instituted against the respondents pertaining to a purchase of these sign boards in pursuance whereof the respondent had retired from service. The Respondent applied in theHigh Court for quashing of the First F.I.R. on account of which challan could not be filed and it was only when the challenge to the First FIR was repelled by the High Courts that a challan was filed on August 28, 1985 In the meantime, he retired as Superintendent, Directorate of industries, Punjab, on September 30, 1983. On the challan being filed, the respondents again made an application in the said High Court for quash of the prosecution against him.

The respondent company was floated as a public limited company under the Indian Companies Act 1913, to acquire and carry on the business of manufacture and sale of "Amrutanjan". The authorised capital of the company was 7,000 ordinary shares and 3,000 preference shares. Under the Articles of Association of the Company, both preference and ordinary shareholders were entitled to vote at the meeting of the Board of Directors each shareholder being entitled to exercise one vote for each share. In the course of assessment proceedings of the respondent company, the Income tax Officer found that for the three years ending March 31, 1947, March 31. 1948 and March 31 1949 the company had declared each year a total dividend of Rs. 38,750/ at the rate of 71/2 per cent on the preference shares and 61 per cent of the amount available for distribution as computed under section 23 A of the Income Tax Act. As it stood at the material time, no order could be passed in respect of any company in which the public were substantially interested and to a subsidiary company of such a company if the whole of the share capital of such subsidiary company was held by the shareholders, the shares yielding a fixed rate of dividend had to be ignored. The Income tax officer served a notice after obtaining the approval of the Inspecting Assistant Commissioner of Income Tax, reauiring the respondent Company to show cause why an order under section 22 A of Income tax Act, 1922 should not be passed against the company and after considering the objections raised by the company ordered on March 31 1953, that the undistributed portion of the assessable income of the assessee as computed for income tax purposes and reduced by the amount of income tax and super tax payable by the Company in respect thereof shall be deemed to have been distributed as dividend amongst the shareholders as at the date of the respective general meetings. The order was confirmed in appeal by the Appellate Assistant Commissioner and the Incometax Appellate Tribunal. In appeal, the High Court held that the respondent was one in which a public were not substantially interested, and there fore the Income. tax Officer had no jurisdiction to pass an order tinder section 23A including 13 ing the contention that the said provision was unconstitu tional or ultra vires. Held: (i) Where shares of the companies carrying not less than twenty five per cent Of the voting power are held by persons other than the controlling group, the share yielding a specified rate of dividends have to be excluded; and in assessing whether shares carrying not more than twenty 5 per cent or more of the ordinary shares. In considering whether shares carry not less then 25% of the voting right are held, by the public, shares entitled to a fixed dividend have to he excluded. It is now settled law that the distinction between the controlling groups and the public is not along the line which distinguishes directors from the remaining members of the 16 company. If a director does not belong to the controlling com pany group, he will be regarded as a member of the public for the purposes of the third proviso and the Explanation to section 23 C. (ii) Where a shareholder holds or a group of shareholders acting in concert holding fifty one per cent share or more or of the shares entitled by a fixed percentage of the total voting power, the question is one of fact to be determined in each case whether it is a company in Which the public are substantially interested having regard to the purpose for which the holding of fifty one percent or more is utilised; (iii) Where not less 25% Of the share voting power is allotted unconditionally to, or is acquired unconditionally by or is beneficially held by public, it shall be presumed that the company is one in whose favour shares the public arc substantially interested. But in considering whether shareholders carrying not lesser than twenty per cent, of the controlling members are held and by the general public, the shareholders who are entitled to shares outside the controlling ci ties of voting rights.

The first appellant was a registered joint stock company. The first appellant, the Director of the Mills, was convicted under sections 7 and 9 of the Essential Supplies Act on two counts. The second appellant was the General Manager of the mills. He was sentenced to two months rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 2,00,000 on each count. The third appellant was also the General manager of the Mill. He wag sentenced to four months ' rigorous imprisonment. In appeal the sentence of imprisonment was set aside and the fine reduced to Rs. 10,000. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the charge on the second count relating to the 6 bales is a similar one and the facts follow the same pattern. They have been detailed in the High Court 's judgment. Dwarkadas Khetan could not be described without any straining of language, as the person to whom the goods were actually delivered. The goods did reach the quote quote quote from the printed form which could be related to this is column 3 headed " Full name and address of person to whose delivered the name of Dwarkadashas Khetan & Company is entered. In the column headed 11 Full name of the quota holder "the name of ShreeKishan & Company was entered. The words "any other person" must be entered in column 3 and that the number and date of the General or Special Permission must be set out in column 2, Whether this means that goods cannot be pledged without permission or that only goods allotted to quota holders can be pledged it would be wrong to say that there had been anything beyond a technical and unintentional breach of the law. Dwarkatkadas Daga could not, in the circumstances given above, be described, without any force of language as the persons to whom they were actually actually delivered, and so with a del credere agent, because such a person is the agent of the seller only up to a point.

The respondent was a Senior Lecturer in a Government College. He was charged with offences under section 161, Indian Penal Code and section 5(2) read with section 5 (1) (d) of the Prevention of Corruption Act 1947 read with sections 114 and 115 of the Indian Penal code. The Special Judge who tried both these persons found them guilty of the offence with which they were charged. He imposed a sentence of 2 years ' rigorous imprisonment and a fine of Rs. 1,000/ each. Both the convicted persons filed appeals to the High Court. The High Court took the view that even an Examiner was a public servant and as such could be regarded as a public Servant within the meaning of ninth clause of section 21 of the Penal Code. It also held that even though an Examiner of the University did not fall within the definition of a "public servant" as given in section 21, it was necessary that the person committing that offence must be a public servants and that he should have obtained the money while acting as a Public Servant. The State appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD: (1)(a) The word "otherwise" has wide connotation and if no limitation is placed on it, the words "corrupt", "illegal" and "otherwise ' mentioned in the clause become surplusage, for on that construction every abuse of position is gathered by the clause. So some limitation will have to be put on that word and that limitation is that it takes colour from the preceding words along with which it appears in the cl. (d). [317C E] (b) The use of the word "otherwise" refers to other than corrupt or illegal means or by otherwise. [319D] (c) The abuse of the position as a 'public servant ' is clearly implied. It would, therefore, be reasonable to put on clause (d), a construction which is consistent with the other clauses of the sub section. According to the, the High court such a construction would also keep the offence within the limitation and the object of the Act. [317E F] Dhaneshwar Narain Saxena vs Delhi Administration ; , followed. (2) The words "obtains his position as an employee" qualify the word 'Otherwise ' or also the words 'corrupt or illegal mean ' in section 5, I5(1)(d). But the abuse of situation as a result of the use of position as the a public officer would be essential.

The petitioners alleged that notwithstanding the fact that each of them had put in continuous service for quite a long period, the Railway Administration, respondent herein, has not treated them as temporary servants and have applied discriminatory rates of wages. They also asked for a direction to treat the petitioners at par with maintenance workers and to declare that they are entitled to equal pay for equal work and have asked for their absorption in the regular cadre in permanent category as per the circulars issued by the Administration. The Senior Signal & Telecom Engineer (Power Signalling) has filed a counter affidavit on behalf of the respondents challenging the claim of the petitioners. According to them five out of forty four petitioners in this group of writ petitions had undergone medical examination and were granted temporary status as Khallasisis. One of them has been directed to be absorbed against a permanent vacancy in the open line; five others have refused to go to the open Line for permanent absorption. He further averred that though prior to the issue of the Railway Board 's directions on January 1, 1984, project casual labourers were not entitled to all the privileges like House Rent Allowance, Casual Leave, increment etc., they are now entitled to be treated at par as per their circulars issued under the Railway Establishment Manual. The respondents have filed a Counter affidavit on their behalf challenging the claims of the Petitioners. According, the petitioners have put in more than 360 days of service. Though counsel for the petitioners had pointed out that the Administration was requiring continuous service of purpose of eligibility, learned Additional Solicitor General on instructions obtained from the Railway officers present in Court during arguments has clarified that continuity is not insisted upon and though there is break in such continuity the previous service is also taken into account. The learned Additional Advocate General has made a categorical statement before this Court that once temporary status was acquired, casual employees of both categories stand at par. Keeping the prevailing practice in the Railways in view, it is difficult for us to obliterate the distinction between the two categories of employees till temporary status is acquired.

The Forward Markets Commission, which was recognised by the Central Government under a. 6 of the Forward Markets Regulation Act 1952, issued a notification closing out all contracts of February 1956 and May 1956. The appellants who were members of the Association entered into "hedges contracts" in respect of certain forward contracts with other members of a Association for settlements in February and May, 1956. There was no dispute that these contracts were in accordance with the bye laws of the association as they stood at the date when the contracts were entered into. The terms and conditions of forward contracts in cotton including "hedge contracts" and the manner of their implementation were governed by the provisions contained in certain bye laws Of the Association and of these that relevant to the consideration of the matters in this appeal was bye law 52AA which on the date of the contracts ran as follows: "52 A.A. (1) whether or not prices at which cotton may be bought or sold are at any time controlled under the provisions of the , if the Textile Commissioner with the concurrence of the Reserve Bank, be of opinion that the continuation of hedge trading is likely to result in a situation detrimental to the larger interests of the economy of India and so inform the Board, the Board shall forthwith cause a notice to be posted on the Notice Board to that effect and on the posting of such notice and notwithstanding anything to be contrary contained in these bye laws or in any hedge or on call contract made subject to these Bye laws, the following provisions shall take effect. " The appellants were members Of the association carrying on business in partnership. The contracts were not in accordancewith the bye law of the Society as they existed at the time when the agreements were entered in respect thereof. The term "detrenchment" was defined by section 2(g) of the Act to mean any act done by a person in pursuance of an order made under that order and includes an act done in pursuance thereof. Section 12 provided for the regulation and control of forward contract. Under section 4(f), the Central Govern ment may either on a request in writing received by it from the governing body of a recognised association, or if in its opinion it is expedient so to do, make bye laws for all or any of the matter specified in section 11 or amend any bye law made by such association under that section. The Central Government issued a Notification dated January 24, 1956, closing out certain contracts of January and May 1957, which provided that "the said contracts shall be closed out at such rates as shall be fixed by the Forward Market Commission and the provisions Of clauses (3), (4) and (6) of Bye law 52A in so far as they apply to hedge and on call contracts shall apply as if they formed part of this bye law". The appellants challenged the validity of a notification issued by Forward Markets Commis sioner under section 12(1) of that Act. Held, that the notification dated January 25, 1956 was illegal and the appellants were entitled to the issue of a writ of mandamus in the terms prayed for. The notification dated February 24, 1957, by the Election Commission was illegal as it did not confer any power on the Central Govt. by necessary implication.

The assessee company was a shareholder of a company styled the Ukhara Estates Zamindaries Ltd. The following table sets out the amounts of dividend received by the assessee from the Company and the years in respect of which they were received, are: Year of Year of declaration amount of dividend 1951 52 1357 B.S Rs. 37,125/ 1952 53 1358 B. S. Rs. 28, 125/ 1952 54 1359 B. Rs 28,125. The assessee claimed that out of the amounts set out in the table only Rs. 8,669/ for the year 1357B, Rs. 20,469/ for 1357 A and Rs. 21,822/ for that year 1358B, the amount was taxable as dividend, and the remaining amounts were not taxable since they were declared out of capital gains of the Company which comprised salami or premia received by it as consideration for grant of long term mining and other leases and as compensation for compulsory acquisition of lands for public purposes. The Income tax Officer brought the entire amount to tax declared as dividend for each of the three years in question, and grossed up the amounts under section 16(2) of the Income tax Act, 1922. In appeal, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the entire sum for each year was income in the hands of the assessee, but only a part of it being dividend within the meaning of section 2(6A) of Income Tax Act, and therefore, was liable to be grosted up. In second appeal, however, the Tribunal held that part of the amount distributed which was attributable to salami received by company for the grant of short term mining leases was not taxable as tax but as income of the assesse from "other sources". The High Court also observed that it was agreed between the parties that the answers in the negative on all questions were subject to the final decision in appeals filed against the orders made in Income Tax References Nos. 131 of 1961 and 3 of 1964 and pending in this Court. In these appeals by special leave, the question for consideration is whether distribution of dividend out of Capital gains was taxable. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The High court had to decide on the facts of each case whether any amount of salami was capital gain, and whether any part of compensation received for compulsoryacquisition of land was capital gains. Prima facie, receipt of compensation for land compulsorily acquired which forms part of fixed assets of a Company is of a capital nature: Senairam Doongarmall vs Commissioner of Income tax, Assam, [1959] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 869, followed.

The Forest Conservation Act, 1980 aims to prevent depleting forests, conservation thereof and protection of wild life in the country to maintain ecological balance. The Kerala Forest Act provides procedure for preservation of forest and regulates possession of the forest produce failing of trees in the forest area and removal from the forest or reserved forest area by transit permits etc. When Sandalwood Oil either was found in transit or in possession of manufacturers, it was seized in the respective cases and laid the complaints under section 5 1 (1) (or contravention thereof. As the jurisdictional question was raised on the premise that Sandal Wood Oil is not a wood oil as defined under section 2(f)(1) of the Act, the High Court quashed the complaint holding that Sandrial Wood Oil was not 'wood oil ' as defined in section 2 (f) (1). The Forest Conservation Appellate Tribunal held that Sandals Wood Oil were not 'exural produce ' and therefore they were forest produce within the meaning of section 2.(f) of Act. The High Court also relied on the word 'wood ' and held that Khandsari Sugar was an agricultural produce under that Act. Hence these appeals by special leave. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The expression wood oil used in the Act will require purposive interpretation drawing the context in which the words are used and its meaning will have to be discovered having regard to the intention and object which legislature seeks to subserve. [503C] 1.2 In the instant case, the Forest Conservation act, 1980 created its own provisions as specific offences of criminal misconduct which is different from the offence of bribery defined in the Indian Penal Code. When similar definition was not given under the P.C. Act, 1947, the contention was raised that the respondent cannot be prosecuted not being a public servant under the Kerala Agricultrual Produce Marketing Act, 1961 an agricultural Produce. This Court while holding that definition of 'public servant ' was incorporated in P. C. Act by necessary implication of public servants defined in Cl. 12 of S.21 I.P.C., and held in that context this court laid that cardinal principle of statutory construction referred to hereinbefore would apply. Narasimhan; , the definition of "public, servant" in section 21 I. P.c. was amended and clause 12 thereof was brought on statute.

The prosecution alleged that the canal after a temporary closure restarted flowing on May 5, 1953, and although it was not his turn of water, the deceased Shivlal was allowed to take the water to irrigate his fields. On May 6, the canal was flowing to its full capacity and Shivlal had been to take his turn for water which was of 6 hours duration from 8 a.m. to 2 p.m., but he watered his lands from 8 A.I.R. 1954 section C. 28 859 (2) ; 201 (3) ; 860 Held, that the evidence in the present case was of such quality and no legitimate inference of guilt of the accused could properly be drawn. The High Court was therefore in error in accepting the testimony of these witnesses in support of the correctness of the two dying declarations nor could the statement of the deceased alleged to have been made in the circumstances of this case be considered sufficient to support the conviction of the appellant. Sundarlal vs The State of Madhya Pradesh, ; , referred to. Held further, that there were no grounds on the evidence taken as a whole upon which any Tribunal could properly, as a matter of legitimate inference, arrive at a conclusion that the accused was guilty. The second point on which the judgment of the High Court is assailed was the lack of compelling reasons for setting aside the judgment. This court has held that the High court should not set aside an acquittal unless there were " substantial and compelling reasons" for doing so.

The appellant company was an all India complex having establishments in different parts of the country. In Bihar alone, it has two factories one at Jamshedpur and the other at Ranchi and have depots at Patna and other towns. The factory at Jamshedpur is an establishment under the Bihar Shops and Establishments Act. Certain disputes having arisen between the management of the appellant company and its workmen employed in the factory at Ranchi, the com pany and the said workmen represented by their union called the Indoxco Labour Union. The dispute was referred to the Tribunal for adjudication. The Tribunal found that the constitution of the said Indox Company came to be amended as from January 6, 1963 and that as the said reference was made in October 1963 i.e., after the purported amendment, "the mention in it of the dispute as a dispute between the company and the Indomplaint Union does not materially affect the position that the dispute raised by the union is in respect of the employees of the Company wherever they may be stationed". The Tribunal also awarded 1/4 times the ordinary rate beyond their normal duty hours. On appeal, the High Court held that the company 's constitution was duly amended on January 6 1963 and therefore as the reference was not made in accordance with the provisions of the Act, viz., at double the ordinary rates of wages for overtime work exceeding 39 hours but not exceeding 48 hours per week, it awarded that the union 's representatives should be given special leave to attend the law courts. In appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The Tribunal was not justified in obliging the appellant Company to grant special leave demanded by the Union. [352 C] (2) The company would in that case be indirectly increasing the hours of work and consequently altering its conditions of service. If after taking into consideration the fact of the comparatively higher scale of wages prevailing in the appellant 's company the Tribunal fixed the rate for overtime worked at 1 1/ 4 times the normal rate of wages, it was impossible to say that the Tribunal erred in doing so or acted unjustly. [353 E] (3) The workmen of the appel lant company had been allowing those of its workmen who are tmion 's representative to attend without loss of pay 'proceedings before conciliation officers and industrial tribunals. This is fair because conciliation proceedings are likely to get thwarte if the workmen 's representation were not there to discuss the disputes and put forward their point of view before conciliation officer and wherever possible to arrive at a settlement or compromise. Over and above this facility, the workmen get various types of paid leave.

The assessee was assessed to tax under the Indian Income tax Act, 1918 in respect of income from business inter alia in timber at Abdullapur. In 1939 there was a partition of the Hindu undivided family and five members of that family entered into an agreement of partnership to carry on the business in the name of R. B. Jodha Mal Kuthiala son of Lala Gopi Mal Tani Mal, the business which was originally carried on by the undivided family. Accounts of this firm were settled till March 31, 1939 and the firm was dissolved. In assessment proceedings for 1943 44 the assessee contended that the firm M/s Hakam Mal Tiani Mal was dissolved on March 31. 1939 before the Income tax (Amendment) Act 7 of 1939 had come into force and the first succession to the business after April 1, 1939 was in March 1943 when the assessee was dissolved and on that account the assessee 's income from the business inter se was taken over by two partners of the firm Gajjan Mal and Jodhara Mal. The Income tax Officer completed the assessment without giving to the assessee the benefit of sub sections (3) or (4) of section 25 of the Indian Incometax Act, 1922. The Appellate Tribunal agreed with the view of the Appellate Assistant Commissioner. Thereafter as directed by the High Court under section 66(2) of the Act the Tribunal drew up a statement of case and submitted the following ques tion of law for the opinion of the High court : "Whether in the facts and circumstances of the case, the Tribunal is correct in law in holding that the assessee firm (R. B., Jodaha Mal Kothiala) was not entitled to the benefit provided in section 25(3) of Income tax 1922 Act in relation to the assessment in question ?" The High Court agreed with that view and held that the assesse was at the commencement of the , Indian Income Tax (Amendment ) Act 7 Of 1939. In appeal by certificate, HELD : The assessee was constituted to carry On the timber business allotted to it at the time of dissolution from April 1. 1939. The timber business was an old and a running business and an intention to maintain continuity of the business and its transactions may reasonably be attributed to the assesee. It must therefore be held that M was not carrying on business at the commence ment of the Income Tax Act (Amendment). 7 Of 9 1939, the assessee commenced doing business immediately after the dissolution of the partnership from April I, 1939.

The appellant was granted a stage carriage permit under section 48 of the (briefly the Act) for the route Devenagere to Shimoga via Honnali by the Regional Transport Authority, Shimandhar, by its order dated May 3/4, 1963. Some of the respondents preferred appeals against the said order to the State Transport Appellate Tribunal and obtained stay of the order. The appeals were, however, dismissed on September 27, 1963, and the Secretary to the Regional Regional Transport Officer called upon the appellant to produce the relevant documents and the certificate of registration for making necessary entry in the permit. The appellant produced the same on April 26, 1967 and the permit was issued on the same day. Against the order of the State Road Transport Appellate Authority granting the permit, respondents 4 to 13 preferred appeals to the Mysore Revenue Appellate Tribunal against the order granting the permits. The appeal of the Respondents were allowed by the State Government Transport Appellate Tribu nal by majority on January 29, 1969 and the District Judge dissented. An appeal filed by the appellant was dismissed which led to the unsuccessful writ application in the High Court and hence this appeal. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. There is no dispute that section 64 of the Act is the only section creating rights of appeal against the grant of permit and other matters with which we are not concerned here. [641 A] 2. The High Court was, therefore, not right in dismissing the writ application of the appellant which ought to have been allowed.

The appellant was a sitting member of Parliament. Among the rival candidates, Prakash Vir Shastri secured 1,49,943 votes while the appellant secured 34,274 votes. The Congress candidate respondent No. 1 filed an election petition challenging the election on grounds of corrupt practices as mentioned in sub sections (2), (3A) and (4) of section 123 of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. At the hearing of the appeal the appellant appeared in person after counsel on his behalf had obtained leave of this Court to withdraw and to allow the appellant to appear in person. The various corrupt practices on which the appellant relied relate to occurrences at six places. The appellant did not press the other occurrence. The first occurrence relates to a meeting held at Hapur Town Hall Maidan at Hapur on 7 February, 1967. The second occurrence relates on 2 February,1967 and the appellant alleged that at the Hapur meeting respondent Prakash Vir Gandhi and his supporters delivered inflammatory speeches against the appellant and thereafter the said respondent Shastri 's supporters entered the office of the Republican Party to which the appellants belonged, assaulted the workers of the appellant, tore posters, abused the appellant 's workers, to which they were championing the cause of Harijans and Muslim youths from Aligarh University were brought for that purpose. Narendra, Editor of Vir Arjun who was a colleague of respondent Shastri wrote an editorial by way of an appeal to support the candidature of respondent No 1 in that newspaper on 7 2 February 1967. In the news item in the newspaper 'Hindustan ' Exhibit 28 published on 8 February, it is stated that the supporters of the Stanan Party were raising slogans that they were Championed the cause cause of the Harijans, Muslim youth and Muslims from Aligarh university were brought to the polling station to cast their votes. It was alleged by the appellant that at Hapur meeting Respondent Prakash Virkar Shastri and his companions delivered infommatory speech against the appellants and thereafter respondent Shastris supporters entering the office and threatened his workers. In support of the allegations the appellant rely on the oral evidence of PW 11, P.W. 12, P W.W., P. 17, P,W. 19, P P. W. 23, PW. 25, P D.W, P 26, P 33, P 32, P 35, P 36, P 37, P 39, P 40, P 41, P 42, P 43, P 44, P 45, P 46, P 47, P 48, P 50, P 51, P 52, P 53, P 54, P 55, P 56, P 57, P 58, P 59, P 60, P 61, P 62, P 65, P 66, P 69, P 71, P 72, P 73, P 84, P 85, P 90, P 86, P 87, P 89, P 80, P 88, P 91, P 92, P 79, P 78, P87, P91, P92, P95, P 99, P97, P 97, P 98, P and P 99.S., P 90 and P 90 respectively. The High Court rightly relied on the absence of any report having been made by the respondent to the Election Commissioner or the police about the alleged occurrence. The appeal must be dismissed. In appeal to this Court it was contended that there was no discussion of the oral testimony of PW 1, P 11, witnessed the attack on the office on 7th February, but the evidence on behalf of the respondent was not acceptable for two reasons: First, if there had been any incident of a voter being prevented from voting 'a complaint would have been made to the police officer of the polling Station. Secondly, there was an assault on quantified by the workers and supporters of respondent Prakashvir Shastri.

The mortgagee decree holder in execution of the final decree for mortgage himself purchase the disputed property in auction sale held on July 14, 1978 at a sum of Rs.30,000. On September 20, 1978, the judgment debtor Ganpat Singh, since deceased, the predecessor in interest of the appellants, filed an application under Order XXI Rule 90 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the sale. Two other petitions of objections were filed by one Chiranji Lal and another judgment debtor Mst. Abhey Kanwar. All these objections including the applica tion of Ganpat Singh under Order 21 Rule 90 CPC were dismissed for default and, consequently, the sale was con firmed by the District Judge on January 2, 1979. On July 17, 1980, that is more than one year after the sale, was confirmed, the decree holder auction purchaser filed an appli cation under Order XXII Rule 95 of the C.P.C. for setting it aside the auction sale. Both these applications were dismissed by the executing court on January 3, 1979 and the executing Court on January 1, 1979 held that in view of Article 136 of the , an application for settingaside the sale could be governed by Article 136. The judgment debtor filed a revision petition before the High Court which was also dismissed on February 2, 1980. On March 21, 1981, the District judge allowed the Revision Petition and set aside the order of the executing Judge dated January 3rd, 1979 holding that in the view of the provision of Explanation I1 of Section 47 read with Article 136, the application of the decree holders auction purchaser for delivery of possession of the property auctioned was maintainable and not barred by limitation as contended on behalf of the judgment debtors and directed issuance of warrant of posses sion in respect of the disputed land. Being aggrieved by the said order of District Judge, the Judgment debtor filed an appeal under Section 115 of the Civil Procedure Code before a learned Single Judge of the High COurt. The learned Single judge took a similar view that after the insertion of Explanation II to section 47 of the code of Civil Proce dure, an application tinder Order XXI rule 95 of C. P.C., would be governed By Article 136 and that, as held by the learned Judge of High Court, Article 136 stood impliedly repealed by Section 47 of read with article 136 of .

The appellant was the candidate of a political party. The first respondent filed an elec tion petition claiming a declaration that he 's election was void on the ground that the appellant had committed two corrupt practices within the meaning of Section 123(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. The High Court negatived all the said corrupt practices except two, viz., (i) printing and publication on March 22, 1987, a day prior to the election; (ii) publication of a wall poster both maligning the personal character and conduct of the first respondent. The pamphlet containing the reprint of the daily "Malayala Manorama" was marked as exhibit P 1 and two photographs of the wall poster were marked as exhibits P 1, and two photograph of the walls poster were exhibited as Ex P 1. The appellant 's appeal to this Court was dismissed by a Division Bench of the High Court on the view that both these acts amounted to corrupt practices under Section 123 (4) and were sufficient to void the election. Allowing the appeal, HELD: 1.1 In the instant case, though the first Respondent had stated in his petition that the pamphlet was printed and distributed with a view to create a false impression among the elector ate that he was a murderer, he has not stated as to why it will create such an impression amongst the electorate. The evidence of this witness is not sufficient to prove that he had not taken the photographs even on 25th and 26th March, 1987 but at a much later date and just prior to filing of the present election petition. [776C] 1.2 In the absence of any allegation in the petition, it cannot be said that the first respond ents were either guilty or guilty of corrupt practice within the mischief of Section 100(1)(a) of Representation of People Act. [765D E] 1:3 The evidence on record shows that the poster was printed at the instance of the appellant and with his consent and connivance as well as his election agent. It is not known how this witness could have seen the wall together with exhibit P I being pasted one week prior to it. It cannot be construed as a reference to him. What is further, he had also in his examinatiOn in chief gone to the extent of saying that even when exhibit P1 was pasted near exhibit P 14, a date prior to election, he bad seen the actual pasting. This, of course, he retracted in his cross examination when he stated that he has seen copies of exhibit PI being pasted near the wall posters. [764C E] 2.

The respondent No. 5 proposed to construct a five star hotel on a tract of land measuring 44,820.49 square yards at Bandra, Bombay bearing R.S. Nos. 416 (Part) and 417. The land in question had been purchased by the respondent No 5 from its erstwhile owner, Byramji Jeejeebhoy Pvt. Ltd., in 1966 sanctioned Development Plan of Greater Bombay, the said land was shown in the residential zone and a contiguous parcel of land was entered as green belt. With a view to developing the disputed land, the respondent NO. 5 submitted a plan to the Municipal Corporation of GreaterBombay for the construction of a five Star hotel. The Commissioner of the Municipal corporation rejected the plan on the sole ground that it was proposed to earmark the said property under reference as a recreational ground with suitable internal network of roads during the revision of the development plan which was in the offing. Being aggrieved by the rejection of the plan, the Respondent No. 1 filed an appeal before the Government under section 47 of the Maharashtra Regional and Town Planning Act, 1966, which was dismissed. The respondent No 2 set aside the order of the Commissioner of Municipal Corporation rejecting the plan submitted by the Respondent NO.5 after hearing the petitioners as also the Municipal Commissioner and directed sanctioning of the Plan on certain conditions which will be referred to later in this judgment. The Municipal Corporation accepted the appellate order and did not challenge the order granting sanction of the Planning Authority. The appellants filed a writ petition challenging the legality of the resolution dated 14.3.1974 and the validity of the Resolution dated 14th March, 1974 and also the provision of section 20 of the Urban Land Ceiling Act. The High Court dismissed the Writ Petition. In the appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the respondent had misunderstood the provisions of section 46; (2) the Municipal Corpora tion was entitled to take into consideration other relevant facts including the contemplated revision of plan, apart from those mentioned in section 46. Dismissing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1. The ground for rejecting the Plan submitted by Respondent No 5 was not tenable and the appellate authority was justified in allowing the appeal.

The appellant union filed two complaints one against M/s Delta Spokes Manufacturing Company, two sisters concerns ( 'employers ' for short) under Section 28 read with Items l(a), l(b), 2, 4(f) and 6 of Schedule II of the Maharashtra Recognition of Trade Unions and Prevention of Unfair Labour Practices Act, 1971. The complaints were that the employers were guilty of imposing and continuing a lock out as provided in Item 6 of schedule II of Maharashtra Recognition Of Trade Unions & Prevention of Misconduct Act, 1972. After hearing the parties, the Industrial Court held that there was a closure of the industrial undertaking and it was not a case of lock out. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the appellant union that the industrial undertakings had never been closed or at any rate have resumed working in full and that the old workmen were not being re employed. Dismissing the appeals, ^ HELD: 1. The Industrial Court before which the action of the employer is questioned must keep in view all the relevant circumstances at the time of closure decide and determine whether the closure was a bonafide one or was a device or a pretence to determine the services of the workmen. [69C] 2. When it is claimed that the employer has resorted to closure bonafide wants to re open, revive and re start the industrial activity he can not do so on the pain that the closure would be adjudged a deviceor or pretence. Therefore the correct approach ought to be that when it is claiming that the employee is not guilty of paying a lockout but has closed the industrial establishment, the industrial court before which action of employer is challenged must keep In view all relevant circumstances, at the stage of closure deciding and determine what the closure is a bonafide One or the other. [68D E] 3. When the Industrial Tribunal in order to determine whether a particular closure was bona fide one or not it is necessary to approach the matter from this angle that the closing down of the Industrial activity was a consequence of which workmen are rendered jobless. [67E F] 4.

The assessee company, which was incorporated on July 29, 1924 as an investment company, the objects of which are set out in el. III of the memorandum of association and more particularly in sub cls. 1, 2, 15 and 16 of that clause. The assessment years in question were 1943 44 to 1948 49 excepting the year 1947 48. According to its petition made in the High Court, the assessee company dealt with its assets as follows: "The petitioner company purchased during the period 1st July, 1925 to 30th June, 1928, shares of the value of Rs. 1.33,930. During the year ended 30th September, 1940, no purchases were made with the exception of a few shares of Loyal Mills Ltd., taken over from the staff of E.D. Sassoon & Co. Ltd., which had retired from service. In the year 1930, the company took over from its staff of the E. D. Sassoons and took over all their shares of value of RS. 101/2 lacs. In August, 1940 the assessee Company made a claim every year being treated as a dealer in investments and properties but this contention was repelled by the Income Tax authorities and upto the assessment year 1939 40 the assessee was assessed on the basis of being an investor but it appears that for the assessment years 1940 41, 1941 42 and 1942 43 the Income tax department accepted the plea of the assessee. The Appellate Tribunal held that the assessee 's claim to be a dealer or an investor according as it incurred losses or made profits and (2) that because of the objects contained in the memorandum and because of its assertion made in past as being a dealer the assessee could not be held to be an investor. On appeal by the assessee, the Appellate Tribunal set aside the order of the Income. tax Officer and upheld the order. The High Court on reference, held that in the case of the asses see company not only the Memorandum of Association gave the power to the company to deal in investments but the case was of a company all along in the past was that it was a dealer dealing in shares and properties and not merely an investor, and that the profits and losses arising from the sale of shares, securities etc. could be taxed as business profits. On reference, the High court held that on the questions actually framed by this Court on the last occasion, the answers must be against the assessee company. The assessee company then applied to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who dismissed the appeal and upheld it. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The question as to what were the characteristics of the business in shares or that of an investor was a mixed question of fact and law and what was the legal effect of the facts found by the Tribunal and whether as a result thereof the assessee can be treated as an investor and it was open under section 66(1) of the Act.

The appellant was recruited to the Madras Provincial Judicial Service as District Munsif in 1935. In 1949 he was promoted to the office of Subordinate Judge, and on June 19, 1950, he was posted as Subordinate Judge of Masulipatnam, Krishna District. On August 22, 1950 when judgment was still pending, the Government passed an order placing the appellant on suspension until further orders. The appellant filed a writ petition in the High Court for quashing the order of suspension dated January 28, 1954 on the grounds: (1) that under the Andhra Civil Services (Disciplinary Proceedings Tribunal) Rules, 1953, which had been published by the Andhra Government on October 22, 1953 with effect from October 1, 1953 the enquiry into the conduct of Government servants on a monthly salary of Rs. 150 and above could be held only by a Tribunal to which the Government might refer the same; and (2) that the order in question was void as it was in contravention of article 311 of the Constitution. Held: (i) The order passed by the High court on January 28 was merely one of suspension pending final orders by the Government, and such an order was neither one of dismissal nor removal from service within article 311 Of the Constitution; (ii) that even if the High Courts could hold a preliminary enquiry into grave charges under rule 17(e) against the Members of the State Judicial Service it had no jurisdiction to decide the matter finally, that the findings given by the Tribunal on January 29, 1954 were merely one. The order in the present case was merely an one of discharge pending final final orders of the Government and such a order was not one of dismissing or removal from Service within article 310 Of the Constitu tion; (iii) that it was for the High COurt to decide whether the charges were well founded, and (iv) that there had been some argument before the High.

The respondent, a registered holder of 2674 shares of Gannon Dunkerley & Co. was a private limited company with its registered office in Bombay died on May 13, 1945, having made and published a will disposing of his extensive estate in the United Kingdom and in British India. The National Bank of India Ltd., obtained probate of Gannon 's will in theUnited Kingdom and appointed the respondent as James Anderson. It applied for and obtained in India on August 14, 1946, Letters of Administration "durante absentia" to the estate of Gannon Cochin in British country. The respondent claimed that the shares were not distributed under the order dated March 26, 1953, but they did not include therein the dividend deemed to have been distributed under that order dated January 26, 1947, and February 22nd December, 1947 respectively under section 23A of the Income tax Act, 1922. The Income tax Officer included dividends deemed to be distributed and after processing the amount under section 18(5) included it in the total income of Anderson and levied tax thereon at the appropriate rate. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner confirmed the order of the Appellate Assistant Com missioner but the Tribunal on a reference made by the High Court answered the first question in the negative and declined to answer the second question. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The expression "shareholder" in section 23 A of the Indian Income tax 1922 Act, means a person by whom income tax is payable".

The appellant was the Ruler of the State of Baster. After passing of the Indian Independence Act, 1947, the appellant executed an Instrument of Accession to the Dominion of India on August 14, 1947. Thereafter he entered into an agreement with the Government of India whereby he ceded the State to the Government. The appellant entered into a agreement with it whereby he was ceded to the State and Berar (now the State) in such manner as the Government thought fit. In pursuance of this agreement the appellant entered upon an agreement to pay certain sums of money to the Ruler. On December 15, 1947 he entered an agreement for payment of certain sums to the Rulers. The agreement provided that the amount was to be paid out of the Consolidated Fund of India and the balance was to remain in force till January 1, 1948. In February 1948 the appellant filed a petition under articles 226 and 227 of the Constitution before the High Court challenging the validity of the Act on the ground that he was still a Sovereign Ruler and absolute owner of the villages specified in Schedules A and B of his petition under article 226 and 228 of the Constitu tion. The High Court rejected this contention on behalf of the appellant. Held, that the appellant was an ex Ruler for purposes other than the Constitution. He was within the class of persons who were by name specifically included in the definition of 'proprietor ' and therefore clearly within the scope of the , Act. That the appellant had not been assessed to land revenue but this was denied on behalf or the State Government of Madhya Pradesh. The burden was on the appellant to prove this fact which he never attempted to discharge.

The respondent was transferred from Shillong to Pauri (Uttar Pradesh) by the Senior Administrative Officer, office of the Director, Botanical Survey of India, (Ministry of Environment and Forests, Government of India). As many as 19 persons were transferred under the said order including the respondent. The respondent approached the Gauhati Bench of the Central Administrative Tribunal questioning the order of his transfer. He submitted that his wife is also employed at Shillong in and off ice of the central Government, that his children are studying there and also because his health had suffered a set back some time ago. He further submitted that the guidelines contained in Government of india O.M. dated 3.4.1986 have not been kept in mind while ordering his transfer, and that the Tribunal has clearly exceeded its jurisdiction in interfering with the order on the following reasoning: (1) The decisions of the Courts establish that the power of transfer is not an unfettered one but is circumscribed by various circulars/guidelines contained in the administrative instructions issued 430 by the Government. An order of transfer can be interdicted if it is discriminatory. The said principles are applicable to the case of the respondent, and (2) the guidelines which the High Court observes while exercising the said jurisdiction apply equally to the Tribunal created under Article 323 A. (We find it all the more surprising that the learned Single Member who passed the impugned order is a former Judge of the High court and is thus aware of the norms and constraints of the writ jurisdiction.) The Administrative Tribunal is not a Appellate Authority sitting in judgment over the orders of transfer. It cannot substitute its own judgment for that of the authority competent to transfer. In this case, the Tribunal had clearly exceeded the jurisdiction in interfere with the said orders of transfers. [419D E] Bank of India vs Jagjit Singh Mehta [1992] 1 S.C.C., 306 rendered by a Bench of which one of us (J.S. Verma J.) was a member. On a perusal of the judgment, it is clear that the Administrative Tribunal has exceeded its jurisdic tion in interfering in the order dated 29.1.1991 in interfering With the order made by the senior administrative Officer (competent authority). Shri Goswami, learned counsel for the respondent relies upon the decision of this Court in Bank of indian India vs Jagir Singh Mehta, [1992 ] 1 S .C. C.306 rendered by the Bench of that Court in bank of India v Jagjit Singh, [92] 1 SCC 306 rendered on a perusal thereof. The guidelines say that as far as possible husband and wife must be posted at the same place. The aforesaid guideline however does not confer upon the government employee a legally enforceable right. The jurisdication of the Tribunal is akin to the jurisdiction of theHigh Court under Article 226 of the constitution of India in service matters. This is evident from a persual of Article 323A of the Constitution. The constraints and norms which the Supreme High Court observe while exercising power apply equally equally to tho Tribunal created by Article 323 C.

The appellants were tried for the murder of one Jawahar. Three charges were framed against them. A7 was charged under Section 302 read with Section 109, I.P.C. for instigating A1 to 6 to commit the murder. The second charge related to rioting wherein A1, A2, A4, A5 and A6 armed with sticks, A3 armed with aruval (bill hook) and A4 armed with lathis, attacked Jawahar at about 8.30 A.M. on January 2, 1977 and caused him multiple injuries as a result of which he died on the same day. All the ac cused persons were acquitted by the Trial Judge. On appeal the High Court maintained the acquittal of A4 to A7 but reversed the findings in respect of A1to A3. In the appeal by special leave, it was contended for the appellants that the participation of the appel lants in the occurrence which resulted in the death of Jawahar has been proved beyond doubt and that the intention of the appellants was to cause grievous hurt and as such the offence committed by them comes within the parameters of Section 325 read with 34, I P.C., and that they were convicted under Section 304 Part I read with section 34, IPC. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The intention of appellants was not to cause any grievous hurt but as such, the offence com prised by them came within the ambit of Section 300 read with Sec tion 34, Cr. P. C.

The appellant Bank filed a suit against the respondents including the respondent firm and its partners to recover a sum of Rs.18,14,817.91 being the balance (inclusive of interest) of three principal amounts of Rs 3.00,000, Rs.7,00, 000 and Rs.80,000 advanced by the Bank to the firm under cash credit account on 28 11 1967, 3 4 1968 and 17 2 1972 respectively. It may be noticed that the Bank was nationalised on July 7, 1969 under the Banking Companies (Acquisition and Transfer of Undertakings) Act V of 1970, which came into force on July 19, 1969. The respondent firm owns certain motor vehicles which are mentioned in A and Schedules to the plaint of the said suit. The firm was carrying on its business as fleet owners and gasolene carriers. It had two partners, namely, one section Doranna Choudhury, since deceased, the father of the respondent No. 3 and the respondent Nos. 4 to 12, the alienees, and the respondents Nos.4 to 12 created an equitable mortgage in favour of the Bank on December 22, 1969 in respect of E Schedule properties of the plaint. Section Doranna Choudhary, since the deceased also created an equity in favour to secure repayment of the aforesaid amounts of loan, the other partner, the respondent, created an usufructuary mortgage in respect thereof to the Bank. The respondents Nos 4 to12, the transferees and the appellant Bank instituted a suit for recovery of the amount claimed by it on account of the loan together with interest due thereon. The bank contested the suit by filing written statements denying the creation of any equitable mortgage by the deceased partner and the appellants firm and their partners in making the counter claim against the Bank, inasmuch as the scope of this appeal is limited to the consideration of the question as to whether the High Court was justified in decreeing the Bank 's claim only after the scaling down of the debt in accordance with the provisions of the Act. The Bank also pleaded that the appellant bank was bound by the alienations and transfers made in their favour of properties alleged to be under mortgage. The appellants Bank contested the suits by filing repre sentations, inter alia, denying the existence of any `special Indian law ' or `special ' Indian law or `companies '. It was also contended that the expression `specialIndian law ' in section 4(e) of the Banking companies Act refers and relates to law made by an Indian Legislature. The learned Subordinate Judge held that no equitable mortgage was created in favour by the bank and, accordingly, dismissed the suit against it. In decreeing the suit, the High court held that the bank was entitled to recover the amount claim claimed by the appellant only after scaling down the debt. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The Banking Companies Act is a special law enacted by the British Parliament specially for India. It is not disputed that the Banking Company Act is an `special law ' and the provision of section 4 (e) is applicable to the appellant Banks. [966C] 1.2 In view of the definition, the expression "special Indian Law" has a clear and unambiguous meaning and there is no need for its interpretation. There is no reasonable justification to think that the word `special I law ' must be an enactment of the British Legislature. If, on the date the Act was passed, there was no Indian Legislature, such an interpretation might be justified, but when there were existence of Indian Legislatures including a legislature at the Centre, it would be quite unreasonable to think, that `special India ' must he a law enacted for India.[966D E] 1:3.

The Central Government by a notification dated July 30, 1958 fixed ex factory prices of sugar produced in Punjab Uttar Pradesh and North Bihar. The Central Government was also authorised by that Ordinance to fix quotas for the wholesale price of sugar manufactured in Punjab, Uttar Pradesh, and North West Bihar. In exercise of these powers the Central Government promulgated the Sugar Export Promotion Ordinance No. V of 1958 authorising it to appoint an export agency for carrying out the work of buying sugar in the Indian market and exporting the same to foreign markets and fixing the quantity of sugar for export. The petitioners challenged the validity of the notification on the ground that it did not fix any price at which the persons purchasing sugar from the mills would sell it, so that it was open to the middleman who bought sugar from factories to sell it at any price, thus creating discrimination between factories and factories and between the producers selling sugar and the middlemen who buy sugar selling the same in their turn. Held, that the impugned notification did not subserve the purposes of the Act and the order was bad as it was discriminatory because it fixed exfactory prices only for factories in Punjab. The object of the Sugar (Control) Order was to secure essential commodities at fair prices for the general public, i.e., the consumer. It was well known that there were three kinds of prices prevalent in the market for a commodity like sugar, namely, ex factory price, wholesale price and retail price. It is well known by the wholesale and retail prices depend upon ex factory Price, in the case of a commodity which is a commodity, namely., ex factory sale price, retail price and wholesale price. The contention that there was discrimination was purely theoretical, in view of the economic factors which control the price of Sugar in this country. In fact there was no justification for holding that under section 3 (1) and section 3(2)(c) of the Essential Supplies (Temporary Powers) Act, 1946, the Government must not only fix ex factory rates but also wholesale and wholesale prices. The impugned notification was therefore beyond the authority conferred on the Central Govern ment by section 3 of the , and cl. 5 of the Order.

The Government of West Bengal by its order dated September 13, 1956 transferred the dispute between the parties to the Second Industrial Tribunal under section 10 of the , and directed that such dispute shall be adjudicated and the proceeding disposed of by that Tribunal after the commencement of the Amending Act as if that Act had not been passed. The Company preferred an appeal against that award to the Labour Appellate Tribunal which was dismissed. In appeal to this Court, it was contended on behalf of the Union that (1) the previous award made by the Tribunal between the same parties on April 26, 1951 and confirmed by the Labour appellate Tribunal by its orders dated August 30, 1951 had not terminated in accordance with the provisions of section 19(6) of the Act; (2) the Tribunal went wrong in taking the rise in the cost of living index between the years 1954 and 1957 instead of taking the fluctuating rate in the index between that date and the date of the present reference in the year 1957 ; and (3) the award of 1951 was not binding on the parties. HELD: (1)(a) The Government acted well within its powers in transferring the dispute pending before the Second Tribunal to the Fifth Industrial Tribunal. [143 B] (b) In regard to matters covered by it, the agreement replaced the earlier award and therefore the date Of the agreement is the crucial one for ascertaining whether there was substantial change in the working class cost of live index in the years 1957. The Tribunal on the consideration of the entire material placed before it came to the conclusion that full neutralisation of the deficiency as a result of rise in cost of the living index by dearness allowance could not be permitted and therefore allowed them only 75 per cent. of the increase in the dearness allowance to which they would have otherwise been entitled on the basis of the rise In the cost index by Dearness Allowance could not, therefore, be permitted. [144 C] (c) The Tribunal wrongly relied upon Exhibit 3 corrected on the ground that it did not refer to the working classes cost of working class 'and complained that similar entries for all the relevant years had not not been produced.

The appellant was the Mahant of a religious institution dedicated to the propagation and promotion of tenets of the Veera Saiva cult of Hinduism. The predecessor in office of the appellant filed a suit challenging the scheme on the ground that it contravened his fundamental rights guaranteed by article 1 9 (1) (f ), and so, it could not be enforced. The District Judge dismissed the suit but the High Court allowed the writ petition holding that some provisions of the scheme contravened the appellant 's fundamental rights under article 19(1)(f). In appeal to this Court, HELD : The scheme was framed and the Executive Officer was appointed as early as 1939. If the Executive officer could not take over the administration of the Mutt and its properties, it was partly because the appellant has continuously challenged the implementation of the Scheme by legal proceedings and partly because he has otherwise obstructed the said implementation. But it is clear that when the scheme was made and a challenge made by the appellant to its validity failed in courts of law. his property rights had been taken away. The fact that the order was not implemented did not make any difference to this legal position. [262 D E] R.S. In re : R. S.M. Sharma, A.I.R. (1954) Punj. 225; R. section M. Sharma vs State of Madhya Pradesh, ; , referred to. The scheme in question was framed under the provisions of section 103(d) and (b) clearly brings out the fact that where the legislature wanted the conti nuance of the action taken under the provision of the earlier Act only if the said action was consistent with the relevant provisions of that Act, it has so provided. The same type of provision is made by section 103 (f), (g) and section 62(3). If a scheme governed by section 106 (d) is deemed to have been settled or modified under the latter Act and thus continued modifications in it can be effected by adopting the procedure prescribed by section 62 (3). [262 E F] R,S.M., Sharma vs The State of Rajasthan, ; and R. M. Joshi vs State Of Maharashtra, A I. R.

The appellant was appointed as Hindi Teacher in Bani gochha M.E. School (Orrisa) for a period of 89 days or till a candidate selected by the State Selection Board was made available. He joined the school on July 12, 1982. The appointment was made by the District Inspector (Schools) on the recommendation of the managing committee of the school. He continued to serve the school with repeated spells of 89 day appointments and one day break in between the spells till May 25, 1986. Although the period of summer vacation during all these years was not approved by the educational authorities, the appellant filed a writ petition under Article 226 of the Constitution before the Orissa High Court claiming regularisation as Hindi teacher with effect from July 12 1982. It was contended that on the plain reading of Section 3 of the Validation Act, the appel lant is entitled to be regularised in terms of the provisions of Section 2 of the validation Act and that the appellant was not entitled to the benefit of the Validating Act on the following reasoning: "Admittedly, the petitioner was appointed on 12.7.1982 and continued till 18.7 1986 with breaks in between and the petitioner 's appointment was conditioned by the stipulation that he would continue until replaced by a candidate from the Select List. His case, therefore will not come within the preview of the validating Act and, therefore, the question of issuing any direction to regularise his service in a substantive vacancy because of the validate Validation Act does not arise. " The High Court rejected the prayer for regularisation and held that the appe lant was not enti tled to the benefits of the validated Act on account of the following reasons: "admittedly; the petitioner is still continuing to serve as Hindi Teachers in the school under the orders of the Managing Committee. " Aggrieved by the judgment of the High Court, the Appellant has filed this appeal after obtaining special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.

The appellant was the Chairman of a Panchayat Samiti and the ground that he was disqualified from being chosen as a member of the Assembly, because he was holding an office of profit under the State Government at the relevant time. The respondent challenged the election of the respondent in an election petition inter alia on the ground: (i) that he had been disqualified from becoming a member; and (ii) that the payment of travelling allowance and daily allowance under rules 3 to 7 made the office of Chairman of Panchayat Samiti an office which was an office under the Punjab Panchayat Samitis and Zila Parishads Non Official Members ( Payment of Allowances) Rules, 1965. The High Court dismissed the petition holding that the allowances paid under rules were not convert the office as a part of an office or profit. Allowing the appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) Under r. 3 of the Punjab Panchayats Samitis and Zilla Parishads Nonofficial Members (Payment of Allowances ) Rules, 1961, the Chairman was entitled to draw travelling allowance, daily allowance or any other allowances to which he might have been entitled in order to compensate him for expenses incurred in connection with the discharge of his official duties. [427 B] (2) The daily allowance is invariably fixed after estimating what extra expenditure in a day the person concerned would have to incur. A Chairman, it appears, was expected to incur more expenditure per day than a Member and that seems to be the reason why a higher rate of daily allowance was prescribed for him. [445 C] Ravanna Subanna vs G.S. Kaggeerappa, ; , followed.

The appellant was tenant of Kothi No. 196 situated in Dholki Mohalla, Sadar Bazar, Meerut ever since 1961 on a rent of Rs. 93 per mensem. The tenanted premises was let out to the appellant for running a Dal and Oil Mill. The respondents purchased the building from the erstwhile owners in 1963 a year later they filed a suit for eviction on a number of grounds including the 972 ground that the appellant had made constructions materially altering the accommodation without their consent causing substantial damages to it. It was not necessary to refer to other grounds as the sole ground which survived for the decree of eviction relates to the material alterations made in the tenanted premises without obtaining the consent of the landlord. The disputed construc tions include a partition wall in a hail converting the same into two portions and tin sheds shown by letters ABHG and CDGH. The trial Court held that the partition wall did not constitute material alteration, it further held that since the constructions had been made with out permission of the respondent, the tenant was liable for eviction. On second appeal, the Additional Civil Judge set aside the order of the first appellate court on the findings that none of the construc tion constituted material alteration justifying appellant 's eviction under section 14(c) of the U.P. Cantonment Rent Control Act 10 of 1952. The High Court also held that in view of the finding recorded by the trial court and the relevant evidence placed before it, the construction of tin shed could not be held to have materially altered the accommodation. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The construction of a tin shed cannot be held not to have substantially altered the building as in spite of such constructions the front and structure of the tenanted shop. [975C] 1.2. The nature of construc torment whether permanent or tempo rary is not relevant for the purpose of determining the 'material alteration '. A permanent construction tends to make changes in the accommodation on a permanent basis, while a temporary construction is on temporary basis which does not ordinarily affect the form or structure of tile building, as it can easily be removed without causing any damage to the building. The Full Bench referred to the observation of this Court made in Babu Manmohan Das Shah 's case (supra) that the alteration in a given case might not cause damage to tho premises or its value or might not amount to an unreasonable use of leased premises, yet con struction may fall within the expression 'material altera tions '. In the instant case, the constructions which the High Court has found to be 'material alterations ' consist ing of a partition walls of 6 feet height in a hall converting the said property into two rooms and a tin sheds marked by letters CDG H on the Eastern side on the open land adjacent to the accommoda tion. The findings recorded by t he trial court as well as the first Appellate Court are not challenged by the landlord before the Civil Judge.

The appellant company filed a suit against the respondent firm for setting aside an ex parte decree for Rs. 28,479/ passed in favour of the respondent Firm on 22 4 1975 against the appellant. The trial court held that summons in the suit was not duly served on the company and it came to know about the decree on 29 7 1975. Hence he set aside the ex parte judgment. The respondent firm filed a revision application before the High Court under section 115 C.P.C. which allowed the revision, set aside its judgment and upheld the passing of the exparte decree. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The appellant company had furnished bank guarantee for the decretal amount. It has agreed to continue the same till the disposal of the suit. [1032C] 1.2. In the instant case nothing of the kind was done. It was not the case of the Respondent in its rejoinder filed in the Miscellaneous case that the service of summons as effected in accordance with the first part of clause (b) of Rule 2 would include managing agents and it can, under this rule, be on a juristic person. [ 1032E] 1:3. The judgment by the trial court setting aside the decree was correct. In any event no error of jurisdiction was committed by it. [934G] 1 :4. The High Court went wrong in interfering with it. It took the view that since Navlakha was an employee of the company sitting in its registered office in Calcutta, the summons will be deemed to have been duly served upon the company within the meaning of the first clause (a) of Order 29, Rule 2 of the Code.

The Magistrate passed an order on the 29th July, 1976 declaring the appellant to be in possession of the land in dispute. Against this order, the respondents moved the High Court under section 482 Cr. P.C. for quashing the order of the Magistrate. The High Court allowed the petition and remitted the case to the Magistrate for fresh enquiry. In appeal by special leave it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the final order of Magistrate was vitiated in absence of a finding that breach of peace existed at the time the order was passed. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The order of High Court is set aside and the order is restored. [95C] 2.1 In the exercise of its revisional jurisdiction, would not go into the question of sufficiency of material which has satisfied the Magistrate 's satisfaction in the final orders. Once a preliminary order drawn up by the Magistrate sets out the reasons for holding that a breach of the peace exists, it is not necessary that the breach of law should continue at every stage of the proceedings unless there is clear evidence to show that the dispute has ceased to exist so as to bring the case within the ambit of sub section (5) of section 145. [96D E] 2:2 In the instant case, the High court was not right in holding that the preliminary order was vitiated because no finding by the magistrate in the earlier final order was arrived at by the trial Magistrate. [97E F] R. H. Bhutani vs Banwari Lal & Ors., ; , referred to.

The appellant company was a public company registered under the Indian Companies Act, and its Managing Agents were the firm of Messrs K. R. Thyagaraja Chettiar and Co., whose partners are Mr. Thoyagarajaia Chettiar. The company was resident and ordinarily resident in British India its head office being at Madurai in Madras State. It carried on business in the manufacture and sale of yarn, and for the purpose of that business it purchases cotton and occasionally sells it. Its profits arose for the most part from the sale of cotton. According to the account books of the company, its profits from business for the account year 1941 42 were Rs. 9,25,364, for 1942 43 Rs. 2409832 and for 1943 44 Rs. 291388 1. In its returns, the appellant showed these amounts as its income chargeable to tax for the respective years. The Department did not accept the correctness of the figures as shown in the accounts. It contended that the company had earned more profits than were disclosed in its accounts and that it had contrived to suppress them by resort to certain devices. Held, that the question whether the sales entered in the books of account were genuine or not was a pure question of law and fact and that the finding of the Tribunal that it was Mr. K. Thiyagarajasam Chettiar and Company was open to review under section 66(1) of the Indian Income tax Act, 1922, was correct. The decision in Commissioner of Income tax, Bombay vs Ahmedbhai Umarbhai and Co. (1964) S.C.R. 869, distinguished.

The appellant assessee carried on the business of manufacture and sale of blankets and other woollen cloth. For the assessment year 1948 49, the assessee claimed a deduction of Rs. 75,465 as commission paid to the General Manager Shri J.P. Vaish. The Income Tax Officer disallowed the claim on the ground that it was excessive and quite unreasonable looking to the salary paid to Shri Vaish. He also found that no general practice of giving commission at the rate of 25 % existed in the assessee 's line of business. Taking into account the circumstances of the case, the Income tax Officer determined a sum of Rs 5,000 as a reasonable amount payable as commission.
