Against the disallowance of Rs 70,465 paid as commission to the general Manager, the appellant preferred an appeal to the Appellate Assistant Commissioner who by his order dated October 31, 1949 found that Rs. 5,00 was not sufficient and it was reasonable to allow the payment of commission at 121/2%. The Appellate Tribunal dismissed the appeal. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (1) The question of law referred to the High Court must be answered in the manner indicated and this appeal is accordingly allowed with costs. [530 D] Swadeshi Cotton Mills Co. Ltd. vs C.I.T., U.P., ; Swadeshy Cotton Mills Company Ltd. V C. I.T. Bombay, ; Swadehi Cotton Mill Co. Pvt. Ltd., vs C .I. T. Bombay vs Walchand & Co. Private Ltd., , referred to. (2) The principle of this decision applies to the present case and it must accordingly be held that in the circumstances established by the assessee the entire amount of Rs 75,467 paid to General Manager was an amount laid out wholly and exclusively for the purpose of the business. [525 E] Swadeya Cotton Mills Ltd. & the Road Products Ltd.

The appellant was a workman employed in the Digha factory of Bata Shoo Company. On January 13, 1954, the management served him with a charge sheet alleging that he had been doing anti union activities inside the factory during the working hours and so was guilty under section 12B(1) of the Standing Orders and Rules of the company. The appellant submitted his written reply denying the charge and asking to be excused. On March 7, 1957, the appellant filed a fresh petition stating that he did not authorised Fateh Singh to enter into any agreement in his case and praying for an issue of an appropriate writ or direction quashing the Tribunal 's order of February 26, 1957 by which the Tribunal had rejected his prayer for representation by a person of his own choice in place of Fateh Singh. The High Court dismissed this application summarily. It was contended on behalf of the appellant that the Tribunal committed a serious error in rejecting his application to be represented by a party of his choice instead of Fateh singh, the Secretary of the Union and thereafter in making an award on the basis of the reference. Held, that the question whether when a dispute concerning an individual workman is taken up by the union of which the workman is a member, as 200 a matter affecting workmen in general and on that basis a reference is made under the Industrial Disputes Act, can be decided independently of the union which has espoused his cause. The Union or those (1)[1954] S.C.R. 956, followed. Central Provinces Transport Service Ltd. vs Raghunath Gopal Patwardhan, [1954] section C. R. 959, applied.

The appellants instituted a suit for ejectment and recovery of rent against two defendants on the allegation that defendant No. 1 was the tenant inchief who had sub let the premises to defendant No 2. The suit was decreed against both the defendants and for arrears of rent. On appeal by defendant No, 2, the District judge set aside the decree for ejectment against defendant No 1 and confirmed rest of the decree against defendant Nos. 2 and 3. The High Court dismissed the second appeal filed in the High Court on February 29, 1952. In view of the decision of this Court in State 's case, the legal representatives could not have taken advantage of r. 4 of O. XLI of the Code of Civil Procedure. Held, that the High court was right in holding that the appellate Court had no power to proceed with the appeal and to reverse and vary the decree in favour of all the plaintiffs or defendants under O.XXII, r. 3. In the absence of the legal representative of the deceased respondent, the appellate court cannot determine anything between the appellants and the legal heirs which may affect the rights of the parties under the decree. It is immaterial that the modification which the Court will do is one to which exception can or cannot be taken. The power cannot be exercised to nullify the effect of the abatement of the appeal so far as it affects the rights Of the various parties. A case like the present was not a case of such a kind.

The appellant tenant of a building in Delhi having been inducted into possession by the respondent landlord under a letting of May 19, 1954 evidenced by a deed which fixed the term merely as less than a year (a circumstance out of which a minor ripple of legal argument has arisen). At the time of the lease the appellant had not been extended to Delhi although later on December 1, 1962, the said Act was made applicable to this area. The landlord filed a petition for eviction under section 106 of the Transfer of Property Act on the ground that no notice to quit had been given nor notice of forfeiture as prescribed by those sections. The Rent Controller dismissed the petition holding that no notices terminating the tenancy under section106 were needed and further that the forfeiture of the tenancy caused by sub letting contrary to the terms of the deed of demise could be availed of by the landlord even in the absence of a notice as contemplated by section 111(g) because the TP Act, as amended by the Amending Act of 1929 did not apply proprio vigore to such demises and their determination, can the principles of justice, equity and good conscience. The High Court dismissed the tenant 's appeal holding that the provisions of the Rent Act had not applied proprio scorely to the lease in question and therefore a forfeiture giving rise to a determination of the leasehold rights under section 111 (g) could be avail of by landlord even if in the Delhi Rent Control Act, 1958 as amended in 1929, had expired by efflux of time. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The provisions of sections 106 and 111 of the PG NO 908 Transfer of property Act would regulate the matter as could be held to be consistent with the rules of equity, justice and good justice. [919A] 2.1 In the instant case, the appellant tenant had all along staked his case on the application of the rules and of justice equity and fair play. He has to stand or fall by his submission that justice, justice, Equity and good sense was the alter ego of section 111 of PG NO 933 PG NO 930 PG NO 993 PG NO 956 PG NO 995 PG NO 960 PG NO 549 PG NO 548 PG NO 547 PG NO 552 PG NO 551 PG NO service jurisprudence. The statutory law as it now stands, however is that the happening of any of the events specified in section 111 does not ipso facto extinguish the lease but only exposes the lessee to the risk of forfeiture and clothes the lessor with the right, if he so chooses, to determine the lease by giving notice in that behalf.

The Governor of Assam was satisfied that Shri P. K. Hore, Superintendent, P.W.D.F.C., and Wing against whom more charges had been received were unfit to be retained in the public service and that he ought to be dismissed from service. The Governor made these orders in terms of article 311(2) as it existed before its amendment by the Constitution (Fifteenth Amendment) Act, 1963 which came into force on October 6, 1963. The amended Article 311(3)(c) was introduced in the judgment of this Court in Khem Chand vs Union of India and Others. The validity of these orders was challenged in a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution by the appellants who were dismissed from serv ice. The High Court held that the satisfaction recorded by the Governor in the language in which the provision in article 311 stood prior to its amendment, was not vitiated by any infirmity or irregularity and that the order of dismissal passed against him was bad. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellants that (1) the satisfaction of the Governor under sub clause (c) of the proviso to cl.(2) of article 31 1 was recorded in the manner prescribed by the amended Article and, therefore, the Governor had no power to pass an order of dismiss without holding an inquiry; (2) the consultation required by article 320(3) continued to be in force and applicable. HELD: (1)(a) The satisfaction recorded under sub cl.(c) is not a condition precedent for the exercise of any statutory right, and it does not confer any rights on a public servant so that the absence of consultation or any irregularity in consultation does not afford him a cause of action in a court of law. [488 F] Khem Chand V. Union of lndia, ; , followed. (b) The Governor 's satisfaction under sub el.(c), is recorded to the effect that it is not expedient to give the said Shri P K.Hore an opportunity to show cause against the action proposed to be taken in regard to him as stated above. [489 G] Khemchand vs Union Of India and Ors., ; , referred to. (2)(a). The satisfaction of Governor under cl.(C) of cl. (3) of Article 31 1 is recorded in a language which was used earlier in the unamended Article and on the interpretation placed on that unamended Article by this Court. [490 G] (b). It is not mandatory and that this Article does not impose any rights upon a public Servant so that he may only do if he is told what the charges levelled against him are and the allegations on which such charges are based .(c)(d) an opportunity of being heard in respect of those charges and where after such inquiry it is proposed to impose on him a penalty he is again to be given a reasonable opportunity of making a representation on the penalty proposed. [491 G] The consultation with the Commission is not prescribed either by the Rules or by the Regulations. The consultation is only under article 320 (3)(C) and that it does no confer any right on a Public servant so as that the absenteees to give him an opportunity for showing cause against his action proposed. The order of the President is, therefore. not invalid. [486 A B] Khem Singh vs Union Territory of Delhi & Ors., [1969] Vol. VI Assam Law Reports 192; State of U.P.

The Shia community of Mohalla Doshipura, Varanasi, which constituted serious infraction and/or infringement of their fundamental rights guaranteed to them under articles 25 and 26 of the Constitution in the matter of enjoying religious faith and performance of religious rites, practices and observances on certain plots and properties situated in the said Mohalla of Doswara, Police Station Jaitpura (formerly Adampur) in the city of Varanasi and in particular are seeking a declaration that the 9 plots of land bearing plot Nos. 245, 246, 247, 248/23/72, 602, 603, 602/1133 and 247/1130 in the Mohalla and buildings and structures thereon belong to the Shia Waqf of Mohalla, Dosakhipura and that the members of Shia Community of that Mohalla have a right to perform their religious functions and practices on the said plots and structures as also an appropriate writ, direction or order in the nature of mandamus commanding respondents 1 to 4 not to prohibit or restrain the Shias of the Mohalla from performing their religious duties and practices thereon. The Shia Muslim Waqf Board and Sunni Central Wakfs Board impleaded as parties to the Writ Petition under Article 32 of the constitution of India and the Shian community of that village had a right of worship over the said plot and structures on the plots and structure thereon and also an order restraining the Shiana Waqf of that property from performing its religious functions. The petitioners and respondents 5 and 6 filed their respective affidavits in the matters and have been heard through their counsel in the case. The two Boards, Shia Central Wakfs Boards and Sunni central Wakfs Board of Waqf (U.P.) constituted under the U.P. Muslim Waqf Act, 1960, were impleaded as respondents to the writ petition under Article 226 of the Consti tution challenging the decision recorded in their Report by the Chief Commissioner of Waqfs dated 28th/31st October, 1938 and the Sunni Central Waqf Board. The Court by its order dated December 12, 1978 not merely granted permission to the petitioners under Order I Rule 8 C.P., but directed at certain stage of the hearing that the two Waqf Boards in U. P. State, namely Shia 1087 Central Waqf Boards and Shia Wakfs be impleaded as party to the petition as their presence was felt necessary for complete adjudication of the controversy and even otherwise under the Uttar Pradesh Muslim Waqfs Act, 1936 concluding in favour of Shias ' title to the concerned plots or structures thereon or their entitlement to the performance of the religious rites etc. on the property in question as claimed; it directed at some stage of hearing that both the Waqf Boards had also been heard by their counsel and in the absence of adequate material no declaration as to the title to plots or the structures or even as to rights in or over the plots, and structures could be granted in favour Of Shia Muslims. The writ petition filed under Article 227 of the Constitu tion challenging the said decision was dismissed by the High Court on the ground that it was not competent to decide the present subject matter and such the bar of res judicata under Section 11 of the Civil Procedure Code 1908 was not attracted, and it would be open to the respondents 5 & 6 and the members to agitate question of title either to the plots or to the structures thereon and even the Shina Waqf Board had also heard through its counsel in this matter. The High Court further held that the decision in this litigation which bore a representative character not merely negatived the Sunnis ' customary rights claimed by them over the plot and structure but adjudicated, determined and declared the Shihatas ' entitlement to their customary rights to perform the religious ceremonies and functions on the properties and structures in question and this decision was binding on both the communities of Mohalla Mohalla Dhalhipura. In the appeal by special leave it was contended for the petitioners that the impugned order passed by a Magistrate under Section 144 of the U .P.

As no further appeal was carried by the assessee with the first appellate order, the matter had become final. In appeal by special leave, it was contended on behalf of the Revenue that: (1) the benefit conferred under section 24 of 1922 Act continued to be given effect to under the 1961 Act and notwithstanding the wordings of section 80 of the latter Act, the High Court was Fight in holding that the claim of setoff was admissible in our view. Dismissing the appeal, HELD: 1. The benefit granted under section24 continued to have been given effect ly under the 1962 Act and the notwithstanding the wordsings of s.

The respondent was recruited as a Senior Scientific Officer on October 12, 1966 in the Defence Science Service. He was posted in the Directorate of Technical Development and Production (Air) (DTD & P). The recruitment when made was always to the Defence Engineering Service, and after the recruitment, the recruits were posted according to the exigency of the service, in any of the three units. Their 22 services were inter changeable and inter transferable be tween the three Units. All, the service conditions of the persons working in the three unit including scales of pay, superannuation age etc. were the same and were regulated by the same set of Rules, viz. Defence Science Services Rules. In the year 1979, the Defence Research Service was trifurcated and reconstituted as Defence Quality Assurance Service (DQAS). The appellant who was working in DTD &P became a member of DAQAS. When the trif arcation was made, the Service Rules governing the three branches had a common Rule which was rat ed in DAQ and DQAS, and Rule 13 in DRDS which reads as follows: "Other conditions of service: (1) The conditions of serv ice of the members of the Service in respect of matters not expressly provided for in these Rules shall mutatis mutandis and subject to any special orders issued by the Government in respect o the service be the same as those applicable to officers (Civil ians) of corresponding status in similar scientific institu tions/organisations under the Government of India. At the time the present controversy arose, and the respondent approached the Administrative Tribunal, he was holding the post of Deputy Chief Scientific Officer. By an Office Memorandum dated July 10, 1986, the said decision was conveyed whereby Scientific and Technical personnel (gazetted) of D.R. & P) were merged as Defence Science Quality Assurance Services (DHQAS), and (3) Directorate General of Inspection (DGI) was reconstituted as defence Quality Assurance service (DNQ). The Tribunal held that respondent K.T. Shastry was entitled to remain in service upto the superannuation age of 60 years, and that he was not liable to be retired at the age of 58 years his superannuation age being deemed to have been increased to 60 years in view of the OM dated July 24, 1987 read with OM dated October 10,2.86 referred to above. It is this decision which is challenged before this Court by the appellants contending that the Government had a right to prescribe different conditions of services for the members belonging to the different units, and merely because the superannuation ages of the employees of the DRDS was increased, it could not be held that the respondent who belonged to another unit, viz DAQ. QAS, was entitled tO & DAQQAS was entitled lo the said benefit. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1. The decision of the Tribunal is both proper and valid, and there is no substance in the present appeal. [85C] 2.1 In spite of the decision of this Tribunal and even pending this appeal when no stay was granted, the appellant Union of India retired the respondent at the time of his re instatement in service as if he had not been retired. The question involved in the instant case is, however, not whether the Government has such power. [86D] 2:2 In spite thereof, the respondent was paid all his retirement benefits. The appellant will not recover any amount so paid to the respondent. The appeal is accordingly dismissed with aforesaid directions and with costs.

The appellant was elected to the Sangli City Municipality. The election of councillors to the Municipality was held under the Maharashtra Municipalities Act, 1965. The counting of votes took place with regard to Ward No. 25 on June 4, 1967. According to the election petition, the results were published in the Official Gazette on June 15, 1967 and the petition was filed on June 24, 1967, i.e., within time prescribed by the Act. The appellant denied that he was responsible for the publication of any of the impugned pamphlets. Of the four issues framed at the hearing of the petition, charges of terrorising voters and securing votes by false personsation were also levelled therein. statements were made in the petition that the appellant 's name as councillor had been declared in the official Gazette on 6 1967 and he gave full particulars as to how he came to receive it. The trial Judge rejected these allegations and held that the ends of justice required that these witnesses should be examined. He fixed August 24, 1968 for further hearing of matters and directed issue of summonses to these two persons. These two persons were examined on the 24th August as court witnesses and thereafter the argument of counsel was resumed and concluded. By judgment delivered on August 30, 1968 the learned Judge allowed the election Petition holding in favour of the appellant on the first issue. The High Court dismissed the writ petition in limine on October 4, 1968 and the appellant has now come up before this Court by special leave. HELD : (i) Under section 21(1) of the Maharashtra Municipal Act, 1966 which does not contain a similar provision it has been held by this Court that "although. the trial court should be at arms length and the court should not really enter into the dispute as a third party, but it is not to be understood that the Court never had the power to summon a witness or to call for a document which would throw light upon the matter, particularly of corrupt practice which is alleged and is being sought to be proved. If the Court was satisfied that a corrupt practice has in fact been perpetrated, may be by one side or the other, it was absolutely necessary to find out who was the author of that corrupt practice. [975 E F] (ii) The High court had jurisdiction to call these two witnesses as witnesses under the provisions of the Act and the High Court was not right in refusing to quash the order. [977 B C] (iii) The trial judge had examined two witnesses, one of whom was examined as court witness and it is quite clear that but for the evidence of these two person, it would have been very difficult. if not impossible, for the Judge to have come to the conclusion he did and find the appellant guilty of corrupt practices.

The petitioner company was carrying on business in the manufacture and sale of jute goods. By a notification dated March 31, 1956, the State of Uttar Pradesh imposed a tax of one anna in the rupee on the sale proceeds of jute. The State of U.P. imposed a sales tax of two anna in rupee on it. The petitioner challenged the validity of the said notification by a writ petition under article 226 of the Constitution. The High Court held that there was no power in the State to issue the impugned notification under section 3 A on March 31. 1956, as that section was itself to come into force only on April 1, 1956 and that therefore the impugned Notification was not saved by the new Act. On appeal by special leave: Held, that the Validation Act is not ultra vires the powers of the legislature under entry 54 in List II of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, comprehended the power to impose income tax with retrospective operation even for a period prior to the constitution. The power conferred on Parliament under article 286(2) is a legislative power and such a power conferred upon a Sovereign Legislature carries with it authority to enact a law either prospectively or retrospectively unless there can be found in the Constitution itself a limitation on that power. The word "section" in entry 54 of List II in the Seventh schedule to the Consti tution includes the power of legislation to impose tax on sales conditional on its making a provision for sellers to collect the tax from the purchasers. Whether a law should be enacted, imposing a sales Tax or validating the imposition of sales tax, when the seller is not in a position to pass it on to the consumer, is a matter of policy and does not affect the competence of the Legislature. The fact that the 1947 Act after the amendment permitted the seller who was a registered dealer to collect sales tax as a tax from purchaser does not alter the real nature of the tax which, by the express provisions of the law, is cast upon the seller. The powers conferred on the Parliament under Article 286(1) are a legislative one and do not affect its competence. It is not an essential characteristic of a sale tax that the seller must have the right to pass the it onto the consumer nor is the power power of the State Legislature to impose a tax on sale conditional on his making a Provision for sellers, to collect tax from purchasers.

The appellant was convicted for the offence of rape under section 376 IPC. The conviction was confirmed by the High Court in appeal. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. A Philanderer of 22, appellant overpowered by sex stress in excess, hoisted himself into his cousin 's house next door, and in broad day light, overpowered the temptingly lonely prosecutrix of twenty four, Pushpa, raped her in hurried heat and made an urgent exist having fulfilled his erotic sortie. The screaming victim complained to her mother working in the field; thereafter a first information, prosecution and conviction ensued, a sentence of 4 years R.I. was imposed by the Sessions Court and the High court affirmed it in appeal.[591E F] 2. The special circumstances of this case constrain us to relent a little on principle because the restorative approach to sentencing has been jettisoned by the courts below. [592F G] 3. In prison treatment must, therefore, be geared to psychic healing, release of stresses, restoration of self respect and cultural normalisation apart from training to adapt oneself to the life outside. The functional failure of our pachydermic prison projects, exacerbated by its tension and trauma on the one hand and the reverse ethos inside on the other, deserves judicial cognizance. [593A B] 4. In jail treatment must therefore be ge Obtained to psychologistaling, released of stressers, restoration or cultural normalization apart from being deterrent. The insulated years behind the insensitive bars must possess a hospital setting if correction is a social purpose, as Gandhiji often insisted.

The respondent company was a limited company dealing in land. It maintained its accounts on the mercantile system. By an order dated June 21, 1946 under rule 75A(1) of the Defence of India Rules read with section 19 of the Act certain plots of land measuring about 19.17 acres in village Kankulia in the District of 24 Parganas and belonging to the assessee were requisitioned by the Government of West Bengal. Subsequently the land was acquired permanently in the State Government under s.5, Requisition of Land (Continuance of Powers) Act, 1951 by a notice of acquisition dated December 27, 1952 published in the Gazette dated January 8, 1953. The Land Acquisition Officer awarded a sum of Rs.24,97,249 as compensation payable to the respondent assessee. The assessee was not satisfied with the amount of compensation and preferred an appeal before the Arbitrator 24 Parganas, Calcutta. The Appellate Tribunal accepted the other contention and held that the compensation received by the assessee related to the acquisition of land which was the stock in trade of the assessee, and was, therefore, a trading receipt of the business carried on by the respondent company, and therefore, was a trading receipts of the commercial nature liable to tax. The High Court also accepted the contention of the Revenue that the sum of compensation received from the assessee was neither a receipt of a revenue nature nor a revenue character. It allowed the appeal accordingly by its order dated February 22, 1964. At the instance of the revenue the Appellate Tribunal referred the question of law set out earlier to the Calcutta High Court for its opinion and by its judgment dated January 9, 1973 answered the question in favour of the respondent and against the Revenue. The question raised in this appeal is limited to the point whether on the facts and circumstances of the case the Revenue can claim that the amount was liable to income tax during the previous year ended March 31, 1956 relevant to the assessment year 1956 57. Allowing the appeal by certificate, the Court ^ HELD: 1.1 The High court is right in the view taken by it and, therefore this appeal must be dismissed. [395E] 1.2 In the majority judgment delivered by N.H. Bhagwati J. it was explained that the words "arising or accruing" describe a right to receive profits, and that there must be a debt owed by some body. Unless and until there is created in favour by the assesee a debt due by somebody", it was observed "it cannot be said that he has acquired a right of appeal by the government to the High Court, and the High court may either disallow that claim or reduce the compensation. [397F G] 1:3 The legal position which emerges is that there is no liability in praesenti to pay an ascertained amount. Till such time, no income can be said to have accrued. [398C D] Kedarnath Jute Mfg. Co. Ltd., vs Commissioner of Income tax, Gujarat, , followed.

The appellants filed a suit against the respondents for eviction from the suit premises and for certain other reliefs. The appellants ' eviction was sought on the ground that the compromise decree was void and inexecutable as being against the provisions of the Act. The trial court accepted the appellants ' objection to execution of the decree and dismissed the execution case. A miscellaneous appeal filed by the respondents was dismissed by the Third Additional District Judge Gwalior. They preferred a second miscellaneous appeal before the Madhya Pradesh High Court. A learned single judge following the decision of that Court in Smt. Chandan Bai vs Surja, ; came to the conclusion that the decree was not a nullity and was executable. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The law is reviewed exhaustively by this Court in K. K. Chari 's case. [83C] 2.1 In order to get a decree or order for eviction against a tenant whose tenancy is governed by any Rent Restriction or Eviction Act the suitor must make out a case for eviction in accordance with the provisions Of the Act, and when the suit is contested the issue goes to trial. The Court passes a decree for eviction only if it is satisfied on evidence that a ground for passing such a decree in accordance therewith has been established. Even when the trial proceeds ex parte, this is so. If, however, parties choose to enter into a compromise due to any reason such as to avoid the risk of protracted litigating expenses, it is open to them to do so. [864D E] 2:2 In the instant case, on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the compromise was clearly valid and executable. [888C D] 3:3 The suit was decreed ex parte and executable; and the Court found that the agreement was legal, that is to say, lawful and was in accordance With the plaint. The order so recorded in this judgment was in full compliance with the requirement of Order 23, Rule 3 of the Code of Civil Procedure. [878C] 4:4 In the present case, it was not necessary to refer to any piece of evidence adduced at the inconclusive trial. [90F G] 5:5 The compromise must indicate either on its face or in the background of other materials in the case that the tenant expressly or impliedly is agreeing to suffer a decree of eviction because the landlord, in the circumstance is entitled to have such a decrees under the law.

The assessee company was assessed on a total income of Rs. 1,61,089/ and taxes paid were Rs. 69,973/ leaving a distributable balance of Rs 91,116/ . The Income tax Officer however, again invoked the provisions of section 23A(1) and levied additional super tax @ 4/ per rupee on the surplus of Rs 60,761/ . In appeal, the Asstt. Commissioner took the view that the loss incurred by the company was a capital loss. But all the same as there was no commercial profits in the relevant accounting years it was not reasonable to expect the assessee company to declare any dividend in respect of those years in view of the capital loss incurred and he therefore cancelled the orders of the Income tax officer under section 23 A(1). The Appellate Assistant Commissioner, however, took the contrary view. In appeal by certificate, HELD : (i) The question is not whether the value of the shares may go up in future but whether the Directors were justified in not declaring dividends in view Of the loss referred to earlier. [85 C] (ii) The assessee had suffered a capital gain of Rs 12,00,000/ as a result of depreciation of the value in the value. of the share held by it in Elphinstone Mill Ltd. of Bombay. The Income Tax Officer took an erroneous view of section 21(1)(Consolidation) Ordinance, 1950 of Tanganyika. That provision corresponds very closely to section 23(1), and dealt with the scope of that provision, their Lordships observed: "It does not follow from what has been said that capital losses should not be taken into account by the Commissioner. Two matters are mentioned specifically in the words which give him a direction the first is 'losses ' (as interpreted above) and the second is 'smallness of profit". The Commissioner, therefore, took an incorrect view of his scope of section 20(1); [85 E F] Commissioner of Income tax West Bengal vs Gangadliar Bannerjee & Co. , Commissioner of Incometax, West Bengal, vs Gangadharshree Banner and Co. (Pvt.) Ltd., ; Commissioner of income tax, WestBengal, vsGangadli Railway Company, , Commissioner Of Income tax, Bengal vs D. M. Mukherjee, [87 E. R. 829, Commissioner of lncome Tax, West Bengisto nt & Co., , Commissioner for Income tax vs Williamson Diamonds Ltd., , and Commissioner of Inland Revenue vs Williamsonson Diana Gyani, , referred to.

The appellants filed objections before the Civil Judge, Aligarh. The Civil Judge modified the award and the award announced by Shri Vikram Singh was accepted. On appeal to the District Judge a preliminary objection was raised that no appeal lay under section 39 of the Act. The District judge overruled the objection and allowed the appeal and set aside the order of the Civil judge modifying the award. The appellants contended that section 37 of the Uttar Pradesh Consolidation of Holdings Act, 1954 applies only as far as procedure is concerned and section 39 provides for appeals does not apply to arbitrations referred to in section 37. Held, that the effect of section 37 is that all the provisions of the except sub section (1) of section 6, sections 7, 12, 36 and 37 apply to arbitration proceedings under the Act, and it is not necessary to rely (1 ) I.L.R. [1959] 1 All. 354, approved. The effect of s.37 of the U.P. Consolidation of Holding Rules, 1954, read with sections 46 and 47 of the , is that the provisions Of section 37 apply only as regards procedure. It is not possible to rely on section 12(6) of the . In the present case, the effect was that all provisions of section 7,12, 36, and 37, apply to the arbitration proceedings before the arbitrator in the matter of procedure only. Attar Singh vs The State of U. P., [1959]. Supp. 1 All,. 66, followed. Atttarar Singh 's case, [1959) Supp. I SCR 928, referred to.

The petitioner was diploma holder in Engineering and holds the post of Executive Engineer in the respondent Corporation. Till 1974, the promotion post of the superintending Engineer was available both for diploma holders and degree holders according to merit cum seniority. This was so according to the practice followed by the Corporation without making any rules or regulations in that behalf. In 1974, a resolution was passed by passing a resolution and continued the same practice. The petitioner challenged the said resolution before the High Court by way of a writ petition. The High Court dismissed the petition. Hence this appeal by special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. For the purpose of promotion, a valid classification can made among the members holding the same post on the basis of their qualification. In State of Jummu & Kashmir vs Triloki Nath Khosa & Ors., ; , a Constitution Bench of his Court has clearly held that such a classification is permissible and does not violate Articles 14 and 16 of the Constitution and must be upheld. [Emphasis supplied]. 1.2. The proposition that in the absence of rule or regulation, the authority can prescribe service conditions by executive instructions and this is what was done till the year 1988 and is also sought to be done since 1988 by the impugned resolution. The principle that in State of Mysore & Anr. vs P. Narasing Rao Rao, ; , relied on. 1.3. In the absence o rule or regulations the authority cannot prescribe service condition by executive instruction and this was what was taken till the years 1988 and was also sought for to be achieved since 1988. [1A B] 1.4. The Court then referred to Roshan Lal Tandon vs Union of India, ; and distinguished it on the facts by pointing out that it was a case of the direct recruits and promotees integrated into one cadre. Once they were integrated they lost their birth marks, viz., the different sources from which they were recruited. [2B C] 2.1 The proposition in State Of Mysore & Ors. vsP. Naradasing Rao, , relied upon.

The petitioners, an advocate practising in this Court, filed applications under Article 32 of the Constitution for a mandamus to the Union of India to fill up the vacancies of Judges in the Supreme Court and the various High Courts of the country and ancil lary orders of directions in regard to the same. The petitions were clubbed together and heard from time to time. In response to the rule, the Union Government took the stand through the Attorney General that the petitions were not maintainable and the filling up of the vacancies in the superior courts was not a justiciable matter. Reliance was placed on the decision of this Court in S.P. Gupta vs Union of lndia, [1982] 2 SCR 365. The objection raised by the Attorney Gener al was overruled by the Court by drawing a distinction between fixing the Judge strength in the Courts or selection of judges on one side and the filing up of vacancies on the basis of sanctioned strength on the other. This Court as an interim measure took the view that while the ratio in S .P. ' Gupta 's case left the matter of fixing up of Judges to the President of India under the constitutional scheme, and the choice of judges to the prescribed procedure, once the sanctioned strength was determined it was the obligation of the Union to maintain the sanctioned cadre in superior courts and these cases were allowed to proceed. The Court also directed that the vacancies should be filled up by the Chief Justice of the High Court and there can be a fresh look at the matter only if the Chief Judge of India permits such a review of the case. [437C D] S.S. Gupta ' s case relating to the status and importance of the process of selection would improve the quality of selection. The matter is not, therefore, to be considered that the final say is the exclusive prorogative of the executive Government. There are preponderant and com pelling considerations why the views of the Chief Justices of the States and that of the chief Justice of India should be afforded a decisive import unless the executive has some material in its possession which may indicate that the appointment is otherwise undesirable. The view which the four learned Judges shared, in Gup ta 's cases, does not recognise the special and pivotal position of the institution of the Judge of the Supreme court. [454E F] S .S.P Gupta vs State of lstia, ; , referred to.

The respondent was charged with misconduct in the K.G. Road Branch of the Bank in Banga lore city availed of 15 days leave from April 17, 1978 to May 1, 1978 and was allowed an advance of Rs.2,500 on April 4, 1978 under LFC to be adjusted later on his submitting the LFC Bill. He submitted a bill for Rs. 2,800 on May 5, 1978 along with a stamped cash receipt purported to have been issued by M/s. Shri Manju Travels of Bangalore and claimed reimbursement for the same. The said bill was passed by the Bank on May 15, 1978 but subsequent investigations revealed that the firm of M/S. Shri Manu Travels was a spurious one which indulged in issuing fake travel receipts. Thereupon the respondent was served with a charge sheet dated October 12, 1978 followed by a departmental enquiry. However during the pendency of the departmental enquiry he retired from service on January 31, 1979. Not withstanding his retirement he continued to function as an Enquiry Officer and concluded the enquiry against the re spondent by the end of 1979. He then gave an opportunity to the respondent to be heard on the question of punishment and then passed the impugned order of discharge on January 14, 1980. The respondent 's departmental appeal was also dis missed on June 17, 1980 on the ground that since the original order was without jurisdiction or competence, there was nothing for the Appellate Authority to confirm '. The Single Judge allowed the writ petition, quashed the order of punishment as well as directed that the respondent be paid all consequential benefits. The appellant preferred a Letters Patent Appeal against the said order of the Single Judge. The Division Bench dismissed it by a single line order: "no ground for interfer ence is made out" and held that on retirement Shri U.B. Menon was nobody in the hierarchy of authorities to impose penalty on the respondent and hence the order imposing punishment was clearly incompetent and without jurisdiction. The learned Single Judge, therefore allowed the appeal and directed that a fresh decision be taken based on the report of the Enquiry Officer. " Aggrieved by the said judgment the appellant has preferred this appeal after obtaining special leave. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. The doctrine of officers de facto performed within the sphere of their assumed official authority, in the interest of the public or third parties and not for their own interest, are generally held valid and binding as if they were performed by a de jure officer. [200E] 1.2. In the instant case, the respondent did not attribute any bias or mala fides to the Enquiry Offi cer nor did he com plain that he was in any manner prejudiced on account of the said Enquiry Officer conducting him domestic enquiry but that will not cure the defect as to his compensence. [201F] 1:3. The High Court was right in quashing the impugned orders of punishment but it should not have ordered payment of 'all consequential benefits flowing from the declaration that the order was bad in law.

The respondents are owners and are in possession of the building bearing municipal door Nos. 3766 to 3776 situated in the main Chawri Bazar, Delhi. As the building was an old construction and required urgent and extensive repairs on October 16, 1965, the respondents submitted to the appellant plans for its sanction for execution of work consisting of repairs, additions as well alterations to the said building. The Commissioner of the appellant Corporation by letter informed the respondents that their application for execution had been refused on the grounds "that the proposal was under acquisition and also effected in the ROW and the land was residential against proposal of commercial". A controversy arose between the parties regarding the construction of a new road which was not material for the present purpose, and the Commissioner by letter dated April 30, 1966 informed the respondent that their request for execution work in respect of house Nos.3766 to3776 had been declined on the ground that the proposal under acquisition was under 'acquisition and also affected in theROW and that the land had been residential against proposals of commercial. The respondents filed a writ petition in the High Court which accepted the writ petition filed by the respondents and issued a mandamus directing the appellant to accord sanction to the plan for execution. The High Court held that the Commissioner could decline the sanction only if there was a contravention of sub section (2) of section 336 or section 340 or any other provision of the Corporation Act or of any other law. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (1) The Master Plan prepared by the Authority for Delhi which has statutory force, has come into operation under section 11, in the area concerned. [172 E] (2)(a) Under section 8(2), the Commissioner is entitled to refuse sanction of a building or work if the building or works or use of the site for building or execution of a work unless such building orwork would contravene any of the provisions of sub s.(2) Of section 336. [173 C] (b) The grounds on which the sanction of the Commissioner was sought to be justified under this provision are: (a) that the building and work or the use of site for the building, by the respondent, would contravene the provisions Of any other laws; (b). that the Master Plan has been prepared under section 7 by the authority on September 1, 1962 and it has come in force, as contemplated by section 11. Though section 8 contemplates the preparation of a Zonal Development Plan simultaneously with the preparation for the Master plan, or as soon as there may be thereafter, no such Zonal Development Plans have been prepared. That assumes considerable importance in this case because it is the Zonal Development plan, under section 8 (2), before it comes into operation in the Zone, the procedure indicated in section 10 will have to be followed and parties will have opportunity of sending their objections and suggestions and representations, which have all to be duly and properly considered by the authorities concerned. Chapter III A deals with modifications to the Master plans and the Zonal development Plan. Section 1 A provides for the Authority and the Central Government making modifications in the Master Plans or the Zonal Planning Plan under the circumstances and after following the procedure, mentioned therein. Sub section (1 ) of section 12 gives power to the Central Govt., by notification in the Official Gazette to declare any area in Delhi to be a development area for the purposes of the Act. [174 E F] (3) The provisions of section 7 of the Development Act clearly indicate and that is borne out by the various matters mentioned in the master Plan that the master plan will only give a very broad outline of DeLhi as it will look in future.

The appellant No. 1 was the Minister of Industries and the appellant No 2 was the Secretary to the Government of the Commerce and Industries Department of the State of Vindhya Pradesh. The appellant No, 2 was charged with having committed offences under sections 120 B, 161, 465 and 466 of the Indian Penal Code and the appellants were tried in the Court of Special Judge at Rewa under the Vindhya Pradesh Criminal Law Amendment (Special Courts) Ordinance No. LVI of 1949 and the Special judge acquitted both of them. The State took an appeal to the Supreme Court by special leave against the acquittal of the appellant Nos. 1 and 2 on the ground that the statement made by the appellant was not recorded under section 164 of the Code of Criminal Procedure and was therefore inadmissible in evidence. Held, that the statements made to these two witnesses were admissible in evidence as there was no doubt that the appellant had brought these moneys from his home These moneys were proved to have been provided by the police authorities and given to Nagindas when the raid was organised with the numbers of the currency notes actually found in the bedroom of the appellants No. I and 25,000 tallied with the number of the notes which had been handed over to Nagandas earlier when the search was organised and which numbers were also specified in the memo prepared at that time was enough enough to establish the falsity of the allegation made by them. Held further, that there was nothing in section 164 Of the Code to suggest that the Magistrate acting as a witness in a particular case did not himself try that case. The basic merit of the administration of criminal justice in the State lies in the fact that the person arrested by the Police is entitled to come before an independent and impartial Magistrate who is expected to deal with the case without the Magistrate himself being in any way a partisan or a witness to police activities. There was another danger and that is the Magistrates are put in the unenviable and embarrassing position of having to give evidence as a witnesses and then being disbelieved.

The respondent was serving the State Police as a constable when an incident took place on 17.2.1971, which led to the prosecution of the respondent along with the Head Constable Kahan Singh and the Sub Inspector Baldev Singh. The charge made against the respondent was that he physically assaulted and detained one Gurdial Singh. On appeal, it was contended on behalf of the appellant that the other accused constable Kahan singh who was also con victed with the plaintiff had also filed a separate suit against his dismissal from service which was decreed with an observation that it was open to the competent authorities to pass fresh order of punishment in accordance with law, but while no further punishment was awarded to the respondent, the respondent 's service stood terminated. The trial court dismissed the suit on the ground of limitation and held that the impugned order of dismissal was void on the grounds of arbitrariness and there fore, the bar of limitation would not apply. It was also observed that this decision would not preclude the authority to award a minor punishment, provided such a punishment has been awarded to tho other police officials tried and con viced along with him. The authority was also permitted to take a decision in regard to the pay and allowance for the period the respondent remained out of service because of his being in jail. The respondent filed a regular second appeal before the High Court against the decree of the first appellate court which was dismissed at the admission stage by merely saving that it would not prevent the authority from awarding a minor penalty, provided the said punishment has already been awarded. Allowing the appeal to this Court, HELD: 1.1 In the instant case, the High court should have examined the plaint for finding out the cause of action for the suit and then in that light deter mined the correct article of the Limitation Act applicable to the case. Serious objection has been taken against the observations of the First Appellate Court permitting the competent authority to inflict only minor punishment on the respondent in certain conditions, and the direction about the payment of salary and other emoluments. After heat ing the learned counsel for the parties, we agree with the appellants that the question involved in this suit should not have been lightly brushed aside by the High COurt in the manner it has been done. [825E F] 1.2 In the event of admission of fresh evidence, the trial court shall permit the plaintiff to file relevant rebutting evidence. The operation of the decree shall remain stayed till the final disposal of the second appeal by the trial Court.

The appellant company entered into certain transactions in jute. On April 17, 1958 the assessee had contracted to purchase 1100 bales of corn sacks: the contract for B Twill and 2500 bales respectively. The assessee had no godown for keeping the goods and had not handled them. The goods were in the godown of the mills and only the delivery orders addressed to the mills changed hands. The amount realised on sale to M/s. Lachhminarain Kanoria & Co. came to Rs. 10,49,865/ . The assessee claimed adjustment of this loss in the computation of its income for the assessment year 1959 60. The Income tax Officer held that the transactions were not speculative and the loss should be treated as business loss relying on two decisions of this Court: Bayana Bhimayya and Sukhdevi Rathi vs The Govt. of Andhra Pradesh, ; , D. M. Wadhwana vs Commissioner of Income tax, West Bengal, ; and D.M. Wadhwani vs Commissioner Of Income tax (supra) overruled. In appeal to the Tribunal it was contended that the transaction was not speculative in nature and could be set off only against speculation profits and as there were no speculation profits in that year he held that loss would be carried forward and set off against speculation profit in the future. The High Court answered the question in the affirmative and against the assessee. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 A transaction which is otherwise speculative would not be a speculative transaction within the meaning of explanation 2 to section 24(1) of the Income Tax Act, 1922. [184 D] 1.2 In enacting the Explanation 2 of section 24 (1) it was not necessary that the transfer in question should be followed up by actual delivery of the goods to the transferee. Even if the goods are delivered to the transferor 's transferee, the first transfer also will be a valid transfer. What has to be seen is whether the ultimate purchaser of the P.D.Os. had taken actual delivery or physical manual delivery of possession in the ultimate analysis eliminating the unnecessary process of each of the intermediate parties taking and in his turn giving actual delivery thereof. [185 E F] 1:3 The object of the explanation is not to invalidate the transaction which are not completed by actual delib erately of the Goods but only to brand them as speculative transactions so as to put them in a special category for income tax purposes. [186 G] 2.1 In enacting Explanation 2 to sec. 24(i) of Income Tax, 1922 the legislature did not intend to affect any transaction of sale wherein the goods were not physically delivered by the seller to the buyer but only laid down that if there was no actual delivery, the loss, if any, would be a loss in a speculative trans action which could be allowed to be set aside only against a profit in a transaction of the same nature. The object is not merely to invalidate speculative transactions which are otherwise not completed but only for brand them and brand them to put themselves in a Special category for Income Tax purposes. The Explanation does not invalidate speculative according to explanation 2 if there is no actual or physical delivery, but only lays down that where there is an actual delivery the loss if any would be loss in speculative transaction which could he allowed to been set off merely against a profits in a transactions of thesame nature. [187 E F; 186 A B] D. R. M Wadhwana v Commissioner of Incometax, WestBengal, ; applied. In construing Explanation 2 it is not necessary for the purpose of this explanation. The definition of "delivery" in section 2(2) of that Act includes both actual and constructive or symbolical delivery has no bearing on the definition of speculative transaction in the explanation.

The first respondent was a candidate for the reserved seat but his nomination was rejected by the Returning Officer at the scrutiny stage and so he was unable to contest the election. The appellant filed an Election Petition challenging the rejection of the nomination papers on the ground that it was not accompanied with the required attestation under section 36(4) of the Representation of the People Act, 1951. Held, that the attestation in the prescribed manner is required in the case of proposers and seconders who are not able to write their names, and the Returning officer rightly rejected them under section 35(2)(d) of that Act because there was a failure to comply with section 33 unless he could and should have had resort to section 36 (4). The attestation in prescribed manner was required in a case where the signature cannot be written it must be authorised in the manner prescribed by the Rules. Whether this attaches exaggerated importance to the authorisation is not for us to decide. What is beyond dispute is beyond controversy that this is regarded as a matter of special moment and that special provision has been made to meet such cases. The General Clauses Act does not define the word "subscribe" any more than the Representation Of the People (Conduct of Election and Election Petitions) Rules, 1951 and if it is improper to exclude the special meaning given to " sign " in the Representationof the People ' Act because the word 'sign " is defined and not " subscribe", it is equally improper to import the special definition of " sign" in the General Clauses Acts because that also defines only "sign".

The appellants, who were employees of the Company, went on an indefinite peaceful strike with effect from August 30, 1972 pursuant to the strike notice given to the Company by their registered union called 'the Association of Chemical Workers ' in support of its demand for re instatement of three of the Unions leaders who had been dismissed by the Company. On September 7, 1972, the Company issued notices to the appellants and 10 others asking them to report for duty on or before September 18, 1972 failing which their absence would be construed as voluntary abandonment of service and their names would be struck off from the muster rolls of the company. The appellants ' union sent separate communications to the Works Manager of the Co operative Workers protesting against the action of the COurt in removing them from service and asserting that the said action was by way of victimization for their participation in the strike. On October 23, 1972 the Company wrote a letter to the appellant company stating that its letter dated September 7. 1972 which had reached them only on September 20, 1972 had already been replied by letter dated Sept. 21, 1972 that they were interested in the service of the co operative Workers ' Union and had neither voluntarily abandoned the service nor did they wish to do so, and that they would report for work the moment the strike was called off by their union. On May 19, 1973 certain proposals for settlements were made on behalf of the employees whose services were terminated by the CO Court. The Assistant Commissioner thereupon summoned the parties for discussion on July 19,1973 but his attempts at conciliation did not bear any fruit. Thereafter, the appellants made the aforesaid complaints before the Industrial Tribunal with the result as stated above. The Company sent separate communication to the appel lants and 10 other workmen informing them that since "by not reporting for duty they had confirmed its presumption that they had abandoned service would constitute a change in the conditions of service of their employees". On October 3, 1973, the CO passed notices to all the appellants calling upon them to submit their reply. The COurt summoned the appellants for discussion and on July 5, 1973 but his attempt at conciliation failed did not yield any fruit, and thereupon the appellants filed the present appeal by special leave against the award of the Industrial Tribu nal. Allowing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1. Abandonment or relinquishment of service is always a question of intention, and normally such an intention cannot be attributed to an employee without adequate eviti dence in that behalf. Thus, whether there has been voluntary abandonment or not is a question Of fact which has to be determined in the light of the surrounding circumstances of each case. Question No. 2: This takes us to the consideration of the second question namely, whether the action was of the Compa ny in removing the names of the appellants from its rolls during the pendency of the proceedings before the Labour Court in respect of the industrial dispute on the presumption that the appellants had abandoned their service would constitutes a change In the condition of service applicable to them immediately before the commencement of the said proceedings which prejud peremptorily affected them. Although the learned counsel appearing on behalf for the respondent has taken us through the certified standing orders as applicable to the petitioners, he has not been able to point out anything therein to indicate that the COCourt could terminate the services of the appellant on the ground of abandonment of serv ice because of their going on strike in enforcement of their demands. Thus there was no abandonment of services on the part of the appe lant. [616C D] 1.2. The fact that back wages have to be computed, if ordered in full, on a much higher scale because of two settlements which have raised the scales of wages substantially.

The respondents were trustees of a public trust. The trustees did not pay the instalments due under the decree, and in an application for execution by the mortgage, the mortgaged property was put up for sale and the bid of the appellant was accepted for Rs. 5,000 by the executing court. The trial Court passed an order disposing of the execution application and directed that Rs. 250 out of the amount deposited by the trustees be paid over to the appellant. In appeal against that order by the appellant, the District Court reversed the order holding that since the trustees had failed to comply with the requirements of r. 89 of 0. 21, Code of Civil Procedure, the executing Court had no jurisdiction to set aside the sale held in execution of the decree. The High Court also held that since a Judge or a Division Bench of a High Court makes a reference on a question of law arising in a matter before a single Judge or Division Bench that there are conflicting decisions of the same court, and that a question which affects a public religious or charitable purpose is involved, the Court shall not proceed to determine such question until after notice "has been given to the Charity Commissioner", made it obligatory upon the Court to issue notice to the trustee and if that officer desires to be joined as a party, to implied him in a proceeding to enforce a mortgage by sale of the mortgaged properties. In an appeal by special leave, HELD: (1) The Legislature did not intend to put any restriction upon the power of the Civil Court executing a decree for recovery of money due from the trust, by sale, of the property of the trust. [459C] (2) A judgment delivered by a Judge and a Division bench of that High Court after due consideration of the points before it was liable to be regarded as irrelevant by Judges of that court on the round of some alleged irregularity in the constitution of the Full Bench. [461D E] (3) The decision of Bhagwati, J. in Pijare Karimbhai 's case did not Jay down the law or rule of practice, it was open to him to recommend to the Chief Justice that the question be considered by a larger Bench. Judicial decorum, propriety and discipline required that lie should not ignore it. [463E] (4) The judgment of Bhagwati J. was binding upon Raju, J., in Pjijare ambhai 'S case, and of Nacleod, C.

Rule 2(2) of the Liberalised Pension Rules, 1950 provides that an officer may retire from service any time after completing 30 years ' qualifying service provided that he shall give in this behalf a notice in writing to the appropriate authority at least three months before the date on which he wishes to retire. The Government servant also may, after attaining the age of 55 years, voluntarily retire after giving three months ' notice or pay in lieu of such notice. Rule 2(1) of Pension Rules provides that such power can only be exer cised in Public Interest '. The respondent joined the Post and Telegraph Department as a clerk on June 4, 1935. He was retired from service under Rule 2 (2) by an order dated April 21, 1970. The Director, Postal Services by an Order dated April 31, 1970 retired him from service on July 30, 1971. The appellant challenged the order of retirement by way of a writ petition before the High Court which held that there was no in firmity in Rule 2.(2) and that there Was no in the firmity. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the Union of India that the Government had issued instruc tions dated July 11, 1955 and February 8, 1956 which lay down that the retirement under Rule II(j) should be effected when such retirement is necessary in public interest. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The Memorandum dated November 30, 1962 and February, 8, 1965 are statutory rules and are identical to Fundamental Rule 56(j). [800G] 2.1 The memorandum has not been issued under Article 309 of the Constitution of India and as such cannot be stat ed with the support of executive instructions. [800C] Union of india & Ors. vs R. Narasimhan, ; , referred to. 2.2 Rule 2046 is a statutory rule and is identical to Rule 56 (j). Para 620 is in the nature of executive instruction but is similarly worded as Rule 2.

The assessee firm was an unregistered firm carrying on business of manufacture and sale of katechu. The chargeable account period was 1 4 1943 to 31st March, 1944. There were two partners of the assessee firm, namely L. Phoolchand and M/s Biharilal Balkishan each having profits in proportion of 11 annas and 5 annas respectively. The work in connection with the extraction of Katechu was carried on in Nepal by 1.4.1943 to 31.3.1944. The sales in this case were effected between 26th July, 1943 to 4th April, 1944, when the business was dis continued. The assessee firm did not maintain any books of account and the entire record of the business transaction was maintained in the books of M/S BiharilalBalkishan in the account styled "Kalyanmal Phoolchand". The assessee Firm had taken a jungle on lease for this purpose and had extracted Katechhu from October, 1940 to September, 1941. The Sales Tax Officer did not set off the said deficiency of profits that accrued in respect of the period 1940 41 out of the profits for the chargeable accounting period from 1st April, 1943, to 31th March, 1943. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner on appeal found that the constitution of the firm during the chargeable year was the same as in 1940 41 and the ac count ing periods were maintained in this fashion; and that the same business of manufacturing Katechinu in Nepal and selling the finished products at kanpur was carried out. The Tribunal, however, held that there could be no profit or loss during the said chargeable accounting periods although there were no sales effected yet profits accrued to the assessee. In appeal by the Revenue, the High Court held that it was not disputed before them that the assessee was carrying on the same dur ing business from 28th October, 1941 to 4.4, 1944 for the purpose of the Act.

The Kerala Public Service Commission invited applications for filling up 130 expected vacancies in the posts of Junior Engineers in the Public Works Department as per notification published in the Kerala Gazette dated 16th May, 1978. The qualifications specified for the posts were B.Sc. in Civil Engineering or Mechanical Engineering of the Kerala University or its equivalent as prescribed by the special rules of the said Kerala Engineering Subordinate Service (General Branch). The applicants had to appear in the written test conducted by the KPSC and there after in an interview held by it. There was a common question paper which contained, in category I, questions in Civil engineering and in Category II, questions were in Civil Engg. The applicants who had qualified in Civil Engineers had to answer the questions in Category I on the one hand and those who had appeared in the viva voce test conducted for filling them in Category 1 on the other hand and these qualified in Mechanical Engineering the questions indicated in Category 11 in the question paper could not rationally be included in a common rank list after the interview. The learned Single Judge of the High Court allowed the Writ Petitions and directed the Government to prepare "two lists, namely, one for the Civil Bench and the other for the Mechanical Branch on the basis of examination already conducted". He proceeded: "With respect to it the Service Commission has not yet published the rank list. On receiving information from the Government on the above lines, the Public Service Commis sioner is directed to prepare the two separate lists, viz., one for Civil Bench & the other and for the Electrical Engineering graduates. The Kerala Government and the K PSC accepted the directions given by the learned Single judge and proceeded to take steps for the implementation thereof. However, some of the aggrieved respondents in the Writ Petition filed appeals before the Division Bench of the high Court. The appeals were ultimately dismissed, in view of the fact that the K.PSC had advised 239 candidates according to separate lists for Civil Engineering graduates and answered questions indicated by Category II in the Question paper couldnot rationally he included in the common rank List after the interviews. The High Court also dismissed all the S.L.Ps. with observations referred to above.

The respondent No. 1, a partner of a partnership business along with his brothers defendant Nos. 1 and 2, was the proprietor of a firm consisting of his brothers and defendant Nos, 2 and 3. Originally it was a proprietary business belonging to Abdul Samad, father of the plaintiff and defendant nos. 1 & 2, and was later converted into a partnership firm by a regular deed. During his life time the business was under the control of Abdul Samad. But on his death the defendants Nos.1 and 2 had effectively taken charge of the business and excluded the plaintiff. A suggestion to re constitute and partnership made and repeated by the plaintiff has been ignored. In reply to the plaintiff 's letter seeking information the defendant No. 2 stated in his letter to the appellant that he has no interest in the firm. The Income Tax Officer passed an order on 26th December 1981 on the basis of the false allegations made by the defendants. The plaintiff challenged the valuation given by the defendant as grossly undervalued and arbitrary. The issues relating to the correct valuation and pecuniary jurisdiction of the Court to enter the suit were taken up as preliminary issues and were decided in favour of the appellant. The trial court decreed the suit. The High Court dismissed the revision application. In appeal to this Court it was contended that relief to the tune of lacs of rupees has been claimed by the respondent in the suit, and that the plaintiff had laid claim to a sum of Rs.1,26,796.72 besides another sum over Rs.84,000 as his share in the profit for a particular period by reference to the proceeding of the Income Tax Department mentioned in paragraph 11 of the plaint, and it was, therefore, preposterous on his part to suggest in paragraph 19 of the Plaint that it could be tentatively valued at Rs.50 only. According to the defence case which is challenged as incorrect by the appellant, the plaintiff requested for and was allowed a larger share 'in the well established and reputed business of auctioneer known as "Russell Exchange" and its assets and goodwill as well as the amount lying in the Habib Bank, Karachi Branch solely and absolutely '. Dismissing the appeal, this Court, HELD: 1.1 In a suit for accounts the plaintiff is not obliged to state the exact amount which would result after taking all the accounts and he may, therefore put a tentative valuation upon the suit but he is not permitted to choose an unreasonable and arbitrary figure for that purpose. At page 392 of the judgment in Meenakshisundaram Chettiar vs Venkatachalam Chettiar, [1945] ILR XXIV Patna 334, the respondent filed a suit praying for accounts from appellant No.1. Rejecting his claim to put any valuation under section 7(iv)(f) of the court Fees Act, the High Court observed that when a plaintiff is required to place the valuation on his claim he must state a valuation which need only be approximately correct but qualified it by saying that "it must not be arbitrary or manifestly inadequate. It is true that in a suit of accounts the defendant is not bound to state exact amount Which would result, after taking into all the account and he might, therefore.

The assesses ' claim for exemption from sales tax for certain periods in question was accepted by the High Court. The State filed appeals and special leave petitions against the judgment of the Full Bench. The assessee contended that the exemption granted earlier to new industrial units claiming exemption from/deferment of payment of sales tax was contingent upon the issue of a certifi cate of eligibility certificate by the Director of Industries, which was subsequently revoked. However, subsequently, a Full Bench of the High court in the case of G.S. Dhall & Flour Mills and, following the Full Court 's decision in the G. S.Dhall & Weaving Mills case and, Following the Full bench decision in G.M. Dhal & Flour Mill case and following the earlier Full Bench decision, the State Government exempted the class of dealers specified in column (1) of the Schedule below who had set up industry in any of the districts of Madhya Pradesh specified in the annexure to this notification and have commenced production after 1st April 1981 from pay ment of tax under the said Act for the period specified in Column (2), subject to the restrictions and conditions specified in columns (3) of that schedule. The High Court rejected the contention of the State that the assessee 's claim that they were eligible for exemption under the notification and that the Director should have granted them a certificate to this effect. Allowing the appeals, this Court, HELD: 1.1 The question of grant of exemption by the Industries Department is not an empty formality but before granting the certificate the Industries Depart ment has to see whether all the requirements as con tained in the instructions are fulfilled and complied with or not. But, here: "as pointed out earlier, column 3 of the 1981 Notification does not contain any guidelines or a procedure in the matter of grant ing exemption certifi fied".

Rule 7 of the Delhi Higher Judicial Service Rules, 1970 provides that recruitment to the Delhi High Court shall be made by the Administrator on the recommendation of the High Court. Rule 17 provides for appointment of promotees to temporary vacancies in the service and, even substantive vacancies in a service can be filled by making temporary appointments. The petitioners who were direct recruits to the said post filed writ petitions in this Court challenging the seniority list contending that seniority between promotees and direct recruits must be determined in accordance with the respective dates of their continuous officiation as Additional District & Sessions Judges and that, direct recruits who are appointed as Additional Distt. and Sessions Judges after the promotees are so appointed cannot rank higher in seniority over the promotees. The respondents contended that seniority was between promotees, and direct recruit must be fixed in accordance With the respective date of continuous officiation in the cadre post i.e. a direct recruit who is appointed after a member of the State Judicial Service is appointed in a substantive capacity to a temporary post of Additional District and Sessions Judge and that the seniority of direct recruits vis a vis promotees shall be determined according to the dates on which direct recruits were appointed to their respective posts and the dates from which the promotees have been officiating continuously either in temporary posts created in the Service or in substantive vacancies to which were appointed in the permanent capacity. The High Court dismissed the writ petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended that the inter se seniority between the promotees and the direct recruits should be determined on the basis of their actual officiation as Addl. District & Session Judges and not according to their dates of continuous officiating officiation as additional District and Session Judges, and that in any case, there is no provision for probation for the appointments under Rules 16 and 17 of the said rules, but sub rule (2) of Rule 12 required that all candidates shall be on probation for a period of two years. Dismissing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1 The seniority of members of Delhi Judicial Service promoted to the service shall be the same as in the Delhi Judicial Services. [362C] 1.2 Under Rule 16, promotees are appointed to temporary posts in the services while under Rule 17 they are appointed in substantive capacity on a regular basis to substantive vacancies In the instant case, the seniority lists which is impugned in this case has been prepared on the foundation that the rule of `quota and rota ' will continue to apply notwithstanding the fact that appointments are made to the Service under Rules16 and 17. [361E] 1:3 The seniority list which is challenged in this petition has been drawn up on the footing that the Rule of ` Quota and Rota ' would continue to operate notwithstanding the non obstante clause contained in the proviso to rule 7 of Delhi Higher judicial Service Rules. [363A B] Chandramouleshwar Prasad vs Patna High Court & Ors., ; , followed. 1:4 The seniority between direct recruits and promotees appointed under Rule 16 must be governed by the rules of continuous continuous officiation, in the Cadre post i,e. direct recruits. [364G H] Chandra Mouleshwar Prashad vs Patna high Court & ors. at 608; , referred to.

The Income tax Officer assessed the Ambala Flour Mills in the three years of assessment. In appeals by Debi Parshad, the Appellate Assistant Commissioner set aside the order of assessment and directed that the direction for assessing the income should be deleted. The Tribunal referred the questions at the instance of the Commissioner of Income tax. The High Court held that the business was carried on by an association of persons and the income from the business could not be brought to tax on that footing. In appeal to this Court, HELD : (i) The expression 'any person ' in section 34(3)(b) of the Income tax Act, 1922, is necessarily confined to a person intimately connected in the said sense with the assessment of the year under appeal. [392 B] Commissioner off Income tax U.P. vs Kanpur Coal Syndi cate, ; , followed. (ii) The word 'any persons ' in the setting in which it appears must be confined to the person intimally connected in that sense with assessment of that year under Appeal. [395 C] Commissioner of lncome tax, U. P., vs Kanpur Sugar Co. Ltd., ; , applied. (iii) The Income tax officer was of the view that the income belonged to Debi Parthshad and he was liable to be assessed personally in respect of the income. The Appellate Assistant Com missioner had directed that he may be personally assessed by the Income Tax Officer in respect Of the income of the Ambala Rice Flour Mills. personally. for in their view Debi Parath, the High Court exercising advisory jurisdiction was incompetent to amend the order.

The appellant, who was the son of Subbiah Chettiar, filed a suit for partition and accounts in respect of his joint family assets. The plaint was valued at Rs. 1,000 under section 7(iv)(f) of the Madras Court Fees Act (which will be described hereafter as the Act). The appellant claimed that he had been adopted by Lakshmi Achi in 1922 and that he was the basis on which a claim for partition was made by him in his suit. The respondent contended that the suit was not maintainable because the suit did not fall under article 17 B of Schedule II of the Act. Held, that the plaint did not attract the provisions of article 17B of Schedule 11 of the Indian , and it could not be reopened at this stage. It was open to the Division Bench to consider the correctness of the view taken by the learned Chamber Judge; but in the present case it had been found by the Division Court that dealt with this matter subsequently that a search of the record did not show any general or special order which would have justified the exercise of jurisdiction under section 5 by Krishnaswamy Naidu J. The appeal must be allowed and the appellant directed to pay additional court fees on his plaint on the basis of the valuation of Rs. 15,00,000 at which he values the relief sought for by him for the purpose of Court fee and the value for the purposes of jurisdiction alone was, therefore, mentioned. Held further, that in view of their prior decision that the present suit fell under section 8 of the Suits Valuation Act, the appellant had been given an absolute right or option to place any valuation whatever on his relief. The fact that in suits for partition the plaintiff attempts to obtain the benefit of article 16 B of schedule II in the matter of payment of court fees arose at the initial stage of the presentation of the plaint or the appeal and the defendant or the respondent was usually not interested in such a dispute unless the question of payment involves also the question whether of jurisdiction of the Court either to try the suit or to entertain the appeal.
