The New Delhi Municipal Committee (NDMC) sought special leave to appeal against the decision of the NDMC dated 18.2.1987 declining to sanction the Revised Plans for construction of "Statesman House" a high rise building on plot No. 148, Barakhamba Road New Delhi of which the first respondent is the lessee. The High Court allowed the writ petition and directed the NDMC to convey its formal sanction of the building plans on or before 5th May, 1989. The NDMC assailed the decision by way of a Writ Petition in the High Court. The main contention of the appellant was that the permissions for the multi storeyed high rise buildings as envisaged in the Building designs, were allayed by the Chief Fire Officer 's clearance and held that thereafter there was no impediment to the sanction. During the course of hearing the standing counsel for the NDMC raised the issue of applicability of Bye law 16.4.8 of the applicable Building Bye laws of the Delhi Municipal Act 1911 and submitted that the clearance of the Chief fire Officer did not prevent the NDMC from enforcing the applicable bye laws. However, the Court in the light of the statement of counsel for respondent No. 1 and 2 held that there was nothing in the Code to show that the rigid interpretation sought to be placed by the appellant on the bye law 16 was not justified. The eligibility of the proposed construction for sanction except on the point of adequacy of "Refuge areas" in the requirement of a "pedestrian walk way" and "Podium/pedest Compulsory walk way", was not otherwise disputed. The objection based on bye law16.4 was also raised by respondent No 1 and the same was rejected by the High Cou rt. In the appeal to this Court, it was contended that the prescriptions in bye law 1.16.8 and 16.2 would detract from the validity of the first respond ent 's claim and establish that the clearances from the Chief Leve nary Development Officer were one of the conditions and not the sole or conclusive test of the adequacy of fire safety measures in terms of the relevant Bye laws. The exemption area envisaged by bye law 2.27 was an additional condition and not a limitation on the power of the Respondent NDMC to satisfy itself that the building plan provide for adequate fire safety precaution in accordance with its bye laws or in a better measure.

The joint family carried on joint family business of a grocery shop, liquor shops, a ration shop, a motor bus service and also money lending under the name of "Sontakke Brothers". The family also Possessed immovable and movable property. Balkrishna sontakke was the eldest of the brothers and was the plaintiff respondent in the present appeal. He will be referred to hereafter as the plain tiff. It is common ground that up to 1944 the brothers were living and messing together and the income from 101 the family business used to be kept with the plaintiff. From April 14, 1945, all the five brothers filed a suit for partition against the plaintiff of all joint family properties including the accounts of all the businesses. The compromise further declared that the plaintiff was to have one sixth share in the motor garage and that defendants 1 and 2 were to pay the price of one sixth to him. These are the material provisions of the compromise. One of the sons of the brother was a minor and the Court finding the compromise to be for the benefit of the minor accepted it and passed a preliminary decree in terms of the compromised on July 25, 1947. The plaintiff filed an application before the Civil Judge praying that accounts of the motor business should be taken up to March 31, 1946, and for determining the amount due up to that date. Each of the two brothers was to get one sixth per cent share in his cash balance as found on March 31. 1946 upon examination of accounts by the arbitrators. All the movable property of the joint family including the stock in trade of all of the family businesses was to be divided equally among all the brothers. The suit was numbered 39 of 1945 and it was compromised on March 7, 1946. By this compromise it was declared that prior to 1942 all the accounts had been correctly maintained and shown, that the parties had agreed to have arbitrators appointed through Court for examining the accounts from 1942 up to the date of final decree. The agreement further declared inter alia that the appellant was to pay one sixth fifth share in a motor garage which he deliberately relinquished. The trial court passed a preliminary decree directing the accounts to be taken from March 31 1946 up to April 14 1945, and on appeal the High Court modified the decree by directing that the accounts were to be made up to date on which a final decree for payment of the amount found to be due would be made. On appeal by special leave: Held, that upon a fair reading of the agreement arrived at between the parties in the circumstances then existing, the only legitimate conclusion was that the party had agreed not expressly negative the right of the plaintiff to an account of motor business. The terms of compromise were clear and unambiguous. The consent decree having been found not to be vitiated by fraud, misrepresentation, misunderstanding or mistake, the decree passed thereon has the binding force of res judicata.

The appellant was employed as a factory in the Salt Works and was working on any day of the preceding twelve months, without obtaining a licence under section 6 of the Bombay Salt Works Act, 1948 read with r. 4 of the Rules framed under the Act. The salt works were carried on in the premises of the firm which consisted of winnowing, cleaning, washing and drying pepper on concrete floor. The appellant was prosecuted for having used the salt work as a raw material for converting it into salt. The trial court acquitted the appellant but convicted him under section 92 of the Act on the ground that the salt works did not come within the definition of the word " factory " in cl. (k) of section 2 of the , and that the process of converting sea water into salt did not amount to "manufacture" as no process for making, altering, packing, cleaning or otherwise treating or adapting any article or substance with a view to its use, sale, transport, delivery or disposal was carried on. Held, that the appellant 's Salt Works were within the meaning of the expression " manufacturing process " and could not be said to be a " factory" within the Act as it was not intended to interfere with persons employed in quarries. The word " premises " is not restricted in scope to buildings alone. The definition of " manufacturing " in section 2(k) is wide enough to include buildings and be not taken to cover open land as well. The expression " premises includes precincts" it has been urged clearly indicated that the word ' premises " must be restricted to mean buildings and are not taken into consideration in construing the definition. The use of the words " manufacturing processes " in the Act is not confined to buildings only but also to buildings which were to be controlled by the respective Factory Acts and that it was intended to include sheds erected in the quarry merely as a protection against the weather; they are only accessories to the quarry and the quarrying processes; and the legislature has not yet declared that open air works shall be within the scope of the factory Acts. The fact that salt works as such do not come under the definition is not decisive of the question whether the salt worked as such did not fall within the word factory " or " premises".

The respondent entered the service of the Princely State in 1935 as Instructor in tailoring and joined duty there on December 1, 1949. He was reverted to his parent department on June 11, 1956, but no order was passed in the case of the respondent despite repeated representations made by the latter. In 1953, the then State of Mysore set up the Department of Technical Education and the Polytechnic at Devangere became part of that Department. The respondent continued tp serve on deputation in that department. In 1955, for no fault of the Respondent, the Government passed orders reverting him to his Principal Department. On June 11. 1956, the respondent was again posted on deputation as Instructor, in tailored and he joined duty thereafter there on 12th December 1949. His specific grievance was that in any case, he could not be discriminated against and treated differently from K. N. Chetty who was junior to him in the parent Department and came on deputation to the Polytechnics subsequently. The State Government referred the respondent 's case to the Public Service Commission who examined it and by a communication dated February 2, 1960 made these recommendations in favour of the respond ent. In November 1958, another batch of 107 persons were similarly promoted as Assistant Engineers with retrospective effect from 1st November 1956 when the new State of Madras emerged under the States Reorganization Act. The appellant contended that this principle was ignored in the matter of absorption and appointment, while his junior K. Narayanaswamy Chetty who had been admittedly junior to the respondent, and was identically situated, was accorded the same treatment. The High Court allowed the writ petition and issued a direction that the absorption of the employees which came on : deputation from a particular date, was a concession which could not he claimed as of right, and consequently, a writ of mandamus should not be issued. Allowing the appeal to this Court, ^ HELD: 1.1 The respondent 'reversion ' to the parent department in 1955 56, was not ordered owing to any fault of his. It is not the case that the respondent had been invidiously discriminated against in the matters of absorption & appointment, and while his juniors were similarly situated, were absorbed from the dates on which they initially joined duty, after deputation to a Polytechnicics. [259A B] 1.2 The acceptance of the respondents ' contentions would have unsettled pre Constitution matter, and it would have been directly productive of results going against section 115(7) of the States Reorganisation Act. Further, acceptance of this respondent ' 's contention would have adversely affected even the Narayanaswamy Mudaliar who was admittedly junior in the previous department. On the` other hand, it is an undisputed fact that sit other employees, who were similarly situate, were promoted from the date on which he initially came on a deputation, was ever departed from, excepting in the cases of the re spondent. This being the case, the High Court was right in holding that the State Government had evolved a principle "that if a person was deputed to the Department from another department and he stayed on in that other department for a reasonable long time his absorption in that Department should be made to relate back to the date of his appointment as such as has been ordered in the ease of Sri K.N. Chetty, [259C D] 1:3 The acceptance by the respondent that his "impermissible reversion" for a short while in 1955 to the Principal Department was no ground to hold that he was not similarly situated as K. Nariayanaswamy Chetty. This so called reversion to the said parent department for the short period in 1955 57 could not by any reckoning, be treated as a break in his service, this period having been treated as leave. Nor did it amount u ' reduction to reduction in rank. [260D E] 1 :4 The acceptance was not made due to any misconduct of the appellant.

The petitioner, an advocate practising in this Court complaining of malpractices indulged in by social organisations and voluntary agencies engaged in the work of offering Indian children in adoption to foreign parents. The letter referred to a press report based on "empirical investigation carried out by the staff of a reputed foreign magazine" called "The Mail", and alleged that not only Indian children of tender age were under the guise of adoption "exposed to the long horrendous journey to distant foreign countries at great risk to their lives but in cases where they survive and where these children are not placed in the Shelter and Relief Homes, they in course of time become beggars or prostitutes for want of proper care from their alleged foreign foster parents. " The petitioner accordingly sought relief restraining Indian based private agencies "from carrying out further activity of routing children for adoption abroad" and directing the Govern ment of India to carry out their obligations in the matter of adoption of Indian children by foreign parents, and directing that the Indian Council of Social Welfare and the Indian council of Social welfare should carry out its obligations in respect of adoption. The Court issued notice to Union of India, the Indian Councils of Social Protection or the Indian County for Child Welfare or any other independent, reputed and publicly recognised social welfare agency to which notice was issued by the court would have to scrutinise the application for guardianship made on behalf of the foreigner wishing to take the child in adoption and after examining the home study report, the child study report as also documents and certificates forwarded by the sponsoring social or child welfare agency and making necessary enquiries, it must make its representation to the Court so that the court may be able to satisfy itself whether the principles and norms laid down by this Court in Bombay, Delhi and Gujarat, are applicable. The petitioner filed a writ petition in the High Court challenging the constitutional validity of the adoption on the ground that the social or Child welfare agency sponsoring the application of foreign parents for guardianship of the child with a view to its eventual adoption was not sponsored by a social or family welfare agency recognised or licensed by the Government of India or the Government, and that it would be in the interest of the children, promotive of its welfare, to be adopted by the foreign parents making the application or in other words, whether such adoption will provide moral and material security to the child alongwith an opportunity to grow into the full stature of its personality in an atmosphere of love and affection and warmth of a family hearth and home. The High Court dismissed the writ petition on the view that it was not necessary for the foreign parent to take a child in adopt any amount in respect thereof, and directed the Government to carryout their obligations. In appeal by special leave, it was contended: (1) The adoption of children by Foreign parents need not wait until social or social welfare agencies are recognised by the government as directed in this order, but pending recognition of social or Children welfare agencies for the purpose of inter country adoptions, which interregnum, the Court hope would be more reluctant to make an order appointing foreign parent as guardian unless it is satisfied that the application is sponsored by such social or children welfare agency. (2) The recognised social orchild welfare agency sponsorship the application must also agree to send to the concerned social or Social or child Welfare agency in India progress reports in regard to the children quarterly during the first year and half yearly for the subsequent year or until the adoption is effected, and it must also undertake that in case of disruption of the family of the foreign foreigner before adoption can be effected, it will take care of the Child and find a suitable alternative placement for it with the approval of the concerned Social or Child Welfare agency through which such child is proposed to be given in inter country.

The appellant company employed workmen numbering over 5000. The gross effective salaries and wages of its employees for the relevant accounting year amounts to Rs. 1,05,32,880. Its accounting year is from 1st April to 31st March of the succeeding year. For the accounting year 1964 65, the Company declared and paid bonus at 20% to all employes in accordance with the provisions of the (hereinafter to be referred as the Act). For the year 1965 66, it calculated a sum of Rs. 23,68,785 as available surplus. This amount represented 13 51% of the wage bill. The workmen were dissatisfied with this offer of bonus at 1351% and demanded payment of bonus on the difference in emoluments drawn by them. A dispute with the Company was referred for adjudication to the National Industrial Tribunal, Calcutta, which held that for the accounting years 1965 66 the quantum of bonus payable by the appellant to its workmen is 20% of their effective salaries or wages with a further direction to set on a sum Of Rs. 14,21,271 being 60% of it as provided in the Act. The Union contended before the Tribunal that the computa tion of allocable surplus by the Company has not been properly made in accordance ' the Act and that several items shown in the profit and loss account as expenditure have to be added back to arrive at the actual gross profits, and deducting therefrom the prior charges under section 6, but not the bonus payable to the employees. The Tribunal held that a sum was paid to keep up the old practice of the Company of paying all the members of the staff without the application of any ceiling. The company appealed to this Court by special leave. HELD: (i) The claim of the Unions is justified. It is not necessary for us to dwell on this point at any great length in view of the decision of this Court in Indian Oxygen Ltd. vs Their Workmen, [1962] Supp. 2 S.C.R. 891. (ii) The Tribunal was justified in disallowing the deduction of certain items from the gross profits for purposes of computing the available and allocable available surplus and the percentage of bonus for the year 1964 66. [114B C] (iii) The contention that the amount of Rs 65,764 has not to be deducted from the net profits under the Act as claimed by the management is untenable. [115C] (iv) The payment of compensation to induce the workmen to retire prematurely was an item of expenditure incurred by the company on the ground of commercial expense in order to facilitate carrying on of the business and it was an expenditure allowable under section 37(1) of the Income tax Act. [116E F] (v) The amount of additional amount that the Company will have to pay by way of bonus to make up the 14.02%, as stated above, is Rs.

The appellant, who was working as a Commercial Tax officer in 1953, was promoted as an Assistant Commercial Tax Officer in 1954. On promotion as Deputy Commissioner of Commercial Taxes he was posted as Member of the Sales Tax Appellate Tribunal in the same cadre. On September 28, 1975 he was retired under Fundamental Rule 56(d) of the Tamil Nadu General Rules for the State and Subordinate Services. The appellant challenged the order before the High Court by way of a Writ Petition. The High Court allowed the writ petition holding that the charges framed against him in consequence of the detailed enquiry conducted by the Vigilance Department cannot be pursued and proved. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1.1. The promotion of the appellant just a few months earlier and nothing even mildly suggestive of ineptitude or inefficiency thereafter, it is impossible to sustain the order of the Government retiring the appellant from service. [80G] 1.2. The previous history of a Government servant should be completely ignored, once he is promoted. Sometimes, past events may help to assess present conduct. But when there is nothing in the present conduct casting any doubt on the wisdom of the promotion, we see no justification for needless digging into the past. [81C] 1:3. The post of a Deputy Commissioner is a Selection post. Under Rule 36(b) (i) of Tamil Nadu Genera! Rules for Commercial Taxes Service: "Promotions in a service or class to a selection grade shall be made on grounds of merit and ability, seniority being considered only where merit and suitability are approximately equal". So, what do we have ? There was an adverse entry in the confidential file of the Appellant in 1969. The basis of the entry 79 was knocked out by the order dated November 29, 1974 of the A Government, and the effect of the Entry was blotted out by promotion of his appellant as Deputy Commis sioner. After his promotion as Dy Commissioner there was no entry in his service Book to his discredit or hinting even remotely that he had outlived his utility as a Govt. servant. If there was some entry, not wholly favourable to the appellant after his promotion, one might hark back to similar or like entries in the past, read them all in conjunction and conclude that the time had arrived for the Government servant to quit Government service. But with nothing of the sort, it was indeed odd to retire a Govt servant a few month after promoting him to a Selection Post. [82D E] 2.1 The post was knocked down by the orders dated November 30, 1974 and November 29. 1974 of A Government.G. O. Ms. No. 1112 dated September 19, 1975, Commercial Taxes Religious Endowments Department, Government of Tamil Pradesh is quashed.

The appellants who were the operators of a motor transport operators whose permits are liable to be modified or cancelled under the provisions of the Schemes on their coming into force, challenged the validity of the schemes framed under Chapter IV A of the . The High Court dismissed the petitions. In appeal to this Court it was contended that (1) the Regional Transport Authority which is specifically mentioned in section 68 C but really the Chief Minister; (2) assuming, however, that the Chief Secretary was actuated by political motives to hit at his opponents still the schemes which were published by the Corporation had been framed by the Corpora tion not at the dictation of the Chief Ministers, but as a result of their own independent judgment; and (3) even assuming that the Regional Secretary directed the order in which districts were to be taken up for nationalisation, still the scheme framed by it could not be assailed as not in conformity with the requirements of section 68C. HELD: (1)(a) The contention that the provisions Of section 68 F(1) are repugnant to section 68F(1), is without substance. [353 E] (b) The Regional Transport Officer which is expressly mentioned in Ch. IV of the , is empowered to issue the permit to the transport undertaking "notwithstanding anything to the contrary contained in Chapter IV" and that the section rendered the provisions o/s 68 F (1). [353 C D] (2)(a), (b), (c) and (d) of the Act are not ultra vires. The Regional A Transport Authority is empowered under Ch. VI of the, but there is some other authority which functions as the Regional Ai dure Authority for the purposes of the Art, such an authority might be that which would be comprehended by section 68 E(1). Therefore, when the judgment in the appeals was pronounced on January 27, 1964, the learned Advocate General for Andhra Pradesh gave an undertaking that in case the appeals succeed succeed, the State will compensate the appellants for the loss incurred by them during the period that the appeals were pending in this Court by reason of the fact that they were not allowed to ply their buses on the routes under the respective permits granted to them. [354 E F] (3)(a). The scheme framed under Ch., IV A, which is a self contained code, is intended to be implemented in every case where the scheme is proposed to be amended as if the modifications proposed were a separate scheme. and struck down. [355 G] Dosa Satyanaraya namurty etc. vs The Andhra Pradesh State Road Transport Corporation, ; , followed. (4) The scheme is not vitiated by non compliance with the provisions in Ch., VI of which applications for State carriage permits by private operators and the permits grant ed to them are required to state the minimum and maximum number of daily services proposed to he provided in relation to each route or area, was an indication that a scheme specifying the maxima and minima of the number of buses and services was in conformity w.e.f. 1st November 1962. [356 C] (5) The provisions of Ch. V of the Road Transport Act, 1950 are not unconstitutional as being violative of article 14 of the Constitution.

The appellant company was a public limited company registered as a dealer under the Bengal Finance (Sales Tax) Act, 1941. In respect of the accounting year ending with 31st December 1954 in the return for the year the assessee had shown its gross turnover at Rs. 70,99,928 10 0 and deposited the tax of Rs. 9 6 on the said amount in the treasury. The Commercial Tax Officer by notice dated April 22, 1955 fixed August 4, 1955, for hearing the assessee in respect of its return. Under section 5(2)(a)(ii) of the Act the appellant in order to claim exemption thereunder had to furnish a declaration forms duly filled in and signed by registered dealers to whom the goods were sold by it. After taking some adjournments of the enquiry it appeared that in the second week 'of January 1957 the assessee found its file containing 147 declarations forms received from its dealers in respect Of the goods received from it was missing. The assessee, therefore, made various attempts to get duplicate forms of declaration form from the dealers but, on account of circumstances over which it had no control and because of the unhelpful and hostile attitude of the Commercial Tax officer within whose jurisdiction the said dealers functioned, it was not able to furnish the duplicate forms for all the declarations that were lost. On August 8, 1957, the assessee applied to the Commercial tax Officer under section 21A of the Bengal Act for summoning the dealers to produce the necessary documents in order that they had issued the declaration forms to it but the said officer did not issue the requisite summons to the parties concerned. The Commissioner rejected the application on the ground that the application was rejected. On appeal, a Division Bench of the High Court confirmed the order of the Commissioner and dismissed the revision petition filed by the assessee. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that (i) the words "on demand" in r. 27A which according to the learned counsel, indicates that the production of the prescribed declaration is not obligatory but only to be made if a demand is made by the authority concerned; and (ii) the proviso qualifies the substantive clause. HELD: The expression "on demanded" only fixes the point of time when the declaration form forms are to be produced; otherwise the rule would be inconsistent with the section. [629 C] In the instant case, the object of section 5 (2)(b)(ii), namely prevention of fraud and collusion in an attempt to evade tax, is self evident. While they are obviously intended to give exemption to a dealer in respect o sales to registered dealers of specified classes of goods, it seeks also to prevent fraud and ' collusion in a attempt to evading tax. [ 630 D] The object of the section 5 is to ensure that fraud and " facilitating administrative efficiency, the exemption given is made subject to a condition that the person claiming the exemption shall furnish a statement in the manner prescribed under the section.[629 E] In view of several transactions that may be entered into between dealers.

The State of Bihar has assured us in the affidavit that several steps regarding the different directions given by the Court are being promptly implemented but due to shortage of time it has not been possible complete the same by 3rd March, 1979. The State of West Bengal has assured this in the affidavits of Mrinmaya Choudhri that necessary steps for transferring women under "protective custody" in jails to the institutions run by the welfare department have been taken and directions to that effect are issued by the Government. It is not uncommon to find that under trial prisoners whose names are set out in the chart filed by Mrs. Hingorani to day have been in jail for periods longer than the maximum term for which they could have been sentenced, if convicted. The Court would like to satisfy itself whether these under trial prisoner whose particulars were given in the list of undertrial prisoners who were directed to be released by the State on their personal bond were periodically produced before the Magistrates in compliance with the proviso to section 167(2). [529C E] Maneka Gandhi vs Union of India, ; and Maneka Gandhi v Union of lndia, ; , referred to. The requirement of the proviso was complied with in their case. The affidavit giving these particulars should be filed by the state Government within three weeks from today. [530D F] Maneka Nehru Gandhi vs State of Delhi, ; ; Maneka Gandhi V. Union of india, [1978] 2 SCR 621; Maneka Gandhi and Anr. vs Union Of India, [1979] 3 SCR 621, referred to; Maneka Nehru Yuwant Singh vs Union Territory of Delhi & Ors., ; , followed.

The appellant landlord gave notice of termination of tenancy to the respondent on December 31, 1951 under section 34(1) of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948. The notice was for one year as required by section 34 (2 A). The tenancy was to terminate from March 31, 1953. The landlord made an application on April 7, 1953, under section 29(2) of Act for obtaining possession of the land to the Mamlatdar. In the meantime, an amendment was made to the Act by the insertion of sub section (2A), which came into force on January 12, 1953 and it was provided that if the landlord bona fide requires the land for any of the purposes specified in sub section(1), then his right to terminate the tenancy shall be subject to the following conditions, namely: (i) The land held by the landlord is in area equal to the agricultural holding or less; (ii) If the land held was more than the agricultural holdings in area, the right of the landlord to terminate that tenancy of the protected tenant shall be limited to an area which shall, after such termination, leave with the tenant half the area of the lands leased. The respondent thereupon applied for possession of his land under section 28(2 A) of Bombay Tenancy & Agricultural Lands (Amendment) Act, 1952, and claimed the benefit of the third clause of subs. (2a), and the question that arose for determination was whether the tenant was entitled to the protection contained in this clause. Held, that the notice given by the respondent under section 24(1 A) is merely a declaration to the tenant of the intention of the landlords to terminate tenancy and no further proceedings may be taken by the land lord in consequence thereof. Durlabbhai Fakirbhai vs Jhaverbhai Bhikabhai (I.L.R. LXVII of 1948), relied on.

The petitioners, who were evacuees and the houses of one Khadim Ali, had not been declared an evacuee and had died on or about October 1, 1950 leaving three sons and five daughters who thereupon became entitled to them in certain shares. The petitioners contended that they had been wrongly deprived of their rights in the houses by the action of the Custodian. Held, that no property could be declared to be evacuee property unless that person had first been given a notice under section 7 of the Act. In the present case there was no judicial determination by the Custodian General of any fact affecting Zafar Ali 's right in the house. The acts of the custodian in so far as they deprive the petitioners of their property cannot be upheld. It was well established that no appeal by him against that order lay or was necessary. The orders of January 10, 1952, were without jurisdiction so far it affected the rights of the petitioners in the properties concerned. There was no legal determination by him on the admitted facts and the acts of Custodian in so much as they deprived the petitioners ' right to their property could not be upheld under section 12 of the , because there was nothing to show that any such notice had been issued to them. The order of January 11, 1952 was without jurisdiction inasmuch as no notice had already been issued under section 8 of the . Held further, that the orders of the High Court were without Jurisdiction so far the rights in respect of the properties were concerned. The act of the respondent Custodian in making the declaration under section 6(1) of the was not a quasi judicial order and it remained so in spite of the appeal. In view of the fact that no notice has been issued, the petitioners had no longer any claim to them and they had no right to them, Held further that the acts were without juris diction so far they deprive them of their properties. The action of Custodian was not quasi judicial or a quasijudicial order. It is well established and not disputed that no person can be declared evacuee property until that person has first been granted a notice in accordance with section 7 Of the Act, see Ebrahim Aboobaker vs Tek Chand Dolwani, , 702, referred to.

The assessee company was running at a loss as a result of which in 1952 the assessee Company decided to instal a plant for manufacture of worsted yarn from imported wool tops by raising a loan of Rs. 7 lakhs from the Industrial Finance Corporation. The plant went into production in September 1952 and the assessee company appointed M/s. Murlidhar Chiranjilal as the sole selling agents on certain specified conditions, the important of which being that the agents were to finance the assessee ' Company to the extent of Rs 2,50,000/ and the latter agreed to pay 6% interest on the advances to be made by the agents and further agreed to Pay 2% commission on the net proceeds of sales of goods in India. Before expiry of this agreement another agreement was entered into by the assessee with the agents on October 20, 1955 under which the agents agreed to share losses on net sales and 50% commission On December 15, 1953 the assessee firm appointed M /s. Ganesh Chiranju as the principal selling agents for the worsted yeast yarn on payment of 2% Commission on net sale proceeds of goods In India. The assessee company entered into an agreement with Mis Saligram Premnath under which it was appointed as the agent on certain conditions, and the important terms of which were that the agency was to finance to the assessee by giving him a loan Of Rs. 6 lakhs from Industrial Finance Corpn. The Plant went into the production in October 1952. The Income tax Officer disallowed the deduction claimed but held that the sum in question was not legal deductions as contemplated under section 10(2)(xv) of the Income Tax Act, 1922 and therefore could not be claimed as a valid deduction under the provisions of the Act. The Appellate Tribunal accepted the contention of the assessee and held that it was a permissible deduction as it was incurred for the purpose of the asses see 's trade in order to facilitate the business ' of the assesses. The High Court also held that there was no express provision in the agreement by which the agent agreed to shares losses which were a provision peculiar to the present transaction and was not at all covered by any authority cited before the Tribunal or the High Court, that itself was proof positive of the fact that the transaction amounted to a joint venture with a view to division of profits; and that it had relied on certain materials which were not at any material time found by the Tribunal in its order nor were those materials mentioned in the statement of case. The Revenue then went up in appeal before this Court. HELD: (1) In order to fall within section 10 (2)(XV) of Income Tax, 1922, the deduction claim claimed must amount to an expenditure which was laid out or expended wholly and exclusively for the purposes of the business profession or vocation as required under section10(2) (xv).

The assessee company maintained an accounts pertaining to him in its books. The balance sheet showed a net profit of Rs. 18,950 np. The assessee was originally assessed for the assessment year 1959 60 on a total income of Rs 43,407. He then became indebted to the company in the sum of Rs 3,757.04 np., and thereafter the Income Tax Officer reopened the assessment by virtue of section 147 of the Income tax Act, 1961. In the assessment proceedings which followed, the assessee claimed that the accumulated profits of the company amounted to Rs. 1,050 only and that amount alone could be considered as "dividend" under section 2(6A)(e) of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922, he reopened the assess ment by virtue Of section 147. The Appellate Assistant Commissioner dismissed an appeal filed by the assessee. The Tribunal in second appeal upheld the claim of the assessee that the words "accumulated profits" in section 2 (6A) (e) could not be construed as including current profits but it rejected the contention that the two sums of Rs 11,000 and Rs. 6,900 had to be taken into account in determining the figure of the accumulated profit. The Revenue applied for a reference to the High Court which was dismissed. In appeal by certificate under section 261 of the Act, the Revenue contended that the question should not have been referred by the Appellate Tribunal to the Supreme Court at the instance of the asses see because no reference application was made by the assessee. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The High Court was right in answering the first question in favour of the appellant and against the Revenue. [949E] 2.1 In view of the finding that the Appellate Assistant Commis sioner had not applied to the second question, and the reference to that extent must be considered void.

The appellant was the Mahant of a religious institution known as Rajgunj Asthal in Burdwan, and the suits out of which the present appeals arose were instituted by him to recover possession of various plots of land in the occupation of the defendants or in the alternative for assessment of fair and equitable rent. The trial court held that the lands were included in Mouza Nala in Thouzi No. 1, which was comprised in the permanently settled estate of Burdwan, that their income was taken into account in fixing the revenue payable by the estate, that they had been granted as Lakheraj to their predecessors in title long prior to the permanent settlement, and that the plea of the defendant that they held them under a Lakhearaj grant made prior to that permanent settlement was not true. The District Judge however dismissed the suits. On appeal the High Court held that there was no proof of the contents of these documents and that they must be excluded. In appeal to this Court, HELD: (i) A presumption of lost grant cannot be founded on the entry in the record of rights. There are also other difficulties in the way of presuming a lost grant in favour of the predecessors of the respondents. [1175 C] (ii) The document relied on by the defendants as containing assertions that they were holding under a Suzheraj grant were not shown to relate to the suit lands. [1108 E F] (iii) A mere presumption of a lost Grant cannot be based on the entries in the Record of Rights. There is no substance in this plea which is accordingly rejected.

The appellant plaintiff filed a suit for specific performance of a contract dated 15th December 1965 for sale of agricultural land. The defendant contended that the land which was the subject matter of the contract was covered by the provisions of the Bombay Tenancy and Agricultural Lands Act, 1948 ( 'Tenancy Act ') and as the intending purchaser, the plaintiff was not an agriculturist within the meaning of the Act, section 63 of the Tenancy Act prohibited him from purchasing the land and, therefore, as the agreement was contrary to the provisions contained in section 70(a) read with sections 85 and 85A of the said Act, the same cannot be specifically enforced. The trial court held that the certificate had no evidentiary value and was not valid. On appeal by the defendant, the High Court agreed with the trial court observing that Civil Court has undoubtedly jurisdiction to entertain a suit in a properly constituted civil suit for Specific performance of contract for sale. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant that if an issue arises in a proper properly constituted Civil Suit which the civil court is competent to entertain, an incidental or subsidiary issue which may arise with reference to provisions of Tenancy Act, then notwithstanding the fact that such an issue arose in a duly constituted civil Suit cognizable by the Civil Court, it would have been necessary for the civil Court not only to arrogate jurisdiction to itself to decide the same treating it as a subsidiary or incidental issue but also to refer the same to the Mamlatdar and on such decision being brought before the Civil court, it will be binding on the civil courts and the civil Courts will have jurisdiction to decide that issue if it arises before it in a civil suit. On behalf of respondent it was submitted that the question whether an acquisition in excess of the ceiling would be invalid would be within the exclusive jurisdiction of the Mamlatdar under section 70 (mb) and that the Civil Courts will not have jurisdiction, and that even when a properly framed suit is brought to the civil suit having jurisdiction to try the same, prima facie on a contention being raised by the respondent an issue may arise which the Civil Judge would not be competent to try and the legislature stepped in to avoid the conflict of jurisdiction by introducing section 85A making it obligatory upon the Civil courts to refer such an issues to the competent authority under the Tenancy Acts. Allowing the appeal, ^ HELD: 1. The jurisdiction of civil court to settle, decide or deal with any question which is required to be settled, decided or dealt with by any competent authority is totally ousted. Therefore, it an issue arising in a suit properly constituted and cognizable by a Civil Court having jurisdiction under the Bombay Act, would alone be barred under section 85. [595C] 2. The civil court as required by a statutory provision contained in Section 85A will have to frame the issue and refer such issues to such competent authority for determination. To avoid any conflict of decision arising out of multiplicity of jurisdiction, by taking one view of the matter and the competent authorities under the Act taking a contrary or different view, an express provision is made in section 85(2) that no order of the competent Authority made under the provisions shall be questioned in any civil court. [596D E] 3. The Bombay High Court which had initially to deal with this problem resolved the problem by holding that in such a situation the Civil suit should be stayed and the parties should be referred to the Competent authority under Tenancy Act for determination, and the suit shall be disposed of in accordance with the decision recorded by the competent authori ty on the relevant issue. [597E] 4.

The assessee, a heavy engineer manufacturing boilers, machinery parts, wagons etc. for the assessment years 1958 59 and 1959 60 claimed exemption of tax under section 15C of the Indian Income Tax Act, 1922 in respect of its profits and gains derived from its Jute Mill Division for the year 1959 60. The assessee had previously in the earlier years bought from outside the castings manufactured in the Steel Foundry Division which was started in the assessment year 1958 59, and continued thereafter. Again in the year '1959 60 in addition to the manufacturing of cast ings in the steel Foundry division, the assessee started the Jute Mill division where the parts made out of the raw material supplied by the Boiler Division by machining and forging them were given to the Boiler Divi sion of the assessee. It was found that out of a total sale of Rs.28,23,127/ of steel castings goods worth Rs.18,39,433/ were used in connection with the various Divisions of the company. The Income Tax Officer and the Appellate Assistant Commissioner held that the new industrial undertakings were formed by reconstruction of the business already existing and hence the assessee was not entitled to exemption under section15C(2)(i). The Tribunal however allowed the appeal of the asses see and accepted the claim for exemption under s 15C(1) of the Act. The High Court held as follows: "The goods which the steel foundry division and the jute mill Division of the assesses were formed out of tho existing business already in existence, namely, the business of heavy engineering. Hence the Tribunal concluded that it could not be said that the undertakings were forming part of the new business to come within the mischief of the exclusion clause in section 15 C(2) (i). The inam lands were granted by Hindu kings for performance of services of watchman, palanquin bearer, background music player, dancing girl, musical instrument player and mason. The inams were confirmed by the British Government. For over 80 years, the inams were in the enjoyment of alienees from inamdars. By an order passed on April 10, 1947 under section 44 B of the Madras Hindu Religious Endowments Act, 1926, the Revenue Divisional Officer resumed the inam lands and regranted them to the temple. On October 17, 1947, this order was confirmed on appeal by the District Collector. The Revenue Divisional officer held that the inams comprised both melwaram and kudiwaram rights in the land. The orders were passed on notice to the alienees. The alienees instituted a suit in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Madurai under the proviso to section 44B(2)(d)(ii) asking for a decree declaring that the inam grants consisted of the melwarom only. The suit was withdrawn to the Court and registered as O.S. No. 3 of 1954. They instituted another suit in which they prayed for a declaration that the order of the Collector dated October 17. 1947 was a nullity. This suit was transferred to the court of the District Judge, and registered under the Proviso to section44 B(2) (d)(iii) asking the Revenue Officer to hold that the Inam grants consisted both melaram and Kudiwarams rights in land. On appeal by Special Leave, the High Court dismissed the suits in respect of the other inams except the Dasi inam. The State appealed to this Court. HELD : (i) The inam lands are resumable under section44B(1)(a)(i). [545 B] (ii) The inams in the present case were not personal inams. They were inams granted to office holders as remuneration for services to be rendered by them and were within the purview of 44 B. The next question is whether section 44 A allows resumption of an inam falling within the ambit of the section where the inam was alienated before the section came into force in 1934. [546 C] (iii) The High Court was right in holding that the grants did not comprise the melarom rights. [544 E F] (iv) The Inam lands were resumrable under section 43 B(1) (a)(ii). There is no period of limitation prescribed for the initiation of proceedings under section 45B(3). The object of section 44A was to define and enlarge the grounds on which the inams could be resumed and to devise a proper procedure for the resumption. On general grounds of public policy, the legislature has declared that the ' inam may be resumed on any of the three grounds mentioned therein. The respondent company was incorporated in 1937 primarily with the object of acquiring and working the rights, title and interest in a match factory belonging to one A. V. Thomas at Medical. The Memorandum of Association empowered the Company to manufacture and deal in acids, alkalis and other chemicals. The assessee company carried on its business of manufacturing matches till the account year ending April 30, 1941. Thereafter, the profits from the business became less and less due to War conditions, and the assessee company started to manufacture plywood chests for tea, paints and lemon grass oil. These were contemplated by cl. (3) of the Memorandum of association. On May 9, 1943, the assessee Company entered into an agreement with one Rao Sahib Natesa Iyer for the sale of the lands, buildings, plant and machinery of its match factory for Rs. 5, 75,000. It was agreed that the price would not include manufactured goods, chemicals and other raw materials or any other asset not shown in the agreement of sale. The purchaser was allowed sixty days ' for the payment of the balance of the price, Rs. 57,500 having been already paid at the time the agreement was 'entered into. The purchasers made a default in payment, and on August 9, 1944, a fresh agreement was entered into between the parties, this time for a consideration of Rs. 7,35,000 and the sale included chemicals and paper for manufacture which had not been sold in the first instance. In a confidential report made on August 1, 1944 to the shareholders, the Directors stated that the prices obtained had shown a capital appreciation of about six times the cost price, and that the sale was of the entire assets including goodwill, and not a business profit, which was liable to tax. The Income tax Officer, however, held that the assessee firm was liable for income tax on a profit of Rs 36,498 6 4. The Commissioner of Income tax on appeal, reduced the assessable profits to Rs. 1,15,259. An appeal filed before the Tribunal at Trivandrum and the appellant Company contented that a stock in trade could only be that which was the subject of trade, and there was no legally a single transaction of the whole match factory inclusive of raw materials. The High Court held that by the sale no business was done, and therefore, the excess represented a capital investment and not an trading profit. In appeal to this Court it was contended on behalf of the appellant company that the amount of Rs 1, 15,259 was properly brought to tax as a trading profit, and since every appreciation of a stock of raw material in trade represented a profit assessable to income tax, it mattered not that the stock in business was sold at once or from time to time. Of this case, the true answer would be the one given by the High Court in the judgment under appeal. Held: (i) The transaction was not during the carrying on of the business or even for the purpose of carrying on the business, but was for the purposes of putting an end to the business and that thus the excess representing a capital invested and not as assessable profit. The case has been accepted as decided on these narrow facts, in Tebrau (Johore) Rubber Syndicate Ltd. vs Farmermer (W. A. 1), and Doughty 's case (3).
